event_4.additional_information: Oberammergau and the British Empire. AN INVITATION (Extracts from a letter to the Press). SIR:— The presentation of the Passion Play at Oberammergau in 1930 made so deep an impression on the Executive Secretary of the National Council of Education of Canada that he was moved by a great desire that when next it was presented the greatest possible number of teachers and students from Canada might share his experience. This desire has gradually taken a wider range. Now, through the National Council of Education of Canada (and the Foreign Students Bureau at Berlin) the Municipality of Oberammergau has invited two thousand Educationists, Teachers and Students (including senior boys and girls of the Secondary schools and Teachers in Training) of the British Empire to attend a special performance of the Passion Play on August 10th, and, moreover, to be the guests of the villagers in their homes. The original invitation was for 5,000, the capacity of the new Auditorium, but at the suggestion of the National Council of Education it is now limited to the number mentioned. The National Council of Education of Canada which, in conjunction with a special London Committee is undertaking the arrangements for this pilgrimage, proposes to organise a short Conference on "The Teaching of Christ and International Goodwill." The Conference will be preceded by a simple service in the great Auditorium, in which the Passion Play Orchestra and Choir will take part. The hope is that the urgent need of peace and goodwill throughout the world may be realised afresh in the wonderful atmosphere of Oberammergau and in the light of the great memories of Calvary and Easter. Some words written by the Archbishop of Canterbury in a letter to the Executive Secretary may here be quoted:—"I have been greatly moved by the generous and gracious invitation of the people of Oberammergau which you are now authorised to extend to the teachers and students of the Empire. I cannot doubt that those to whom the invitation is addressed will be eager, so far as they can, to accept it. I hope that a great gathering may assemble at Oberammergau to receive for themselves the deep impression which the Passion Play cannot fail to give and with its inspiration to hasten the time when, forgetting the misunderstandings of the past, the nations may live together in mutual understanding and goodwill."

O God our help in ages past,
    Our hope for years to come,
Our shelter from the stormy blast,
    And our eternal home.

Under the shadow of Thy throne,
    Thy saints have dwelt secure;
Sufficient is Thine arm alone,
    And our defence is sure.

Before the hills in order stood,
    Or earth received her frame,
From everlasting Thou art God,
    To endless years the same.

A thousand ages in Thy sight
    Are like an evening gone,
Short as the watch that ends the night
    Before the rising sun.

Time, like an ever rolling stream
    Bears all its sons away;
They fly forgotten as a dream
    Dies at the opening day.

O God our help in ages past,
    Our hope for years to come,
Be Thou our guard while troubles last,
    And our eternal home.  Amen.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Lead us, Heavenly Father, lead us
O'er the world's tempestuous sea,
Guard us, guide us, keep us, feed us,
For we have no help but Thee.
Yet possessing every blessing,
If our God our Father be.
Saviour, breathe forgiveness o'er us;
All our weakness Thou dost know,
Thou didst tread this earth before us,
Thou didst feel its keenest woe;
Lone and dreary, faint and weary,
Through the desert Thou didst go.
Spirit of our God descending,
Fill our hearts with heavenly joy,
Love with every passion blending,
Pleasure that can never cloy:
Thus provided, pardoned, guided,
Nothing can our peace destroy. Amen.

performance_2.performance_name: Now thank we all our God
performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Now thank we all our God
    With hearts and hands and voices,
Who wondrous things hath done,
    In whom His world rejoices;
Who from our mother's arms
    Hath blessed us on our way,
With countless gifts of love,
    And still is ours to-day.
O may this bounteous God
    Through all our life be near us,
With ever-joyful hearts
    And blessed peace to cheer us,
And keep us in his grace
    And guide us when perplexed,
And free us from all ills
    In this world and the next.
All praise and thanks to God
    The Father now be given;
The Son, and Him who reigns,
    With them in highest heaven,
The one eternal God,
    Whom earth and heaven adore;
For thus it was, is now,
    And shall be evermore. Amen.

Dear Madam,

I write to acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 25th, but I am afraid I can give you no information about the 25th Anniversary Record of the Overseas Education League.

Mr. Heywood, who was then Secretary of the League, left some time ago, and as far as I have been able to ascertain the Record in question was never published.

I will however bring the matter to Major Ney's notice when he returns to this country from Canada - which will not be for some weeks.

Yours faithfully,

[signature]

event-2-section-1-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
"RÉCIT ET AIR DE LIA."

L'année en vain chasse l'année!
A chaque saison ramenée
Leurs jeux et leurs ébats m'attristent malgré moi,
Ils rouvrent ma blessure et mon chagrin s'accroît.
Je viens chercher la grève solitaire
Douleur involontaire! Efforts superflus!
Lia pleure toujours l'enfant qu'elle n'a plus!
    Azaël! Azaël! Pourquoi m'as tu quittée?
    En mon cœur maternel ton image est restée
    Azaël! Azaël! Pourquoi m'as tu quittée?

Cependant les soirs étaient doux dans la plaine d'ormes planté,
Quand, sous la charge récoltée, ou ramenait les grands bœufs roux
Lorsque la tâche était finie, enfants vieillards et serviteurs,
Ouvriers des champs ou pasteurs,
Louaient de Dieu la main bénie.

Ainsi les jours suivaient les jours, et dans la pieuse famille
Le jeune homme et la jeune fille échangeaient leurs chastes amours
D'autres ne sentent pas le poids de la vieillesse ;
Heureux dans leurs enfants ils voient couler les ans.
Sans regret comme sans tristesse.

Aux cœurs inconsolés que le temps? sont pesants !
Azaël! Azaël! Azaël! Azaël!
Pourquoi m'as-tu quittée ? Pourquoi m'as-tu quittée ?

E. Guinand.

Translation.

The years roll by, no comfort bringing,
Spring comes smiling, gay flowers flinging,
The birds' sweet song but makes my heart the sadder pine,
My wounds bleed fresh, my heart cries for joys that once were mine.

Along this silent shore I wander lonely,
My grief God knoweth only, ever, evermore
Lía mourns for her child, the child that once she bore.

    Azaël! Azaël!  Ah! wherefore didst thou leave me?
    On my heart thou art graven; I sorrow for thee;
    Azaël! Azaël!  Ah! wherefore didst thou leave me?

Happy days to my memory start when the elm trees waving o'er us,
Homeward the ruddy oxen bore us,
Weary with toil, but light of heart.

Then as the shadows 'gan to fall,
We all the evening hymn did sing
Thankfully to God, our King,
To God the Lord who giveth all.

Sweetly we slept, and glad uprose,
Youths and pure maidens wandered free,
Plighted vows in sincerity.

Evening shades brought rest and calm repose,
Happy ye parents! when to earth your children bind ye:

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
"CELESTE AIDA."

Se quel guerrier io fossi!
Se il mio sogno si av verasse!
Un esercito di prodi da me guidato
E la vittoria, e il plauso di Menfi tutta!
E a te, ma dolce Aida,
Tornar di lauri cinto,
Dirti; per te ho pugnato.
Per te ho vinto!
Celeste Aida, forma divina,
Mistico serto di luce e fior.
Del mio pensiero tu sei regina,
Tu di mia vita sei lo splendor.
Il tuo bel cielo vorrei ridarti,
Le dolci brezze del patrio suol,
Un regal serto sul crin posarti,
Ergeti un trono vicino al sol.

English Version.

What if 'tis I am chosen, and my dream be now accomplished!
Of a glorious army I the chosen leader,
Mine glorious victory, by Memphis received in triumph,
To thee returned, Aida, my brow entwined with laurels,
Tell thee, for thee I battled—for thee I conquered.
Heavenly Aida, beauty resplendent,
Radiant flower, blooming and bright,
Queenly thou reignest, o'er me transcendent,
Bathing my spirit in beauty's light.
Would that thy bright skies once more beholding,
Breathing the soft airs of thy native land,
Round thy fair brow a diadem folding,
Thine were a throne next the sun to stand.
Heavenly Aida, etc.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
A trusting little leaf of green,
A bold audacious frost,
A rendezvous, a kiss or two
And youth for ever lost.
    Ah me! Ah me!
The bitter, bitter cost.

A flaunting patch of vivid red,
That quivers in the sun,
A windy gust, a grave of dust
The little race is run.
    Ah me! Ah me!
Were that the only one.
performance_1.additional_information: Marked as (a).

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Falling leaf and fading tree,
Lines of white in a sullen sea,
Shadows rising on you and me;
The swallows are making them ready to fly,
Wheeling out on a windy sky,
Good-bye, summer! Good-bye! Good-bye!

Hush! a voice from the far away,
"Listen and learn," it seems to say;
"All the to-morrows shall be as to-day."
The cord is frayed—the cruse is dry,
The link must break, and the lamp must die,
Good-bye to hope! Good-bye! Good-bye!

What are we waiting for? O, my heart,
Kiss me straight on the brow and part,
Again, again, my heart!
What are we waiting for, you and I?
A pleading look—a stifled cry,
Good-bye for ever! Good-bye! Good-bye!
performance_2.additional_information: Marked as (b). "By special request)."

O flow'rs, all your sweets and splendour!
'Neath my hand you tremble, you thrill,
You hold in chalices tender,
His voice, softly sounding still.
As on that day, dear past naming,
In that hour of joy divine,
When a kiss, like fire forth flaming,
My love's lips laid on mine;
    O flow'rs, etc.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
You were my past, my day by day,
You were my life to be,
You were my thoughts, my words, my dreams,
You were the world to me.

You are my past, an echo now,
That dwells in a ling'ring sigh,
You are a memory hard to crush,
Of a love that has long passed by.

performance_1_1_1.lyrics_transcript:
Rod. O soave fanciulla,
O dolce viso di mite circonfuso alba lunar,
il sogno ch'io vorrei sempre sognar!

Rod. Fre mon gio nel l'anima le dolcezze streme, more!
Fremon nell'anima dolcezze estreme fremon dolcezze estreme,
Nel bacio freme amor!

Mim. Ah! tu sol comandi, amor
Tu sol comandi, amore!
Oh! come dolci scendono le sue lusinghe al core
Tu sol comandi, amor!

Mim. No, per pieta!
Rod. Sei mia!
Mim. V'aspettan gli amici.
Rod. Guai mi mandi via?
Mim. Vorrei dir ma non oso
Rod. Di'
Mim. Se venissi con voi?
Rod. Che? Mimi!
Sarebbe così dolce restar qui
C'è freddo fuori
Mim. Vi staro vicina!
Rod. E al ritorno?
Mim. Curioso!
Rod. Dammi il braccio mia piccina
Mim. Obbedisco, signor!
Rod. Che m'ami di
Mim. Io t'amo!
Rod. & Mim. Amor! Amor! Amor!

Translation.

Rod. Lovely maid in the moonlight!
Your face entrancing,
Like radiant seraph from on high appears!
The dream that I would ever, ever dream, returns.

Rod. Heart to heart and soul to soul
Love binds us in his fetters.
Love now shall rule our hearts alone,
Life's fairest flower is love!

Mim. Love alone o'er hearts has sway.
Ah Love! to thee do we surrender.
Sweet to my soul the magic voice
Of love its music chanteth,
Life's fairest flower is love!

Mim. No, I pray you!
Rod. My Sweetheart!
Mim. Your comrades await you?
Rod. Do you then dismiss me?
Mim. I should like—no, I dare not!
Rod. Say!
Mim. Could I not come with you?
Rod. What, Mimi?
It would be much more pleasant here to stay.
Outside 'tis chilly!
Mim. To you I'll be neighbour! I'll be always near you.
Rod. On returning?
Mim. Who knows, sir?
Rod. Take my arm, my little maiden!
Mim. I obey you, my lord!
Rod. You love me? Say!
Mim. I love thee!
Rod. & Mim. My love! My love!

Hark, brothers, hark! the trumpet's warning blast!
Arm, brothers, arm! the foe is gather'ring fast;
The dawn of the day's at hand,
Fierce muttering comes,
With tramp of hurrying feet;
And the senses reel
In the tumult's wild,
Where the flashing squadrons meet.

Fight, brothers, fight for home and liberty!
Charge, brothers, charge; the hirelings turn and flee.
Like avalanches they rush,
From the ice-king's world,
With thunderous crash we go;
And the mighty host
Of the Tyrant's boast
Has melted away like snow.

Mourn, brothers, mourn for those who bravely fell:
Pray, brothers, pray for those who fought so well.
In their graves we laid
As they nobly died
With face to the foe, they're laid;
We will carve each name
In the stone of fame.
Their memory shall not fade.

March, brothers, march in sight of home again;
Sing, brothers, sing a loud triumphant strain;
Let our lov'd ones hear
The notes of the new song;
For which they have yearn'd so long;
At each hill and dale,
And each hill and dale,
Resound with the joyful song!

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Let all creation praise the Lord,
Ye nations, bow before Him;
In choral strains with one accord,
Exalt Him and adore Him.
Ye orbs of day that roll in light,
Ye beams of morn from morn to night,
O praise your great Creator!
Angel hosts repeat the song,
Ye prophets clad in glory,
Ye nations, raise your voice prolong.
Repeat the wondrous story;
Ye spirits, who are flames of fire,
Awake and sing, and stirke your lyres,
O praise your great Creator!

Let our theme of praise ascending,
Blest in music's lofty strain,
Soaring through the starry main,
Peal in echoes never ending.
Lovingly did, its light arose;
Thus the sun and moon arise,
Faith and Hope began to banish
Doubt and soul-appealing fear.
Spirits of light, your beams so clear,
Error in their beams will vanish
Mortals roam'd without a guide,
Dread the night and shun the region;
Not a ray could be descried,
All was gloom and desolation,
Till the earth with one accord
Shall adore and praise the Lord.

The Word went forth, the Word was Light;
God spoke, His radiance darted.
Light made chaotic darkness bright,
And night when the light was parted.
In space the starry hosts are sung,
The Universe in music sung
Its great Creator's glory
Still in their courses orbs above,
Hail Him in concert as they move,
His praise in everlasting song
Rings through the vast celestial throng.
Soon may we join the lay,
In His presence, in His praises,
And stand in bright array
To harp and sing our praises.
Where shining Cherubim,
And seraphim blend,
Their hallelujahs blend
In strains that never end.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
Night around is gently closing,
As the light of day doth fail
Every sorrow's dispelling:
See the fire in the Alpine vale.
See, the meadows darkly shaded
Bid thee, Wanderer, depart;
Alpine light with thee is hid,
Ah, how beautiful thou art.
Softest winds are idly blowing,
Like elves' music in the trees.
Thou, the silver-clad mountains lowing
Hoodoos amongst the breeze.
Swift the eagle homeward flying,
Stirs the slumbering ev'ning air,
Alpine night, in shadow lying,
Thou art fair, ay, passing fair!

Like grim giants darkly frowning,
Mountains rise, steep and clear.
But the stars in their heights are crowning
And the stars are bright and clear.
And a fitful light is gleaming
On the lake's silvered outset,
Alpine night so full of dreaming,
Thou art passing and fair!

When the pale moon mutely gazes
On the scene so still, so fair,
In the east a bright sight she raises,
Like a pious and reverend pray'r.
From my eyes the tears are flowing,
Rest, oh! rest thou too, my heart!
Alpine night, with beauty glowing,
Ah, how fair thou art!

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
The starlight pale is waning,
Ere long will the dawn appear,
The deepest silence is ringing,
From the woods no sound I hear.

What joys and what griefs will be given,
Ere this coming day is done.
Let me raise then my heart to Heaven,
In pray'r from the mountain lone.

Alone on the hilltop I wander,
And watch thro' the chill night air,
In the dark horizon yonder,
The light that will glimmer there.

The sigh of the forest grows stronger;
Morning light suddenly breaks.
The lark's song grows louder and longer,
From night's slumber Earth now awakes.

While here in darkness lonely,
I wait for the coming ray,
One voice I hear, and one only,
'Tis the torrent far away.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
SUR LA ROUTE DE COME A MILAN, EN 1815

DES gendarmes viennent d’arrêter une calèche où se trouvent Fabrice del Dongo et sa tante, la jeune comtesse Gina. Fabrice, grand admirateur de Napoléon s’est compromis en allant prendre part comme volontaire, à la bataille de Waterloo ; il est en fuite pour Milan. Il se croit arrêté par ordre du gouvernement autrichien. L’arrivée de deux autres prisonniers dévoile un quiproquo. On recherchait le général Conti, grand chambellan du Prince de Parme et sa fille Clelia qui avaient quitté Côme sans passeports. À la vue de Clelia, Fabrice s’éprend pour elle d’un grand amour. Les explications du général avec les gendarmes sont orageuses et menacent de tourner mal. Gina alors offre du vin à la troupe. Tout s’arrange. La calèche peut repartir avec les quatre voyageurs.

UNE LOGE, A LA SCALA DE MILAN

Quelques jours plus tard. Avec des libéraux milanais, Gina recherche les moyens
de soustraire Fabrice aux poursuites de la police. Il doit partir à minuit pour le Piémont. Survient le Comte Mosca, premier ministre du Prince de Parme. Il aime Gina et veut l'entraîner à la Cour où, tout puissant, il peut faire d'elle une Duchesse et sauver Fabrice. Celui-ci qui vient faire ses adieux à sa tante, apprend qu'il ira à Naples étudier la théologie pour devenir peut-être un jour une Eminence... Dans la loge, il retrouve Clelia. Le spectacle interrompt les conversations...

LE TRATTORIA DE THEODOLINDE

Gina a suivi les conseils de Mosca : elle est venue à Parme et a épousé le vieux Duc Sanseverina qui l'a rapidement laissée veuve et fort riche. Elle mène une vie fastueuse et fort enviée. Auprès d'elle veille amoureusement le Comte Mosca, mais elle ne cesse de penser tendrement à Fabrice qu'elle protège de loin. Nous la retrouverons plus tard.

Fabrice, de son côté, est allé à Naples étudier la théologie. Il a déjà reçu le titre de Monsignore qui ne l'empêche pas toutefois de continuer sa vie aventureuse. Le voici, quelques années plus tard, dans une pauvre auberge campagnarde sur le bord du Pô, à la frontière des États autrichiens où il est venu se réfugier. Il a tué le protecteur d'une petite danseuse à laquelle il
faisait la cour et qui lui cherchait querelle. Il risque maintenant d’être emprisonné pour meurtre. Sa bonne étoile l’a conduit ici, chez Théodolinde dont l’amant est l’ancien cocher de sa tante. L’aventure de la première fuite de Fabrice est évoquée. Il songe à la petite Clélia... Les gendarmes le recherchent de nouveau. Il faut se hâter. On le déguisera en paysan et il pourra, la nuit venue, gagner l’autre rive et s’échapper. Avant de s’enfuir il écrit à Gina pour lui annoncer son prochain retour. À Parme, il la retrouvera et peut-être aussi reverra-t-il Clélia qu’il n’a point oubliée, qu’il aime.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
LA COUR DE LA PRISON DE PARME

La nuit. Ronde de sentinelles, inspection du Général Conti, gouverneur de la citadelle. On attend un prisonnier d’importance : c’est Fabrice, qui est amené, menottes aux mains. Les adversaires politiques de Mosca (dont est Conti) triomphent. Voici le protégé de la Duchesse en leur pouvoir. Il se débat et, débarrassé de ses menottes, gifle le terrible Barbone, gardien-chef de la prison. On l’enchaîne de nouveau : il sera enfermé dans le plus haut des cachots, la cellule de l’Obéissance Passive.

Alors que les gardes l’entraînent, Clélia survient en robe de bal. Fabrice ébloui, la
salue. Interdite, elle ne lui répond pas. Seule, elle se rappelle leur première rencontre et sent renaître avec ardeur son amour pour celui qui va avoir besoin de son aide désormais.

LA PLATE-FORME DE LA CITADELLE

On voit la tour où Fabrice est enfermé, le balcon et la terrasse de Clelia. Elle soigne ses oiseaux. Son père survient et la menace de l'envoyer au couvent si elle persiste à refuser les maris qu'il lui propose. En entendant que la vie du prisonnier est menacée, elle accepte de recevoir les hommages du dernier prétendant : le Marquis Crescenzi. Le général la laisse seule. La nuit tombe. Fabrice est parvenu à retirer les panneaux qui masquent la lucarne de sa cellule. Clelia est terrifiée par son audace. Il lui parle d'amour. Elle le supplie de ne songer qu'à s'enfuir : sa vie est en danger. Il refuse et lui demande un rendez-vous.

LA CELLULE DE L'OBEISSANCE PASSIVE

Fabrice est désespéré. Clelia ne vient plus à son balcon. On entend une sérénade. Le geolier qui apporte son repas lui annonce le prochain mariage de Clelia. Mais soudain Clelia, affolée, fait irruption dans la cellule, jette à terre le repas qui était empoisonné et supplie Fabrice de fuir. Tout est préparé pour
cela : les gardes sont ivres, la Duchesse est en bas avec des hommes et voici une corde pour la terrible descente. Fabrice se débat : il veut rester près de celle qu'il aime. Clélia le menace de s'enfuir pour toujours au couvent. Il accepte l'évasion. Après s'être dit leur amour, ils se séparent et, pendant que Fabrice s'évade, Clélia, pour réparation du péché qu'elle commet en trahissant son père, fait à la Sainte Madone le vœu de ne plus revoir Fabrice, s'il échappe à tout danger.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
L'ATELIER DE FABRICE, A LOCARNO

Sur le lac Majeur où il est venu retrouver Gina après son évasion. En vain sa tante l'entoure-t-elle de tendres soins. Il ne songe qu'à son cachot et à sa chère Clélia dont il est sans nouvelles. Mosca va lui en apporter. Le prince de Parme est mort. Une insurrection a été soulevée à l'avènement du nouveau prince que Mosca a pu maîtriser. Sa puissance est maintenant extrême. Fabrice et Gina vont pouvoir rentrer à Parme. Mais Clélia est sur le point de se marier. Fabrice s'enfuit pour arriver à temps. Gina se laisse aller à la mélancolie. Mosca lui offre son amour de nouveau. Peut-être enfin l'acceptera-t-elle ?

(Voir la suite de l'analyse après les distributions)

LE JARDIN DE CLELIA, LA NUIT

Elle a accepté d’entendre Fabrice une dernière fois. En vain celui-ci tente-t-il de l’arracher à son voeu. Sous son voile, pour que « ses yeux ne le voient plus », Clelia demande à Fabrice la permission d’épouser le Marquis : ils ne trouveront le bonheur éternel que par un acte de renoncement...

LE SERMON AUX LUMIERES

Dans la petite Eglise de la Visitation, à Parme, Fabrice, par son austérité, sa modestie, sa piété, son talent de prédicateur, soulève l’enthousiasme des fidèles qui sont venus en foule l’entendre ce soir. La fatigue interrompt son sermon. Pendant la pause, Clelia, maintenant Marquise Crescenzi, vient écouter celui qu’elle continue de chérir. Fabrice est remonté en chaire. Il la voit. Il va décider de se retirer pour toujours à La Chartreuse de Parme. S’approchant de Clelia, il lui dit un dernier adieu.

    And pluck'd the ripen'd ears,
We fell out—my wife and I—
    O we fell out, I know not why,
        And kiss'd again with tears.
And blessings on the falling out,
    That all the more endears,
When we fall out with those we love.
        And kiss again with tears.
For when we come where lies the child
    We lost in other years,
O there above the little grave
    We kiss'd again with tears.

2. Sweet and Low.

Sweet and low, sweet and low,
    Wind of the western sea,
Low, low, breathe and blow,
    Wind of the western sea.
Over the rolling waters go,
Come from the dying moon and blow,
Blow him again to me.
While my little one, while my pretty one sleeps.
Sleep and rest, sleep and rest.
    Father will come to thee soon;
Rest, rest, on mother's breast,
    Father will come to thee soon.
Father will come to his babe in the nest,
Silver sails all out of the west;
Under the silver moon
Sleep my little one, sleep my pretty one, sleep.

    The horns of Elfland faintly blowing!

O love, they die in yon rich sky,
    They faint on hill or field or river.
Our echoes roll from soul to soul,

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
Tears, idle tears; I know not what they mean;
Tears from the depth of some divine despair,
Rise in the heart, and gather to the eyes,
In looking on the happy autumn fields,
And thinking of the days that are no more.

Fresh as the first beam, glitt'ring on the sail,
That brings our friends up from the under world,
Sad as the last which reddens over one
That sinks with all we love below the verge,
So sad, so fresh the days that are no more.

Ah! Sad and strange, as in dark summer dawns,
The earliest pipe of half-awaken'd birds to dying ears,
When unto dying eyes the casement slowly grows a glimm'ring square;
So sad, so strange the days that are no more.

Dear as remember'd kisses after death,
And sweet as those by hopeless fancy feign'd on lips of others:
Deep as love, deep as first love, and wild with all regret;
O Death in Life. The days that are no more.

performance_14.lyrics_transcript:
O swallow, swallow, flying, flying south,
Fly to her, and fall upon her gilded eaves,
And tell her what I tell to thee.
O tell her, swallow, that thou knowest each,
That bright, and fierce, and fickle is the south,
And dark, and true, and tender is the north.

O swallow, swallow, if I could follow
And light upon her lattice,
I would pipe and trill, and cheep and twitter
Twenty million loves.

O were I thou that she might take me in,
And lay me on her bosom,
And her heart would rock the snowy cradle till I died.

Why ling'reth she to clothe her heart with love,
Delaying as the tender ash delays to clothe herself,
When all the woods are green.

O tell her, swallow, that thy brood is flown,
Say to her I do not wanton in the south,
But in the north long since my nest is made.
O tell her brief is life, but love is long,
And brief the sun of summer in the north,
And brief the moon of beauty in the south,
Fly to her, and pipe and woo her, and make her mine
And tell her that I follow thee.

performance_15.lyrics_transcript:
Thy voice is heard thro' rolling drums
That beat to battle where he stands,
Thy face before his fancy comes
And gives the battle to his hands.
A moment, when the trumpets blow,
He sees his brood upon his knee.
The next, like fire, meets the foe.
And strike him dead for thine and thee.

performance_16.performance_name: 7. Home they brought her Warrior dead.
performance_16.lyrics_transcript:
Home they brought her warrior dead,
She nor swoon'd nor utter'd cry,
All her maidens, watching, said
"She must weep or she will die."
Then they praised him soft and low,
Called him worthy to be loved;
Truest friend and noblest foe.
Yet she neither spake nor moved.
Stole a maiden from her place,
Lightly to the warrior slept.
Took the facecloth from the face,
Yet she neither moved nor wept.
Rose a nurse of ninety years,
Set his child upon her knee.
Like summer tempest came her tears—
"Sweet, my child, I live for thee."

performance_17.lyrics_transcript:
Our enemies have fall'n!
The seed—the little seed they laughed at in the dark,
Has ris'n and cleft the soil and grown a spanless girth
That lays on every side a thousand arms,
And rushes on the sun.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They came—the leaves were wet with women's tears.
They heard a noise of songs they would not understand;
They marked it with the red cross to the fall,
And would have strown it, but are fall'n themselves.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They came—the woodman with their axes. Lo, the tree!
But we will make it faggots for the hearth,
And shape it plank and beam for roof and floor,
And boats and bridges for the use of men.
Our enemies have fall'n!
They struck—with their own blows they hurt themselves,
Nor knew there dwelt an iron nature in the grain.
The glitt'ring axe was broken in their arms—
Their arms were shatter'd to the shoulder blade.
Our enemies have fall'n!
But this shall grow a night of summer from the heat,
A breath of autumn, dropping fruits of pow'r.
And rolled with music in the growing breeze of time,
The tops shall strike from star to star,
The fangs shall move the stony bases of the world.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,
The flying cloud, the frosty light;
The year is dying in the night.
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new.
Ring, happy bells, across the snow;
The year is going, let him go.
Ring out the false, ring in the true
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind,
For those that here we see no more;
Ring out the feud of rich and poor,
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,
And ancient forms of party strife,
Ring in the nobler modes of life.
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the old, ring in the new;
Ring, happy bells, across the snow.

The year is going, let him go.
Ring out the false, ring in the true,
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,
The civic slander and the spite:
Ring in the love of truth and right,
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease,
Ring out the narrowing lust of gold:
Ring out the thousand wars of old,
Ring in the thousand years of peace;

Ring in the valiant man and free,
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be!

Ring out the old, ring in the new,
The year is going, let him go:
Ring out the false, ring in the true,
Ring out the old, ring in the new.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
(b) Like silver lamps in a distant shrine
The stars are sparkling bright;
The bells of the city of God ring out,
For the Son of Mary was born tonight;
The gloom is past, and the morn at last
Is coming with Orient light.

Never fell melodies half so sweet
As those which are filling the skies:
And never a palace shone half so fair
As the manger bed where our Saviour lies;
No night in the year is half so dear
As this which has ended our sighs.

Now a new power has come on earth,
A match for the armies of Hell:
A Child is born who shall conquer the foe,
And all the spirit of wickedness quell;
For Mary's Son is the Mighty One
Whom the prophets of God foretell.

The stars of heaven still shine as at first
They gleamed on this wonderful night:
The bells of the city of God peal out,
And the Angels' song still rings on the height:
And love still turns where the Godhead burns,
Hid in flesh from fleshly sight.

Faith sees no longer the stable floor,
The pavement of sapphire is there:
The clear light of Heaven streams out to the world.
The Angels of God are crowding the air:
And Heaven and earth, through the spotless birth,
Are at peace on this night so fair.

performance_4.performance_name: Three Geistliche Lieder from the Spanish Lieder Collection
performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
SPANISH SONGS.
No. 1.
(Free Translation)
Now I am thine, flower of all flowers!
And sing always only of thy glory!
I will be zealous to consecrate myself
To you and your suffering!
Selected woman,
Thou art all my hope.

My inmost feelings will always be open to thee.
Come to deliver me from the curse of evil
That struck me so hardly,
Ye star of the sea.
Ye port of all happiness!
Before I die.
Look down from Heaven,
O Queen of all suns!
The spring of thy mercy will never cease.

Thou aid to victory to those laden with ignominy.
To be near to thee and to sit at thy feet.
That cures all harm and injury.
I suffer hard and well-earned punishment.
I am afraid of my eternal sleep.
Do stay with me and lead me through the sea to the haven.

No. 2.
Ah! the eyes of the holy boy appeared so beautiful and clear to me.
And something shines out of them that wins all my heart.
He looks with his sweet eyes to my eyes;
If he would see his face therein he would greet me kindly:
So I surrender myself perfectly to him only to serve his eyes,
For something shines out of them that wins all my heart.

No. 3.
You that float around these palms in night and wind,
You holy angels, calm the tops of the trees.
There slumbers my child;
You palms of Bethlehem in the storm,
How can you blow so furiously to-day?
Do calm the storm.
Be silent and bow softly and gently;
There slumbers my child.
The heaven's child suffers pains;
Ah, how tired he was from grief of earth!
Ah, in his sleep softly passes his torment.
Do calm the storm.
There slumbers my child.
Grim cold strikes down:
With what shall I cover my child's limbs?
Ah, you angels, flying winged through the night.
Do calm the storm;
There slumbers my child.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Hath passed so soon away.
My soul is filled to sadness
With lil' of olden lay.
The air is dewy and darkling,
And calmly floweth the Rhine.
The crest of the hills is sparkling
In light of even shine.

There sitteth a maid in the gloaming,
A maid divinely fair.
'Mid gleam of her gems is combing
Her curls of golden hair.

From golden comb she is raining
Her tresses, and sings from on high
A passionate, soul enchanting,
Entrancing melody.

The sailor with wild pangs thrilling
Is chained by magic tone,
While breakers his skiff is filling.
He gazes on her alone.
He, with the surge descending,
Is swept along with his boat.
And such is e'er the ending
Of Lorelei's witching note.

"I began, by idle accident, to associate the Christmas time of year with human interest, and with some inquiry into, and some care for, the lives of those by whom I found myself surrounded. ... A good time: a kind, forgiving, charitable time: the only time I knew of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely.... performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
The wheel of time is turning,
Yet heed we not its flight:
The world in vain allureth.
While Love alone endureth:
We vow ourselves to love, by day, by night.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Holy night! Holy night!
Starbounded Heaven's peace!
All is united that the day has separated,
All wounds bleed sweetly in evening glow.

Bjelborg's spear! Bjelborg's spear
Sinks into the depth of the elated earth.
Which dives with happy air to the bosom
of dark lusts.

Holy night! Sweet bride! Sweet bride!
Hide your sweet shame.
When the wedding cup's sweetness descends,
The day enters into the lustful night!

Holy night! etc.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
(Why Should We Seek to Hide Our Passion?)
Why should we seek to hide our passion—
    The bliss that bids our hearts o'erflow?
Nay, every human creature living
    Our soul's exultant joy shall know!
When two fond hearts with love are beating
    A shout of joy through Nature goes,
And o'er the hours of lovers' meeting
    Soft summer eve its shadow throws
E'en from the oak's decaying trunk,
    That saw a thousand years go by,
A crown of green once more doth blossom—
    It lifts those aged branches high.
Each leaf, each flower, awakes to gladness,
    Their choicest colours they display:
The brooklet murmurs softer music,
    And blossoms' fragrant splendour tell 'tis May!
Why should we seek to hide our passion—
    The bliss that bids our hearts o'erflow?
Nay, every human creature living, all earth,
    Now I am thine, flowe. of all flowers!
performance_3.additional_information: English subtitle appears in parentheses: '(Why Should We Seek to Hide Our Passion?)'.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Love, fear not if sad thy dreaming
    All thro' the night.
Though o'ercast bright stars are gleaming
    All thro' the night.
Joy will come to thee at morning,
    Life with sunny hope adorning.
Tho' sad dreams may give dark warning
    All thro' the night.

Angels watching ever round thee
    All thro' the night.
In thy slumbers close surround thee.
    All thro' the night.
They should of all fears disarm thee;
    No forebodings should alarm thee:
They will let no peril harm thee,
    All thro' the night.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
Ev'ry rustling tree is at peace,
    The whisp'ring winds do cease,
And no sound is heard.

The birds are all sunk in slumber:
    Wait-a-while, wait-a-while,
Soon shalt thou, too, rest in peace.
    Wait-a-while, wait-a-while.
Soon shalt thou, too, rest in peace.
    Thou shalt rest in peace.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
While moon and stars above us
    Their airy dance renew.
Say, why should sadness move us.
    Or earth-born care pursue?
Behold! the soft beams play, love.
    Come in my bark away, love.

And glide from bondage free,
    Across the dark blue sea.
Now midnight's boding number
    From good Saint Mark's I hear.
And all are hushed in slumber
    Except Thy Gondolier.

event-1-section-1-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
Great is Jehovah the Lord!
The heaven and the earth both proclaim
His mighty power.
We hear Him when roareth the storm,
When the wind through the woods rushes along.
Great is Jehovah the Lord!
Mighty in His power.

Thou hear'st it in the green budding boughs of the forest.
Seest it in the cornfields that glow like gold.
In flowers ye may see it in bright varied hues.
And in the stars still His marvellous power behold.

Awful rolls He in thunder on high,
The flame of His lightning darts in terror below,
And each beating heart, every soul feels His wondrous power and might.

We bow to the power dwelling in Him.
The Lord of all, and up to the Father.

Thou to Him look for aid,
In hope to gain His love and grace.
Turning then, we implore His love and grace and protection.
Great is Jehovah the Lord!

event-1-section-1-performance-9.lyrics_transcript:
The Heav'ns with praise to the Lord are abounding.
His name to hear afar they rejoice;
The earth, the sea, to His honour are sounding;

Give ear, O man! to Nature's voice.
The stars above us, who is it upholdeth?
Who leadeth from his tent the sun?
He cometh, laughing. His glory unfoldeth.
A giant who His course would run!

event-1-section-1-performance-11.lyrics_transcript:
Good King Wenceslas look'd out
    On the feast of Stephen,
    When the snow lay round about,
        Deep, and crisp, and even.
    Brightly shone the moon that night,
        Though the frost was cruel,
    When a poor man came in sight,
        Gather'ring winter fuel.

Baritone Solo:
    "Hither, page, and stand by me,
        If thou know'st it, telling,
    Yonder peasant, who is he?
        Where and what his dwelling?"

Treble Solo:
    "Sire, he lives a good league hence,
        Underneath the mountain;
    Right against the forest fence,
        By St. Agnes' fountain."

Baritone Solo:
    "Bring me flesh, and bring me wine,
        Bring me pine-logs hither:
    Thou and I will see him dine
        When we bear them thither."

Chorus:
    Page and monarch forth they went,
        Forth they went together;
    Through the rude wind's wide lament
        And the bitter weather.

Treble Solo:
    "Sire, the night is darker now,
        And the wind blows stronger:
    Fails my heart, I know not how:
        I can go no longer."

Baritone Solo:
    "Mark my footsteps, my good page:
        Tread thou in them boldly;
    Thou shalt find the winter's rage
        Freeze thy blood less coldly."

Chorus:
    In his master's steps he trod,
        Where the snow lay dinted;
    Heat was in the very sod
        Which the saint had printed.
    Therefore, Christian men, be sure,
        Wealth or rank possessing,
    Ye who now will bless the poor
        Shall yourselves find blessing.
event-1-section-1-performance-11.additional_information: Marked (a). Includes Baritone Solo, Treble Solo, and Chorus passages.

event-1-section-1-performance-12.lyrics_transcript:
Here we come a-wassailing
        Among the leaves so green;
    Here we come a-wandering,
        So fair to be seen.

Chorus:
    Love and joy come to you,
        And to your wassail too:
    And God bless you and send you a Happy New Year.
    And God send you a Happy New Year.

    Our wassail-cup is made
        Of the rosemary tree,
    And so is your beer
        Of the best barley.
    Love and joy, etc.

    Call up the butler of this house,
        Put on his golden ring;
    Let him bring us a glass of beer,
        And the better we shall sing.
    Love and joy, etc.

    Bring us out a table,
        And spread it with a cloth;
    Bring us out amply cheese,
        And some of your Christmas loaf.
    Love and joy, etc.

    God bless the Master of this house,
        Likewise the Mistress, too;
    And all the little children
        That round the table go.
    Love and joy, etc.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
HALLO! hallo! to cover!
Where waves the forest far around,
And thro' the waving branches
I hear the horn resound.
    Tra-ra!

Then sound aloud the hallo
O'er forest, meadow, stream, and crag,
To startle and to follow
And track the bounding stag.

And homeward when returning,
Beneath the moon's effulgent light,
I seek my lady's window,
To sing a soft good night.

Sleep well! O my beloved,
And may no dream thy peace annoy;
My heart is thine for ever,
Thou art the hunter's joy.
    Sleep well!

And then hallo to cover!
Where waves the forest, &c.

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Day again his race has run,
And the tranquil night comes on,
Soothingly her pinions waving,
Heated hill and valley laving,
Spreading from her starry chart
    Holy peace to every dwelling,
    Holy peace to every heart.

All who rest in slumber's arm—
Void of trouble, void of harm—
Heavenly angels now are guarding,
Every danger from them warding—
Powers of evil must depart
    Holy peace to every dwelling,
    Holy peace to every heart.

(b) When in thy dreams thou sayest:
    "Who taps the window there?"
    Then shall the wind make answer:
    "I, and a message bear.
    Thy lover e'er for thee doth long.
    I bring thee greeting, kiss and song."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

When in thy dreams thou sayest:
    "What shineth there so clear?"
Then shall the moon make answer:
    "I, and a blessing bear.
I come from one who night and day
For thee doth ever watch and pray."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

When in thy dream thou sayest:
    "What doth so soft bewail?"
Then shall a bird make answer:
    "I am the nightingale.
Of love and longing sing to thee
Until thine eyes the morning see."
        Slumber soft, slumber soft.

performance_11.lyrics_transcript:
'Neath the vine tree's garlands bending
Spread, dear maid, the festive board.
With thy fair hands on us tending;
Speeds the day with joyous ending.
Thee we'll pledge with glad accord.
Slumber deep is reigning o'er us,
We alone are now astir
Clink the glasses round in chorus,
Gaudiamus igitur.
Each in turn the tale recount then,
Whence his wandering steps have strayed.
From the distant vale and mountain,
By the mossy dell and fountain,
All in nature's best array'd.
All seems dancing now before us.
As the golden wine we pour,
Joining in the merry chorus,
Gaudiamus igitur.
Blessings rich from heav'n descending,
Rest upon the students free.
Loud in song our voices blending,
Beauty's praise on high ascending,
Praise of maidens true like thee.
Long may heav'n's rich blessings flowing
On our hills and valleys pour,
Where the fruitful vine is growing.
Gaudiamus igitur.

performance_12.performance_name: Mon cœur s'ouvre à ta voix
performance_12.lyrics_transcript:
("Softly awakes my Heart.")
(From the Opera Samson and Delilah.)
(Translation.)
Softly awakes my heart, as the flowers awaken
To Aurora's tender zephyr!
But say, O well-belov'd, no more I'll be forsaken;
Speak again, O speak for ever!
O say that from Delilah you never will part!
Your burning vows repeat—vows so dear to my heart.
    Ah, once again do I implore thee,
    Ah, once again then say you adore me.
    Ah, I here implore thee,
    See, I implore thee!
E'en as to whis'ring winds sways the waving grain,
    To and fro so gently moving,
So sways my trembling heart, consoling all its pain,
    To thy voice so dear, so loving.
The arrow in its flight is not swifter than I.
When, leaving all behind, to your arms I fly!

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
DRAKE'S DRUM.

Drake, he's in his hammock, and a thousand miles away
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot in Nombre Dios Bay,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Yonder lumes the island, yonder lie the ships,
With sailor lads adancing heel-an'-toe.
And the shore-lights flashing, and the night-tide dashing,
He sees it all so plainly as he saw it long ago.

Drake, he was a Devon man, and ruled the Devon seas,
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Roving tho' his death fell, he went with heart at ease,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.

Drake, he's in his hammock, and a thousand miles away
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot in Nombre Dios Bay,

Yonder lumes the island, yonder lie the ships,
With sailor lads adancing heel-an'-toe.

Drake, he was a Devon man, and ruled the Devon seas,
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)

"Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore,
Strike it when your powder's running low;
If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port of Heaven,
And drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago."

Drake, he's in his hammock till the great Armadas come.
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot, list'ning for the drum,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Call him on the deep sea, call him up the Sound,
Call him when ye sail to meet the foe;
Where the old trade's plying and the old flag flying,
They shall find him ware and waking, as they found him long ago!

event-1-section-1-performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
Dear Earth, near Earth, the clay that made us men,
    The land we sowed.
    The heart that glowed,—
O Mother, must we bid farewell to thee?
Fast dawns the last dawn, and what shall comfort then
    The lonely hearts that roam the outer sea?

Gray wakes the daybreak, the shivering sails are set,
    To misty deeps
    The channel sweeps,—
O Mother, think on us who think on thee!
Earth-home, birth-home, with love remember yet
The sons in exile on the eternal sea.

event-1-section-1-performance-6.performance_name: DEVON, O DEVON, IN WIND AND RAIN.
event-1-section-1-performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
DRAKE in the North Sea grimly prowling,
    reading his dear Revenge's deck.
Watch'd, with the sea-dogs round him growling,
    Galleons drifting wreck by wreck.
    "Fetter and Faith for England's neck,
    Faggot and Father. Saint and chain,--
Yonder the Devil and all go howling,
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"

Drake at the last off Nombre lying,
    Knowing the night that toward him crept.
Gave to the sea-dogs round him crying
    This for a sign before he slept:--
    "Pride of the West! what Devon hath kept:
Devon shall keep on tide or main:
Call to the storm and drive them flying,
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"

Valour of England gaunt and whitening,
    Far in a South-land brought to bay.*
Locked in a death-grip all day tight'ning,
    Waited the end in twilight gray.
Battle and storm and the sea-dog's way!
Drake from his long rest turn'd again.
Victory lit thy steel with lightning.
    Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!

event-1-section-1-performance-7.lyrics_transcript:
AFTER long labouring in the windy ways,
    On smooth and shining tides
        Swiftly the great ship glides,
Her storms forgot, her weary watches past!
Northward she glides, and thro' the enchanted haze
    Faint on the verge her far hope dawns at last.

The phantom sky-line of a shadowy down,
    Whose pale white cliffs below,
        Thro' sunny mist aglow.
    Like noonday ghosts of summer moonshine gleam—
Soft as old sorrow, bright as old renown.
There lies the home of all our mortal dream.

event-1-section-1-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
The wind was rising easterly, the morning sky was blue,
The straits before us opened wide and free;
We look'd towards the Admiral, where high the Peter flew,
And all our hearts were dancing like the sea.
The French are gone to Martinique with four and twenty sail.
The "Old Superb" is old and foul and slow!
But the French are gone to Martinique, and Nelson's on the trail,
And where he goes the "Old Superb" must go.
So Westward ho! for Trinidad, and Eastward ho! for Spain.
And "Ship ahoy!" a hundred times a day;
Round the world if need be, and round the world again,
With a lame duck lagging all the way.

The "Old Superb" was barnacled and green as grass below,
Her sticks were only fit for stirring grog;
The pride of all her midshipmen was silent long ago,
And long ago they ceased to heave the log.
Four year out from home she was, and ne'er a week in port,
And nothing save the guns aboard her bright;
But Captain Keats he knew the game, and swore to share the sport,
For he never yet came in too late to fight.

So Westward ho! &c.

"Now up, my lads," the Captain cried, "for sure the case were hard
If longest out were first to fall behind;
Aloft, aloft with studding-sails, and lash them on the yard,
For night and day the Trades are driving blind."
So all day long and all day long behind the fleet we crept,
And how we fretted none but Nelson guessed:
But ev'ry night the "Old Superb," she sail'd while others slept,
Till we ran the French to earth with all the rest.

O 'twas Westward ho! &c.

event-2-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Thou comest here to the land, O friend.
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows:
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove.
    Where the voices of nightingales
    Resound, floating in dulcet strains
        Thro' their temples of verdure:
    Where the thick-woven ivy clings.
    Spreading over the sacred aisles:
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine,
    Unscathed by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god,
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays.
    Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

    Fair and fragrant at dawn of day.
    See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus,
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
        Worn by them in the days of old.
    See the Crocus array'd in gold:
        Hear the slumberless waters.
    While they glide in Cephisus' tide.
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
    Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

    Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia;
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear.
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway: yet here it freely springeth:
    Rever'd by friends, and feared by foes,
        In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold, ours is the rich oil-dropping olive;
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree,
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure,
Everheeded by Morian Jove.
    Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva.

    Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts deigned to my country:
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder-guided;
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent.

Mighty god Poseidon,
Thou didst give us the rein formed for the courser;
Guided thus, or curbed, he yields obedience.
Through the billows we dash, stemming the deep,
    Speeded along by the ear and helm,
    Bounding on with the dancing nymphs—
    Nereus' hundred-footed daughters.

event-2-section-1-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
The drooping flow'rs their buds are closing,
    The silver stars keep watch above;
The world in tranquil sleep reposing,
    My wakeful bosom yields to love.
While here in hopeless grief I languish,
    Could I behold thy vision bright,
Then would I fondly breathe my anguish,
    Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.
Tho' all unmoved by love's appealing,
    No kindling passion lights thy brow,
No voice of love thy heart revealing,
    Still all the world to me art thou.
Bend softly down, ye golden tresses:
    Beam kindly once, bright orbs of light;
List, lady, list to love's distresses,
    Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.

event-2-section-1-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
(a) There is nought on earth so still as the snow!
    Shrouding all the world in silent glamour;
    Muffling ev'ry sound: on the frozen ground
    Hushing ev'ry footfall's noisy clamour.
    There is nought on earth as pure as the snow!
    Swan's down loosed from winter's pions spreading,
    On the hand a flake doth a teardrop make,
    Through the crystal air white thoughts are threading.
    Nought so lulling on the earth as the snow!
    Sinking light as slumber on the weary.
    Till the silence so into sound doth grow
    Fine as silver bells, as music ringing.

(b) Ah, me! Up here it is bright and gay,
    On the mountain!
The zephyr rippling in sprightly play
    On the mountain!
Our feet are dancing, our eyes are bright,
Our heart rejoicing with new delight,
    On the mountain!
Come up, come up! From the vale ascend
    To the mountain!
Refreshing odours with zephyrs blend
    On the mountain!
The grass is studded with flowers untold,
The sun is shedding her rays of gold
    O'er the mountain!
Ah, dearest boy of mine! come to me
    On the mountain!
Day after day I have longed for thee
    On the mountain!
Come, let us talk till the sun has set,
And in our loving our grief forget
    On the mountain.

event-2-section-1-performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
In the lakes and flowing rivers
Dwells a race of free good livers;
Always laughing, swimming, croaking;
Always singing, always joking;
And is heard the whole day long,
Loud and clear their ringing song.
    Quack! quack! Reck! eck! eck!

Eyes like diamonds brightly flashing,
Limbs on lake and riplet splashing,
Sporting, playing, chatting, laughing,
Feasting richly, nectar quaffing,
And is heard the whole day long,
Loud and clear their ringing song.
    Quack! quack! Reck! eck! eck;

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
Recitative.

How bravely o'er the floods so bright,
Ellida flies to shore now in sight!
Although the king with demon spell
Invoked the horrid goblin brood,
And unloosed the wings of the tempest,
My Northland courage bore me
Through ardent strife
To glory's height;
From mighty Jarl the tribute I obtained:
I greet thee gladly, Baldur's grove,
Where oft by break of night
Hope filled my heart with sweet delight!
My Ingeborg, but where art thou now?
Beloved maiden, art thou true to me?

See, I vie with the winds and their heavenly train.
Ellida, O hasten and fly o'er the main.

Chorus.

Oh, 'tis delight when the land afar appeareth,
And from the hearth of thy home beloved
The smoke curls upwards
And thou art near to childhood's scenes
For ever dear.

Solo—Frithjof.

On the tomb of my father I planted the lime-tree,
Is the delicate stem still alive?
Give, earth, thy growth,
And thou O heaven, send fostering dew.
Oh, 'tis delight!

performance_4.performance_name: Scene II. Ingeborg's Bridal Procession to King Ring.
performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
March—Orchestra

Chorus.
Sadly the Skald walks before the train.
Pale sits the bride on the coal black palfrey:
The angry Norma her arrow darteth:
She rules the mortals,
As their lot is cast.
From thunder-clouds ruin falls at last.

Solo, Ingeborg—and Chorus.
My heart, with sorrow overflowing,
Heeds not the flowers entwined with my ringlets:
For ever away from my home I go,
By my brother forced to wed his foe!
And endless woe in my bosom burneth.
But Bele's daughter pity spurneth!
Yet bear to Frithjof greetings from Ingeborg!
Great is my grief, but I do not hate.
    All-father judges
    I bear my fate.

performance_5.performance_name: Scene III. Frithjof's Revenge—Temple in Flames—Curse
performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
Chorus of Priests.
Midnight sun on the mountain burns,
    Red like blood appearing,
And through the strange mysterious light
    Helge's train is nearing.
Lo, he comes, while the glare is spread,
Splendid crown adorns his head,
    Helge, mighty monarch!

Recitative—Frithjof.
Go to Hela's dark abode.
    Seek ye there the mighty rover:
Slain upon the horse he rode,
    Helge's life is over!

Chorus.
Woe! Oh! wicked deed!

Frithjof.
Hush, wretched priests with gory knives.
    Moonlight's pallid princes!
Hush! or tremble for your lives,
    Long our blades have thirsted!
Where my father rests,
Where my childhood passed,
Nought save a ruin I found aghast!
And sold to the foe my beloved bride.
    The armlet which to her I left,
Behold, now the God wears it proudly,
    And she is bereft!
Ah, Baldur! is this thy valiant deed?
By theft this armlet was given to thee!
Thou must, O Baldur, restore it to me!
How dar'st thou hold this ring in thy keeping.
Which once my Ingeborg blessed with weeping?
    No longer on thine arm it shall rest!
My hope, my joy, thou could'st destroy,
But, mind! not me shall thou decoy!

Chorus—Priests and People.
Woe! he rags with all his might at the ring
    —O fright!
Ah! the God, now filled with wrath,
    'Midst the flames is rushing,
And the consecrated hearth
    By his weight is crushing.
    Fane in flames!
    Pour water on!
The waves of the sea bring either!
    Lo! clouds of smoke are bursting forth.
Morning winds blow from the North!
    How the flames are glaring!
What availeth human might!
Now from branch to branch they spring
    Through the combat daring!
Blazing flames in the grove abound.
    Onward like rivers flowing,
Sunlight smileth,
    But fiend and sound
Blood-red with fire are glowing.
    Woe! Woe! Woe!

Priests.
Mischief bringer! malediction on thy head!
accurs'd!

People and Priests.
Mount, smoke, and upwards to heaven ascending.
    Valhalla enter, Valhalla enter.
Cry to the Gods, who o'er earth are bending.
And thou, O flame, the deed proclaim.
Fly, and proclaim to the Gods the accursed deed!

Frithjof's Followers
Ashes our temple soon will be:
Frithjof from his home must flee!
Happy he who departs not for ever!

performance_6.performance_name: Scene IV. Frithjof Goes Into Exile
performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
Solo—Quartette
Sun in the sky
Now mounteth high.
The winds are blowing
And gently flowing,
The waves advance
In joyful dance.

Chorus.
Sadly Frithjof goes his way;
See, he weepeth, while morning gloweth!

Solo—Frithjof and Chorus.
World's grandest region thou mighty North,
From thy dominions I'm driven forth.
Within thy borders I lov'd to dwell!
Midsummer sun, fare thee well!
My love is foiled, my rooftree rent!
With honour soiled, in exile sent!
Cheerless is my soul within me.
Hopeless, I must bear my lot.
Ye rugged mountains where heroes dwell,
And Thor commandeth clouds and winds:
Ye azure lakes that I love so well.
Ye woods and brakes, fare ye well!

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
Solo—Ingeborg.
Storms wildly roar!
Billows break madly upon the shore.
Would 'neath the sod I were lying,
Winds o'er me sighing!
Sad and oppress,
Thee I did watch, flying sail in the west!
Onward with Frithjof thou glidest,
With him abidest.
Falcon, beloved! thee he left here;
Falcon for his sake to me thou art dear.
Shake not thy pinions, stay near me,
O, why should'st thou fear me?
Here on his hand,
Worker on the canvas, thou proudly shall stand,
Silver thy pinions unfolden;
Thy claws shall be golden.
Thou darling bird!
Sit on my shoulder, and list to my word!
When I'm no more
He will come hither, and his heart will be sore:
Greet from me Frithjof.
Who loves me, and never forgets me.

performance_8.performance_name: Scene VI. Frithjof On the Sea
performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
Chorus—Frithjof's Followers.
Now he crossed the floods of the salt desert waste.
Far off like a falcon he flew!
But for warriors on board he wrote maxims and rules!
List to the laws of his crew!

Frithjof and Chorus.
On this deck raise no tent,
And ashore do not sleep:
Within houses the foe lurks for thee!

On thy shield sleep, Viking.
Thy sword in thy hand:
Let the heavens thy canopy be.
Now hold high your lances—
Your lances hold high—
Our banners unfold ye,
The triumph is nigh.
To climes of the south we shall wander.
When hurricanes rage,
Hoist the canvas on high!
Let them come as they may:
He who flinches must die.
Rise, rise, unfold ye our banners!

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
Holy night, oh soothe my breast
With thy solemn tranquil calm:
Give the weary wand'rer rest,
O'er his sorrows shed thy balm.
Stars brightly o'er me gleaming,
From azure fields are beaming,
They set my soul a-dreaming
Of rest above.
Hallowed sounds fall on my ear,
Wafted on the nightwind's sighs:
Murmurings from some blissful sphere.
Echoes from love's paradise.
On high my glances turning,
Where heaven's stars are burning,
I dream with fervent yearning
Of peace and love.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
If thou are sleeping, maiden,
Awake, awake, and open thy door,
'Tis the break of day, and we must
away
O'er the meadow and mount and
moor.
Wait not to find thy slippers,
But come with thy naked feet.
We shall have to pass thro' the dewy
grass
And the waters wide and fleet.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
I've never sailed the Amazon,
I've never reached Brazil!
But the "Don" and the "Magdalena,"
They can go there when they will.
Ah!
Yes, weekly from Southampton,
Great steamers, white and gold,
Go rolling down to Rio,
And I'd like to roll to Rio
Some day before I'm old!

=== Page 14 ===
〈地の口は速い〉について

この作品は1964〜65年にかけて作曲された室内オーケストラのための作品である。題名の Quick are the mouths of Earth はいささか奇妙だが、これはアメリカの小説家トマス・ウルフから引用されたのだという。「大地の口はすべて貧欲である」とも訳されるほか、さまざまな意味がふくまれているらしいが、ここでは作曲者の意向によって、むしろ直訳的に〈地の口は速い〉としておく。

18分ほどの作品だが、6つの部分にわかれている。そしてそれぞれのパートは、さらに6つの部分に分割できる。また各部分の楽器の音のうごきも、それぞれ6つの要素にわけられる。つまりここでは〈6〉のプロポーションで曲が構成されているといえる。このような構成方法は、かれはすでに2度とこころみないだろうといっていいる。それはそのご時間に関するつここんだ追求の結果、新しい時間構造への方向をあゆみだしているからだという。心理学によれば、人間は時間のプロポーションというものは知覚できないらしい。心理学上では、人間には最大5秒程度の時間のプロポーションしかわからないことになっている。つまり、それは時間というよりは、むしろ多くの小さな瞬間（あるいはモメント）の集合としてうけとっているというべきだろう。

しかしこの曲での構造の特色は、むしろ時間的なプロポーションよりも、このような小さなモメントの集合構造にあるといえるようにおもわれる。音のテクスチュアは、つねにすばやく変化しつづけているものと、あまり変化しないものとが濃密にくみあわされている。聴衆は、こうした激しい変化とうごきの複雑なテクスチュアの中に、つねに新しい要素を発見していく。

楽器のグループのうえからみると、大きくわけて3つの群に分割されている。そして①多くの異った音が星座のように散らばる各群間のとびかうような交錯。②まったく同じではないが、同質といえる音色の対比。③同じ音の前後の関係——といった音のインタープレイがみられる。

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom their dark crests rearing.
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot of land,
E'en like the waves, the royal desire
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard upleaping,
"Yonder snow-covered peaks o'er cloud bands peeping."

And it was Olav Trygvason,
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted.

Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring.
Swayed in the stormy wind, the forest strangely was murmuring
Sounds as of churchbells chiming.
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming;
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards.
On to Him, the All Creator,
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning
God, to thee alone be glory.
    On to God! On to God!"

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Holy night, oh soothe my breast
    With thy solemn tranquil calm;
    Give the weary wand'rer rest,
    O'er his sorrows shed thy balm.

    Stars brightly o'er me gleaming,
    From azure fields are beaming,
    They set my soul a-dreaming
    Of rest above.

    Hallowed sounds fall on my ear,
    Wafted on the nightwind's sighs;
    Murmurings from some blissful
    sphere,
    Echoes from love's paradise.

    On high my glances turning,
    Where heaven's stars are burning,
    I dream with fervent yearning
    Of peace and love.

(b) Birdling's flying to his nest,
    Wings are weary roaming,
    Boats are sailing home to rest,
    From the ocean's moaning.
    Twilight soothes the sun to sleep,
    Far has he been coming,
    Now he sinks in heaven's bed,
    In the crimson glooming.
    Birdling rests in his warm nest,
    Boats at anchor rocking,
    Fast asleep is now the sun,
    Hush, my darling's nodding, hush.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
DRAKE'S DRUM

Drake, he's in his hammock, and a thousand miles away
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot in Nombre Dios Bay,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
Yonder lumes the island, yonder lie the ships.
With sailor lads advancing heel-an'-toe,
And the shore-lights flashing, and the night-tide dashing,
He sees it all so plainly as he saw it long ago.

Drake, he was a Devon man, and ruled the Devon seas
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Roving tho' his death fell, he went with heart at ease,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.
"Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore,
Strike it when your powder's running low;
If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port of Heaven,
And drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago."

Drake, he's in his hammock till the great Armada's come
(Captain, art thou sleeping there below?)
Slung atween the round shot, list'ning for the drum,
And dreaming all the time of Plymouth Hoe.

Call him on the deep sea, call him up the Sound,
Call him when ye sail to meet the foe;
Where the old trade's plying and the old flag's flying,
They shall find him ware and waking, as they found him long ago!

OUTWARD BOUND

Dear Earth, near Earth, the clay that made us men.
The land we sowed,
The heart that glowed.—
O Mother, must we bid farewell to thee?
Fast dawns the last dawn, and what shall comfort then
The lonely hearts that roam the outer sea?

Gray wakes the daybreak, the shivering sails are set,
To misty deeps
The channel sweeps,—
O Mother, think on us who think on thee!
Earth-home, birth-home, with love remember yet
The sons in exile on the eternal sea.

DEVON, O DEVON, IN WIND AND RAIN

Drake, in the North Sea grimly prowling,
Treading his dear Revenge's deck.
Watch'd, with the sea-dogs round him growling,
Galleons drifting wreck by wreck.
"Fetter and Faith for England's neck,
  Faggot and Father, Saint and chain,—
Yonder the Devil and all go howling,
  Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"
Drake at the last off Nombre lying,
  Knowing the night that towards him crept,
Gave to the sea-dogs around him crying
  This for a sign before he slept:—
"Pride of the West! what Devon hath kept
  Devon shall keep on tide or main:
Call to the storm and drive them flying,
  Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!"

Volour of England gaunt and whitening,
  Far in a South-land brought to bay*;
Locked in a death-grip all day tight'ning,
  Waited the end in twilight gray.
Battle and storm and the sea-dog's way!
  Drake from his long rest turn'd again,
Victory lit thy steel with lightning,
  Devon, O Devon, in wind and rain!!
*Waggon Hill, 6th January, 1900.

HOMEWARD BOUND

After long labouring in the windy ways,
  On smooth and shining tides,
Swiftly the great ship glides,
  Her storms forgot, her weary watches past!
Northward she glides, and thro' the enchanted haze
  Faint on the verge her far hope dawns at least,
The phantom skyline of a shadowy down
  Whose pale white cliffs below,
Thro' sunny mists aglow,
  Like noonday ghosts of summer moonshine gleam—
Soft as old sorrow, bright as old renown,
  There lies the home of all our mortal dream.

THE OLD SUPERB

The wind was rising easterly, the morning sky was blue,
  The straits before us opened wide and free;
We looked towards the Admiral, where high the Peter flew,
  And all our hearts were dancing like the sea.
The foe are gone to Martinique with four and twenty sail,
  The "Old Superb" is old and foul and slow!
But the foe are gone to Martinique, and Nelson's on the trail,
  And where he goes the "Old Superb" must go.

So Westward ho! for Trinidad, and Eastward ho! for Spain,
  And "Ship ahoy!" a hundred times a day;
Round the world if need be, and round the world again,
  With a lame duck lagging all the way.
The "Old Superb" was barnacled and green as grass below,
  Her sticks were only fit for stirring grog;
The pride of all her midshipmen was silent long ago,
  And long ago they ceased to heave the log.
Four years out from home she was, and ne'er a week in port,
  And nothing save the guns aboard her bright;
But Captain Keats he knew the game, and swore to share the sport,
  For he never yet come in too late to fight.
  So Westward ho; etc.

"Now up, my lads," the Captain cried,
  "For sure the case were hard,
If longest out were first to fall behind;
  Aloft, aloft with studding-sails, and lash them on the yard,
For night and day the Trades are driving blind."
So all day long and all day long behind the fleet we crept,
  And how we fretted none but Nelson guessed;
But ev'ry night the "Old Superb," she sail'd while others slept,
  Till we ran the foe to earth with all the rest.
  O 'twas Westward ho! etc.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
How mild the balmy summer night!
Upon the heights what fires are glowing!
All is around us fragrant, bright,
The boatmen chant below as rowing.
The azure heav'n above is beaming.
Now rests the world, the waters glide,
A wondrous dome outstretching wide,
And earth its broad foundation seeming.
Oh, summer night! in holy light,
With perfume, light, and grace o'erflowing,
With stars like eyes of angels bright,
Their placid smile on all bestowing!

There floats a chord of love along
And earth with heav'n is thus united,
And silenced too are sin and wrong,
As love alone could here be plighted.
Oh, therefore lighted is the blaze
Upon the heights, and fire is gleaming;
Oh, therefore all the planets gaze,
And earth and heav'n alike are beaming.
Now rests the world, and as the wind
Now in the tree-tops gently rustleth,
Such peace and beauty are combined,
That man rejoiceth, prayeth, list'neth.

performance_1.performance_name: Setting of God Save the King

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
(a)
My bonny lass, she smileth,
When she my heart beguileth,
Fa, la, la!
Smiles less, dear love, therefore,
And you shall love me more,
Fa, la, la!
When she her bright eye turneth,
O, how my heart it burneth,
Fa, la, la!
Dear love, call in their light,
Or else you burn me quite.
Fa, la, la!

(b)
Now is the month of Maying,
When merry lads are playing,
Fa, la, la.
Each with his bonny lass,
A-dancing on the grass,
Fa, la, la.
The spring, clad all in gladness,
Doth laugh at winter's sadness,
And to the bagpipes' sound
The nymphs tread out the ground,
Fie, then, why sit we musing?
Youth's sweer delight refusing?
Say, dainty nymphs, and speak,
Shall we play barley-break?

I love, and schall untyl I dye

Through bushes and through briars
I lately took my way,
All for to hear the small birds sing
And the lambs to skip and play.
I overheard my own true love,
Her voice it was so clear:
"Long time I have been waiting
For the coming of my dear.
Sometimes I am uneasy and troubled in my mind,
Sometimes I think I'll go to my love,
And tell to him my mind,
And if I should go to my love,
My love, he will say nay;
If I show to him my boldness,
He'll ne'er love me again.
If I show my boldness he'll ne'er love me again."

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
Ca' Hawkie, through the watter,
Hawkie is a sweir beast,
And Hawkie winna wade the watter,
Hawkie is a bonnie coo!
Tho' she's loath to wade the watter,
While she waits the work'll stand,
So ca' Hawkie through the watter,
Hawkie winna wade the watter,
Hawkie is a prettier coo!
All the children do adore her,
For she gives them all the milk,
There is none they prize before her!
Girls, be not too nice or coy,
If you swear a man to marry;
Ne'er say nay, but quickly comply,
As 'tis hazardous to tarry.
Now, young maids, my counsel take,
Since that it can be no better:
Cast off baith your hose and shoon,
And safely drive her through the watter.

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
Some talk of Alexander, and some of Hercules;
Of Hector and Lysander, and such great names as these;
But of all the world's brave heroes there's none that can compare
With a tow row row row row row row
To the British Grenadiers.

Those heroes of antiquity ne'er saw a cannon ball,
Or knew the force of powder to slay their foes withal;
But our brave boys do know it, and banish all their fears;
Sing tow row row row row row row,
For the British Grenadiers.

When e'er we are commanded to storm the palisades,
Our leaders march with fuses, and we with hand grenades;
We throw them from the glacis about the enemies' ears;
Sing tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

And when the siege is over, we to the town repair,
The townsman cry, "Hurra, boys! here comes a Grenadier."
Here come the Grenadiers, my boys, who know no doubts or fears,
Then sing tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

Then let us fill a bumper and drink a health to those
Who carry caps and pouches and wear the louped clothes;
May they and their commanders live happy all their years,
With a tow row row row row row row
For the British Grenadiers.

performance_11.lyrics_transcript:
All welcome the bowl!
A full flowing soul,
    Unfathomed by care!
What boots it the bandit,
If hunted and branded,
    So wine be his share!

    To play, sirs!
Treasure is merely a pleasure
    That flies soon as come!
And play hath a duty,
It charmeth when beauty
    Inconstant may roam.

Thrice welcome the bowl!
Whose glorious soul
    Doth bleed at our call!
The bowl, the bowl,
Whose glorious soul, sirs,
    Doth bleed at our call.

Ernani, still pensive?
    Quick thought grows apprehensive
        To view his cheek so blanch'd
    Where life's tide hath motion,
On Death's shoreless ocean
    Our one bark is launched.

    To give, then thy willing
Immediate fulfilling,
    Ere will'd we prepare.
The hawk's speed 'gan tarries
In hitting her quarries,
    If ours ye compare.

    Come, welcome the bowl,
Whose glorious soul
    Can drown all thy care!

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
I may no longer dream
Here by the solitary tulip-tree
That Leirion waits for me;
Nor in the cool
Shade of the sombre cypress look to see
Narcissus, bowed above the marble rim,
Blurring with crystal tears his image in the pool.

I may no more esp'y
By yonder mouldering plinth,
Lord Eros, veiled, with lanthorn lifted high,
Guiding his virgin train,
Hippolytus, Adonis, Hyacinth,
Hylas and Agathon—
Lilies new-blown and clear of earthly stain—
Home to the unguessed heights of his serene domain.
Ah me! ah me!
Must I go mourn for earth-born phantoms fled,
And those Uranian summers lived in vain?
Nay, fond, inveterate lover!

Now, now at last lift up a joyful head!
Thy perilous day is done,
The blessed night draws on—
Love is no dream, as thou wilt prove tomorrow,
When thou shalt wake to find Him standing at thy side.
See where the quiet garden waits for thee!
The sheltering boughs their evening balm have shed;
Dear memories, undefiled;
Gather like dew; closer the shadows creep.
Beneath thy chosen Leirion-haunted tree
Make thou thy lonely bed;
Lie down and rest, by no false dreams beguiled;
With folded hands pray God thy soul to keep,
Even as a little child,
Weary, and very glad because of coming sleep.

—Paul England.

performance_15.lyrics_transcript:
Defeated and slain with half of his host,
Was Theodemerus, King of the Goths.
The Huns were shouting with fiendish mirth,
The vultures hastened down to earth:
The moon was bright, the wind was cold,
The wolves were howling in distant wold.
Three men were riding through heather and field,
Their helmets battered, and broken their shield.
The first one bore in his saddle sling
The broken spear of his murdered King;
The second, he bore the King's crown, Oh, woe!
Split straight in two, by the axe of a foe.
The third, he hid in faithful arm
A secret veiled in his mantle warm,
A veiled secret!
And when they the river Iser espied,
The first one rested his horse and cried:
"Save a battered crown and a broken spear,
Of the Gothic Kingdom is naught to fear"!

And the second, he said, "In those waters deep,
Let us bury our treasure for ever to sleep,
Then follow ourselves, by a leap from the sand;
Why tarry, Master Hildebrand?"
"Ye carry the King's own crown and spear:
My faithful companions, far more have I here."

Thus saying, he opened his cloak so warm;
"I carry the hope of the Goths in my arm.
Ye saved crown and spear, 'twas bravely done;
I—I have rescued the King's own son!
Awake now, my boy, see how homage I bring.
I greet thee Young Dietrich, the Goths' new King."

I've never sailed the Amazon,
I've never reached Brazil!
But the "Don" and the "Magdalena,"
They can go there when they will.
Ah!

Great steamers, white and gold,
Go rolling down to Rio,
And I'd like to roll to Rio

Some day before I'm old!
I'd like to roll to Rio
Some day before I'm old!

I've never seen a jaguar,
Nor yet an armadill—
O dillowing in his armour,
And I s'pose I never will. Ah!
Unless I go to Rio
These wonders to behold,
Go rolling down to Rio!
Roll really down to Rio!
Oh, I'd love to roll to Rio,
Some day before I'm old!
I'd love to roll to Rio
Some day before I'm old!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
Cries "Boatman, do not tarry!
And I'll give thee a silver pound
To row us o'er the ferry."

"Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle
This dark and stormy water?"
"Oh, I'm the chief of U'vas' Isle,
And this, Lord Ullin's daughter."

And fast before her father's men,
Three days we've fled together,
And should he find us in the glen,
My blood would stain the heather.

His horsemen hard behind us ride;
Should they our steps discover,
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
When they have slain her lover?

Out spake the hardy highland wight,
"I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
But for your winsome lady.

And by my word, the bonny bird
In danger shall not tarry,
So though the waves are raging white,
I'll row you o'er the ferry."

By this the storm grew loud apace,
The water wraith was shrieking,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
Grew dark as they were speaking.

But still as wilder blew the wind,
And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
Their tramping sounding nearer.

"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
"Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
But not an angry father."

The boat has left the stormy land,
A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
The tempest gather'd o'er her.

And still they rowed amidst the roar
Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
His wrath was changed to wailing.

For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
And one was round her lover.

"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

'Twas vain: the loud waves lashed the shore,
Return or aid preventing,
The waters wild went o'er his child,
And he was left lamenting.
performance_1.additional_information: Hamish MacCunn. Liedertafel, Associated Ladies' Choir, and Orchestra.
