performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
WHY linger, why turn back, why shrink, my heart?
Thy hopes are gone before: from all things here
They have departed; thou should'st now depart!

The soft sky smiles, the low wind whispers near;
'Tis Adonais calls! Oh, hasten thither,
No more let Life divide what Death can join together.

That Light whose smile kindles the universe,
That Beauty in which all things work and move,
That Benediction, which the eclipsing Curse
Of birth can quench not,
Now beams on me
Consuming the last clouds of cold mortality.

The breath whose might I have invoked in song,
Decends on me: my spirit's bark is driven
Far from the shore, far from the trembling throng
Whose sails were never to the tempest given;
The massy earth and spher'd skies are riven!
I am borne darkly, fearfully, afar;
Whilst burning through the inmost veil of Heaven
The soul of Adonias, like a star,
Beacons from the abode where the Eternal are.
performance_3.additional_information: Specially Composed for and Dedicated to the Melbourne Liedertafel By August Siede (Conducted by the Composer.) MR. SIEDE'S composition is for full chorus and orchestra, and is entitled "Elegy," the words being selected from the three last wonderful stanzas of Shelley's "Adonais." This work bears few or no traces of the novice, its technique is mastery, both in the severe grip of form and in the polyphonic style of the part writing. It is above all fermented by vivid poetic feeling from first to last. Its deep sadness shows never a touch of morbidity, but is permeated by a certain objective grandeur, which at times is imposing.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
A Sacrificer—
THOU to whom fancy lends many titles,
    Giver of runes and of magic!
Working before the world's beginning,
Thou who outgazeth from Lidskialf.

Men—
Hear us!

A Woman—
Tender mother Frigga, sorrowing for Balder;
Bearing in thy bosom all worldly woe;
Comforter of Odin, nourisher of nature,
Drawing all life and care into Fensal.

Women—
Hear us!

The Sacrificer—
Trudyang's Hlorrida, Bilskirner's Yireflame,
Thou of the strength-belt and hammer,
Shield of the Aesir and of the Northmen,
Ever the dread of the giants.

Men—
Hear us;

The Woman—
Beauteous weeping goddess, silent widow Vannadis
Love's dis-tress thine own loss taught unto thee!
Let our tears of sorrow with thine own be mingled;
Thou who dost govern half of the living.

Women—
Hear us!

The Sacrificer—
Horn-beating Heindal, Ull in Ydaler,
Nyord, mighty north-dweller, hear us!
Algenheim's joy, Landvida's sorrow,
Long-bearded minstrel, and thou Tyr.

Men—
Hear us!

The Woman—
Ever-youthful Idun, Sif of golden harvests,
Saga of the streamlet, Skada of the hills,
All ye mighty Aesir, Vanir and Valkyrie,
Here our complaining, earthward oh hasten!

Women—
Here us!

Men and women—
Other gods are now arising,
Gods of power, gods of battle:
Help us, Mitgard trembles,
Gods alone with gods can wrestle!

(All kneeling.)
Ye who from the Urdar fountains pour life-strength
into our bosoms,
Ye alone who know his will, the Father in gold-caped Gimle;
Ye in Odin's ear who whisper softly as each day
awakens,
Ye who were ere world's beginning,
Ye who will be when 'tis wasted,
Show our fates the way to him, the god so long
awaited—
Hear us!

The Volva—
(From an elevation in the foreground)—

'Tis not enough that ye invoke Nornir and Aesir,
Runes must be graven duly
Evil to disperse from the pathway which to the gods
doth lead.
There, see the gathered hosts
Upon their horns howling, to hide our voices,
That the gods never may hear us!

Men and women—
O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

The Volva—
(Raises herself so that she stands high above all the others)—

Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the
southland,
With Hel soon shall feast be holden!
Plague shall gnaw, serpents send through your veins
deadly venom!
Let Hel's hounds awake, howling and foaming,
Monsters filled with madness, for your blood thirsting
blindly!
For Hel no fitter food can afford them!

With Hel! spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland,
With Hel, here in the north, your feast is.

Men and women—
O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

The Volva—
(Who has been carving runes now continues to cut eagerly)
Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland,
To Hel soon shall your way be wended!
Evil ones away! the Thunderer's weapon awaits ye!
Runes I wrote on a staff I rent from the altar of Odin.
To Hel straightway its charm consigns ye.
To Hel! Runes will lead Lokis lot unto the doors of his daughters,
With Hel ye shall devour that writing.

(She casts the Rune-staff on the holy fire, which immediately bursts into flames that ascend to the roof of the Temple. A horrible din, accompanied by thunder in the distance, shakes the Temple.)

Men and women—
(Kneeling in terror)-
Wondrous word of Odin goes
To black abyss, to heaven's height,
Aweful, returneth the answer.

The Volva—
Answer came from Hel, from high gods;
All fear it, yet not I.
Now let us kneel to them!
Every path is free!
So I will pray them first.
Gods, ye holy, eternal gods!
Are ye here? Then heed me!
Where find we the fiat which governs our fate?
Where bends your balance, ordering all?
Show, ah! show to me, ye mighty ones,
Where ye will strike the evil Olaf?
Gods all-governing, endless, omnipotent Aesir; I pray;
Devoted to Odin from my youth.
By the grey wolf's heart, by the raven's tongue,
By my sacrifice in sleepness nights, I pray you!
Show me, mighty ones, where ye will strike the evil Olaf.

(A crash of thunder and the back of the Temple is shattered. The Temple is seen in the distance enclosed in flames and smoke. Thunder continually heard until the Temple becomes invisible.)

The Volva, men and women—
Here! here! hasten the holy ones!
Here! here! strikes him the vengeance of heaven!

In our hall he must enter,
Let him go in, ne'er to come forth again.

(With Mockery.)
Let this be told to him—
We will believe if he comes safely forth.
Let his god go in to our gods!
If he safely come forth, we will believe.

All— (Turning towards the gods)—
Thanks for the token, solace it sends to us.
Thanks for the token, faith it confirms!
Choice of thy children, come then, oh king, to us;
Come to thy children, strife will be short!
Now will the gods themselves go on their gladsome way,
Now will the gods themselves grant us their grace!
Lit from our land by fire, lo, he shall leave us;
Loki shall lighten him hence unto Hel!

(Assembling round the images of the gods.)
Three nights besought we, suing like son to sire,
Three nights we pleaded, heard is our prayer.

The Sacrificer and Elders having procured horns form a circle round the three "Holy Firs," afterwards advancing and seating themselves at the sides. The Sacrificer, having made the "hammer sign" over the horns, proceeds to render the following song.

The Sacrificer—
Raise high the horn, great host-father, Odin's horn,
Raise high the horn, upheave it for him.
High altar fires, and Akethor's hammer-sign.
High altar fires have hallowed it.

Men and women—
Gladly we join in
Games for the gracious god,
Gladly we join in
Outbursts of joy!

(Preparations are made by the people for a dance. The men leap over the "Holy Fire," lifting the women over on both sides. Then commences a Temple dance in which all join.)

Quartette—
Give to all gods a grace-cup of gratitude,
Give to all gods your greatest of gifts.

Men and women—
Horns fill for Akethor, Drontheimer's deity,
Fill them to Akethor, daring in fight.
    Gladly then, etc.
Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest and fish they send,
Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest fair, haul of fish,
To freedom, and faith.
    Gaily then, etc.

Beakers to Braga, bring we with holy vows,
Beakers to Braga, brimming we raise!
Offerings of flesh and blood
To Braga we all freely bring.
    Gaily then, etc.

    Women—
O ye Asynier, honour we offer thee,
All ye Asynier, honour and praise!
Nourish, oh mild ones, men with your mother milk,
Nourish us ye who move us with might!
Young men and maidens, grandsire and grandmother,
Honour for aye the gods ever green?
    Gaily then, etc.

    Men and women—
Glorious Disir, gliding like doves around!
Glorious Disir, death making glad!
Guarding ye, follow friendly our future fate,
Guarding ye, follow us, hail to your flight!
Fortune of fathers, holdeth the hamingja
Fortune of fathers and of the race.

    Women—
O ye Asynia, etc.

    Men and women—
Earthmen and Kobalds, deepening the ground for us
Earthmen and Kobalds, hail to your kind!
Hail to the highest spirit that hides in the hills!
Hail I tiny elves who frolic in flow'rs.
Hail our upholder, guardian of house and halls,
Hail who upholdshest harbour and holm.
    Gaily then, etc.

Faith of our fatherland, love thou dost light in us,
Faith of our fatherland, moving all men.
We will defend thee, fight for our father's faith,
We will defend thee, future be ours,
We will defend thee, source of our weal and woe,
We will defend thee, fount of great deeds.

Three nights besought we suing, like son to sire,
Three nights we prayed, and heard was our prayer
The first night offered we bowls of bloody sacrifice,
On the first offered we oxen with prayer.
Next night guest-offering gave we the gracious gods,
Over their images uttering prayer.
On the third night fair dream faces favoured us,
On the third night we danced and we sang,
Gladly we joined in games to the gracious gods
Gaily we joined in outbursts of joy.
performance_5.additional_information: Scenes from... OLAV TRYGVASON (BJÖRNSTERNE BJÖNSON) For Solo Voices, Choir and Orchestra. By Edvard Grieg Op. 50. OLAV TRYGVASON, a descendent of Harold Haarfager (the first king of Norway), was brought up at the court of Gardarikke (Russia), and was baptised in England while on a Viking raid. When he learned that Norway was dissatisfied with her king (a scion of an older branch of the same race), he resolved upon conquering the kingdom and converting the people to Christianity. Richly endowed by nature, he was superior of all his contemporaries in bodily and spiritual gifts, and so comely to behold that none had seen his like; he was revered in the middle ages as the noblest example of the Norman race; he conquered more by his personality than by his sword. He commenced his struggle in the Drontheim district, and the beginning of this conflict is depicted in the scenes of the drama here set to music. The action takes place in an ancient Norman temple in the Drontheim district, at the time of Olaf Trygvason's appearance. Period—End of the tenth century. Cast shown in this chunk: A Woman Miss Hesketh Jones; The Volva Mr. E. A. Ure; A Sacrificer. Performing forces: Liedertafel. Associated Ladies' Choir, and Orchestra.

event_5_11.additional_information: Page 3 gives: "16 March 1968", "Asahi Hall, Tokyo", "sponsored by the American Cultural Center with the cooperation of the Asahi Newspaper company", and Japanese line "主催 アメリカ文化センター　後援 朝日新聞社". Page 4 describes CROSS TALK activities: In the 1967-68 season, CROSS TALK presented Japanese first performances of works by the following composers and film makers: ASHLEY, AUSTIN, BABBITT, BEHRMAN, CAGE, CHIHARA, FREUND, ICHIYANAGI, IIMURA, IVES, KOSUGI, LUCIER, MARTIRANO, MATSUDAIRA, MIZUNO, MORRIS, MUMMA, NELSON, SATIE, SCHILLING, SUBOTNICK, REICH, REYNOLDS, TAKAHASHI, TAKEDA, TAKEMITSU, YUASA. Future plans also described: During the winter of 1968-69, CROSS TALK will sponsor the first festival of live electronic music in Japan. Several guest composer/engineers from the United States are expected. In addition, general demonstrations for the public; special work sessions on basic technical resources (e.g., ring modulators, photo cells, computer applications, etc.); open rehearsals; experimental presentations; and public events are planned. Later in the spring of 1969, several days of intermedia events will be held, including performances of IANNIS XENAKIS' Terretektorn for 88 players seated among a circularly arranged audience; JOHN CAGE's as yet incomplete HPSCHD for fifty computer-derived tapes and harpsichord soloist; and the premiere of Flight-Operatic by TORU TAKEMITSU, for orchestra, mime, dancers, film, tape, and so on. Various other events on a smaller scale will be presented from time to time, as announced.

■〈クロス・トーク〉コンサートはアメリカ文化センター（館長ドナルド・オーブライト）の主催のもとに、企画・構成ロジャー・レイノルズ、カレン・レイノルズ、湯浅謙二、秋山邦晴によって、今回も組織されました。

■今回の再生装置には、トリオ株式会社のご好意により、総合アンプ、スピーカー・システムが提供されました。
■1967～68年のシーズンに、〈クロス・トーク〉は下記の作曲家および映画作家の作品を、世界初演、または日本初演をふくめてとりあげました。
アシュレー、オースティン、バビット、バーマン、ケージ、千原、フルンド、一柳慧、飯村隆彦、アイヴス、小杉武久、ルシエ、マルティラーノ、松平顕隆、水野修孝、モリス、ムンマ、ネルソン、サティ、シリング、スポットニック、ライヒ、レイノルズ、高橋悠治、武田明倫、武満徹、湯浅譲二（5月に予定されている作品を含む）
■〈クロス・トーク〉では、1969年の春にライヴ・エレクトロニック・ミュージックの音楽祭を計画、進行中です。
アメリカから、数人の作曲家と技師を招待して、さまざまなデモンストレーションやコンサートをおこなう予定です。それと同時に、日本の若い作曲家や技術者のために、電子音響機械（リング・モデュレーター、フォト・セル、コムピューター、変調器その他）を使用するゼミナールを行います。電子工学と芸術との新しい結びつきや、その可能性が活発にこころみはじめられている今日、こうしたエンジニアリングへの新しい視野をひろげることは意味のあることでしょう。
■1969年春以降の予定としては、目下さまざまな構想を検討中ですが、次のような、いわゆるインター・メディアともいうべき動向をうかびあがらせるコンサートを計画しています。
88人の奏者と聴衆を参加させるイアニス・クセナキスの〈テレテクトール〉1966、ジョン・ケージが目下イリノイ大学のコムピューターを使って作曲中の〈HPSCHD〉（これは50チャンネルにわけられたテープとハープシコード奏者による作品）、さらにアメリカから帰国した武満徹がオペラティックな作品として構想中の〈フライト〉（オーケストラ、マイム、舞踊、映画、テープその他を使用）などを予定しています。
■このほか、特別コンサートと、定期的なコンサートも継続しておこなう予定ですが、いずれ詳細は追ってお知らせします。

section_1.additional_information: FOR SOLI, CHORUS, AND ORCHESTRA. JOHANNES BRAHMS, (Op. 45).

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
CHORUS.

Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall have comfort. They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. Who goeth forth and weepeth, and beareth precious seed, shall doubtless return with rejoicing and bring his sheaves with him.
performance_1.additional_information: Program note begins on Page 9 and continues on Page 13: "The first chorus (I.) opens with the calm utterance of the words \"Blessed are they that mourn\"; succeeded by the promise \"They that sow in tears shall reap in joy,\" set to music of the most consolatory character. In this movement an indescribable richness of tone is produced by the skilful management of the stringed band, from which the violins are altogether excluded."

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
CHORUS.

Behold all flesh is as the grass, and all the goodliness of man is as the flower of grass: for lo! the grass withereth, and the flower thereof decayeth. Now therefore be patient. O my brethren, unto the coming of Christ. See how the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early rain, and the latter rain. So be ye patient. Behold all flesh is as the grass, &c.

Albeit the Lord's word endureth for evermore. The redeemed of the Lord shall return again, and come rejoicing unto Zion; gladness, joy everlasting, joy upon their heads shall be; joy and gladness, these shall be their portion, and tears and sighing shall flee from them.
performance_2.additional_information: Program note on Page 13: "The next number (II.) opens with a Funeral March. The idea is that of the whole human race marching in solemn procession to the grave, and this idea has inspired Brahms to the composition of a march unlike all marches that were ever written. It is in triple-time—the measured tramp of no ordinary host. The effect is heightened by the employment of unison in the vocal parts at the words \"Behold all flesh is as the grass.\" The imagery of these words, perhaps connected with the \"sowing in tears\" of the preceding chorus, suggests the passage from the Epistle of St. James, \"The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth\"; and this leads to the beautiful fugal setting of the words \"The redeemed of the Lord shall return.\" The repetition of the words \"joy everlasting,\" with which the chorus closes, is a most striking contrast to the gloom of the beginning."

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
BARITONE SOLO and CHORUS.

Lord, make me to know the measure of my days on earth, to consider my frailty, that I must perish. Surely all my days here are as an hand-breadth to Thee, and my lifetime is as nought to Thee.

BARITONE SOLO.

Verily mankind walketh in a vain show, and his best state is vanity. He passeth away like a shadow, he is disquieted in vain, he heapeth up riches, and cannot tell who shall gather them.

CHORUS.

Verily mankind walketh in a vain show, and his best state is altogether vanity.

BARITONE SOLO and CHORUS.

Now, Lord, O what do I wait for? My hope is in Thee.
But the righteous souls are in the hand of God, nor pain nor grief shall nigh them come.
performance_3.additional_information: Program note on Page 13: "The third number (III.) starts with a Baritone Solo, \"Lord make me to know,\" melodious, expressive, and pre-eminently vocal. The Chorus then repeat the same words, as also in the next section, \"Verily mankind walketh in a vain show.\" At the words \"Now, Lord, O what do I wait for,\" the voice parts become more involved and the music more agitated, leading up to a very fine climax at the words \"My hope is in Thee.\" Here the four sections of the choir enter successively from the lowest register of the bass to the high soprano, suggesting the idea of a hope built upon a sure foundation, and leading into the splendid fugue \"But the righteous souls are in the hand of God,\" in which the same impression of stability and permanence is conveyed, and is indeed accentuated by its being constructed throughout one continuing Pedal note."

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
CHORUS.

How lovely is Thy dwelling place, O Lord of Hosts!
For my soul it longeth, yea fainteth for the courts of the Lord; my soul and body crieth out, yea for the living God.
Blest are they, O blest are they that dwell within Thy house. They praise Thy name evermore; they praise Thee.
performance_4.additional_information: Program note on Page 13: "After the assurance as to the destiny of the \"righteous souls,\" it is natural to turn to the joys of their abode, and in the next number (IV.) \"How lovely is thy dwelling place!\" the perfect peace of heaven is reflected. Attention may be drawn to the fine fugal treatment of the words \"They praise Thy Name evermore,\" towards the end of this movement."

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
SOPRANO SOLO.

Ye now are sorrowful, howbeit ye shall again behold Me, and your heart shall be joyful, and your joy no man taketh from you.

CHORUS.

Yea I will comfort you, as one whom his own mother comforteth.

SOPRANO SOLO.

Look upon me! Ye know that for a little time labour and sorrow were mine, but at the last I have found comfort.

CHORUS.

Yea I will comfort you.
performance_5.additional_information: Program note on Page 13: "The subject of the next number (V.) is that of comfort to mourners, based on the happy state of the holy dead. The loss of the composer's mother is said to have determined its form, which is that of a soprano solo, accompanied by a quiet chorus, which repeats the words \"As one whom his own mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.\"

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
CHORUS.

Here on earth have we no continuing place: howbeit we seek one to come.

BARITONE SOLO and CHORUS.

Lo, I unfold unto you a mystery. We shall not all sleep when he cometh, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the sound of the trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and all we shall be changed.

BARITONE SOLO.

Then what of old was written, the same shall be brought to pass:—

CHORUS.

For death shall be swallowed in victory. Grave, where is thy triumph! Death, O where is thy sting!

CHORUS.

Worthy art Thou to be praised, Lord of honour and might, for thou hast earth and heaven created, and for Thy good pleasure all things have their being, and are and were created.
performance_6.additional_information: Program note on Page 13: "The sixth chorus (VI.) begins with a passage of simple four-part harmony, \"Here we have no continuing place,\" and the baritone solo entering at the words \"Lo! I unfold unto you a mystery,\" the thoughts are led on to the change from mortality to immortality, on which the burial service lays stress. To English ears the re-setting of \"For the trumpet shall sound,\" &c., may seem almost sacrilegious; but it must be remembered that the Messiah is far less familiar in Germany than here. The dramatic passages descriptive of the \"mystery\" serve as a preparation for the calm dignity and devotional grandeur of the double fugue, \"Lord, Thou art worthy.\"

But who goes there apart? In the brake his pathway is lost;
Close behind clash the branches together, the grass rises again, the desert engulfs him.
Who can comfort his anguish?
Who, if balsam be deathly,
If the hate of men from the fulness of love be drained.
He that was scorned turned to scorner, lonely now devours all he hath of worth in a barren self-seeking.

But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart!
Lift up his o'er-clouded eyes where are the fountains hard by the thirsty one in the desert.
But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,

event_1_43.additional_information:
Biographical/program-note style text on JOHANNES BRAHMS, with adjacent lyric/transcript text and page marker. Visible text includes: "JOHANNES BRAHMS, born 1833 at Hamburg; as a boy excited great attention both by compositions and pianoforte playing. In 1874, he was made a member of the Academy of Arts at Berlin. Excepting opera, Brahms cultivated nearly every branch of musical composition. Powerful, original and versatile, Brahms, more than any other, sums up in his strongly-marked individuality the varying elements: classical as well as romantic, of contemporaneous culture. His imagination, to which he at first allowed too free a scope (about to Op. 10), he bridled by severe study and rigid self-criticism; and although reflection plays a large part in his compositions, he produced abundance of music of a thoroughly spontaneous and inspired character. His melodies possess inexhaustible variety, ranging from naive simplicity and a dreamy poetical tenderness peculiar to himself, to stirring pathos, striking force, and glowing passion; always remaining pregnant and concise. His harmony, often surprisingly bold and original, is subordinated to the dictates of a high artistic idea, which permeates and controls the formal construction of his works, in which an admirable mastery of contrapuntal art is often exhibited. His songs extend from the simplest specimens of popular melody to the richest and most complicated forms of art."

section-1.additional_information: Characters Represented: Gerontius — Mr. Gregor Wood.; Assistants — THE LIEDERTAFEL.; The Priest — Mr. Horace Stevens. ARGUMENT: Gerontius, lying at the point of death, sees in a dream the passing of his soul from earth towards the judgment seat of the Almighty. Part I. of the Poem is descriptive of the last moments on earth of the departing spirit. Gerontius, surrounded by his friends, feels that he is being called away, and prays for the sustaining presence of the Almighty in his extremity. A sense of impending ruin disquiets his thoughts from time to time, but supported by the intercessory prayers of the priests and his friends, he repeats the Creed and gradually falls into a sleep ending in death.

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
JESU, MARIA—I am near to death.
And Thou art calling me; I know it now.
Not by the token of this faltering breath,
This chill at heart, this dampness on my brow.

(Jesu, have mercy! Mary, pray for me!)
'Tis this new feeling, never felt before,
(Be with me, Lord, in my extremity!)
That I am going, that I am no more.
'Tis this strange innermost abandonment.
(Lover of souls! great God! I look to Thee.)
This emptying out of each constituent
And natural force, by which I come to be.
Pray for me, O my friends; a visitant
Is knocking his dire summons at my door,
The like of whom, to scare me and to daunt,
Has never, never come to me before:

So pray for me, my friends, who have not strength to pray.

performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison.
Holy Mary, pray for him.
All holy Angels, pray for him.
Choirs of the righteous, pray for him.
All Apostles, all Evangelists, pray for him.
All holy Disciples of the Lord, pray for him.
All holy innocents, pray for him.
All holy martyrs, all holy Confessors,
All holy Hermits, all holy Virgins,
All ye Saints of God, pray for him.

performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
Rouse ye, my fainting soul, and play the man;
And through such waning span
Of life and thought as still has to be trod,
Prepare to meet thy God.
And while the storm of that bewilderment
Is for a season spent,
And, ere afresh the ruin on me fall,
Use well the interval.

performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Parce mihi, Domine.

Firmly I believe, and truly
God is Three, and God is One:
And I next acknowledge duly
Manhood taken by the Son.
And I trust and hope most fully
In that Manhood crucified;
And each thought and deed unruly
Do to death, as He has died.
Simply to His grace and wholly
Light and life and strength belong
And I love, supremely, solely,
Him the holy, Him the strong.
Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Parce mihi, Domine.

And I hold in veneration,
For the love of Him alone.
Holy Church, as His creation,
And her teachings, as His own.
And I take with joy whatever
Now besets me, pain or fear,
And with a strong will I sever
All the ties which bind me here.
Adoration aye be given.
With and through the angelic host.
To the God of earth and heaven,
Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
Sanctus fortis, Sanctus Deus,
De profundis oro te,
Miserere, Judex meus,
Moruis in discrimine.

I can no more; for now it comes again,
That sense of ruin, which is worse than pain,
That masterful negation and collapse
Of all that makes me man.

And, crueller still,
A fierce and restless fright begins to fill
The mansion of my soul. And, worse and worse,
Some bodily form of ill
Floats on the wind, with many a loathsome curse
Tainting the hallowed air, and laughs, and haps
Its hideous wings,
And makes me wild with horror and dismay
O Jesu, help! pray for me, Mary, pray!
Some Angel, Jesu! such as came to Thee
In Thine own agony—
Mary, pray for me. Joseph, pray for me.
Mary, pray for me.

performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
Rescue him, O Lord, in this his evil hour,
As of old so many by Thy gracious power—
Now from the waters in a saving home:
(Amen.)
Job from all his multiform and fell distress; (Amen).

Moses from the land of bondage and despair.
(Amen.)
David from Golia and the wrath of Saul:
(Amen.)

section-2.additional_information: In Part II. the disembodied soul of Gerontius awakens to consciousness and feels itself being borne onward by unseen hands. The song of the Guardian Angel is heard, rejoicing in the completion of his work, and that the child of clay confided to his care is saved. The Soul questions the Angel, and learns that it is being carried towards the Throne of God. On the way they encounter a cloud of Demons, hungry and wild to gather souls for hell, who mock and jeer at the heavenly aspirations of "low-born clods of brute earth." On approaching nearer to and passing through the gateway of the House of Judgment they are met by a Choir of Angelicals singing praises and thanksgiving. Then, as the veiled presence of God is reached, echoes are heard of the earthly voices of the friends of Gerontius, and the priests reciting the "Subvenite," while the Angel of the Agony pleads before the Throne of Grace for the dying and the dead. The soul is then tenderly consigned to the penal waters by the Guardian Angel, who promises to return, after the night of trial, and awaken the Soul to a glad to-morrow. The voices of the Angelicals are again faintly heard singing the hymn, "Praise to the Holiest," and the work closes with a beautiful seven-fold Amen.

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
I would have nothing but to speak with thee
For speaking's sake. I wish to hold with thee
Conscious communion; though I fain would know
A maze of things, were it but meet to ask,
And not a curiousness.

performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
You cannot now
Cherish a wish which ought not to be wished.

performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
Then I will speak. I ever had believed
That on the moment when the struggling soul
Quitted its mortal case, forthwith it fell
Under the awful Presence of its God,
There to be judged and sent to its own place.
What lets me now from going to my Lord?

performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
Thou art not let; but with extremest speed
Art hurrying to the Just and Holy Judge.

performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
Dear Angel, say,
Why have I now no fear at meeting Him?
Along my earthly life, the thought of death
And judgment was to me most terrible.

performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
It is because
Then thou didst fear, that now thou dost not fear.
Thou hast forestalled the agony, and so
For thee the bitterness of death is passed.
Also, because already in thy soul
The judgment is begun.

performance-7.lyrics_transcript:
A message falls upon thee, as a ray
Straight from the Judge, expressive of thy lot.
That calm and joy uprising in thy soul
Is first-fruit to thee of thy recompense,
And heaven begun.

performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
Now that the hour is come, my fear is fled;
And at this balance of my destiny,
Now close upon me, I can forward look
With a serenest joy.

But hark! upon my sense

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
What's a saint?
One whose breath
Doth the air taint
Before his death;
A bundle of bones,
Which fools adore.
Ha! ha!
When life is o'er.

Virtue and vice,
A knave's pretence,
'Tis all the same;
Ha! ha!
    Dread of bell-fire,
Of the venomous flame.
    A coward's plea.
Give him his price,
Saint though he be.
Ha! ha!
    From shrewd good sense
    He'll slave for hire.
Ha! ha!
    And does but aspire
To the heaven above
    With sordid aim,
And not from love.
    Ha! ha!

SOUL.
I see not those false spirits: shall I see
My dearest Master, when I reach His throne?

ANGEL.
Yes,—for one moment thou shalt see thy Lord.
One moment; but thou knowest not, my child,
What thou doth ask: that sight of the Most Fair
Will gladden thee, but it will pierce thee too.

SOUL.
Thou speakest darkly, Angel! and an awe
Falls on me, and a fear lest I be rash.

ANGEL.
There was a mortal, who is now above
In the mid glory: he, when near to die,
Was given communion with the Crucified,—
Such, that the Master's very wounds were stamped
Upon his flesh, and, from the agony
Which thrilled through body and soul in that embrace,
Learn that the flame of the Everlasting Love
Doth burn ere it transform.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:

ANGEL.
    . . . . Hark to those sounds!
They come of tender beings angelical,
Least and most childlike of the sons of God.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!

To us His elder race He gave
To battle and to win,
Without the chastisement of pain.
Without the soil of sin.
The younger son He willed to be
A marvel in His birth;
Spirit and flesh His parents were:
His home was heaven and earth.
The Eternal blessed His child, and armed,
And sent Him hence afar,
To serve as champion in the field
Of elemental war.
To be His Viceroy in the world
Of matter, and of sense;
Upon the frontier, towards the foe.
A resolute defence.

ANGEL.
We now have passed the gate, and are within
The House of Judgment. . . .

SOUL.
The sound is like the rushing of the wind—
The summer wind—among the lofty pines.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Glory to Him, who evermore
By truth and justice reigns:
Who tears the soul from out its case.
And burns away its stains!

ANGEL.
They sing of thy approaching agony,
Which thou so eagerly didst question of.

SOUL.
My soul is in my hand: I have no fear,—
But hark! a grand mysterious harmony:
It floods me, like the deep and solemn sound
Of many waters.

ANGEL.
And now the threshold, as we traverse it,
Utters aloud its glad responsive chant.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest in the height.
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!
O loving wisdom of our God!
When all was sin and shame.
A second Adam to the fight
And to the rescue came.
O wisest love! that flesh and blood
Which did in Adam fail,
Should strive afresh against the foe.
Should strive and should prevail:
And that a higher gift than grace
Should flesh and blood refine,
God's Presence and his very Self,
And Essence all divine.

O generous love! that He who smote
In man for man the foe,
The double agony in man
For man should undergo.

And in the garden secretly,
And on the cross on high,
Should teach His brethren and inspire
To suffer and to die.

Praise to the Holiest in the height,
And in the depth be praise:
In all His words most wonderful;
Most sure in all His ways!

ANGEL.
Thy judgment now is near, for we are come
Into the veiled presence of our God.

SOUL.
I hear the voices that I left on earth.

ANGEL.
It is the voice of friends around thy bed.
Who say the "Subvenite" with the priest.
Hither the echoes come; before the Throne
Stands the Great Angel of the Agony.
The same who strengthened Him, what time He knelt
Lone in the garden shade, bedewed with blood.
That Angel best can plead with Him for all
Tormented souls, the dying and the dead.

ANGEL OF THE AGONY.
Jesu! by that shuddering dread which fell on Thee;
Jesu! by that cold dismay which sickened Thee;
Jesu! by that pang of heart which thrilled in Thee;
Jesu! by that mount of sins which crippled Thee;
Jesu! by that sense of guilt which stifled Thee;
Jesu! by that innocence which girdled Thee;
Jesu! by that sanctity which reigned in Thee;
Jesu! by that Godhead which was one with Thee;
Jesu! spare these souls which are so dear to Thee,
Souls, who in prison, calm and patient, wait for Thee;
Hasten, Lord, their hour, and bid them come to Thee,
To that glorious home, where they shall ever gaze on Thee.

SOUL.
I go before my Judge.

VOICES ON EARTH.
Be merciful, be gracious; spare him, Lord.
Be merciful, be gracious, Lord, deliver him.

ANGEL.
Praise to His name!
O happy, suffering soul! for it is safe,
Consumed, yet quickened, by the glance of God

SOUL.
Take me away, and in the lowest deep
There let me be,
And there in hope the lone night-watches keep,
Told out for me.
There motionless and happy in my pain.
Lone, not forlorn,—
There will I sing my sad perpetual strain,
Until the morn,
There will I sing, and soothe my stricken breast,
Which ne'er can cease
To throb, and pine, and languish, till possess
Of its Sole Peace.
There will I sing my absent Lord and Love:—
Take me away.
That sooner I may rise, and go above,
And see Him in the truth of everlasting day.

SOULS IN PURGATORY.
Lord, Thou hast been our refuge: in every generation;
Before the hills were born, and the world was: from age to age Thou art God.
Bring us not, Lord, very low: for Thou hast said, Come back again, ye sons of Adam.
Come back, O Lord! how long: and be entreated for Thy servants.

ANGEL.
Softly and gently, dearly-ransomed soul,
In my most loving arms I now enfold thee.
And, o'er the penal waters, as they roll,
I poise thee, and I lower thee, and hold thee.
And carefully I dip thee in the lake,
And thou, without a sob or a resistance,
Dost through the flood thy rapid passage take,
Sinking deep, deeper, into the dim distance.
Angels, to whom the willing task is given,
Shall tend, and nurse, and lull thee, as thou liest;
And Masses on the earth, and prayers in heaven,
Shall aid thee at the Throne of the Most Highest.
Farewell, but not for ever, brother dear,
Be brave and patient on thy bed of sorrow:
Swiftly shall pass thy night of trial here,
And I will come and wake thee on the morrow.

SOULS.
Lord, Thou hast been our refuge, &c.
Amen.

CHOIR OF ANGELICALS.
Praise to the Holiest, &c. Amen.

CARDINAL NEWMAN.

GLORY and love to the men of old.
Their sons may copy their virtues bold:
Courage in heart and sword in hand,
Ready to fight or ready to die for Fatherland.
Who needs biddig to dare by a trumpet blown?
Who lacks pity to spare when the field is won?
Who would fly from a foe if alone, or last,
And boast he was true, as cowards might do when peril is past?
Now to home again we come, the long and fiery strife of battle over;
Rest is pleasant after toil as hard as ours beneath a stranger sun.
Many a maiden fair is waiting here to greet her truant soldier lover,

(a) Good King Wenceslas look'd out,
    On the feast of Stephen;
    When the snow lay round about,
    Deep, and crisp, and even.
    Brightly shone the moon that night,
    Though the frost was cruel,
    When a poor man came in sight,
    Gath'ring winter fuel.

Tenor Solo. "Hither, page, and stand by me,
    If thou know'st it, telling,
    Yonder peasant, who is he?
    Where and what his dwelling?"

Treble Solo. "Sire, he lives a good league hence
    Underneath the mountain;
    Right against the forest fence,
    By St. Agnes' fountain."

Tenor Solo. "Bring me flesh, and bring me wine,
    Bring me pine-logs hither;
    Thou and I will see him dine,
    When we bear them thither."

Chorus. Page and monarch forth they went,
    Forth they went together;
    Through the rude wind's wild lament
    And the bitter weather.

Treble Solo. "Sire, the night is darker now,
    And the wind blows stronger;
    Fails my heart; I know not how,
    I can go no longer."

Tenor Solo. "Mark my footsteps, my good page
    Tread thou in them boldly;
    Thou shalt find the winter's rage
    Freeze thy blood less coldly."

Chorus. In his master's steps he trod,
    Where the snow lay dinted;
    Heat was in the very sod
    Which the saint had printed.

    Therefore, Christian men, be sure,
    Wealth or rank possessing,
    Ye who now will bless the poor,
    Shall yourselves find blessing.

event-1-section-1-performance-1.additional_information: L. van Beethoven. The ORCHESTRA. THANKS to Plutarch's stirring "Life" and Shakespeare's yet more stirring drama, everyone can know how that mighty warrior Caius Marcius, surnamed Coriolanus, delivered Rome repeatedly from the greedy grasp of her foes; and how that, having done so, he was shamefully handled by the ungrateful people he had saved spirited out as though he were a few ignorant and envious mob orators; how that he was banished the city and reviled with nothing vengeance, with a vast and invincible army; how that on the eve of the fulfilment of his just wrath his wife and little son and mother penetrated to the hostile camp and after long entreaty prevailed on him to withdraw his troops, conscious as he was that this course was tantamount to signing his own death-warrant—these several events subsequently proved. It is this tragic crisis with which Beethoven has dealt in the present powerful tragic overture, how truthfully and well he felt by those who can sympathise with the contending passions which must have torn the warrior's heart during the terrible interval.

event-1-section-1-performance-2.performance_name: (a) "Now is the Month of Maying"; (b) "Awake! Sweet Love"
event-1-section-1-performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
(a) NOW is the month of Maying, when merry lads are playing,
Fa la la, etc.
Each with his honey lass, a dancing on the greene,
Fa la la, etc.
The Spring clad all in gladness, doth laugh at Winter's sadness,
Fa la la, etc.
And to the Bazpipes' sound, the nymphs tread out their ground.
Fa la la, etc.
Fie then, why sit we 'musing, youth's sweet delights refusing?
Fa la la, etc.
Say, dainty nymphs, and speak, shall we play harley break?
Fa la la, etc.

(b) AWAKE, sweet love! thou art return'd;
My heart, which long in absence mourn'd,
Lives now in perfect joy.
Only herself hath seemed fair,
She only I could love,
She only drove me to despair
When she unkind did prove.

event-1-section-1-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
E' STRANO! in coro scolpiti ho quegli Scutia che amore, è il palpit' dell'universo intorno misterioso orvce o delizia alcor!
Saria per me sventura un serio amore?
Che risolvi, turbata anima mia?
Nell'uomo ancora tacendeva,
Oh gioia ch'io non conobbi, esser amata amando!
E sdegnar la poss'io per l'aride follie del viver suo?
Ah, fors'è lui che l'anima solinga ne' tumulti,
goda sovente pingers de' suoi colori oculti!
Lui che, modesto e virile, all'egregio soglio ascese
destandomi all'amor!
A quell'amor che e' palpit' dell'universo, dell'universo intero, misterioso, altero,
crese e alizia al cor mio.
A me fioristi un araldo e tregiolo desira
quest'efficio dolceissimo signor dell'avvenire, quando ne' cieli il raggio di sua belta veda e tutta me paseca de quel divino error.

Follie! follie! delirio vano è questo!
Povera donna, soa, abbandonata in questo pozzoloso deserto che appallano.
Parigi, che spero or più? che far degg'io?
gioire di voluta ne' vorrici, di voluta gioir? gioir! gioir!
Sempre liberi degli' folleggiare di gioia in gioia, via che scorra il viver mio pel seno del passato.
Nasca il giorno o il giorno muoja, sempre lieta ne' ri rovi a diletti sempre nuovi del volare il meo pensier.

event-1-section-1-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
MATONA, lovely maiden,
O listen to the song
I sing beneath thy window,
While night clouds roll along.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

I pray you hear my ditty,
'Tis sweet and not too long,
'Tis pointed, if not witty,
And sharpened like a prong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

The words of choicest tissue,
To shoot love's aim, belong,
Then from your window issue,
Or else you do me wrong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

You'll say if once you catch them,
And note their fine ding dong
Petrarca could not match them,
They are so sweet and strong.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

But if you think the more,
Should to all scorn belong,
A more complying treasure,
I'll choose from out the throng.
Dong, dong, derry, derry, etc.

event-1-section-1-performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
Here is a Rose unfolken,
Out of a tender shoot;
As sung to us of olden,
From Jesse sprung its root.
It bloom'd for our delight
And bid the frosts of winter,
Nigh on the noon of night.

That Roselet blest of Heaven,
Isaiah did forshow,
By Mary to us given,
The Virgin pure as snow.
She thro' God's holy might,
Gave birth unto an infant,

event-1-section-1-performance-8.additional_information: L. van Beethoven. Movements: Adagio Molto; Allegro con brio; Andante cantabile con moto; Allegro molto e vivace (Minuetto and Trio); Adagio; Allegro molto e vivace. The ORCHESTRA. This the first of the great master's symphonic works, will be especially interesting, owing to the rarity of its performance and the opportunity it affords us of observing the development of the genius of Beethoven. Throughout the work the influence of Haydn and Mozart is felt, and it has been said that the Andante un rit. even have been written by a Mozart or a Haydn. The Third Movement, however, clearly prophesies the scherzo of the later symphonies, as do some of the earlier chamber works of the master. With the last Movement we are carried back to the graceful time of Haydn, with all its quaintness and light-hearted gaiety.

event-1-section-1-performance-9.performance_name: (a) "April is in my Mistress' Face"; (b) "Flora gave me Fairest Flowers"
event-1-section-1-performance-9.lyrics_transcript:
(a) APRIL is in my Mistress' face,
And July in her eyes hath place,
Within her bosom is September,
But in her heart is cold December.
O were it July all the year,
Then April show'rs I would not fear,
Nor blight that falleth in September,
Nor frost that chills in cold December.

(b) FLORA gave me fairest flowers,
None so fair in Flora's treasure.
These I placed in Phillis' bowers,
She was pleas'd and she's my pleasure.
Smiling meadows seem to say,
Come ye wantons, here to play.

performance_2.additional_information: Movements listed as: Adagio Molto; Allegro con brio; Andante cantabile con moto; Allegro molto e vivace (Minuetto and Trio); Adagio; Allegro molto e vivace. Performed by The ORCHESTRA. Program note: "This the first of the great master's symphonic works, will be especially interesting, owing to the rarity of its performance and the opportunity it affords us of observing the development of the genius of Beethoven. Throughout the work the influence of Haydn and Mozart is felt, and it has been said that the Andante un rit. even have been written by a Mozart or a Haydn. The Third Movement, however, clearly prophesies the scherzo of the later symphonies, as do some of the earlier chamber works of the master. With the last Movement we are carried back to the graceful time of Haydn, with all its quaintness and light-hearted gaiety."

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
APRIL is in my Mistress' face,
And July in her eyes hath place,
Within her bosom is September,
But in her heart is cold December.
O were it July all the year,
Then April show'rs I would not fear,
Nor blight that falleth in September,
Nor frost that chills in cold December.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
FLORA gave me fairest flowers,
None so fair in Flora's treasure.
These I placed in Phillis' bowers,
She was pleas'd and she's my pleasure.
Smiling meadows seem to say,
Come ye wantons, here to play.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
SINCE yesterday I've sought in vain my master.
Oh Capulet, perhaps he yet honours thy house!
I'll sing a stave—so the servants will come
Flocking out to repair yesternight's sad disaster.

Gentle dove wherefore art thou clinging
To a wild vulture's nest?
Soon, we trust, thou wilt be a-winging
To a far dearer rest.

Fond shepherdess, thy loves fight and foray,
And to tear and mangle his quarry
Hath beak both sharp and strong.
Unlike thine, soft and true and slender.
Oh may thine bend to lips more tender,
With kisses warm and long.

See you guard her safely,
They that live will know
For your dove may flutter
From her cage and go.

Now, it happ'd, that a ringdove flying
From her woodland so green.
To that eyrie came one eve sighing
For her young love, I ween.

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
The cold blast of winter why heed we,
If only thy bright face be near,
And with thy smile, what cheer?
Here standing at thy door what need we?
Of the brightness that springtime bringeth
Thine abode at all times can tell,
And fair lady, where thou dost dwell
Ever the nightingale singeth.
And to know is thy bosom longing
What gleam of light these may be.
performance-1.additional_information: Performed by Mr. H. M. Lee.

performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
O Sons of Art, man's dignity to you is given:
Preserve it man!
It falls with you, with you ascends to heaven!
The hallowed themes of Magian dreams,
Founded in woman's vast creation,
Gliding like rivers find their ocean,
That great harmonious plan.

Eternal truth tho' oft rejected,
Exists not ever unprotected;
She finds a refuge with a truthful throng,
She turns to them for all her glory,
Mighty when veil'd in mystic story;
She wakes the lay of lofty voices,
And over all her foes rejoices,
Her vengeance flashing, peals in song.

To your free mother homage render,—
Boldly to gain her height aspire;
Enthroned she dwells in radiant splendour
No other throne her lustre desert.
While you her thousand paths are tracing
Press onward, keeping Truth in sight;
Come altogether, stand embracing
Before the Throne where paths unite!

performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
Fling wide the gates! come out!
Dauntless and true;
Brothers, of heart be stout,
We must not go,
Bring from the battlements
Our flag again;
Tho' by the leaguer rent
It hath no stain.

Mothers and wives to pray'r,
From this eve,
The Lord of Hosts will care
For all we leave.
Plead that we sought not fight,
Nor chose the field;
But ev'ry free heart's right
We dare not yield.

Mother and wives, to prayer
Relief is nigh,
For you each man will dare
Deeds not do die.
For sure as fire doth blaze,
Or foaming wine, you
Yield well-to-night upraise
Songs of the free.

performance-9.lyrics_transcript:
And more than all, the folly
That from the winecup flows.
The people drudge and labour,
Debited as they are,
The sword rules and sabre,—
'Tis pity to behold!
Such misuse and detraction,
By Stry Thine eyes no more!
Look to our gay subjection
The world we must restore.
And therefore, children of the berry,
Ye wine both wise and merry, all take heed—
A King we'll choose both wise and merry,
So haste, approach, and to the poll proceed!

Chorus of Wines: Great Bacchus, hail!
Thy plan is wise, it cannot fail.
Our faith we plight by red and white,
The best of wines, wherever grown,
We loyally as king shall own.

Bacchus: See Don Sherry then, Spain's redoubtable knight,
He first appears your kind votes to invite;
By churchmen and laymen he e'er was beloved,
By the King of Prussia, All England's lord,
And e'en Isabella, the fond-hearted queen,
Regarded our knight with affectionate mien.
Where to sound of castanet
Gave the King of Wines his title
Where the sun doth never set,
Choose ye there the King of Wines?

Chorus: Oh no, no, no!
A Philistine and bigot he,
Our king Don Sherry cannot be!

Bacchus: Preferreth then Tokay, the valiant Magyar,
Who has off prov'd his mettle in love and in war;
The spirit of fortune auxiliarily bold,
Carried by the best of the young and the old.
Marianas—a many his honey have sipp'd,
And sturdy young Wenceles he many has tripp'd.
He drinks the wine of the strays,
Fiddling his fantastic lays,
Spurs the nut-brown maidens wear—
Will ye choose your monarch there?

Chorus: Oh no, no, no!
The Baron of Grünberg by far is he—
Tokay our king can never be!

Bacchus: The Baron of Grünberg now comes to view,
Whoever molesteth him, his boldness shall rue;
A cion of old and august name,
His "vinegar aspect" belies not his fame.
No enemy yet could against him prevail—
He drank, made grimaces, and so quickly turned tail.
That if a monarch you select
This candidate sardonically
Your stoutest foes you may defy,
They'll conquer, taste, and conquer'd fly!
Ye, then, O King, a king elect,
Will prove a bitter toad.

Chorus: No, no, no, no!
This is a false deceitful wine,
He never shall be king of mine!

Bacchus: Behold then the Freischutz! Pretender
In chivalry!
The lord of Champagne is, in all men's belief.
The elements four as his sponsors have stood,
And lavished their gifts in a generous mood.

From Fire he had the fervid glow
That animates his flow;
And Water gave the beads that swim
Like pearls on goblet's rim.
The air the fragrant, golden dress,
The garb of joyousness;
And Air gave him the spirit free,
That he may sing and be.
Piff, paff! see the froth
Mounting in the cup, sir!
Piff, paff! be not loth,
Quickly fill, quicky fill, sir!
Fill again, drink again,
Sparkling vintage of Champagne—
Crown him king and let him reign
O'er all the world, sir!

Chorus: No! 'tis an uproarious wine,
A bragart and vain-glorious wine!
Howe er he fume and rave.
He fills your glass to half, the knave!
A knave who will conquer's bent,
But whose élan is quickly spent.
No, no! Champagne
As King of Wines shall never reign!

Bacchus: Then lo! by the Rhine-river's beautiful
Behold the vine of Rauenthal grow!
From pure Teutonic blood 'tis sprung,
Make glad the heart, the spirit young—
The noble Rhine's vines,
Shall be as King have sway!

Chorus: In crystal green the golden wine,
The heart's blood of dear Father Rhine,
Yes, sent the strain of land and sea
This shall be King! O, our joy be!
All joyous hearts in concord sing,
The glorious Rhine-wine shall be King!

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
ONAWAY, awake, beloved,
Thou wild flower of the forest,
Thou the wild bird of the prairie,
Thou with eyes so soft and brown!
If thou only lookest at me,
I am happy, I am happy!
As the lilies of the prairie,
When they dew upon them feel!

Sweet thy breath is as the fragrance of the flowers in the morn.
As their fragrance is at evening, in the Moon when leaves do fall.
Does not all the blood within me leap to meet thee, Onaway.
As the springs to meet the sunshine in the Moon when nights are bright?
    Onaway!

    Onaway! my heart sings to thee,
    Sings with joy, when thou art near,
    As the sighing, singing branches
    In the pleasant Springtime Moon.
    When thou art not pleased, beloved,
    Then my heart is sad and dark,
    As the shining river darkens
    When the clouds on it throw shade.

    When thou smilest, my beloved,
    Then my troubled heart is brightened,
    As in sunshine gleam the ripples,
    That cold winds in rivers make.

    Smiles the earth, and smile the waters,
    Smile the cloudless skies above,
    But I lose the way of smiling
    When thou art no longer near.
    Onaway! I myself, behold me!
    Blood of my beating heart, behold!
    O awake, awake, beloved,
    Onaway! beloved awake,
    Onaway! Onaway! Onaway, wake,
    Awake! loved one, Onaway!

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
AGAIN our march we resume, going on
Across the weary wastes alone,
The depths of the desert beholding,
We forward press throughout the day,
Though days are long, and long the way,
Life no joys unfolding:
And as we go, we yearn to know
How Fate our course is moulding.
We take our way, with a song we march,
With full delight, we onward fare,
Beneath this blue overhanging arch
We freely breathe in ample air.
We sing, we march

Allah, Allah, to Thee I render homage,
Allah, Allah, of Thine eternity, of Thine immensity,
I am the created image.
    Allah, Allah!
To Thee be praise, Thou ruler of creation,
That dwellest in eternity.
The solitude of the desert
Thou fillest with Thy majesty,
    Allah, Allah!

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
O Sanctissima! O Piissima!
Dulcis Virgo, Maria,
Mater amata intemerata;
Ora, ora pro nobis!

HAL-LOH! Hal loh! Hal-loh!
Hal-loh! o'er hill and dale we go,
Thro' smiling forest bounding,
No fear of danger can we know,
While loud the hunter's horn we blow,
The woods and craigs resounding
Echo as we go.

Tra-ra.

The sunbeams fill our hearts with glee,
With rapture now our souls are free,
All dangers then we laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the twanging horn,
All dangers then we laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the horn.

Tra-ra.

The eager chase to follow,
O'er hill thro' break and hollow.
And when the nimble deer we spy,
With ecstasy our hearts beat high,
All dangers laugh to scorn,
While merry sounds the horn,
    Tra-ra.

Our homeward way now wending,
We pause awhile at even's close,
Beneath some dear one's window,
And wish her sweet repose,
We pause beneath her window,
And sing at even's close.
Repose thou dearest maiden,
May heav'nly angels guard thy rest,
For thou with joy and beauty,
The hunter's life has blest.
Beneath thy chamber window,
The happy day we close,
Repose! Repose!
Hal-loh! Hal-loh! etc.

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
HAIL, O Night!
    Calm and bright;
    From care all hearts set free:
    Peace restoring,
    Come in thy majesty!
Shine brightly on us with thy mild beaming eye,
From thy glad presence all sorrow shall fly,
    As with the merry dance and song,
    The happy hours will pass along
        In harmony and revelry.

While pleasure reigning holds her radiant sway,
And hearts unfeigning glad homage pay,
While joy and beauty on life's pathway shine,
Why should we sorrow, why then repine?
Youth, happy youth, is life's richest prize!
Then love, then young love, beams in beauty's
    bright eyes
Banish maiden, all thoughts of sorrow,
Cares that sudden thee leave till morrow;
    And lightly as thy twinkling feet,
    Light my fond heart doth beat;
    Thy fond glance I meet,
        When thou art near.
    List to the beeze, love.
    Softly whisp'ring through the trees, love,
While the moon in her splendour sheds her rays
    from above;
Gently, so gently, on zephyrs borne, love stealing,
Softly in whispers, two fond hearts appealing;
Thine's my heart, dearest maiden,
    With love's bliss ever laden;
Thine are my thoughts, ever thine.

Hark! Hark! 'tis the midnight chime,
Wafted on the sweet wing of time;
    It sighs farewell, with parting knell.
Farewell, fair maiden, we shall meet again;
Joy's in the future though parting is pain;
Parting is brief, joy shall remain.
Fare thee well!

PRÉFACE
La Fête fédérale de chant qui aura lieu à Lausanne au mois de juillet 1928 réunira environ quatorze mille chanteurs. C'est-à-dire que ce sera une manifestation musicale très importante. Or, selon la coutume, les sociétés lausannoises offriront à nos confédérés un concert, dit « de réception ». L'œuvre qui sera interprétée à cette occasion sera la Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner, qui, outre ses qualités de style et d'expression dont le public jugera, aura cet avantage de convenir à l'immense hall de Beaulieu où auront lieu les concerts et dans lequel des œuvres plus délicates ne feraient aucun effet. La Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner est une partition où trouvent leur emploi les qualités de simplicité et de grandeur que l'on s'accorde à reconnaître au maître autrichien ; c'est une fresque sonore, et, pour en saisir la beauté, il convient de faire abstraction du détail pour considérer l'ensemble de la composition. Elle n'est pas longue, mais elle est traitée dans un style large qui répondra, nous l'espérons, à l'ampleur de la salle. Il eut été imprudent de ne pas tenir compte de cette question de convenance.
Les organisateurs du « concert de réception » ont pensé bien faire en offrant au public de la Suisse romande une audition de la Messe en fa mineur de Bruckner quelques semaines avant la Fête fédérale. Le concert du mois de mars servira ainsi de prélude aux manifestations du mois de juillet.
Le Chœur du Conservatoire de Lausanne est renforcé, pour la circonstance, par un groupe important de dames de Lausanne et de Vevey.
HERMANN LANG
Chef des auditions de la Messe en fa mineur.

event-1-section-1-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
In fear of the Gods shall ye dwell, sons of men!
So the empire they hold in their hands everlasting
And wield at their pleasure the lightnings of fate.

He doubly shall tremble whom they have exalted!
On turrets of cloudland enthroned they banquet,
Pour golden libations.

But are they offended, they hurl forth the guest,
To dishonour and ruin, where shadows are deepest.
There vainly he waiteth, in darkness and bondage,
For justice and judgment.

But they hold, the Immortals, eternal carousals,
Pour golden libations.
They stride over height unto height thro' the heavens.

event-1-section-2-performance-3.performance_name: THE BIRTH OF HERCULES, FROM THE LYRIC DRAMA ARISTODEMUS.
event-1-section-2-performance-3.additional_information: G. W. L. Marshall-Hall. THE LIEDERTAFEL AND ORCHESTRA. THE lineal descendants of Hercules, the Messenians, have, by pestilence and their foes, been driven to their last stronghold, the citadel of Ithome. There they await the oracle of the god, which shall determine their fate, and in worship to Zeus recall the ancient splendid legend of the birth of their ancestor Hercules, and of the wrath of Hèrè (Juno), to whom they ascribe all their misfortunes. They implore Zeus to remember his erewhile love towards his offspring, and to avert from them "the wrath and the doom." The music is an attempt to realize something of the dignity and splendour with which the Greeks surrounded their gods, in whom they embodied the most vital characteristics of their race. There is nothing in the wonderful symbolism of their mythology more inspired than the conception that their Heroes were the offspring of the intercourse of gods with mortal beings. Thus alone did it seem to them, could the pre-eminence of certain of the greatest among men be accounted for.

event-1-section-2-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
In fear of the Gods shall ye dwell, sons of men!
So 'le empire they hold in their hands everlasting
And wield at their pleasure the lightnings of fate.

He doubly shall tremble whom they have exalted!
On turrets of cloudland enthroned they banquet,
Pour golden libations.

But are they offended, they hurl forth the guest,
To dishonour and ruin, where shadows are deepest.
There vainly he waiteth, in darkness and bondage,
For justice and judgment.

But they hold, th' Immortals, eternal carousals,
Pour golden libations.
They stride over height unto height thro' the heavens,
From earthy abysses arises the groaning
Of long smother'd Titans,
A fragrant oblation, faint cloud on the azure.

The all-ruling Gods shut the gates of their blessings
On whole generations,
Avoiding the once cherish'd, still speaking features
Of Grandsire in far distant and blameless sons.

Thus chanted the Sisters; below, 'mong the Shadows
The Exil'd one hearken'd the Fates' dread foreboding
He thinks on his children, all darkness and doubt.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
AND the beautiful too, must die!
    Even the beautiful die,
What men and gods has conquered, melts not the iron heart,
Melts not the stygian Jove.
Only once, for love! the Monarch of Shadows relented,
But at the threshold called back.
    Called he back his gift!
Aphrodite staunches not the wound,
Which in the lovely body, the Cruel Boar has torn.
Nor could mother immortal save the godly hero falling at the gate of Troy,
    Falling, his fate fulfilled!
But from the sea she arises, with the daughters of Nereus,
And in loud lamenting, mourns for the son now glorified.
    See, how mourn the gods!
    See, how mourn the goddesses all!
That the beautiful Fades!
Mourn that the Highest dies!
And a song of lament from heart of the loved is glorious!
    Ah! to go songless and silent to Orcus dark reign!
And a song of lament from heart of the loved is glorious!

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Evil Spirit—
How diff'rent, Gretchen, was it
When thou cam'st with pure heart
Here to the altar,
Thy well thumb'd little book didst clasp,
Thy pray'r's soft lisping;
Thy thoughts half playful,
Half turned to Heaven.
Gretchen,
Where now thy thoughts?
And in thy bosom
What misdeed hast thou?
Ist for thy mother's soul thou'rt praying,
Who through thee, to never ending pain,
Slept on and on?
Upon the threshold, whose the blood?
What stirs beneath thy heart?
Hath it not dawning Life
That scares itself and thee
With its forboding presence!

Gretchen—
Woe! Woe!
Could I from the thoughts escape,
That pierce through my being
And, accusing me,
Haunt me still!

Chorus—
Dies irae, dies illa,
Solvent sæculum in favilla.

Evil Spirit—
Tremble thou!
For the trumpet sounds!
The graves are quaking!
And from its ashy rest,
Thy heart,
For flaming tortures
Afresh created,
Starts forth;

Gretchen—
Would I were hence!
'Twould seem as though the organ's tone
Could hinder my breathing;
The singing
Thrills my heart with torture!

Chorus—
Judex ergo cum sedebit,
Quidquid latet ad parebit,
Nil inultum remanebit.

Gretchen—
Oppress'd I feel!
The cluster'd pillars
Imprison me,
And the groined roof
Whelms me—Air!

Evil Spirit—
Ah, hide thee! Sin and shame
Are never hidden.
Air? Light?
Woe's thee.

Chorus—
Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?
Quem prætonum rogaturus,
Cum vix justus sit securus?

Evil Spirit—
Their faces from thee
The blessed turn away,
The pure from thee withhold
Their hands with shudd'ring!
Woe!

Chorus—
Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?

Gretchen—
Friend your help!
Or I faint.

DAY again his race has run,
    And the tranquill night comes on,
    Soothingly her pinions waving,
    Heated hill and valley laving,
    Spreading from her starry chart.

        Holy peace to ev'ry heart.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
THRO' forest deep at dead of night,
    The mail is slowly borne;
    While sleep the weary travellers,
    The post-boy winds his horn.

    The forest-ranger's dwelling
    Within the wood is seen,
    The horn a tale is telling—
    What can its echoes mean?

    It's tunes so soft and sweetly flow,
    The winds, in passing by,
    Pause at an open window,
    And mingling with them fly.

    Where sleeps the forest maiden,
    While beams the moon above;
    With love her dreams are laden—
    With melody and love.

    "The horn sounds, and produces a general bustle. . . . As the coach rattles through the village, everyone runs to the window, and you have glances on every side of fresh country faces, and blooming, giggling girls." —Washington Irving.

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
Thou art, O Lord, my star by night,
    By day my sun above me;
    Thou art my confidence and might,
    That onward ever move me;
    With Thee o'er deserts do I go,
    And brave in trust no terror know.

    Give me the power my sword to wield,
    And steel my blade to serve me,
    That ere my purpose I shall yield,
    No foe may e'er unnerve me;
    Aid me when I oppose the foe,
    And guide my eye to strike the blow.

    On mountain's height wher'er I stray
    From faltering horse protect me,
    And let Thy angel on my way
    Thro' wood and wild direct me;
    And when upon the trackless sand,
    Be Thou my ever-guiding hand.

    The balmy breeze upon me send,
    To cooling shade convey me,
    E'er head and heart in conflict end,
    And foot and eye betray me;
    And fill me into quiet rest,
    In dreams of home afar caressed.

    Thou art, O Lord, my star by night,
    By day my sun above me.

"Here pause we gentle, for a space;
    And if our tale hath won your grace
    Grant us brief passage, and again
    We will renew the Minstrel strain."
    —Scott.

performance_10.additional_information: Weber. Adagio. Allegro con fuoco. The ORCHESTRA. Program note: "SINCE the creation of Shakespere's \"Midsummer Night Dream,\" no such delightfully picturesque suggestion of the world of sprites, elves and fairies has been given to us as is contained in this romantic Overture. From the mysterious horn call, with which the introduction opens, and the gradual awakening of the drowsy little hamsters of the woodland, to the brilliant and lively theme of the Allegro, and the delightful suggestion of sweet melodies which follow, everything is invested with a profound sympathy with Nature, whose myriad life seems here informed with soul understanding. As we listen to this deeply penetrating poet, the line of demarcation between higher and lower organisms fades away, and their hidden secrets, the unity of life, is disclosed. It is this highly beautiful revelation which causes us to experience such aesthetic pleasure, unmixed with any feeling of incongruity. —G. W. L. M. H."

event_1_section_2_perf_3.lyrics_transcript:
WHILE through a valley I was straying,
A rose fresh blooming met my sight,
Such ample store of charm displaying,
My bosom felt unknown delight.

With fragrant moss around it swelling,
Appeared the gem of lustre mild;
Oh, ne'er from out a fairer dwelling;
The angel face of virtue smiled.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

A strange yet pleasing sense came oe'r me,
I felt new life within me bound,
While I beheld the flow'r before me,
Unwonted rapture then I found.
That image fair of heav'nly pleasure,
Upon my heart is deeply traced;
It is my bosom's dearest treasure,
And never can it be o'ersc'd.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

When sorrow's clouds are round me low'ring
At once the rose's form appears,
A charm such anguish overpow'ring,
It stills my sighs, it dries my tears.
Oh flow'r that 'mid the darkness springing,
By heav'n's decree upon me shone;
To thee my heart is fondly clinging,
And will not cease till life is gone.
Beautiful form, tarry, oh, tarry with me.

event_1_section_3_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
"The rosy tints of morning pierce the haze—
The eastern sky illumining with its rays,
From the heav'n above,
The star of day, like a loud hymn of praise,
Fills all the Desert with new light and love.

Chorus.
With cheerful heart
On our way let us start,
Toil heeding not, our aim to gain
We roam through the Desert dreary;
Still! on we press nor stay for rest,
Nor stay for rest, though the days are long
And our limbs are weary.
Away we march, ever free and gay,
So pure the air, so bright the day!
We blithely sing as we march along,
Our feet keep time to our rhythmic song.

Chorus.
STLLAH! Allah! To Thee I homage render.
Of Thine immensity,
Of Thine eternity,
Image am I, my praise I tender.
Allah!
All praise to Thee; Thy glory is unbounded,
The Sovereign of the world Thou art;
In solitude though I should wander,
Yet Thou art there, in every part.
Allah!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
NORTHWARD from Denmark came Eric and Jorund,
    To Upsal came sailing to win back their own
From Hakon the Sea-king, who, conquering Sweden,
    Their kinsman had slain, and had seized on his throne,

King Hakon of Sweden was strong, brave and fearless,
    And though half his warriors were roaming the sea,
And cruising as vikings from Norway to Bretland,
    As fierce as the tempest, as wild and as free,

Yet fought he the brothers with spirit undaunted,
    Until by his sword-stroke King Eric fell dead;
Until with his forces all broken and scattered,
    Back to his warships King Jorund had fled.

But Hakon, the fearless, was mortally wounded,
    His men, dead and dying, were strewn on the shore,
The tide was fast ebbing and so was his life-blood,
    He knew that by nightfall he'd enter death's door.

Sadly, yet bravely, he turned his glance seaward,
    He saw his great warship at rest on the strand;
The ship that had borne him through storm and through battle,
    Her helm ever faithful beneath his firm hand.

Then all the old mem'ries came thronging and throbbing:
    Of cruises so many, so long and so far,
Of storms on the ocean, of salt spray a-dashing,
    Of fights in the Baltic, of wounds, and of scar.

Of midnight in summer, the sky flushed with crimson,
    The waters reflecting the northern light's bars.
Of loyal companions, and telling of sagas,
    While sailing on swiftly beneath the bright stars.

"And now a long cruise we shall sail for the last time."
    The dying King said to those gathered near,
"His heroes with Hakon will set out undaunted,
    To death as to battle we go without fear.

"Launch then the warship, her deck pile with dead wood.
    And thereon rest gently my battle-men dead,
Your King place among them all clad in his armour,
    And bright shield untarnished laid under his head.

"Free let the helm be, set all the flags flying,
    The great anchor hang in its place at the rail,
And then fire the death pile, thus passing in glory
    Straight east to Walhalla and Odin we'll sail."

Just as the low sun had gilded with splendour
    The wild rocky islands that bounded the bay,
And then sunk in crimson behind the far mountains,
    The soul of King Hakon from earth passed away.

In the grey gloaming the moorings were severed,
    The fresh wind blew off shore, the fire leaped up red,
In clear flame a-burning between the dark islands,
    Straight eastward to Odin, King Hakon's ship sped.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
Soft the glassy waves are flowing,
  Gently, gently let us glide;
Golden stars and sunset glowing
  Flash upon the silent tide.
As the day and night are blending,
  Floating o'er the waves along,
From the depths below ascending
  Comes a strange and ghostly song.

The king's enchanted daughter
  Has swept the golden strings;
And under the depths of the water
  She sweetly, sadly sings.
She sings of echoing forest,
  She sings of flowery plain.
And how she, in longing and sorrow,
  Thereunder must ever remain.

She sings of days in childhood,
  Of joyous, lovely May;
And how they are now all departed,
  How that has faded away.
It floated over the water,
  And died away on the air,
That song of a joy now departed,
  That sorrowful song of despair.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!
Rescue my castle before the hot day
Brightens to blue from its silvery grey.
Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

Ride past the suburbs, asleep as you’d say,
Many’s the friend there will listen and pray
God’s luck to the gallants that strike up the lay.
Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

Forty miles off, like a roebuck at bay,
Flouts Castle Brancepeth the Roundheads' array,
Who laughs "Good fellows ere this, by my fay?"
    Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

Who? My wife Gertrude, that, honest and gay,
Laughs when you talk of surrendering. Nay!
I've better counsellors, what counsel they?
    Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!

(b) King Charles! and who'll do him right now?
King Charles! and who's ripe for the fight now?
    Give a rouse
Here's in Hell's despite now
    King Charles.

Who gave me the goods that went since?
Who raised me the house that sank once?
Who helped me to gold I spent since?
Who found me in wine you drank once?
    King Charles.

For whom used my boy George quaff else
By the old fool's side that begot him?
For whom did he cheer and quaff else
While Noll's damn'd troopers shot him?
    King Charles.

(c) Kentish Sir Byng stood for his king,
Bidding the crop-headed Parliament swing,
And pressing a troop, unable to stoop,
And see the rogues flourish and honest men droop,
Marched them along, fifty score strong,
Great-hearted gentlemen singing this song.

God for King Charles! Pym and such carles
To the devil that prompts their treasonous parles!
Cavallers up! lips from the cup!
Hands from the pastry, nor bite take or sup,
    'Till you're marching along, fifty score strong.
    Great-hearted gentlemen singing this song.

Hampden to hell, and his obsequies knell.
Serve Hazelrig Fiennes and young Harry as well.
England good cheer. Rupert is near,
Kentish, and loyalists keep we not here.
    Marching along, &c.

Then God for King Charles! Pym and his snarls
To the devil that pricks on their treasonous parles,
Hold by the right, you double your might,
So onward to Nottingham, fresh for the fight.
    March we along, fifty score strong.
    Great-hearted gentlemen singing this song.

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
Ah, were I on yonder plain,
Where now our undaunted sons
Stand arm'd for the hostile fray;
There, where the shrine of Phoebus gleams,
And torches are burning;
Where mortals bow down to the awe-inspiring pair,
Whose hallow'd rites are mystic deeds,
Wrought by Eumolpidan priests,
And never breath'd to mortal ear.
    There, glowing with ardour,
    Panting to rush against the foe,
        See, see all our legions.
With Theseus they wave their swords, and cry,
    Rescue the sisters!

    Or westward perchance they rush.
    Where snow-cover'd mountains rise
        O'er Gea's enamell'd meads;
There dancing cars and prancing steeds
    Will clash in the onset!

There on the foe soon will impending vengeance fall,
    For Theseus leads our valiant bands:
    See their arms and armour gleaming
Bright as the trappings that grace their steeds!
        Now proudly exulting,
They, who honour the deeds of sage Minerva
And Rhea's great son, earth-encircling ocean's king,
        Press to the battle!

    Do they await, pursue or fight?
        My heart thrills with hope
That they will soon rescue the captive maid,
Who hath endur'd, and still endures her kindred's woe.
    This day, Jove will restore her,
Crown your deeds, heroes, with glory!
Like a dove high soaring,
Sped along by the storm-wind,
I, from the verge of a cloud,
Would look down on the contest,
And see my country's cause triumphant!

    Dread Pow'r, that fillest heav'n's high throne,
O all-seeing Jove, defend our great ruler!
        On him the victor's palm bestow!
        With verdant laurels deck his brow!
            We call on thee, Pallas Athene!
            Mighty hunter, Pcebus, hear us!
And thy sister, fleet in chase, whose dart unerring
        Pierceth the far distant hart:
        O come, defend our guardians!
        We pray ye, aid our native heroes!

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
The drowsy woods are wrapped in shadow;
    The dreamy clouds hang o'er the lake;
The quiet moon sleeps on the meadow;
    But love now watches for thy sake.

The ocean now in silence slumbers,
    Unheard the billows gently break,
And so to thee, in whispered numbers,
    Comes love, who watches for thy sake.

Then rouse thee not, tho' love be singing,
    Or from thine eyes their slumbers shake,
If in thy soul the tones are ringing
    Of love, who watches for thy sake.

performance_15.lyrics_transcript:
Freedom dwells thro'out our own beloved land:
    Up to heav'n its voice is swelling.
From the mountain heights afar to ocean strand
    Ev'ry breeze the tale is telling.

Never weary of the ever joyous song,
Heart and voice united bear along.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend!
Foe within and out repelling.

War's alarum has but lately died away,
    Yet the echo rolls around us.
But the patriot host has overthrown the sway
    Of the haughty pow'r that bound us.
Freedom dwells where freedom never dwelt before,
Cries and groans shall grieve the land no more.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend
Has the suff'ring captive found us.

Freedom dwells thro'out our own beloved land,
    Wide as heav'n arches o'er it.
Like the rising sun, the patriot's armed hand
    Clouds of wrong hath swept before it.
Sound aloud the joyous word from crag to crag.
Plant on ev'ry peak our starry flag.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend!
Guard and like a shrine adore it!

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where the peaks are white with snow,
Where the alpine roses grow;
Where the horn gives out a strain,
That in echo comes again.

Where is heard the sheep-bell's sound,

Where the torrent's noisy flow

event-2-section-1-performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
The sun has now descended,
The woodland notes are ended.
Soft in the swaying trees
Sighs now the evening breeze,
While from afar yet hover
The sounds of day, scarce over,
And all to rest incline.
O heart, what rest is thine?

On heav'n's broad arch encroaching,
The night is fast approaching,
And in the vault above
Shines now the star of love.
And nightingales are singing,
And onward softly winging,
For love the spirit yearns,
And restless, homeward turns.
