event-2-section-1-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
I heard the trailing garments of the night
    Sweep through her marble halls!
I saw her sable skirts all fringed with light
    From the celestial walls!

I felt her presence, by its spell of might,
    Stoop o’er me from above:
The calm majestic presence of the night,
    As of the one I love.

I hear the sounds of sorrow and delight
    The manifold soft chimes,
That fill the haunted chambers of the night,
    Like some old poet’s rhymes.

From the cool cistern of the midnight air
    My spirit drank repose;
The fountain of perpetual peace flows there,
    From those deep cisterns flows.

O holy night! from thee I learn to bear
    What man has borne before!
Thou layest thy finger on the lips of care,
    And they complain no more.

Peace! peace! Orestes-like I breathe this prayer.
    Descend with broad-winged flight,
The welcome, the thrice prayed for, the most fair,
    The best-beloved night!

event-2-section-2-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
In evening stillness lies the lake,
    And mirrors the waning glow of the west,
Their thirst come timorous deer to slake,
    And swans fly, encircling its tranquil breast.

The fisher boy unfastens his boat,
    The plash of his oar thro' the silence steals:
In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright,
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the waterlily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar;
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,
    "Why trouble the children within their home?"
And the forest complains, "These long have I loved,
    Why force these delightful sisters to roam?"

But the red-glowing moon then fiercely cries,
    "How darest thou to address my bride?"
And in terror the boy with tears homeward flies,
    That there, with his mother, his grief he may hide.

    "O mother, the roar of the lake I heard,
        Against me the forest with fury shook,
Before me, in anger, the full moon appeared,
        O mother, I but a lily took!"

event-2-section-2-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
Hear us, Almighty One!
Hear us, All Holy one!
    Dark rolls the battle before us.
Father, all praise to Thee!
Father, all thanks to Thee!
    That freedom's banner is o'er us!

Like a consuming brand,
Stretch forth Thy mighty hand,
    Over oppression victorious.
Help us maintain the right,
Help us, oh, God of Might.
    Help us, Thy cause must be glorious.

Help us! though we may fall,
From out the grave we call
Praise to Thy mercy for ever.
All pow'r and glory be Thine
Thro' eternity. Amen! Amen! Amen!

event-2-section-2-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
On the sparkling snow so lightly we go,
    While the moon's full glow you cloud is dividing.
To the whip's cheerful crack the bells tinkle back
    As gaily we go on the snow swiftly gliding.
So light we go, on th' sparkling snow.
In the winter night, by the pale moon-light,
The fancy hath leisure to follow her pleasure.

    Good steeds gallop on, with the wind we fly,
    As it wanders by with a whisper'd sigh!

Care begone, you are no great treasure,
You spoil every pleasure.  Crick, crack!  Hurrah!
With the wind we fly, as it wanders by
With a whispered sigh, gallop on!
Never look behind!  Hurrah!  &c.

Happy hearts we bring, gay laughter shall ring,
Tho' the fleet hoofs fling snow-dust in our faces.
    And swift as we fly, our fortune we try,
And just for the fun, we will run friendly races.
    So swift we fly, we'll pass you by,
In the winter breeze, while the leafless trees,
Now shake their clear shadows o'er frost-bound white meadows.

    Good steeds gallop on, &c.

Care good-bye, for now we must part,
Don't fancy the loss will break my heart.
    Crick, crack!  Hurrah!  &c.

In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright.
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the water-lily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar:
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,
    "Why trouble the children within their home?"

And the forest complains, "These long have I loved,
    Why force these delightful sisters to roam?"
But the red-glowing moon then fiercely cries,
    "How darest thou to address my bride?"
And in terror the boy with tears homeward flies,
    That there, with his mother, his grief he may hide.

    "O mother, the roar of the lake I heard,
    Against me the forest with fury shook,
Before me, in anger, the full moon appeared,
    O mother, I but a lily took!"

event_3_section_1_perf_6.lyrics_transcript:
ALONE! ah, forsaken!
    Forsaken am I!
Not a maiden smiles on me,
    They all pass me by.
Far off to the church-yard
    In sorrow I stray,
And lowly there, kneeling,
    In sorrow I pray.

A mound in the green-wood,
    White flow'rets bloom there,
And softly she sleepeth
    Who once was so fair.
And since my own loved one
    From earth scenes hath gone,
'Mid life and its pleasure
    I am always alone.

event_3_section_1_perf_7.lyrics_transcript:
Ever sweet art thou, O Night!
    In the forest sweeter far,
Where thy starry eyes gleam bright,
    Where thy soft enchantments are!
Where the leaves, like fairy goblets,
    Overflow with dewy wine,
And the moon's unclouded radiance
    Fills each glade with light divine.

Murmuring breezes sing of thy pleasures,
Silvery moonbeams weave thee thy treasures;
All whom thy lips have silently press'd,
Closing their eyes, sink sweetly to rest!

But who would sleep on night so clear?
Arise! the horn rings far and near,
And wakens with its gladsome sound
Each slumberer in the groves around.
    Wake! wake! wake!

It echoes the woods and the mountain tops o'er,
The birds, all awaking, think night is no more;
The wandering deer in affright flee away,
They fancy it heralds the dawn of the day;
The lords of the forest shout loud in their might,
The fountain awakes with a song of delight!

Then sing we as we wander,
    "The woods are the home of the Night!"
And echo answers yonder,
    "The woods, thy home, O Night!"
Yes, here within thy forest home,
    We'll greet thee, lovely, lovely Night,
Where smiling from thy heav'nly dome,
    Thou reign'st in all thy might!
event_3_section_1_perf_7.additional_information: (PART SONG WITH ACCOMPANIMENT OF HORNS) Liedertafel

event_3_section_1_perf_9.lyrics_transcript:
Come love, the sea invites us,
    Our barque is on the shore;
Say now if I shall sing thee
    Of wond'rous deeds of yore,
Of heroes slain on battle plain?

Solo—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, the twilight darkens,
        The stars now greet our eyes;
Say now if I shall sing thee
        Of Freedom's high emprise?
Of patriots grand, of Fatherland?

Solo—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, my heart is longing
        For thy dear presence bright;
Say now if I shall sing thee
        Of mirth and gay delight?
Shall themes of joy my lute employ?

Solo—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, let us together
        Sail o'er the waters clear;
Say now with legend olden
        Shall I enchant thine ear?
Some magic store of fairy lore?

Solo—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Great is Jehovah, the Lord!
The heavens and the earth proclaim His wondrous might;
    In storms his dread accents are heard,
In the wild forest stream He calls by night;
        Great is Jehovah, the Lord!

Thou hearest it in the green budding boughs of the forest,
    See'st it in the corn fields that glow like gold,
In flowers ye may see it in bright varied hues,
    And in the stars still His marvellous power behold.

Sounds His voice in the dread thunder roll,
    And flames in the lightning on its swift blinding flight,
And each beating heart, every soul
    Feels His wondrous power and might;
        The eternal God, the Lord!

Thou to Him dost look for aid,
    In hope to gain His love and grace,
Trust in Him, be not afraid,
    He ne'er will turn away His face.
        Great is Jehovah, the Lord!

performance_12.lyrics_transcript:
Fair Semel's high-born son,
Thou many-named one,
Thou who callest thy father the Thunderer Jove!
Object of beautiful Italia's love:
Thou who crownest what Ceres bestoweth on all.
To thee now we cry:
Hear us, Bacchus, in Thebes, thy Bacchantes' home.
Where the bright Ismene, rolling her waters,
Unites the Dragon's sons and daughters.

On thy mount's double-crested heights,
Thy votive flames ascending,
With Corycian nymphs attending,
Grace the mystic rites:
While pure Nysian fates laves the ground,
The lofty Nysian summit sings, ivy crowned,
Thy praise!
Vine and tree
Warble to thee.
Thy votive train chant thy lays:
Thy sacred chorus raises
And Thebes' fanes resound thy praises.
Hear us, Bacchus!

Above all the rest,
Thebes thou hast guarded and blest.
She was its pride,
When slumbering the Thunderer died;
And now, nothing the lost repose,
We pray thee to come and heal its woes.
O, hither bend
From thy Parnassian heights descend.
Or from over Euboea's billows:
Hear us, Bacchus!

Thou whose power inspires
All our torch-lit star-vising choirs,
Guide our dance and lead our song.
Son of Jove for ever young!
Come with mirth and revelry!
Bring thy Naxian nymphs with thee:
Come, and let them, sounding before us,
Chime and blend with the thine chorus,
To praise thee, adore thee, great Bacchus!
Hear us, Bacchus!

performance_14.lyrics_transcript:
As the gloaming shadows creep
Through the forest deep,
Fra Nightingale sings sweet
Through the forest deep.

As through the trees the moonbeams sweep,
A maid with eager feet
Seeks in vain her lover to greet,
Ah, sweet! why moan and weep!

For aye, old Time will stealthy reap,
And hearts will cease to beat.
Still Fra Nightingale sings sweet,
Sings sweet when love is deep.

performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
One by one the pale stars die before the day now,
One by one the great ships are stirring from their sleep.
Cables are all rumbling, anchors all a-weigh now,
Now the fleet's a fleet again, gliding towards the deep.

Now the fleet's a fleet again, bound upon the old ways.
Splendour of the past comes shining in the spray:
Admirals of old time, bring us on the bold ways!
Souls of all the sea-dogs, lead the line to-day!

Far away behind us town and tower are dwindling,
Home becomes a fair dream faded long ago;
Infinitely glorious the height of heaven is kindling.
Infinitely desolate the shoreless sea below
Now the fleet's a fleet again, &c.

Once again with proud hearts we make the old surrender,
Once again with high hearts serve the age to be,
Not for us the warm life of Earth, secure and tender.
Ours the eternal wandering and warfare of the sea.
Now the fleet's a fleet again, &c.

performance-7.performance_name: (b) THE SONG OF THE SOU' WESTER.
performance-7.lyrics_transcript:
The sun was lost in a leaden sky,
And the shore lay under our lee;
When a great Sou' Wester hurricane high
Came rolling up the sea.
He played with the fleet as a boy with boats
Till out for the Downs we ran,
And he laughed with the roar of a thousand throats
At the militant ways of man:

    Oh! I am the enemy most of might,
    The other be who you please!
    Gunner and guns may be all right,
    Flags a-flying and armour tight,
    But I am the fellow you've first to fight—
    The giant that swings the seas!

A dozen of middies were down below
Chasing the X they love,
While the table curtsyed long and slow
And the lamps were giddy above.
And the lesson was all of a ship and a shot,
And some of it may have been true,
But the word they heard and never forgot
Was the word of the wind that blew:
    Oh! I am the enemy most of might, &c.

The Middy with luck is a Captain soon,
With luck he may hear one day
His own big guns a-humming the tune,
    "Twas in Trafalgar's Bay."
And whenever he goes, with friends or foes,
And whatever may there befall,
He'll hear for ever a voice he knows
For ever defying them all:
    Oh! I am the enemy most of might, &c.

performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
In a blue dusk the ship astern
Uplifts her slender spars,
With golden lights that seem to burn
Among the silver stars.
Like fleets along a cloudy shore
The constellations creep,
Like planets on the ocean floor
Our silent course we keep.

    And over the endless plain,
    Out of the night forlorn
    Rises a faint refrain,
    A song of the day to be born—
    Watch! Oh watch till ye find again
    Life and the land of morn!

From a dim West to a dark East
Our lines unwavering head,
As if their motion long had ceased
And Time itself were dead.
Vainly we watch the deep below,
Vainly the land above:
They died a thousand years ago—
Life and the land we love.
    But over the endless plain, &c.

performance-9.lyrics_transcript:
Stand by to reckon up your battleships,
Ten, twenty, thirty, there they go.
Brag about your cruisers like Leviathans—
    A thousand men a-piece down below.
But here's just one little Admiral,
We're all of us his brothers and his sons,
And he's worth, O he's worth at the very least
Double all your tons and all your guns.
    Stand by, &c.

See them on the forebridge signalling—
    A score of men a-hauling hand to hand.
And the whole fleet flying like the wild geese
Moved by some mysterious command.
Where's the mighty will that shows the way to them.
    The mind that sees ahead so quick and clear?
He's there, Sir, walking all alone there—
    The little man whose voice you never hear.
    Stand by, &c.

There are queer things that only come to sailormen
    They're true, but they're never understood:
And I know one thing about the Admiral,
    That I can't rightly tell as I should.
I've been with him when hope sank under us—
    He hardly seemed a mortal like the rest,
I could swear that he had stars upon his uniform,
    And one sleeve pinned across his breast.
    Stand by, &c.

Some day we're bound to sight the enemy,
    He's coming, tho' he hasn't yet a name.
Keel to keel and gun to gun he'll challenge us
    To meet him in the Great Armada game.
None knows what may be the end of it,
    But we'll all give our bodies and our souls,
To see the Little Admiral a-playing him
    A rubber of the old Long Bowlist!
    Stand by, &c.

performance-10.lyrics_transcript:
Mother, with unhobed head
    Hear thou across the sea
    The farewell of the dead.
    The dead who died for thee.
Greet them again with tender words and grave,
    For, saving thee, themselves they could not save

To keep the house unharmed
Their fathers built so fair,
Deeming endurance armed
Better than brute despair.
They found the secret in the word that saith,
"Service is sweet; for all true life is death."

So greet thou well thy dead
Across the homeless sea.
And let them be confounded
Because they died for thee
Far off they served, but now their deed is done,
For evermore their life and thine are one.

performance-11.lyrics_transcript:
While moon and stars above us
Their airy dance renew,
Say, why should sadness more us,
Or earth-born care pursue?
Behold! the soft beams play, lore.
Come, let my bark away, love,
And glide o'er the waves free,
Across the dark blue sea.
Now midnight's boding number
From good Saint Mark's I hear,
And all are hushed in slumber.
Except thy gondolier.

performance-12.performance_name: Una Voce poco fa (Barbiere di Siviglia)

performance-13.additional_information: (a) Wilt Thou be my Dearie? G. Bantock; (b) Always More R. Seifert

performance-14.lyrics_transcript:
When sorrow wrings thy gentle heart,
O wilt thou let me cheer thee?
By the treasure of my soul
That's the love I hear thee:
I swear and vow that only thou
Shall ever be my dearie.

Lassie, say thou lo's me.
Or, if thou will not be my ain,
Say thou't not refuse me.
If it winna, winna, canna be,
Thou for thine may choose,
Let me lassie quietly dee.
I'm true, that thou lo's me.
Only thou, I swear and vow,
Shall ever be my dearie.

performance-15.performance_name: (b) Would I again might see her,
performance-15.lyrics_transcript:
Ah, only once again!
But when I then had seen her,
Yet should I long to see her,
A thousand times again!

Her hand would I might hold now,
Ah, only once again!
But when I then had held it,
Yet should I long to hold it,
A thousand times again!

Would I again might kiss her,
Ah, only once again!
But when I then had kiss'd her,
Yet should I long to kiss her,
A thousand times again!
performance-15.additional_information: Part of grouped Part Songs. Program heading gives title as "Always More".

performance-18.lyrics_transcript:
Full fathom five thy father lies,
Of his bones are coral made:
Those are pearls that were his eyes.
Nothing of him that doth fade
But doth suffer a sea change
Into something rich and strange.
Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell
—Hark! now I hear them, Ding-dong bell.

event_4_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
AND it was Olav Trygvason,
Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom, their dark crest rearing,
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land,
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See I!" cried the bard unleaping,
"Yonder snow covered-peaks o'er cloud bands peeping."
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring,
Swayed in the stormy wind the forest strangely was murmuring,
Sounds as of church bells chiming,
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God to thee alone be glory."

"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator."
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God to thee, alone be glory
    On to God! On to God!

event-1-section-1-performance-3.additional_information: Beethoven. ALLEGRO CON BRIO—ANDANTE CON MOTO— ALLEGRO \( \frac{3}{4} \) —ALLEGRO \( \frac{2}{2} \) —PRESTO. Beethoven, when asked what he meant by the remarkable phrase which opens this Symphony, replied—"Fate knocks at the door." Throughout the first movement there seems to be a conflict between the human element and that mysterious force which overshadows it—we are reminded of the hapless Odysseus of Homer driven to and fro, ever striving towards the land of his hopes. The second movement seems to be "an outburst of love divine," not unmingled with sorrow, and doubt; especially is the "sehnsuchtvoll" theme of the wind, which follows on the melody of the 'cellos, to be noted. The third movement partakes more of the nature of the opening, and may be likened to the wanderer in his restless and fruitless search for the desired goal, interrupted only for a moment by the strange scene opened out by the Trio, which speedily is covered from sight as by the falling of a mist. The former mood is resumed, and leads into the triumphant finale, in which, as Balzac said, "we are held in the grasp of our most sacred hopes, which are realised for an instant as we listen."

event-1-section-2-performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
I SAW the trailing garments of the night
    Sweep through her marble halls;
I saw her sable skirts all fringed with light
    From the celestial walls.
I felt her presence, by its spell of might,
    Stoop o'er me from above,
The calm majestic presence of the night,
    As of the one I love.
I heard the sounds of sorrow and delight.
    The manifold soft chimes,
That fill the haunted chambers of the night
    Like some old poet's rhymes.
From the cool cistern of the midnight air,
    My spirit drank repose,
The fountain of perpetual peace flows there,
    From those deep cisterns flows.
O holy night, from thee I learn to bear,
    What man has born before,
Thou layest thy finger on the lips of care
    And they complain no more.
Peace! Peace! Orestes like I breathe this prayer,
    Descend with broad-winged flight;
The welcome, the thrice paid for,
    The most fair, the best beloved night.

event-1-section-2-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
ONAWAY, awake, beloved,
Thou wild flower of the forest,
Thou the wild bird of the prairie,
Thou with eyes so soft and brown!
If thou only lookest at me,
I am happy, I am happy!
As the lilies of the prairie,
When they dew upon them feel!

Sweet thy breath is as the fragrance of the flowers
in the morn,
As their fragrance is at evening, in the Moon when
leaves do fall,
Does not all the blood within me leap to meet thee,
Onaway,
As the springs to meet the sunshine in the Moon
when nights are bright?
Onaway!

Onaway! my heart sings to thee,
Sings with joy, when thou art near,
As the sighing, singing branches
In the pleasant Springtime Moon.
When thou art not pleased, beloved,
Then my heart is sad and dark,
As the shining river darkens
When the clouds on it throw shade.

When thou smilest, my beloved,
Then my troubled heart is brightened,
As in sunshine gleam the ripples,
That cold winds in rivers make.

Smiles the earth and smile the waters,
Smile the cloudless skies above,
But I lose the way of smiling
When thou art no longer near.
Onaway! I myself, behold me!
Blood of my beating heart, behold!
O awake, awake, beloved,
Onaway! beloved awake,
Onaway! Onaway! Onaway, awake
Awake! loved one, Onaway!

event-1-section-2-performance-6.lyrics_transcript:
The Nation's glory into your hands now is given.
    Oh, guard it well,
To sink with you, or with you rise to heaven.
    The magic spell of art and song
    Links all the worlds that roll along,
So may they ever blended be in richest harmony.
Her voice is like the dreadful thunder,
    Terrible in its mighty anger.
It rises on victorious pinions, and vengeance
takes on foes and minions—
    Strikes terror to the tyrant's heart.
If truth to exile e'er be driven.
Then to her aid the Muse arisen
Shall find revenge in lofty tuneful song.
    Oh, freeborn sons of art arise!
    Lift up your head to beauty's throne,
And as with her you mount the skies,
    All lesser crowns disown.
The thousand various ways unending
    Of rich humanity explore,
Till, from the summit's height extending,
    Behold the vast eternal shore.

a.
I stand here all the day,
Calling my roses,
Under a summer sky,
"Oh! who will buy
My pretty posies,
My Lords and Ladies gay?"

Thirteen summers are dead
With all their roses.
Now call I down the street,
"Oh! buy my sweet,
My pretty posies!
My flowers white and red."

The wind sings all the day
Swaying my roses.
"Oh! come, my little one!
Come, heed the sun
And drop your posies,
My little one, and play."

I bend my weary head
Down to my roses,
"He would not be unkind
The gentle wind,
My pretty posies
But Oh, that I were dead!"

And still I stand all day
Calling my roses,
So old, so old am I.
"Oh! will you buy
My pretty posies,
My Lords and Ladies gay."

b. Close to the sod there can be seen
A thought of God in white and green.
Unmarried, unsoiled it left the clay,
Serene, unspoil'd it views the day.

It is so holy, yet so lowly,
Would you enjoy its grace and dower
And not destroy the living flower?
Then you must, please, fall on your knees.

c. O my deir hert, young Jesus sweit,
Prepare thy creddil in my spriet,
And I sall rock thee in my hert
And never mair from thee depart.

But I sall praise thee ever muir
With sangis sweit unto thy gloir.
The knees of my hert sall I bow
And sing that right Balulalow.

d. I have desired to go
Where springs not fail,
To fields where flies no sharp and sided hail,
And a few lilies blow.

And I have asked to be
Where no storms come,
Where green swell is in the Heavens dumb—
And out of the swing of the sea.

event_1_section_1_perf_2.lyrics_transcript:
In evening stillness lies the lake,
    And mirrors the waning glow of the west,
Their thirst come timorous deer to slake,
    And swans fly, encircling its tranquil breast.

The fisher boy unfastens his boat,
    The plash of his oar thro' the silence steals:
In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright.
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the water-lily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar;
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,
    "Why trouble the children within their home?"

And the forest complains, "These long have I loved,
    Why force these delightful sisters to roam?"
But the red-glowing moon then fiercely cries,
    "How darest thou to address my bride?"
And in terror the boy with tears homeward flies,
    That there, with his mother, his grief he may hide.

"O mother, the roar of the lake I heard,
    Against me the forest with fury shook,
Before me, in anger, the full moon appeared,
    O mother, I but a lily took!"

event_1_section_1_perf_6.lyrics_transcript:
ALONE! ah, forsaken!
    Forsaken am I!
Not a maiden smiles on me,
    They all pass me by.
Far off to the church-yard
    In sorrow I stray,
And lowly there, kneeling,
    In sorrow I pray.

A mound in the green-wood,
    White flow'rets bloom there,
And softly she sleepeth
    Who once was so fair.
And since my own loved one
    From earth scenes hath gone,
'Mid life and its pleasure
    I am always alone.

event_1_section_1_perf_7.lyrics_transcript:
Ever sweet art thou, O Night!
    In the forest sweeter far,
Where thy starry eyes gleam bright,
    Where thy soft enchantments are!
Where the leaves, like fairy goblets,
    Overflow with dewy wine,
And the moon's unclouded radiance
    Fills each glade with light divine.

Murmuring breezes sing of thy pleasures,
Silvery moonbeams weave thee thy treasures;
All whom thy lips have silently press'd,
Closing their eyes, sink sweetly to rest!

But who would sleep on night so clear?
Arise! the horn rings far and near,
And wakens with its gladsome sound
Each slumberer in the groves around.
    Wake! wake! wake!

It echoes the woods and the mountain tops o'er,
The birds, all awaking, think night is no more;
The wandering deer in affright flee away,
They fancy it heralds the dawn of the day;
The lords of the forest shout loud in their might,
The fountain awakes with a song of delight!

Then sing we as we wander,
    "The woods are the home of the Night!"
And echo answers yonder,
    "The woods, thy home, O Night!"
Yes, here within thy forest home,
    We'll greet thee, lovely, lovely Night,
Where smiling from thy heav'nly dome,
    Thou reign'st in all thy might!

event_1_section_1_perf_9.lyrics_transcript:
COME love, the sea invites us,
    Our barque is on the shore;
Say now if I shall sing thee
    Of wond'rous deeds of yore,
Of heroes slain on battle plain?

SOLO—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, the twilight darkens,
        The stars now greet our eyes;
Say now if I shall sing thee
    Of Freedom's high emprise?
Of patriots grand, of Fatherland?

SOLO—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, my heart is longing
        For thy dear presence bright:
Say now if I shall sing thee
    Of mirth and gay delight?
Shall themes of joy my lute employ?

SOLO—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

    Come love, let us together
        Sail o'er the waters clear;
Say now with legend olden
    Shall I enchant thine ear?
Some magic store of fairy lore?

SOLO—Oh, no! oh, no! in sweeter strains my song must flow.

event_1_section_1_perf_10.lyrics_transcript:
Great is Jehovah, the Lord!
The heavens and the earth proclaim His wondrous might;
    In storms his dread accents are heard,
In the wild forest stream He calls by night;
    Great is Jehovah, the Lord!

Thou hearest it in the green budding boughs of the forest,
    See'st it in the corn fields that glow like gold,
In flowers ye may see it in bright varied hues,
    And in the stars still His marvellous power behold.

Sounds His voice in the dread thunder roll,
    And flames in the lightning on its swift blinding flight,
And each beating heart, every soul
    Feels His wondrous power and might;
    The eternal God, the Lord!

Thou to Him dost look for aid,
    In hope to gain His love and grace,
Trust in Him, be not afraid,
    He ne'er will turn away His face.
    Great is Jehovah, the Lord!

event_2_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
No star is o'er the lake
    Its pale watch keeping;
The moon is half awake,
    Through gray mist creeping.
The last red leaves fall round
    The porch of roses,
The clock hath ceased to sound,
    The long day closes.

Sit by the silent hearth
    In calm endeavour
To count the sounds of mirth
    Now dumb for ever.
Heed not how hope believes
    And fate disposes;
Shadow is round the eaves,
    The long day closes.

The lighted windows dim
    Are fading slowly;
The fire that was so trim
    Now quivers lowly.
Go to the dreamless bed
    Where grief reposes;
Thy book of toil is read.
    The long day closes.

event_2_section_2_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
THOU comest here to the land, O friend.
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows:
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove,
    Where the voices of nightingales
    Resound, floating in dulcet strains
        Thro' their temples of verdure;
    Where the thick-woven ivy clings,
    Spreading over the sacred aisles;
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine.
    Unscath'd by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god.
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays,
    Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

    Fair and fragrant at dawn of day,
    See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus.
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
    Worn by them in the days of old.

See the Crocus array'd in gold;
    Hear the slumberless waters,
While they glide in Cephisus' tide,
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia:
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear.
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway: yet here it freely springeth:
    Rever'd by friends, and fear'd by foes.
    In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold, ours is the rich oil-dropping olive;
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree,
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure.
    Ever heeded by Morian Jove,
    Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva.

Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts deigned to my country:
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder-guided:
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent.
        Mighty god Poseidon,
Thou didst give us the rein formed for the courser;
Guided thus, or curbed, he yields obedience.
Through the billows we dash, stemming the deep,
    Speeded along by the oar and helm,
    Bounding on with the dancing nymphs—
        Nereus' hundred-footed daughters.

event_2_section_2_perf_4.lyrics_transcript:
I hear thee speak of the Better Land,
Thou call'st its children a happy band;
Mother, where is that radiant shore?
Shall we not seek it and weep no more?
Is it where the flow'r of the orange blows,
And the fireflies dance thro' the myrtle boughs?
    Not there, not there, my child.

Is it far away in some region old,
Where the rivers wander o'er sands of gold,
Where the burning rays of the ruby shine,
And the diamond lights up the secret mine,
And the pearls gleam forth from the coral strand?
Is it there, sweet mother, that better land?
    Not there, not there, my child.

Eye hath not seen it, my gentle boy;
Ear hath not heard its sweet songs of joy;
Dreams cannot picture a world so fair:
Sorrow and death may not enter there;
Time doth not breathe on its fadeless bloom:
For beyond the clouds, beyond the tomb.
    It is there, my child, it is there.
event_2_section_2_perf_4.additional_information: (Composed expressly for the Society). JOSEPH KENDALL. Liedertafel.

event_2_section_2_perf_5.lyrics_transcript:
HARK! the tattoo the hour is beating,
    The sound obey;
Come, troopers, come away.
Disgrace on him will fall
Who disregards the call.
To quarters now retreating,
    Come, troopers, come away,
    The sound obey.
Shadows of darkness o'er us hover,
No friendly form can we discover.
    Night reigns around,
Loud rolls the drum, the horns replying,
And echo's voice in distance dying
    Repeats the sound.
Yon fortress tow'ring,
With an aspect low'ring,
Obscure as night,
Conceals from sight
Each roof and dwelling height.
While all are sleeping
Our watch we are keeping.
With sword and lance
And eagle glance
The ready troops advance.

event_2_section_2_perf_6.additional_information: Haydn. ALLEGRO MODERATO—ADAGIO CANTABILE—MENUETTO—FINALE VIVACE. Mr. Geo. Weston, Mr. F. O. Schieblich, Mr. H. Schrader, Herr L. Hattenbach

event_2_section_2_perf_8.lyrics_transcript:
O SUMMER night serenely still!
No sound the forest haunting,
In hollow glade alone, the rill
Its song is ever chanting.
The flow'rs are nodding with sleep-laden eyes.
A dream of dawn on the branches lies,
And peace on valley and hill.

Hark! 'tis the lark's thrilling note on high
The forest's silence breaking:
Ye sleepers, arise, in the Orient sky
The rosy morn is awaking.
Trill on, sweet herald, in jubilant lay,
Welcome the kiss of the joyous day.
As westward the shadows hie.

Now sweetly faint the distance o'er
The matin chimes are stealing,
And soon within the bosom's core
The joy bells all are pealing.
Adoring sound, exultant song,
It rings and sings the world along:
Praise God for evermore!

event_2_section_3_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
Great is Jehovah the Lord!
The heavens and the earth both proclaim His mighty power.
We hear Him when roareth the storm,
When the wind through the woods rushes along.
    Great is Jehovah the Lord!
    Mighty is His power.

Thou hear'st it in the green budding boughs of the forest.
Seest it in the cornfields that glow like gold,
In flowers ye may see it in bright varied hues,
And in the stars still His marvellous power behold.
We see Him in heaven's high arches of starry splendour.

Awful rolls He in thunder on high,
The flame of His lightning darts in terror below,
And each beating heart, every soul feels His wondrous power and might.
We bow to the power dwelling in Him,
The Lord of all, and God everlasting.

Thou to Him look for aid,
In hope to gain His love and grace.
Turning then, we implore His love and grace and protection.
    Great is Jehovah the Lord!
event_2_section_3_perf_1.additional_information: Mr. Gregor Wood and Liedertafel. Schubert-Liszt.

event_2_section_3_perf_4.lyrics_transcript:
Poom, poom, poom! home!
The distant bell is pealing,
Down the mountains slowly stealing
    The morning sunbeams play.
When God, his hand revealing,
    Beckons darkness away,
In songs of grateful feeling.
We hail the rising day.
    Oh! behold the day.

We sing of Tyrol, her mountains and waters,
    The gloomy ravine, the wild shaggy wood;
Her true-hearted sons, her fair blooming daughters,
    The valiant and free, the gentle and good.
And chiefly we sing that sweet, simple strain,
Which echo returns from yon rocks again.
Dear strains of Tyrol, how sweet to the soul;
    Gentle song, float along.

    Ah, ah! la la la la! la la la la!
Oh! once we were fond of carelessly saying,
    Our home was the world in which we would roam,
And half round the world we might have gone straying,
    And never have found for our hearts a home.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Poom, poom, poom! home!
The distant bell is pealing,
Down the mountains slowly stealing
    The morning sunbeams play.
When God, his hand revealing,
    Beckons darkness away,
In songs of grateful feeling.
We hail the rising day.
    Oh! behold the day.

We sing of Tyrol, her mountains and waters,
    The gloomy ravine, the wild shaggy wood;
Her true-hearted sons, her fair blooming daughters,
    The valiant and free, the gentle and good.
And chiefly we sing that sweet, simple strain,
Which echo returns from yon rocks again.
Dear strains of Tyrol, how sweet to the soul;

    Ah, ah! la la la la! la la la la!
Oh! once we were fond of carelessly saying,
    Our home was the world in which we would roam,
And half round the world we might have gone straying,
    And never have found for our hearts a home.

Till passing one day thro' the mountains near,
    Sweet echo let fail this strain on our ear:
Dear strains of Tyrol, how sweet to the soul;
    Gentle song, float along.

    Ah! ah! Hoo! hoo!
What dismal sounds are crashing athwart the air?
See lightning flashing everywhere.
    It is the thunderstorm!
    How the wind roars!
    How the rain pours!
    Hark how loud the thunders crash!
    The wind doth roar,
    The rain doth pour,
    Ah, that fearful crash!
    The storm winds shatter the pines around.
'Tis the hurricane:
Hailstones clatter upon the ground.
Flee away, mountaineers!
The lightning dazzles every eye.
It flashes nigher and more nigh:
Ah, the hailstones lash the flying mountaineer
The rain torrents pour.
Ah! how it doth roar;
The storm wind doth roar;
Ha, but the thunder farther away doth run,
Clouds rent asunder, out shines the sun!
Sound again, tender strain, sound again,
    We'll sing la la la la la'!

Gaily dancing,
Swiftly glancing,
Tripping lightly,
Now skipping sprightly,
Tread we now a gay mincing measure,
Dance and song will sweeten our leisure;
Softly treading, nimbly threading,
In and out the merry rout.

Singing, dancing, take we our pleasure,
Pray, keep step, beat the time to the merry rout.
'Tis of Tyrol we sing, this gentle strain we sing.
Once again, gentle strain. 'tis lovely Tyrol
    We sing, la la la!

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
All welcome the bowl!
A full flowing soul,
    Unfathomed by care!
What boots it the bandit,
If hunted and branded,
    So wine be his share.

    To play, sirs!
Treasure is merely a pleasure
    That flies soon as come!
And play hath a duty,
It charmeth when beauty
    Inconstant may roam.

Thrice welcome the bowl!
Whose glorious soul
    Doth bleed at our call!
The bowl, the bowl,
Whose glorious souls, sirs,
    Doth bleed at our call.

Hernani, still pensive!
Quick thought grows apprehensive
    To view his cheek so blanch'd.
Where life's tide hath motion,
On Death's shoreless ocean
    Our one bark is launch'd.

To give, then, thy willing
Immediate fulfilling,
    Ere will'd we prepare;
The hawk's speed e'en tarries
In hitting her quarries,
    If ours ye compare.

Come, welcome the bowl.

event_15_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
AND it was Olav Trygvason,
Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
Far on the other side
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom, their dark crest rearing,
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land,
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard unleeping,
"Yonder snow covered-peaks o'er cloud bands peeping."

And it was Olav Trygvason,
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring;
Swayed in the stormy wind the forest strangely was murmuring,
Sounds as of church bells chiming,
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator."
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God to thee, alone be glory
    On to God! On to God!

    On to God! On to God!

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Last night the nightingale 'woke me,
    Last night when all was still,
It sang in the golden moonlight
From out the woodland hill.

I open'd the window so gently,
I look'd on the dreaming dew,
And oh! the bird, my darling, was singing,
    Singing of you, of you,
    Yes, singing of you.

I think of you in the day time,
I dream of you by night,
I wake and would you were here, love,
And tears are blinding my sight.
I hear a low breath in the lime tree,
The wind is floating through,
And oh! the night, my darling,
Is sighing, sighing of you, of you,
    Is sighing of you.

Oh think not I can forget you;
I could not if I would,
I see you in all around me—
The stream, the night, the wood,
The flowers that slumber so gently,
The stars above the blue,
Oh! Heaven itself my darling,
Is praying, praying for you, for you,
    Is praying for you.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
'NEATH the ships' gay 'broidered awning,
    Brightly coloured by the setting sun,
Let us drink, friends, 'till day's dawning,
Wine that makes the blood more swiftly run;
And let each repeat again, again,
The hardy sailors' say refrain.
'Neath the ships' gay 'broidered awning,
Comrades drink here 'till day's dawning;
To the Admiral give all homage,
Laud his glory, and his courage;
Let the crew with one accord,
To-day some pledge of love afford;
Of courage, courage, let us sing,
To work this same true spirit bring.
Ah! yes, through wine's aid all danger scorning,
Comrades, comrades, drink here till day's dawning.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
"Hark, the tempest rages fierce!
When thy accents soft are falling:
See, the flames but grow in fury
Whilst thy image lures my heart.

"Tremble, if I to thy wooing
Yield, and leave my spheres, the fiery
Torture lurks in my embraces,
And my kiss it seals thy death!"

CHORUS (TENORS). Lightly laughs the lovely Mila,
Gaily shakes her golden tresses.

MILA. "Even I, the little maiden,
Make thee, mighty spirit, quail!
Vulcan, see, for that I like thee;
Fume and reek and blaze and thunder
To thy heart's content, beloved,
Fume, but rise and come to me!

For I do not fear thy fury
See, the learned Monks have taught me
Instantly thou must surrender
If I utter the word: 'Cross.'

See, the spell doth tell already,
Quickly quelling flame and flashes,
And the storm grows faint and fainter
Since that mystic word I spoke."

(QUARTETTE.) Linden blossoms' balmy fragrance
Weave a web of magic sweetness,
And the nightingale sings softly
Its alluring lay of love.

CHORUS (TENORS). 'Gainst the rugged rock is nestling
Mila, fearlessly and fondly,
And she whispers words of longing
Down into the dark abyss.

MILA. "Prithee, rise, beloved spirit!
Pray, come forth! Devouring passion
Burns within my bosom fiercely,
Fiercer far than all thy flames!

Weary am I of frail mortals'
Weakly wooing; thee I crave for,
Mighty spirit; still my longing,
Fill the void within my heart!"

CHORUS.  Lo, the earth with crash terrific,
Quakes and quivers and cleaves open,
Out of crimson clouds of vapour
Awe-inspiring steps the god.
On his head a crown of fire,
Raven tresses on his shoulders,
Dreamy sadness droops the eyelids,
Yet each glance a vivid flash.

Stately, with majestic grandeur
Wide his mighty arms he opens,
And a robe of purple splendour
Brilliant radiance sheds around.

(SOLO 1ST BASS)  Spell-bound, lost in awe and rapture,
Mute and motionless stands Mila:
Heeding not the priestly wisdom
She but whispers:

MILA: "Ah! sublime!"

CHORUS.  Stately, still, with solemn grandeur
Wide his mighty arms he opens,
And upon his breast sinks Mila.

Through the ravine roars the thunder,
Through the clefts the lightning flashes,
Lo, the rocks are rent asunder,
Burning lava belching forth.

Through the fiercely seething torrents,
To his fiery realm bears Vulcan
Triumphantly down his bride.

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
Tell me, Flora, tell me truly,
    Why this heart no more is free,
Why my thoughts are so unruly,
    Why they only turn to thee?
If a studious mood comes o'er me,
    And to reading I incline,
Tell me why I see before me
    Flora's name in every line?
Tell me Flora, tell me truly,
    Why my thoughts but turn to thee?

Tell me when soft zephyrs playing,
    Sportive thro' the leafy dell,
Why they sound like voices saying,
    Flora scarce on earth should dwell?
Why, when o'er the waters stealing,
    Village bells' sweet measures come,
This the burden of their pealing,
    Flora, hasten to thine home.
Tell me, Flora tell me truly,
    Why this heart no more is free?

performance_11.lyrics_transcript:
A SACRIFICER—

THOU to whom fancy lends many titles,
Giver of runes and of magic!
Working before the world's beginning,
Thou who outgazest from Lidskialf.

MEN—
    Hear us!

A WOMAN—
    Tender mother Frigga, sorrowing for Balder:
    Bearing in thy bosom all worldly woe;
    Comforter of Odin, nourisher of nature,
    Drawing all life and care into Fensal.

WOMEN—
    Hear us!

THE SACRIFICER—
    Trudyang's Hlorrida, Bilskirner's Yireflame,
    Thou of the strength-belt and hammer,
    Shield of the Aesir and of the Northmen,
    Ever the dread of the giants.

MEN—
    Hear us!

THE WOMAN—
    Beauteous weeping goddess, silent widow Vannadis,
    Love's distress thine own loss taught unto thee!
    Let our tears of sorrow with thine own be mingled;
    Thou who dost govern half of the living.

WOMEN—
    Hear us!

THE SACRIFICER—
    Horn-bearing Heimdal, Ull in Ydaler,
    Nyord, mighty north-dweller, hear us!
    Algenheim's joy, Landvida's sorrow,
    Long-bearded minstrel, and thou Tyr.

MEN—
    Hear us!

THE WOMAN—
    Ever-youthful Idun, Sif of golden harvests,
    Saga of the streamlet, Skada of the hills,
    All ye, mighty Aesir, Vanir and Valkyrie,
    Hear our complaining, earthward oh hasten!

WOMEN—
    Hear us!

MEN AND WOMEN—
    Other gods are now arising,
    Gods of power, gods of battle;
    Help us, Mitgard trembles,
    Gods alone with gods can wrestle!

    (All kneeling.)

Ye who from the Urdar fountains pour life-strength into our bosoms,
Ye alone who know his will, the Father in gold-canopied Gimle;
Ye in Odin's ear who whisper softly as each day awakens,
Ye who were ere world's beginning,
Ye who will be when 'tis wasted,
Show our fates the way to him, the god so long awaited—
    Hear us!

THE VÖLVA—(From an elevation in the foreground)—
    'Tis not enough that ye invoke Nornir and Aesir,
    Runes must be graven duly
    Evil to disperse from the pathway which to the gods doth lead.
    There, see the gathered hosts
    Upon their horns howling, to hide our voices,
    That the gods never may hear us!

MEN AND WOMEN—
    O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
    Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

THE VÖLVA—(Raises herself so that she stands high above all the others)—
    Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southlands,
    With Hel soon shall feast be holden:
    Plague shall gnaw, serpents send through your veins deadly venom!
    Let Hel's hounds awake, howling and foaming,
    Monsters filled with madness, for your blood thirsting blindly!
    For Hel no fitter food can afford them!
    With Hel! spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland,
    With Hel, here in the north, your feast is.

MEN AND WOMEN—

O prophetess mighty, rise in thy magic!
Fill heaven and earth with Odin's word!

THE VÖLVA—(Who has been carving runes, now continues to cut eagerly)—
Spirits base, basely mastered, ye who come from the southland;
To Hel soon shall your way be wended!
Evil ones away! the Thunderer's weapon awaits ye!
Runes I wrote on a staff I rent from the altar of Odin.
To Hel straightway its charm consigns ye.
To Hel! Runes will lead Lokis lot unto the doors of his daughters,
With Hel ye shall devour that writing.

(She casts the Rune-staff on the holy fire, which immediately bursts into flames that ascend to the roof of the Temple. A horrible din, accompanied by thunder in the distance, shakes the Temple.)

MEN AND WOMEN—(Kneeling in terror)—
Wondrous word of Odin goes
To black abyss, the heaven's height,
Awful, returneth the answer.

THE VÖLVA—
Answer came from Hel, from high gods;
All fear it, yet not I.
Now let us kneel to them!
Every path is free!
So I will pray them first.

Gods, ye holy, eternal gods!
Are ye here? Then heed me!
Where find we the fiat which governs our fate?
Where bends your balance, ordering all?
Show, ah! show to me, ye mighty ones,
Where ye will strike the evil Olaf?
Gods all-governing, endless, omnipotent Aesir; I pray:
Devoted to Odin from my youth.
By the grey wolf's heart, by the raven's tongue,
By my sacrifice in sleepless nights, I pray you!
Show me, mighty ones, where ye will strike the evil Olaf.

(A crash of thunder and the back of the Temple is shattered. The Temple is seen in the distance enclosed in flames and smoke. Thunder continually heard until the Temple becomes invisible.)

THE VÖLVA, MEN AND WOMEN—

Here! here! hasten the holy ones!
Here! here! strikes him the vengeance of heaven!

In our hall he must enter,
Let him go in, ne'er to come forth again.

(With mockery.)

Let this be told to him—
We will believe if he come safely forth.

Let his god go in to our gods!
If he safely come forth, we will believe

ALL (Turning towards the gods)—
Thanks for the token, solace it sends to us.
Thanks for the token, faith it confirms!
Choice of thy children, come then, oh king, to us;
Come to thy children, strife will be short!
Now will the gods themselves go on their gladsome way,
Now will the gods themselves grant us their grace!
Lift from our land by fire, lo, he shall leave us;
Loki shall lighten him hence unto Hel!

(Assembling round the images of the gods.)

Three nights besought we, sung like son to sire,
Three nights we pleaded, heard is our prayer.

The Sacrificer and Elders having procured horns, they form a circle round the three "Holy Fires;" afterwards advancing and seating themselves at the sides. The Sacrificer, having made the "hammer sign," over the horns, proceeds to render the following song.

THE SACRIFICER—
Raise high the horn, great host-father, Odin's horn,
Raise high the horn, upheave it for him.

High altar fires and Akethn's hammer-sign,
High altar fires have hallowed it.

MEN AND WOMEN—
Gladly we join in
Games for the gracious god,
Gladly we join in
Outbursts of joy!

(Preparations are made by the people for a dance. The men leap over the "Holy Fire," lifting the women over on both sides. Then commences a Temple dance in which all join.)

QUARTETTE—

Give to all gods a grace-cup of gratitude,
Give to all gods your greatest of gifts.

MEN AND WOMEN—

Horns fill for Akethor, Drontheimer's deity,
Fill them to Akethor, daring in fight.
    Gladly then, etc.

Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest and fish they send,
Fill up to Nyord and Frey, harvest fair, haul of fish,
To freedom, and faith.
    Gaily then, etc.

Beakers to Braga, bring we with holy vows,
Beakers to Braga, brimming we raise!
Offerings of flesh and blood
To Braga we all freely bring.
    Gaily then, etc.

WOMEN—

O ye Asynier, honour we offer thee,

Program note: 'OLAF TRYGVASON, a descendant of Harold Haarfager (the first king of Norway), was brought up at the court of Gardarike (Russia), and was baptized in England while on a Viking raid. When he learned that Norway was dissatisfied with her king (a scion of an older branch of the same race), he resolved upon conquering the kingdom and converting the people to Christianity. Richly endowed by nature, the superior of all his contemporaries in bodily and spiritual gifts, and so comely to behold that none had seen his like; he was revered in the middle ages as the noblest example of the Norman race; he conquered more by his personality than by his sword. He commenced his struggle in the Drontheim district, and the beginning of this conflict is depicted in the scenes of the drama here set to music.' Setting note: 'The action takes place in an ancient Norman temple in the Drontheim district, at the time of Olav Trygvason's appearance. Period—End of the tenth century.' performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
On board! On board!
From land away!
'Mid billows whirling,
Our canvas unfurling,
We'll weather the tide;
With pennants streaming,
Like serpents gleaming,
We'll boldly ride.
Tho' tempests be rocking,
'Tis jovial mocking
To man's daring mood;
But rapturous jesting
To us is the breasting
Of storm and of flood.

For many days and many nights
Onward we have sailed.
With vigour fresh and courage bright
A lofty goal pursuing.
We trembled not 'mid storms sublime,
Nor anxious felt 'mid calm most dismal;
Yet the ocean's endless swell
Upon our vessel's keel would break,
And no friendly starry sign
The lonesome, gloomy night illumed.
Our courage sinks, our hope's lamed,
And troubled scruples leave us never;
When will the day be dawning
That ev'ry ardent dream fulfils?

Oh, fear not now! Have faith in me, your leader,
The blessed day is drawing near,
When we shall reach the hallowed harbour,
And view the longed-for unknown land.

In spirit there before me lying,
I see its wonders without end;
Through vistas long of distant ages,
My wond'ring gaze doth rove.
I see the mighty surging masses
Of people seeking the untried shore;
A weary combat, bloody struggles,
Then high a noble banner waves;
A mighty banner, peace defender,
Hoard of freedom and of light.
    Press forward, comrades, boldly steer!
    We'll hasten on our grand career,
    So long ago forshadowed;
    Whate'er the hindring power unfurled,
    We'll soon behold a new, fair world,
    Emerging from the billows.

Once more the days and nights have vanished,
No token courage new doth rouse,
The sought-for goal proclaiming.
Yet lo! what wondrous blaze of glory
The horizon displays!
Is this the goal, the land we've yearned for?
Ah, no, 'tis but a fond illusion,
The ocean's tremulous mirage,
The work of Fay Morgana.
It holds my ev'ry sense imprisoned,
It lures me on, as dreams have lured
    Islands fair, like gems beaming,
        Adorn the trackless blue,
    Transfigured heroes seeming
        To my enraptured view.

The billows all resplendent,
    With marble arches glow,
They mirror groves transcendent,
    Where gloomy palm-trees blow,
And women with beauty dowered,
    Than sleeper's dream more fair,
'Neath flow'ry trees embowered.
    Soon quiet all our care,
Now stately as Valkyries
    Are they; with one accord
They now are kind and gracious
    And promise love's reward,
And wide open doors they're flinging,
    Proud harps we hear and song;
We enter, heroes, singing,
    A joyous, merry throng.

The dream hath flown, the magic long departed,
The endless breakers ebb and flow;
The waves they roll, the tempest threatens

event-1-section-1-performance-1.additional_information: Music kindly lent by Charles Levy, Esq. Performed by Orchestra. Program note: "Schubert's Unfinished Symphony in B Minor was composed in 1822. In this and the great C Major Symphony, Schubert seems to have struck out a real, independent symphony style for himself, thoroughly individual in every respect, both of idea, form and orchestration. The first movement of the B Minor is entirely unlike any other symphonic first movement that was ever composed before. It seems to come direct from the heart, and to have the personality of the Composer in it to a most unusual degree. The orchestral forces used, are the usual ones, but in the management of them there are numbers of effects which are perfectly new in this department of art, indicating the tendency of the time towards direct consideration of what is called "colour" in orchestral combinations, and its employment with the view of enhancing the degree of actual sensuous enjoyment of a refined kind, to some extent independent of the subjects and figures.—C. H. H. P."

event-1-section-1-performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
March along, march along, with weapons all glittering bright,
March along, for freedom and country we fight.
Raise our battle cry, loud and high, to the sky,
March along, march along, our cause is the just and the right.

Life is short at best, 'tis an empty jest,
Then join our jovial song as we thus march along.
Soon shall we be at rest 'neath the earth's chilly breast,
But while we march along let us be gay.

Soldiers live and die, widows mourn and cry,
    War is rough weather,
Cowards quail and fly, but not you or I.
    Comrades happy and jolly together.
Soldiers, close up the ranks.
    Fight for fatherland, freedom and glory,
    Let the battle be gory, living in story,
Earning a nation's thanks, hurrah!

Fatherland, thy blessing is o'er us, goes before us,
And for fatherland chant we our chorus.
    Safe in that glorious name.
For our fatherland we yield up our being, all agreeing
That for fatherland danger's worth seeing.
    For death can bring no shame.
    Let us onward go, lead us onward.

Gaily the trumpets call,
Forward, ye warriors all,
Soon will the foemen fall,
    Onward we're going.
Fear not yon iron hail,
Ne'er let your cheek grow pale,
Our arms shall yet prevail,
    Onward we go.

Then away, march away,
    For the day we shall gain,
Then away, march away,
    O'er the hill and the plain.
        March along, march along, &c.

event-6-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where the peaks are white with snow,
Where the alpine roses grow;
Where the horn gives out a strain,
That in echo comes again.

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where is heard the sheep-bell's sound,
Where the herds are grazing round;
Where the torrent's noisy flow
Pours in thunder far below.

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where the heart with joy can glow,
Leaving pain and care below;
Where the eye its glance can raise,
And on Heaven thankful gaze

event_1_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
Liedertafel

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where the peaks are white with snow,
Where the alpine roses grow;
Where the horn gives out a strain,
That in echo comes again.

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where is heard the sheep-bell's sound,
Where the herds are grazing round;
Where the torrent's noisy flow
Pours in thunder far below.

Oh! How bright the mountains rise,
Grand and glorious to the skies.
Where the heart with joy can glow,
Leaving pain and care below;
Where the eye its glance can raise,
And on Heaven thankful gaze

event_1_section_1_perf_5.lyrics_transcript:
The sun has now descended,
The woodland notes are ended.
Soft in the swaying trees
Sighs now the evening breeze,
While from afar yet hover
The sounds of day, scarce over,
And all to rest incline.
O heart, what rest is thine?

On heav'n's broad arch encroaching,

Shines now the star of love.
And nightingales are singing,
And onward softly winging,
For love the spirit yearns,
And restless, homeward turns.

event_1_section_1_perf_8.lyrics_transcript:
I HEARD the trailing garments of the night
    Sweep through her marble halls!
I saw her sable skirts all fringed with light
    From the celestial walls!

I felt her presence, by its spell of might,
    Stoop o'er me from above:
The calm majestic presence of the night,
    As of the one I love.

I hear the sounds of sorrow and delight
    The manifold soft chimes,
That fill the haunted chambers of the night,
    Like some old poet's rhymes.

From the cool cistern of the midnight air
    My spirit drank repose;
The fountain of perpetual peace flows there,
    From those deep cisterns flows.

O holy night! from thee I learn to bear
    What man has borne before!
Thou layest thy finger on the lips of care,
    And they complain no more.

Peace! peace! Orestes-like I breathe this prayer.
    Descend with broad-winged flight,
The welcome, the thrice prayed for, the most fair,
    The best-beloved night!

event_1_section_2_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
Miss Maggie Stirling and Liedertafel

In evening stillness lies the lake,
    And mirrors the waning glow of the west,
Their thirst come timorous deer to slake,
    And swans fly, encircling its tranquil breast.

The fisher boy unfastens his boat,
    The plash of his oar thro' the silence steals;
In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright,
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the waterlily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar;
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,
    "Why trouble the children within their home?"
And the forest complains, "These long have I loved,
    Why force these delightful sisters to roam?"

But the red-glowing moon then fiercely cries,
    "How darest thou to address my bride?"
And in terror the boy with tears homeward flies,
    That there, with his mother, his grief he may hide.

    "O mother, the roar of the lake I heard,
    Against me the forest with fury shook,
Before me, in anger, the full moon appeared,
    O mother, I but a lily took!"

event_1_section_2_perf_4.lyrics_transcript:
Hear us, Almighty One!
Hear us, All Holy one!
    Dark rolls the battle before us.
Father, all praise to Thee!
Father, all thanks to Thee!
    That freedom's banner is o'er us!

Like a consuming brand,
Stretch forth Thy mighty hand,
    Over oppression victorious.
Help us maintain the right,
Help us, oh, God of Might.
    Help us, Thy cause must be glorious.

Help us! though we may fall,
From out the grave we call
Praise to Thy mercy for ever.
All pow'r and glory be Thine
Thro' eternity. Amen! Amen! Amen!

event_1_section_2_perf_8.lyrics_transcript:
On the sparkling snow so lightly we go,
    While the moon's full glow yon cloud is dividing.
To the whip's cheerful crack the bells tinkle back
    As gaily we go on the snow swiftly gliding.
So light we go, on th' sparkling snow.
In the winter night, by the pale moon-light,
The fancy hath leisure to follow her pleasure.

    Good steeds gallop on, with the wind we fly,
    As it wanders by with a whisper'd sigh!

Care begone, you are no great treasure,
You spoil every pleasure. Crick, crack! Hurrah!
With the wind we fly, as it wanders by
With a whispered sigh, gallop on!
Never look behind! Hurrah! &c.

Happy hearts we bring, gay laughter shall ring,
Tho' the fleet hoofs fling snow-dust in our faces.
    And swift as we fly, our fortune we try,
And just for the fun, we will run friendly races.
    So swift we fly, we'll pass you by,
In the winter breeze, while the leafless trees,
Now shake their clear shadows o'er frost-bound white meadows.

    Good steeds gallop on, &c.

Care good-bye, for now we must part,
Don't fancy the loss will break my heart.
    Crick, crack! Hurrah! &c.

GOD SAVE THE QUEEN

event_1_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
O! Sweet May night, so calm, so still,
    All forest tones are sleeping,
Save voice of yonder purling rill
    That o'er the stones is leaping.

O! Sweet May night, so calm, so still,
    The flowers in their dreaming are swayed by the breeze,
    Of golden sunlight breathe the trees,
And sweet sleep shrouds vale and hill.

Hark! 'tis a blackbird's sweet song begun;
    The slumbering world is waking.
Arouse thee, to welcome the morning sun;
    The trees their boughs are shaking.

The lark soars up to the bright'ning skies,
Pouring forth song even as he flies,
    Rejoicing that night is gone!

And with the fuller glow of day,
    The morning bells are ringing.
The burden of their fervent lay,
    Our heart with them is singing.

This is their burden, this their song,
That fills all the world, as it flows along:—
    "Praise be to God!  Praise be to God alway!"

event_1_section_1_perf_7.lyrics_transcript:
In the convent of Drontheim,
Alone in her chamber
Knelt Astrid the Abbess,
At midnight, adoring,
Beseeching, entreating,
The Virgin and Mother.

She heard in the silence
The voice of one speaking
Without in the darkness,
In gusts of the night-wind
Now louder; now nearer,
Now lost in the distance.

The voice of a stranger
It seemed as she listened,
Of some one who answered,
Beseeching, imploring,
A cry from afar off
She could not distinguish.

The voice of Saint John,
The beloved disciple,
Who wandered and waited
The Master's appearance,
Alone in the darkness,
Unsheltered and friendless.

"It is accepted,
The angry defiance,
The challenge of battle!
It is accepted.
But not with the weapons
Of war that thou wieldest!

"Cross against corselet,
Love against hatred,
Peace-cry for war-cry!
Patience is powerful:
He that o'ercometh
Hath dower o'er the nations!

"As torrents in summer,
Half dried in their channels,
Suddenly rise though the
Sky is still cloudless—
For rain has been falling
Far off at their fountains—

"So hearts that are fainting
Grow full to o'erflowing,
And they that behold it
Marvel, and know not
That God at their fountains
Far off has been raining!

"Stronger than steel
Is the sword of the spirit;
Swifter than arrows
The light of the truth is;
Greater than anger
Is love, and subdueth.

"Thou art a phantom,
A shape of the sea mist,
A shape of the brumal
Rain, and the darkness
Fearful and formless;
Day dawns, and thou art not!

"The dawn is not distant,
Nor is the night starless;
Love is eternal;
God is still God, and
His faith shall not fail us!
Christ is eternal!"

event_1_section_3_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
SLEEP, dear one, sleep, may thy rest be unbroken,
    Save by pure thoughts wrapt in harmony divine,
Visions of night, heavenly voices, words unspoken,
    Call us to meet in devotion at thy shrine.
        Sleep, dear one, sleep.

Dream, fair one, dream, while we sing in sweet numbers,
    Angels of light hover round thee ever near,
Nought can approach to disturb thy peaceful slumbers,
    Guarded from harm by thy faithful watchers here.
        Dream, fair one, dream.

Wake! loved one, wake; lo! the day breaks in splendour,
    Earth's fairest flowers are responsive to the call,
Rise on our night, while this homage we would render.
    Be thou our sun, pouring brightness over all.
        Wake! loved one, wake.

event_1_section_3_perf_3.lyrics_transcript:
O world, thou art wondrous fair,
O how fair, so fair, so fair!
    The birds they all know it well,
While over the woods they flutter,
And joyful sweet carols they utter,
    To the heav'ns their melodies swell.

O world, thou art wondrous fair,
O how fair, so fair, so fair!
    They know it the waters all,
Reflected in them all nature
Stands, mountain and mead and creature,
    And the clouds as they float and fall.

The minstrels and painters know it,
    So does many a shepherd boy,
They copy all and feel it,
And those who sing reveal it,
    Their hearts so full of joy.

event_1_section_3_perf_8.lyrics_transcript:
No star is o'er the lake
    Its pale watch keeping,
The moon is half awake,
    Through gray mist creeping.
The last red leaves fall round
    The porch of roses,
The clock hath ceased to sound,
    The long day closes.

Sit by the silent hearth
    In calm endeavour
To count the sounds of mirth,
    Now dumb for ever.
Heed not how hope believes,
    And fate disposes:
Shadow is round the eaves,
    The long day closes.

The lighted windows dim
    Are fading slowly.
The fire that was so trim
    Now quivers lowly.
Go to the dreamless bed
    Where grief reposes;
Thy book of toil is read,
    The long day closes.

event-2-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
How mild the balmy summer night!
    Upon the heights what fires are glowing!
All is around us fragrant, bright,
    The boatmen chant below us rowing.
The azure heav'n above is beaming,
    Now rests the world, the waters glide,
    A wond'rous dome outstretching wide,
And earth its broad foundation seeming.

Oh, summer night! in holy light,
    With perfume, light, and grace o'erflowing,
With stars like eyes of angels bright,
    Their placid smile on all bestowing.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
How mild the balmy summer night!
    Upon the heights what fires are glowing!
All is around us fragrant, bright,
    The boatmen chant below us rowing.
The azure heav'n above is beaming,
    Now rests the world, the waters glide,
    A wond'rous dome outstretching wide,
And earth its broad foundation seeming.

Oh, summer night! in holy light,
    With perfume, light, and grace o'erflowing,
With stars like eyes of angels bright,
    Their placid smile on all bestowing.
There floats a chord of love along,
    And earth with heav'n is thus united,
And silenced too are sin and wrong,
    As love alone could here be plighted.

Oh, therefore lighted is the blaze
    Upon the heights, and fire is gleaming;
Oh, therefore all the planets gaze,
    And earth and heav'n alike are beaming.
Now rests the world, and as the wind
    Now in the tree-tops gently rustleth,
Such peace and beauty are combined,
    That man rejoiceth, prayeth, list'neth.
performance_1.additional_information: Liedertafel

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
I love to vaunt
My rustic haunt:
For fairer graces
Than all around
The eye embraces
Nowhere are found.
Here spreads the glory
Of ripening corn,
There woodlands hoary
The scene adorn;
The white flocks daily
On yonder lea,
And in the valley
Stands "Sorrow-free."
For thus my hamlet
I love to greet,
My hermitage,
My blest retreat:
Where morn comes bracing
To cheerful task,
And, interlacing,
The vine and elmtree
The noonday mask.

The wild sloes' tangle
Defines yon ravine,
The poplars spangle
With silvery sheen;
And softly rustling
By fernshaded nook,
Now idling, now bustling,
Meanders the brook:
Through furtive shadows
Of arching boughs,
And sun-gilt meadows
Serenely it flows;
Then lucently glasses
The green hills it passes,
Where lambkins stray;
It mirrors the flowers,
And cool in its bowers
The groundlings play.
See, darting and gliding,
The clear flood dividing,
The roach and trout:
Now downward feigning,
Then swiftly about,
The surface regaining.
    O happy state!
May Time and Fate
Undo thee never;
To strength renewed
And joyous mood
Restore me ever!

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
Ye little birds that sit and sing
    Amidst the shady valleys,
And see how Phyllis sweetly walks
    Within her garden alleys;
Go, pretty birds, about her bower;
Sing, pretty birds, she may not lower;
Ah me! methinks I see her frown!
    Ye pretty wantons, warble.

Go, tell her through your chirping bills,
    As you by me are bidden,
To her is only known my love,
    Which from the world is hidden.
Go, pretty birds, and tell her so;
See that your notes strain not too low,
For still, methinks, I see her frown!
    Ye pretty wantons, warble.

Go, tune your voices' harmony,
    And sing, I am her lover;
Strain loud and sweet, that every note
    With sweet content may move her.
And she that hath the sweetest voice,
Tell her I will not change my choice,
Yet still, methinks, I see her frown!
    Ye pretty wantons, warble.

Oh fly! make haste! see, see, she falls
    Into a pretty slumber.
Sing round about her rosy bed,
    That, waking, she may wonder.
Say to her, 'tis her lover true
That sendeth love to you, to you;
And when you hear her kind reply,
    Return with pleasant warblings.
performance_8.additional_information: Liedertafel. Cobb

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
CONCEALED in the leafy recess of a grove
Sweet Philomel warbled the beauty of love,
She sang of its rapture, its longing and pain
In jubilant cadence, in thrilling refrain.

Her own bosom's yearning gave voice to her throat,
Each tone spoke of passion, a sigh was each note;
Then died into silence at last, like the bliss
Of true hearts in union grown mute in a kiss.

Thus often, O friends, have our souls been regaled,
When Cynthia's lamp o'er the darkness prevailed,
When ecstasy came on the pinions of song,
And love in our hearts linger'd gladly and long.

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
The winds rush onward, the clouds they drift,
But question them never: "Say whither so swift?"
The clouds and the winds ne'er an answer give they,
But joyless and painless they drift on their way.

The brooklets and rivers flow murm'ring along,
But question them never: "What meaneth your song?"
They ripple and murmur their self-same refrain,
Thou waitest unheeded, and askest in vain.

The wild swans fly southward when summer is o'er,
But question them never: "Return ye no more?"
They follow the summer, they reckon not where,
Their home is the wide world, be summer but there.

But thou, my heart, look'st back with a sigh!
O question it never: "For why, ah why?"
Who never has felt it, will ne'er understand,
My heart turns to thee still, beloved native land.

performance_14.lyrics_transcript:
'Tis night! upon the Cornish coast full loud the breakers roar,
And helplessly yon gallant bark drifts on the dark lee shore,
And quickly now the signal guns boom high above the gale,
Oh! many a dark-eyed Cornish girl at that wild sound grows pale.

The life-boat's mann'd, stand clear ahead, there's death upon the gale,
Cheer up, dear lass, one parting kiss, your lips look cold and pale.
The life-boat's mann'd, stand clear ahead, no time to sigh for home,
Hurrah! the gallant life-boat sweeps thro' the seething foam.

Bend boldly to your task, brave hearts, it is a glorious strife,
On ev'ry oar-blade flashing high, there hangs some loved one's life.
A cheer so faint comes down the wind, all hands we yet may save,
Now lift our gallant life-boat like lightning o'er the wave.

performance_18.lyrics_transcript:
FREEDOM dwells thro'out our own beloved land:
    Up to heav'n its voice is swelling.
From the mountain heights afar to ocean strand
    Ev'ry breeze the tale is telling.

Never weary of the ever joyous song,
Heart and voice united bear along.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend!
Foe within and out repelling.

War's alarum has but lately died away,
    Yet the echo rolls around us.
But the patriot host has overthrown the sway
    Of the haughty pow'r that bound us.
Freedom dwells where freedom never dwelt before,
Cries and groans shall grieve the land no more.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend
Has the suff'ring captive found us.

Freedom dwells thro'out our own beloved land:
    Wide as heav'n arches o'er it.
Like the rising sun, the patriot's armed hand
    Clouds of wrong hath swept before it.
Sound aloud the joyous word from crag to crag,
Plant on ev'ry peak our starry flag.
    Loyal to the end!
    Ready to defend!
Guard and like a shrine adore it.

event-1_23.additional_information: Page 4 includes 曲目解説 by 秋山紀夫 and a section titled ●武蔵野音楽大学ウインドアンサンブルについて. It states: 武蔵野音楽大学管合奏の歴史は、古く、第二次大戦中にまでさかのぼるが、本格的な活動を開始したのは、1953年日本で初めて“ウインドアンサンブル”の名称を用いた時からである。“ウインドアンサンブル”とは、従来の“プラス・バンド”のイメージを一新し、現代的且つ高度な管合奏の技術を目指して名付けたもので、当時としては、ごくモダンな名称であった。又活動としても音楽大学中唯一のウインドアンサンブルの方向づけを示し、現代作曲家によるオリジナル作品の紹介、演奏旅行、管楽器による室内楽の演奏会等、多様な活動を進め現在に至っている。1973年よりアントニン・キューネル客員教授がその指導にあたり、75年北海・76年東海・東北・77年上越と演奏旅行を行ない好評を博している。 演奏旅行日程: 7月17日＜月＞ 6:30 ●弘前市民会館 / 7月18日＜火＞ 6:00 ●青森市民会館 / 7月20日＜木＞ 6:00 ●秋田県民会館 / 7月21日＜金＞ 6:30 ●横手市民会館. Antonin Kühnel profile text: 1941年プラハに生まる。プラハ・コンサヴァトリとプラハ・アカデミーにおいて指揮法と打楽器を学んだ。コンサヴァトリ時代にすでに打楽器奏者として活躍をはじめ、アカデミー在学中にも国立劇場オーケストラのティンバーニ奏者をつとめた。1970年6月にオルミュッツで行われた青年指揮者コンクールに入賞（第2位）チェコ文化省より給費を受けプラハ・FOK交響楽団において指揮の実際を学んだ後、チェコ国内各地の交響楽団と協演好評を博す。その後テヘラン・オペラの音楽監督として在任中、1973年本学の招聘により客員教授として来日、管弦楽を始め、吹奏楽、室内楽等数々の演奏会を成功させている。 Tetsuro Ishikawa profile text: 東京芸術大学卒業。同大学大学院を経て、1972年より2年間ポーランド政府給費留学生として国立ワルシャワ高等音楽院大学院に学び、院長レギナ・スメンジャンカ女史の薫陶を受ける。その間、ポーランド国立放送のテレビ等に出演の他、ワルシャワを始めポーランド各地において演奏会等を行い、1975年に帰国。平田小百合、松野景一、福井直俊、永井進の各氏に師事。現在、武蔵野音楽大学講師。 Page numbers present in chunk: === Page 4 ===, === Page 5 ===, === Page 6 ===.
