event_2_55.additional_information: Page 7. Text consists of institutional news and descriptive prose rather than a specific musical event. Includes the headings: 「大成功に終わった管弦楽団の西独演奏旅行」, 「広大な自然に恵まれた入間校地の開設」, 「明年を迎える創立50周年」, and 「入間校舎：IRUMA CAMPUS」. Visible text: 「昨昭和52年9月8日から約1ヶ月間、西独ボン市およびドイツ音楽評議会の主催による、ベートーヴェン没後150年祭の公式行事に参加するとともに、同国13都市で演奏を行なった武蔵野音楽大学管弦楽団は、訪問地先々で大成功を収めた。大統領府におけるシェーン大統領への感謝の対面（写真）、日・独・英の若人の共演による“第9シンフォニー”ボン市ベートーヴェンホールでの演奏会、各都市での心温まる歓迎レセプション、民宿先でのドイツ家族との交流、史跡や音楽関係施設の見学など、この旅行が教育上または文化交流と国際親善に果たした役割は大きい。今秋、本管弦楽団は山陽地方への演奏旅行が計画されている。昨今、大都市内の多くの大学が、その狭隘と都市公害などから受ける制約を憂慮して、抜本的な学園環境改善策としての脱都心、キャンパス移行計画を進めているが、武蔵野音楽大学ではすでに10数年前、他大学に先駆け、いち早く大自然に恵まれた広大な（校地面積45万㎡）入間市の新校地建設に着手した。計画した諸施設は写真のように現在建設中の大講堂を残し、ほぼ全部完了し、ここでは昭和51年以降音楽学部1部1・2年生生徒約1,000名が自然の深緑と白亜の校舎群の中で活気に満ちた青春を送っている。武蔵野音楽大学の前身である武蔵野音楽学校は昭和4年に創立されたので、昭和54年には創立50周年を迎える。大学の歴史として半世紀は決して長いとは言えないが、わが国音楽界の揺籃期、第2次大戦をはさんでの社会の激動期を、現在の“武蔵野”にまで輝やかしく発展できたことは、関係各位のご支援とともに建学の精神である“和”の心が脈々と息づいてきたからに他ならない。優れた職員と整備された施設のもとで、豊かな人間性に根ざした音楽芸術の追求を目標としている武蔵野音楽大学では、わが国において音楽教育に占める私学の重要な役割と大きな責任を再確認し、明年を迎える創立50周年を契機として一段と大きく飛躍をしようとの意気に燃えている。」

event_1_section_1.additional_information: Cantata—"The Maid of Orleans". Program note text follows describing the work and labeling internal divisions PART I., PART II., and PART III. Those internal labels appear within the cantata text and are preserved as performance text rather than separate event sections.

event_1_section_1_performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
PART I.—A brief orchestral prelude—sostenuto—leads to a spirited chorus wherein the pleasures of the vintage and the virtues of wine are duly set forth. This joyous strain is interrupted by the arrival of a band of peasants with tidings of the ravages caused by the conquering English troops, and all
bewail their own weakness and the restless might of the foe. Joan appears, and after declaring her supernatural mission, breaks into a triumphant song in which the chorus, infected by her dauntless spirit, subsequently join. The stirring melody of this number, with its fine instrumentation and the effective use made of the harp, cannot fail to appeal to all who hear it.

PART II.—After a few characteristic bars of introduction, the King welcomes his soldiers, who have brought Joan to him, clad in full armour. In answer to his inquiry, the King is told that when the troops were on the point of yielding, this young maid had come to their assistance, and that by her aid they had routed the enemy. Joan's solo, telling of the mysterious command she had received whilst praying before a picture of the Madonna in her native village, is preceded by a striking passage from the clarionet, and the opening subject in A minor is accompanied alternatively with the woodwind and the muted strings; the same motif is then given in the major, an almost martial character being here imparted to it by the use of trumpets. In answer to further questions from the King, Joan foretells that she will bring him victorious to Rheims, and the army with a shout demands that she shall at once lead them against the foe. This concluding number of Part II. is a finely-written double chorus, the two divisions, after a brief duet for Joan and the King, uniting in an ensemble which, from a musical standpoint, is undoubtedly the climax of the whole work.

PART III.—Joan of Arc, betrayed into the hands of the English, has miraculously escaped, and once more led her countrymen to victory, but at the cost of a fatal wound. The French soldiers, believing her to be dead, sing a solemn funeral march; but reviving a little, she asks where she is, and is surprised to find herself with her friends. The cantata concludes with the death of Joan, who gives utterance to her belief in the everlasting joys in store for her, while the chorus indulge in lamentations at the untimely death that thus overtakes the saviour of her country.

FIRST PART

The autumn is coming, full ripe is the vine,
The rich juices rising to burst from their shrine;
    Warmest glow of summer sunshine
        Drinking deep in quiet might,
    Haply of their own joy dreaming,
        Waxing strong to fulness bright.
Press out the rich juices, free, glowing and clear,
That bring to all hearts strength, joy and good cheer.

Half-chorus.—He whom fate unkind hath driven,
    All.—Drink its juices, comfort rife;
Half-chorus.—Who his heart from hope hath riven,
    All.—Findeth here new strength and life.
Half-chorus.—Who his love to vow not daring,
All.— Courage drink for love's first kiss.
    He who love's delight is sharing,
    Laud in vine, laud in wine,
        His joy and bliss.
        The juices are flowing,
            Now fill high the cask,
        Its fires all glowing
            In slumber to bask.
Now that deeper sleep may darkle
    Let the hammer stroke resound,
That in golden life it sparkle,
    As the glass goes round and round.
        Then pour out its juices, &c.
Hold! and silence all your merry singing;
Not glasses' clangour, sabre stroke
Demands our Fatherland from ye.

Vintagers.—
Why startle us here 'mid our pleasure?
Your tidings tell—what hath befallen us?

Chorus of Peasants.—
England's rudest lords are coming,
    O'er the sea t' invade our land—
To make desolate our meadows,
    Spreading death with sword and brand.
Ev'rywhere are they victorious,
    Ruin threatens all our host;
Only Orleans ours remaining,
    Last defence our land can boast.
Even there now stand our foemen,
    In their strong o'erpow'ring might,
With their thousand throats of fire,
    Scatt'ring ruin, death, and night.

Vintagers and Peasants.—
Woe unto us! Our joys, but just beginning,
    Already die at danger's breath.
A nobler blood than blood of vintage
    Asks the cruel Vintager—Death.

Woe, woe, too powerless our arm,
    To save our routed host from flight;
Who here will rescue, and who be guarding,
    Our native hearth, our toils requite?
Help us, O God! Preserve our firesides
    From war's red flaming fire and death!
Woe unto us! Our joys, but just beginning,
    Already die at danger's breath.

Joan.—
Who will your saviour be?
    I have that task!
Of God anointed, me 'tis given,
    Our Fatherland's deliverer to be.

That which an army may not dare,
Shall I achieve by Heaven's might alone!
Ask not that which my mouth may never dare to tell:
The King alone shall know it all.
Look up in hope!
Your own fair meadows shall still remain war's carnage far:
My footsteps victory shall order,
Farewell, farewell! I follow mine own star.

    Lo, what a wonder, doth here her holy presence wake!
        The simple maid, transfigured, shining,
        Words of mystery she spake.

Joan.—Now to Thy care, all pure and holy,
    Leave I my dear ones in their stress:
        Thy ray divine illumine lowly
            The way my land to save and bless.
A simple maid Thou hast appointed,
    To show the might of God, to war;
For Thee raised up, of Thee anointed,
    Following to victory my star.
Thy ray divine aye lighting me,
The way my land to save and bless.
I follow to victory my star. Farewell!

SECOND PART.

King.—My welcome to ye, noble warriors!
    What bring ye me? have tidings had?
    And who is yonder lovely maid,
    In glittering armour clad?

Warriors' Chorus.—
    We would, o'ercome in bloody battle,
        Our host surrender to its foes,
    When lo, before us, our eyes beheld it,
        A sudden, mighty wonder rose.
    For from the wood toward us gliding,
        Darted a virgin glorious fair,
    Adorned with armour of a goddess,
        The battle watching there.
    A holy light from heavenly height
        O'ershone her armour, splendour rife,
    And with strong hand she caught high our banner,
        And led us on to war and strife.
    Then fled our foemen in wildest tumult,
        No leader's voice they hear or know;
    From terror dazed, plunge man and horse,
        O'er rocks into the stream below.
    And so we won the awful fight,
        By this fair virgin's wondrous might.

King.—How marvellous!
    Who art thou, mighty presence?—speak!

Joan.—Only a shepherd's child am I.

King.—And how hath God thee victor crowned?

    Chorus.—Speak! How hath God us victors crowned?

Joan.—Near my home, my native village,
    Stands an old Madonna shrine;
    And there, on my knees, I oft have knelt,
    In fervent, ardent prayer.
    And I prayed to God's own mother:
    O, avert the tide of war,
    And in mercy guard from danger
    Our King for evermore.

Then near me the Holy Virgin stood and spake:
Joan, arise! Leave thy hearthstone,
For the Lord hath thee to higher duty called.
Bear this sword, and bear this banner,
Forth away to holy war;
Slay, destroy my people's foemen,
For thou shalt aye victor be.

Before this mighty wonder, still every doubtful feeling,
In lowliness we bend us, before the Virgin kneeling.

King.—Thine eye sweet innocence is beaming,
    Most marvellous seems what thou hast wrought.
If thou the future, too, can'st tell me
    (Hear well the question I have brought)——
Shall I to Rheims as conquering victor go?

Joan.—Thro' thousand foes I'll lead thee safely—go!

Chorus.—
Give us the maiden as our army's leader,
We'll follow blind, where'er the godly maid shall guide.
Her seeress eyes aye be our leader,
To guard her well, we draw our daring swords.
Not e'en a world in arms have we to fear,
If she before our armed host doth go.
The god of victory beside her rideth,
She lead us on, we'll follow blind,
Where the godly maid shall guide,
She lead us on, the mighty one in battle, she lead us on.
She lead us on to holy battle, she lead us on to war.

Joan.—Not e'en a world in arms have ye to fear,
    If I before your armed host may go. I lead ye on.
    The god of victory beside me rideth, I lead ye on.
    Not e'en a world in arms have ye to fear,
    If I before your armed host may go,
    I lead ye on to war, to holy war.

THIRD PART

Warriors' Chorus.—

Mourn, mourn for our lost heroine—
Comrades, mourn for the glorious maiden;
She that us from our foes hath saved,
God hath called to Himself on high.
She is no more—no more will she watch o'er us;
Her eyes no more of earth shall ever see,
She soars above, a spirit glorious,
Seeing our grief no more, sees not our sorrow.
She opens, see, her eyes, she lives!
Here to us from the grave returned?
Conquering death?

Joan.—Where am I?

King.—In thy true friends' hold, in thy King's own arms,
    With thine own folk, with thine own people.

Joan.—No, I am no enchantress, believe me I am not!

King.—Thou art holy as the angels;
    And our dull eyes were but with night bedimmed.

Joan.—And am I truly here, with mine own folk,
    And am no more despised and rejected?
    Ye curse me not, look on me kindly here?
    I'd see my banner, see it not; where is it?
    Never without my banner dare I near ye;
    From my high Master given me in trust,
    Before His throne I lay it down for ever.
    I dare to show it, for I bore it true.

King.—Lo, here an angel dieth!

Joan.—The Holy Virgin nears again to greet me;
    See ye yon rainbow span the ether blue,
    And heaven opening its golden portal?
    Amid the angel choir she brightly stands;
    She holds the Eternal Son upon her breast,
Her arms outstretching smilingly toward me.
O whither? Lightest clouds upbear me high,
The heavy armour winged robe outspreading.
Away, the earth is left behind,
Brief is all pain, and joy eternal.

King.—Ah soon was her pure holy spirit
    From earthly woe to sever,
And angels bear her to that land,
    Where joy shall reign for ever.

event-1-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Mourn, mourn for our lost heroine—
Comrades, mourn for the glorious maiden;
She that us from our foes hath saved,
God hath called to Himself on high.
She is no more—no more will she watch o'er us;
Her eyes no more of earth shall ever see,
She soars above, a spirit glorious,
Seeing our grief no more, sees not our sorrow.
She opens, see, her eyes, she lives!
Here to us from the grave returned?
Conquering death?

Joan.—Where am I?

King.—In thy true friends' hold, in thy King's own arms,
    With thine own folk, with thine own people.

Joan.—No, I am no enchantress, believe me I am not!

King.—Thou art holy as the angels;
    And our dull eyes were but with night bedimmed.

Joan.—And am I truly here, with mine own folk,
    And am no more despised and rejected?
    Ye curse me not, look on me kindly here?
    I'd see my banner, see it not; where is it?
    Never without my banner dare I near ye;
    From my high Master given me in trust,
    Before His throne I lay it down for ever.
    I dare to show it, for I bore it true.

King.—Lo, here an angel dieth!

Joan.—The Holy Virgin nears again to greet me;
    See ye yon rainbow span the ether blue,
    And heaven opening its golden portal?
    Amid the angel choir she brightly stands;
    She holds the Eternal Son upon her breast,
Her arms outstretching smilingly toward me.
O whither? Lightest clouds upbear me high,
The heavy armour winged robe outspreading.
Away, the earth is left behind,
Brief is all pain, and joy eternal.

King.—Ah soon was her pure holy spirit
    From earthly woe to sever,
And angels bear her to that land,
    Where joy shall reign for ever.

event-1-section-3-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
On a bank two roses fair,
    Wet with morning showers,
        Filled with dew in fragrance grew,
As I, pensive, full of care,
    Gathered two sweet flowers.
        Tell me roses, truly tell
        If my fair one loves me well.

This in leaves of white array'd,
    Not a speck to dim them,
        So I find the spotless mind
Which adorns my lovely maid—
    Innocence's emblem.
        Tell me then, and truly tell
        If my fair one loves me well.

Like her cheeks, the blushing ray
    Which thy bud encloses,
        Brighter far than you they are;
But her charms if I should say,
    Ye'll be jealous, roses.
        Tell me then, and truly tell
        If my fair one loves me well.

event-1-section-3-performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
HALLO! Hallo!
Now hunters come away, for early breaks the day;
With rifles prov'd and tried we range the mountain side,
Keep distance every man, each nook and covert scan:
From by the forest end to where the two ways blend.

Yoho, yoho, yoho! There something crouches low;
What eyes can shine like that? It is a mountain cat.
'Tis only so I fear: It is a crouching deer;
Surround it every way, before it steals away.

See now he springs and flies, and for the forest tries,
But there the hunters stand, with steady eye and hand.
And crack it goes, yoho! the ball has laid him low;
A noble beast is he, and killed most manfully.

Here from the waterfall we send a hunter's call,
To glad the list'ning ear of wives and sweethearts dear.
So gently timid they, that if we shoot they say—
"Ah me! there's someone hurt to-day."

O sweethearts in the vale, you from afar we hail,
With joyful notes that tell that all with us is well,
Yet here awhile we roam: and with the evening come
To seek our dear and quiet home.

Tra la, la la, la la! then there's hurrah, hurrah!
For such a bonny land, for vales and mountains grand.
And here's hurrah, hurrah! for wives and maidens true.
Sweethearts, we shout for you, hurrah!

An eye that never fails, a heart that never quails,
A cheek aglow with health, is more than idle wealth.
Hallo! hallo, hallo! a-hunting we will go;
By topmost crag and peak our timid prey we seek,
Hallo! hallo, hallo! a-hunting we will go:
Full quickly flies the day: Hallo, hallo, away!

event-1-section-3-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
The moon is bright, the skies are clear,
And as of old, we two are here,
Tra la la!
In these old scenes of wild delight
In old Venetia here to-night.
Yes, we are here, Love, you and I,
Alone to breathe and sigh,
Our heart's deep love for ever true,
O! love me, Love, for I love you.

While the stars in heaven are shining,
I will love thee evermore,
Love for thee this heart is pining,
Love is waking as of yore.

Thou hast my heart and I have thine,
I know my Love that thou art mine,
Tra la la!
With all my heart I love but thee,
Venetia has but one for me.
In all my dreaming thou art nigh,
To love thee not would be to die,
Oh! life is young, and all is bright,
In old Venetia here to-night.
While the stars, &c.

event-1-section-3-performance-5.lyrics_transcript:
When sorrow sleepeth, wake it not,
    But let it slumber on;
If grief is for a while forgot,
    Its power that while is gone.
The mind may from the pause gain strength
    To grapple with its foe,
And thence may rise to prove, at length,
    Triumphant over woe.
When sorrow sleepeth, wake it not,
    O wake it not.

To mourn the lost, we sigh for care,
    We grieve, by sin opprest;
And all a secret burden bear,
    For earth is not our rest.
Then watch thy thoughts, thy words restrain,
    Each heart its burden knows;
One little word, all light and vain,
    May break that heart's repose.
When sorrow sleepeth, wake it not,
    O wake it not.

event-1-section-3-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
FAIR Semele's high-born son,
Thou many-named one,
Thou, who callest thy father the Thunderer Jove!
Object of beautiful Italia's love;
Thou, who crownest what Ceres bestoweth on all
To thee now we call!
Hear us, Bacchus, in Thebe, thy Bacchante's home,
Where the bright Ismenus, rolling her waters,
Unites the Dragon's sons and daughters.

On thy mount's double-crested heights,
Thy votive flames ascending,
With Corycian nymphs attending,
Grace thy mystic rites;
While pure Castalia laves the ground,
Thy lofty Nysian summit sings, ivy crowned,
    Thy praise!
    Vine and tree
    Warble to thee.
Thy votive trains chant thy lays;
Thy sacred chorus raises
And Thebes' fanes resound thy praises.
    Hear us, Bacchus!

Above all the rest,
Thebes thou hast guarded and blest.
She was its pride,
Who, clasping the Thunderer, died;
And now, seeking its lost repose,
We pray thee to come and heal its woes.
O, hither bend,
From thy Parnassian heights descend,
Or from over Euboea's billows;
    Hear us, Bacchus!

Thou whose power inspires
All our torch-lit star-vieing choirs,
Guide our dance and lead our song,
Son of Jove for ever young!
Come with mirth and revelry;
Bring thy Naxian nymphs with thee;
Come, and let them, bounding before us,
Chime and time the tip-toe chorus,
To praise thee, adore thee, great Iacchus!
    Hear us, Bacchus!

In evening stillness lies the lake,
    And mirrors the waning glow of the west,
Their thirst come timorous deer to slake,
    And swans fly, encircling its tranquil breast.

The fisher boy unfastens his boat,
    The plash of his oar thro' the silence steals;
In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright,
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the waterlily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar;
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,

In evening stillness lies the lake,
    And mirrors the waning glow of the west,
Their thirst come timorous deer to slake,
    And swans fly, encircling its tranquil breast.

The fisher boy unfastens his boat,
    The plash of his oar thro' the silence steals;
In Fancy's realm does he appear to float,
    He knows not why in his heart thus he feels.

Around him whisper the darkling waves,
    And sing in their motion, far and wide,
The water a dim wooded margin laves,
    And the spectre-like mountains tower in pride.

The cooling breath of the evening air,
    It plays thro' his locks all golden and bright,
A fragrance comes from the flow'rets fair,
    As low they are bending for sleep at night.

But the waterlily is yet awake,
    Though nodding in slumb'rous mood is she;
She bends unto him from her native lake,
    Tho' evening invites her at rest to be.

His dream is dispelled, and he quits his oar;
    His face is on fire with longing confessed;
He stoops from the boat, the spot to explore,
    He plucks off a lily, thus decking his breast.

But hark! with fury the forest shakes,
    The lake uplifts its roaring on high,
And sudden over a mountain breaks
    The ruddy full moon, so wrathful of eye.

And the lake exclaims, with heart deeply moved,
    "Why trouble the children within their home?"
And the forest complains, "These long have I loved,
    Why force these delightful sisters to roam?"

But the red-glowing moon then fiercely cries,
    "How darest thou to address my bride?"
And in terror the boy with tears homeward flies,
    That there with his mother, his grief he may hide.

    "O mother, the roar of the lake I heard,
    Against me the forest with fury shook,
Before me, in anger, the full moon appeared,
    O mother, I but a lily took!"

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Dioscuri! shining twin stars,
    Ye who light us o'er the ocean;
    Mighty helpers, guide us safely,
    Still the waves to gentle motion.

    Tho' with firm hearts, fear unknowing,
        Undismayed with storms contending.
    We would see your mild rays beaming,
        Hope and courage to us lending.

    This strong oar that bears us onward,
        O'er the waves your rule obeying.
    At your shrine we then will offer,
        At your altar homage paying.

(b) Again fill your glasses with bright sparkling wine,
    Once more will I pledge ye, dear comrades of mine!
    Farewell, hoary mountains and dear native home,
    Farewell! to a far distant land I must roam.

    The bright sun above us at rest does not stand,
    His course he fulfils over ocean and land:
    The billows disperse and recede from the shore,
    The storm rushes onward its fury to pour.

    With swift-speeding pinion the bird flies away,
    Still singing and soaring it pours out its lay.
    Thus youth's glowing visions will urge to the race,
    Thus earth wanders on thro' regions of space.

    The birds of his own land the wanderer greet,
    Its flow'r's meet his eye with their odour so sweet;
    They bring to his heart thoughts of home and of love,
    The meadow beneath and the blue sky above.

He dreams that once more he his fatherland sees,
And sweet scents of home life come borne on the breeze;
Thus love e'er will follow the lov'd one afar,
And shine through the distance his one guiding star.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Theseus, followed by the citizens of Athens, again appears, and, learning what Creon has done, sends for soldiers and renews his promises of protection to Oedipus, declaring that his daughters shall be restored to him, and that Creon shall not be allowed to bring such a disgrace upon Athens. The Chorus describes the contest, and invokes the aid of the Gods in favour of Theseus and his followers.

Ah, were I on yonder plain,
    Where now our undaunted sons
        Stand arm'd for the hostile fray;
There, where the shrine of Phoebus gleams,
        And torches are burning;
Where mortals bow down to the awe-inspiring pair,
    Whose hallow'd rites are mystic deeds,
        Wrought by Eumolpidan priests,
    And never breath'd to mortal ear.
        There, glowing with ardour,
            Panting to rush against the foe,
                See, see all our legions,
        With Theseus they wave their swords, and cry,
            Rescue the sisters!

Or westward perchance they rush,
Where snow-cover'd mountains rise
    O'er Œa's enamell'd meads;
There dancing cars and prancing steeds
    Will clash in the onset!
There on the foe soon will impending vengeance fall,
    For Theseus leads our valiant bands:
    See their arms and armour gleaming
Bright as the trappings that grace their steeds!
    Now proudly exulting.
They, who honour the deeds of sage Minerva,
And Rhea's great son, earth-encircling ocean's king,
    Press to the battle!

    Do they await, pursue or fight?
        My heart thrills with hope
That they will soon rescue the captive maid,
Who hath endur'd, and still endures her kindred's woe.
    This day, Jove will restore her,
    Crown your deeds, heroes, with glory!
    Like a dove high soaring,
    Sped along by the storm-wind!
    I, from the verge of a cloud,
    Would look down on the contest,
And see my country's cause triumphant!

    Dread Pow'r, that fillest heav'n's high throne,
    O all-seeing Jove, defend our great ruler!
        On him the victor's palm bestow!
        With verdant laurels deck his brow!
            We call on thee, Pallas Athene!
            Mighty hunter, Phœbus, hear us!
And thy sister, fleet in chase, whose dart unerring
    Pierceth the far distant hart:
    O come, defend our guardians!
    We pray ye, aid our native heroes!

The Athenians are successful, and Theseus returns with Antigone and Ismene. Œdipus expresses his gratitude to the King, who announces the arrival of Polynices, seeking an interview with his father. The Chorus describes the sorrows of life, and the blessing of death when old age has come.

II

When the health and the strength are gone.
He that still would be lingering here,
Borne down by a load of care,
Is, I consider, devoid of wisdom.
Old age bringeth disease and pain,
Grief, anguish, and regret remain.
For youth's bloom and its fleeting joys
Never, never return again.
Life's varied journeys lead to death!
Smooth or rugged, all its pathways,
Even its wishes, end in Hades.
Love hymeneal, revels, dances, strains of music
    Cease, when the Foe appeareth!

Better not to exist;
Or, if born, in early childhood to die,
And escape all the cares and pains.
They, living longest, endure the longest.
Youth and Folly and Sorrow roam
Hand in hand to their destined home:
For none liveth devoid of care;
None escapeth what all must bear.
Envy, Sedition, Murder, Strife,
Fear and rage hover around us:
And, in conclusion, feeble, helpless,
Old and friendless, all these ills together meeting
    Crush their devoted victim.

On man, poor mourner, all these evils fall,
Fall as billows rushing beat the north strand,
Dashing onward, urged by the blast of winter.
Thus, then, storms of affliction, never-ending, assail us.
    Thus lowering sorrows around us gather;
    Whether from Helios' western bound,
        Or from his eastern gate,
        Or where its rays beam brightest,
        Or down from the home of Arcturus.

The Chorus sing the praises of Colonos,

Thou comest here to the land, O friend,
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows;
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove,
    Where the voices of nightingales
    Resound, floating in dulcet strains
        Thro' their temples of verdure;
    Where the thick-woven ivy clings,
    Spreading over the sacred aisles;
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine,
    Unscath'd by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god,
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays,
    Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

Fair and fragrant at dawn of day,
See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus,
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
    Worn by them in the days of old.
See the Crocus array'd in gold;
    Hear the slumberless waters,
While they glide in Cephisus' tide,
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia;
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear,
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway! yet here it freely springeth;
    Rever'd by friends, and fear'd by foes,
    In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold, ours is the rich oil-dropping olive!
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree.
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure,
    Ever heeded by Morian Jove,
        Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva.

Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts deigned to my country;
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder-guided;
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent,
        Mighty god Poseidon,
Thou didst give us the rein form'd for the courser;
Guided thus, or curbed, he yields obedience.
Through the billows we dash, stemming the deep,
    Speeded along by the oar and helm,
    Bounding on with the dancing nymphs—
        Nereus' hundred-footed daughters.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Ever sweet art thou, O Night!
        In the forest sweeter far.
    Where thy starry eyes gleam bright,
        Where thy soft enchantments are!
    Where the leaves, like fairy goblets,
        Overflow with dewy wine,
    And the moon's unclouded radiance
        Fills each glade with light divine.

Murmuring breezes sing of thy pleasures,
Silvery moonbeams weave thee thy tresses;
All whom thy lips have silently press'd
Closing their eyes, sink sweetly to rest;

But who would sleep on night so clear?
Arise! the horn rings far and near,
And wakens with its gladsome sound
Each slumb'rer in the groves around.
    Wake! wake! wake!

It echoes the woods and the mountain tops o'er,
The birds, all awaking, think night is no more;
The wandering deer in affright flee away,
They fancy it heralds the dawn of the day;
The lords of the forest shout loud in their might,
The fountain awakes with a song of delight!

Then sing as we wander,
    "The woods are the home of the night!"
And echo answers yonder,
    "The woods, thy home, O Night!"
Yes, here within thy forest home,
    We'll greet thee, lovely, lovely Night.
Where smiling from thy heav'nly dome,
    Thou reign'st in all thy might!

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
ROLLING along, bowling along, over the sea we go,
    And heave our anchor singing our song,
With a yeo! ho! cheery men, yeo!
    The wind and the waves may beat us about,
And rocks' lie waiting below,
    But our yards they are trim, and our timbers are stout,
So yeo! ho! cheery men, yeo!

Monstrous and terrible roars the old sea,
    When winds make his wild rage grow;
Grim death lurks then in his heart "for we,"
    But yeo! ho! cheery men, yeo!

For well are we nurst on his broad boon breast,
    When his rage shall overblow,
Fed full of the bold free life which is best,
    Yeo! cheery men, yeo! ho!

How he swings him along 'neath his ocean of air,
    In his great heart's careless flow;
How we win his love when his wrath we dare,
    Sing yeo! ho! cheery men, yeo!

event-1-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Of Nelson and the North
Sing the glorious day's renown,
When to battle fierce went forth
All the might of Denmark's crown,
And her arms along the deep proudly shone.
By each gun the lighted brand
In a bold determined hand;
And the prince of all the land
    Led them on.

Like leviathans afloat
Lay their bulwarks on the brine;
While the sign of battle flew
On the lofty British line.
It was ten of April morn by the chime;
As they drifted on their path,
There was silence deep as death,
And the boldest held his breath
    For a time.

But the might of England flushed
To anticipate the scene;
And her van the fleeter rushed
O'er the deadly space between.
"Hearts of oak!" our captains cried, when each gun
From its adamantine lips
Spread a death shade round the ships,
Like the hurricane eclipse
    Of the sun.

Again! again! again!
And the havoc did not slack,
Till a feeble cheer the Dane
To our cheering sent us back;
Their shots along the deep slowly boom—
Then ceased—and all is wail,!
As they strike the shattered sail,
Or, in conflagration pale,
    Light the gloom.

Then cried the victor,
As he hailed them o'er the wave:—
"Ye are brothers! ye are men!
And we conquer but to save:—
So peace instead of death let us bring:
But yield, proud foe, thy fleet,
With the crews, at England's feet,
And make submission meet
    To our King."

Now joy, old England, raise!;
For the tidings of thy might,
By the festal cities' blaze,
While the wine cup shines in light;
And yet amidst that joy and uproar,
Let us think of them that sleep,
Full many a fathom deep,
By thy wild and stormy steep,
    Elsinore!

Brave hearts! to Britain's pride
Once so faithful and so true,
On the deck of fame that died,--
With the gallant good Riou:
Soft sigh the winds of heaven o'er their grave
While the billow mournful rolls,
And the mermaid's song consoles,
Singing glory to the souls
    Of the brave.

event-1-section-1-performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
Hear those soothing sounds ascending
    From the winding path below;
Each in each other sweetly blending,
    On the breezes as they flow.
    Jubilate, Amen.
'Tis the ev'ning choir now wending
To the vespers chanting low.
    Hark! Hark! Jubilate, Amen.
Bear, ye breezes, gently breathing,
    Sounds of peace far o'er the land,
Now all our best affections wreathing
    With a chaplet light and bland.
    Jubilate, Amen.
Heart to heart in love bequeathing
By thy soft divine command.
    Hark! Hark! Jubilate, Amen.

event-1-section-1-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
HALLO!
HALLO! hallo! to cover!
Where waves the forest far around,
And thro' the waving branches
I hear the horn resound.

Tra-ra!

Then sound aloud the hallo
O'er forest, meadow, stream, and crag,
To startle and to follow
And track the bounding stag.

And homeward when returning,
Beneath the moon's effulgent light,
I seek my lady's window,
To sing a soft good night.

Sleep well! oh my beloved,
And may no dream thy peace annoy;
My heart is thine for ever,
Thou art the hunter's joy.

Sleep well!

And then, hallo to cover!
Where waves the forest, &c.

event-1-section-2-performance-1.performance_name: Ah! were I on Yonder Plain (Antigone)
event-1-section-2-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Ah, were I on yonder plain,
Where now our undaunted sons
Stand armed for the hostile fray!
There where the shrine of Phoebus gleams,
And torches are burning;
Where mortals bow down to the awe-inspiring pair,
Whose hallowed rites are mystic deeds,
Wrought by Eumolpidan priests,
And never breathed to mortal ear!
    There, glowing with ardour,
    Panting to rush against the foe,
    See all our legions!
With Theseus they wave their swords, and cry,
    Rescue the sisters!

    Or westward perchance they rush,
    Where snow-covered mountains rise
        O'er Œa's enamelled meads;
    There dancing cars and prancing steeds
        Will clash in the onset!
There on the foe soon will impending vengeance fall;
    For Theseus leads our valiant bands.
    See their arms and armour gleaming,
Bright as the trappings that grace their steeds;
    Now proudly exulting,
They who honour the deeds of sage Minerva,
And Rhea's great son, earth-encircling ocean's king,
    Press to the battle!

Do they await, pursue, or fight?
    My heart thrills with hope
That they will soon rescue the captive maid,
Who hath endured and still endures her kindred's woe.
    This day Jove will restore her;
    Crown your deeds, heroes, with glory!
    Like a dove high soaring,
    Sped along by the storm-wind,
    I, from the verge of a cloud,
Would look down on the contest,
And see my country's cause triumphant!

Dread Power, that fillest heaven's high throne,
O all-seeing Jove, defend our great ruler!
    On him the victor's palm bestow,
    With verdant laurels deck his brow!
    We call on thee, Pallas Athene;
    Mighty hunter, Phœbus, hear us!
And thy Sister, fleet in chase, whose dart unerring
Pierceth the far-distant hart.
    Oh come, defend our guardians!
    We pray ye, aid our native heroes!

event-1-section-2-performance-3.lyrics_transcript:
Softer than the sunlight dying
    In the golden ev'ning shine,
Moon and starlight sweet is lying
    In thy chamber, love of mine.

II

With the far light of the starlight,
    Softly on the breeze,
    Thro' the linden trees
    Softly blending,
    Love's song ascending,
Now greets thee, O my soul's delight,
    Good night!

Love in true heart slumbers never,
    Watchful faith is constant there;
Yearningly the spirit ever
    Broods on hope and anxious care.

    With the far light, &c.

event-1-section-2-performance-8.lyrics_transcript:
HALLO! Hallo!
Now hunters come away, for early breaks the day;
With rifles prov'd and tried we range the mountain side.
Keep distance every man, each nook and covert scan;
From by the forest end to where the two ways blend.

Yoho, yoho, yoho! There something crouches low;
What eyes can shine like that? It is a mountain cat.
'Tis only so I fear: It is a crouching deer;
Surround it every way, before it steals away.

See now he springs and flies, and for the forest tries,
But there the hunters stand, with steady eye and hand.
And crack it goes, yoho! the ball has laid him low;
A noble beast is he, and killed most manfully.

Here from the waterfall we send a hunter's cheer,
To glad the list'ning ears of wives and sweethearts dear.
So gently timid they, that if we shoot they say—
"Ah me! there's someone hurt to-day."

O sweethearts in the vale, you from afar we hail,
With joyful notes that tell that all with us is well.
Yet here awhile we roam: and with the evening come
To seek our dear and quiet home.

Tra la, la la, la la! then there's hurrah, hurrah!
For such a bonny land, for vales and mountains grand.
And here's hurrah, hurrah! for wives and maidens true.
Sweethearts, we shout for you, hurrah!

An eye that never fails, a heart that never quails,
A cheek aglow with health, is more than idle wealth.
Hallo! hallo, hallo! a-hunting we will go;
By topmost crag and peak our timid prey we seek.
Hallo! hallo, hallo! a-hunting we will go;
Full quickly flies the day: Hallo, hallo, away!

event_7_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
1.—The Departure

Up, up, and away, every sail widely spanned,
The anchor set free, and the yards all bemanned.
Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

High swells his heart, and he longs for the bride,
Her all of his soul and his life doth confide,
Beauteous will adorn her with purple and gold,
With gems and pearls as his queen enfold.

An island hides her in ocean afar,
There brightly she shines as a radiant star,
The Maid of the Sea, demons guard day and night,
But our hero will win her all valiant in might.

Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

2.—On the Strand

An Old Sailor:

Depart, farewell! thou'lt see this port aye never,
    Your fatherland greets ye the last to-day,
Soon raging storm as foam the ship shall sever,
    Ye all shall be of fish and fowl the prey.

    Storm birds I see are flying,
    The wolf to forest hieing;
    Signs these that hell aye keepeth,
    When low the eagle sweepeth.

These signs full oft I read descrying,
    But younger folk their doubt will cast,
High rolls the tide, the winds are sighing,
    What is to be, must be, at last.

    Shout then and revel,
    Soon thy song shall die away,
    The raven croaks, deep caverns yawn,
    Thy fatherland greets ye the last to-day.

3.—On the Sea

Beauteous prize our zeal engageth,
    Be thou gracious, seaman's fate!
Lead us safe though tempest rageth,
    Back to native port elate.

Where we wander, where abiding
    In the hand of God we are,
On, great ship, the waves dividing,
    Aye before goes God's fair star.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Liedertafel

1.—The Departure

Up, up, and away, every sail widely spanned,
The anchor set free, and the yards all bemanned.
Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

High swells his heart, and he longs for the bride,
Her all of his soul and his life doth confide,
Beauteous will adorn her with purple and gold,
With gems and pearls as his queen enfold.

An island hides her in ocean afar,
There brightly she shines as a radiant star,
The Maid of the Sea, demons guard day and night,
But our hero will win her all valiant in might.

Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

2.—On the Strand

An Old Sailor:

Depart, farewell! thou'lt see this port aye never,
    Your fatherland greets ye the last to-day,
Soon raging storm as foam the ship shall sever,
    Ye all shall be of fish and fowl the prey.

    Storm birds I see are flying,
    The wolf to forest hieing;
    Signs these that hell aye keepeth,
    When low the eagle sweepeth.

These signs full oft I read descrying,
    But younger folk their doubt will cast,
High rolls the tide, the winds are sighing,
    What is to be, must be, at last.

    Shout then and revel,
    Soon thy song shall die away,
    The raven croaks, deep caverns yawn,
    Thy fatherland greets ye the last to-day.

3.—On the Sea

Beauteous prize our zeal engageth,
    Be thou gracious, seaman's fate!
Lead us safe though tempest rageth,
    Back to native port elate.

Where we wander, where abiding
    In the hand of God we are,
On, great ship, the waves dividing,
    Aye before goes God's fair star.

So we're full of valour daring,
    Fear naught deep nor storm award,
Joy all earthly treasure sharing,
    For the Lord our house doth guard.

Harald's Song:

From the sea all darkly flowing,
    High the sun ascends and higher,
Fills the mead with radiance glowing,
    Wakes the Nereidian choir.
Love's bright star is beck'ning me,
    O! I'll follow, follow thee!

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.
I will listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

Swell, ye sails, and call, ye billows,
    Roar and blow, ye strong winds wild,
That I with my warriors daring,
    Soon may reach the darling child.

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

4.—The Storm

The God of Storms and the Demons of the South Sea:

Ye storms there on high,
    And fiends of the deep,
O tarry ye not,
    Where'er ye may sleep!

For battle prepared,
    Your God calleth ye,
Roll on as the thunder,
    And plough ye the sea.

O shiver the masts,
    Shake the bed of the sea,
Make known to them all
    Sons of hell ye be.

On the Ship:

    Hark, storm-spirits dark are nighing,
        Threat'ning clouds all downward fly.
        For the storm spirit's nigh!
    Reef the sails, the yards all lower,
        On the deck then every man.

    Billow rises wild on billow,
        Piping raves the furious wind,
Is the anchor fast and steady?
        Still our hope to that we bind.

Woe! The mast broke, shrouds all shriven,
    Cleft the great ship's mighty bow,
Flash on flash red lightning driven
    Wraps in flame the anchor tow.

On and on the storm is waging,
    'Gainst the hellish rocks they dip.
See the furies, hear their raging,
    In the great deep sinks the ship.

The God of Storms:

    To the deep she went down!
    Come, O sun, here downward pour thee,
    Ne'er that ship will sail before thee.

The Demons:

Victoria! That ship we sank for ever,
    Of shameless robbers quick revenge obtain
O'er us hath mortal had victory never,
    Ancient and mighty ocean race we reign.

Ill fares who seeks the prize 'tis ours to guard,
    And woe! shall sink in deepest wave.
Who his desire and hope our waves award,
    Earns for his daring bold an early grave.

5.—Closing Song

The Spirits of the Sea:

Slumber soft in deep sea lying,
    Lulled by billow-throng for aye.
Our ear heareth all your sighing,
    When ye plaint to plaint reply.

Calmly moon and stars are bending
    From high heaven unto the wave.
Far and wide night shadow blending,
    God doth guard your silent grave.

And the spirit choir are mourning
    With the nymphs thy fate's decree,
And the spirit choir are saying:
    Slumber soft in deepest sea!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
The drowsy woods are wrapt in shadow;
The dreamy clouds hang o'er the lake;
The quiet moon sleeps on the meadow;
But love now watches for thy sake.

The ocean now in silence slumbers,
Unheard the billows gently break,
And so to thee, in whispered numbers
Comes love, who watches for thy sake.

Then rouse thee not, tho' love be singing,
Or from thine eyes their slumbers shake,
If in thy soul the tones are ringing,
Of love, who watches for thy sake.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
1.—Rakocsky March

2.—Easter Hymn

CHRIST is risen from the dead.  
Has broken the tomb,  
Gladly hail the token.  
Sin's fetters are broken,  
Reversed is the doom.  
Now the Master hath ascended,  
    Rejoice for your bondage is o'er,  
And the reign of sin is ended,  
    Praise him for evermore!

Alas! those He loved can but languish,  
    Suffer mid pain and annoy.  
Master, we envy Thy joy,  
Forget not the depth of our anguish.  
    Hosanna!

3.—Danse des Sylphes

4.—Chorus of Soldiers and Students

Soldiers.

Fortresses defended with strong ramparts high,  
Fair maidens who daringly love's power defy,  
Of conquest we're certain soon as we take the field,  
We reck not of danger, to us they must yield.  
At the sound of the trumpet we soldiers so  
To revel or battle at once march away.

Students.

Jam nox stellata vel amina pandit,
Nunc bibendum et amandum est,
Vita brevis fugax que voluptas,
    Gaudeamus igitur.

Nobis sub ridente luna,
Per urbem quaerentes puellas eamus.
Ut cras fortunati Caesares dicamus,
Veni, vidi, vici, gaudeamus igitur.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
Ah! must we part for ever?
One kiss before we sever.
Beside my bold commander
I far away must wander.
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!

I ne'er again may greet thee,
On sunny pathway meet thee;
The foe will stand before me,
And battle clouds roll o'er me.
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!

I long for thee when parted.
Weep thou for me true hearted!
When life's last pulses flutter,
My latest breath shall utter,
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!
performance_5.additional_information: Rinkel.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
Why should we sigh, and mirth decry,
And why from content seek banishment?
With care why alloy the cup of joy,
To vainly repent o'er days misspent?
No! cherish the hours, while youth is ours;
And give not to care life's better share:
    But the sage old device
    Let us prize,
That this world's both good and fair!
Though in lane and street,
Oftsoe'er you meet
    Gloomy faces, sorrow's traces,
Think that evermore.
When the clouds pass o'er,
Lips will smile that smil'd before, Once more!
Ever thus sweet Spring
Weaves his flow'ry ring,
    Gladness wooing, world renewing;
And like airy sprite,
Ceaseless day and night,
Joy doth weave a new delight, With might.

    Her shapes are manifold
    Her voices all untold,
    She dwells in ev'ry place
    Where pure hearts may follow
        Her fairy trace.
She roams on sunlit hills,
Or lurks by babbling rills,
Or rocks on ocean's breast,
    Or sings where the woodlands
        In shadow rest.

But, oh! sweet is the image of joy,
    In human face that dwells,
When love new-born, of its pure ecstasy
    In humid glances tells,

O'er joy-illumined eye
Night spreads no starless sky;
And love-filled heart can hear
    The chime of earth's joy-bells
        Sound far and near.

O ye, that look through a darkening veil,
And ye, faint souls, that life's sorrows bewail,
Look up! and trust to Nature's decree:
    Where life is, love can be.

Come, haste your dull doleful creed to forsake,
To brighter faiths let your spirits awake,
Nor doubt that towards a heaven-lov'd end
    All joyful things will tend.

Then silence not the voice
That would in glee rejoice,
Nor dim in darksome night
Eyes made to bask in light;
Hush not the silv'ry note
That falls from Mirth's gay throat,
But when the maid thou hast,
    O hold her fast!

No wanton sprite is she,
That would avoided be,
But in each guileless breast
A gladly harbour'd guest;
Love that hath such bridesmaid,
By her more lovely's made—
Blest, where in cot or hall,
    Joy's footsteps fall.

And oft, when adrift in thought's rudderless boat,
    Calmly we float
    From life's noise remote,
Across the still waters her bright glances beam,
And bathe all in sunlight our dream.
Or when at Humanity's glorious shrine
    Men's hearts entwine
    In love half-divine,
'Tis joy that her glow to our pulses imparts,
And throbs in our grateful hearts.
    O rejoice! Heart and voice
    Raise to heav'n above, laud the Source of Love.
    He is good, great and wise;
    Wraft from earth to skies
    Hymns of gratitude!
Now to the gay dance's rhythmical sound
See the golden-haired hours circle round,
While our thoughts in harmonious rhyme
To their soul-stirring cadence keep time!
Stealing us far from the sorrows of life,
Shedding balm o'er its heart-paining strife,
Guiding gently to sweet spots of rest
For the heart that with gladness is blest!
    Joy and song
    Be our theme life-long,
    And in jocund strain
    Sound again the refrain!
    Sing and laugh, laugh and sing—
    Come what fate may bring!
    Let joy's paeans rise
    In glad songs to the skies!
        Then sing, yes sing, O sing!

GOD SAVE THE QUEEN.

event_2_section_1.additional_information:
とき：18世紀のなかごろ
ところ：ナポリ

event_2_section_1_perf_1.additional_information: 幕があがるとナポリのカフィー。ナポリに住む2人の青年士官フェルランドとグリエルモが、年老いた哲学者のドン・アルフォンソと女性の貞節について論争している。まずフェルランドが、自分は恋人のドラベルラを絶対に信頼しているというと、グリエルモもまけじとばかり自分の恋人フィオルディリージの様をたたえる。2人の青年士官の恋に浮かされた熱っぽい話をきいたドン・アルフォンソは、かつて若いころその道で苦労したことがあるだけに、2人の青年の話がおかしくて仕方がない。そこで彼は、女は移り気なもので、フィオルディリージとドラベルラ姉妹とで例外ではない、と強く主張する。すると2人の士官は立腹してその証拠を出すようにドン・アルフォンソに追り、あげくの果て決斗を挑む。しかしアルフォンソは平然としたもので、2人の青年の人のよさを笑う。ついに青年士官たちと老哲学者の間に奇妙な賭けが成立し、どちらが正しいか決着をつけようということになる。賭することにあたってアルフォンソが出した条件は、2人の士官はこの賭のことを恋人たちに一切秘密にすること、これから24時間、何事も自分の指示に従うこと、というものであった。賭に勝つことをすこしも疑わない2人の青年は、その条件を受け入れ、賭勝って大金がころがり込んだら盛大な宴会を催そうと相談しながら、愛の女神を請えて乾杯する。

event_2_section_1_perf_2.performance_name: ナポリ湾を見下す庭園の場
event_2_section_1_perf_2.additional_information: ここは見晴らしのいいフィオルディリージ、ドラベルラ姉妹の家の庭。フィオルディリージとドラベルラが、お互いの恋人の肖像の描かれているメダルを見ながら、恍惚として恋人のことを考えていると、アルフォンソが、あわてた様子でやってきて、フェルランドとグリエルモの2人がすぐに戦場に行けなくなればならなくなったと告げる。あまり突然のことでぼう然とする姉妹。やがてアルフォンソの招きの声に応じて、出発の準備を整えた2人の士官が姿をみせる。2組の恋人たちは、思いがけない突然の別離を悲しみ合う。いよいよアルフォンソの工作がはじまったのである。

event_2_section_1_perf_3.additional_information: 遠くから行進曲が聞こえ、出征する兵士たちを讃える歌が力強く歌われる。頃はよしと、アルフォンソは2人の士官に出発を命ずる。これが計略とは知らないフィオルディリージとドラベルラは、「この胸は張り裂けるばかり……」と歌うが、2人の士官は、この歌に合わせていかにも悲しそうに芝居をしてみせる。そばではアルフォンソが「おかしくて死にそうだ」といしながら、自分の計画がうまく図にあたったことを喜んでいる。やがて2人の士官は出発し、その姿を見送りながら、フィオルディリージ、ドラベルラ姉妹とドン・アルフォンソは、それぞれの気持を三重唱で歌う。

event_2_section_1_perf_4.additional_information:
女中のデスピーナがチョコレートを作っている。そこに恋人を見送ったフィオルディリージとドラベルラが入ってくる。ドラベルラはデスピーナが差し出したチョコレートの盆をひっくり返したうえ、恋人と別れた悲しみを歌う。するとデスピーナは、男は他にいくらでもいるし、それに男、とりわけ軍人は浮気であてにならないものであるから、私たち女も負けずに大いに浮気しましょう、と姉妹を元気づける。
さて、姉妹が退場した隙に、ドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、デスピーナに取り入り、自分がつれてきた2人のアルバニアの貴族と姉妹の仲を取り持つことを引き受けさせる。このアルバニアの貴族というのが、実は変装したフェルランドとグリエルモである。アルフォンソがこの奇妙な変装した2人の男をデスピーナに紹介してから身を隠すと、姉妹が部屋に帰ってきて、見知らぬ奇妙な男が2人いるのを見て驚ろく。2人の貴族は、アルフォンソのいいつけ通りに、燃ゆる想いを姉妹に打ち明けるけれど、2人は服を立てて見向きもしない。するとそこにドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、アルバニアの貴族は懐しい旧友であるといって姉妹に紹介する。2人の男はそれに力を得て、さらに恋の言葉を述べ立てるけれど、姉妹はまるで取り合わず、自分たちは恋人がいて、しかも自分たちの愛は絶対に揺がないものである、と歌う。それを聞いて2人の貴族、すなわち変装したフェルランドとグリエルモは勝ち誇って退場する。あとに残ったドン・アルフォンソは新しい計略を思いつき、それをデスピーナに伝える。

event_2_section_1_perf_5.additional_information: ここから第一幕のフィナーレとなる。フィオルディリージとドラベルラが、恋のほかなさを嘆いていると、アルバニアの貴族に変装したフェルランドとグリエルモが、手に毒薬のピンをもち、いかにも毒薬を飲んだかのようによろめきながら出てくる。それを追ってドン・アルフォンソがあわてた様子でやってくる。突然の騒ぎに姉妹が驚いていると、ドン・アルフォンソは2人の命がないといってデスピーナとともに医者を呼び出てゆく。やがてドン・アルフォンソは医者をつれて帰ってくるがこの医者が実は女中のデスピーナである。彼女は磁石を使って怪しげな治療をほどこし2人の貴族の命をとりとめる。われにかえった2人の若者は、ふたたび恋の芝居をはじめるが、姉妹はまだ心を動かす気配はない。

event_2_section_2_perf_1.additional_information: 女中の姿に戻ったデスピーナは、手を変え、品を変え、真節などというもののはもう時代遅れのたわ言ですよ、と主人である姉妹に吹きこむので、ついに姉妹は、それでは2人のアルバニア人に会ってみようという気持になる。すかさずデスピーナは、娘は年頃になったら男を御する術を覚えなくてはいけません、と歌って姉妹の気持を焚きつける。アルバニアの貴族の自殺さわぎ以来、かなり気持の動いていた妹のドベルラは、デスピーナの巧妙なワナにかかって、ちょっとした浮気なら構わないだろうと思うようになり、その浮気の相手にグリエルモの変装したアルバニア貴族を選ぶことにする。そして妹にも浮気をすすめるので、フィオルディリージは妹の恋人フェルランドを浮気の相手にすることになる。姉妹が意見の一致を見、恋愛遊戯の楽しさを歌っているところにドン・アルフォンソがやってきて、姉妹を庭園に誘い出す。

event_2_section_2_perf_2.performance_name: ナポリ湾を見下す庭園の場
event_2_section_2_perf_2.additional_information: アルバニア貴族に変装したフェルランドとグリエルモが、姉妹にセレナード、つまり愛の歌を歌ってきさせ、やがて庭に入ってくる。するとデスピーナはドベルラの手をとってグリエルモのそばに連れてゆき、ドン・アルフォンソはフィオルディリージの手をとってフェルランドのそばに連れてゆく。そうしてデスピーナとドン・アルフォンソはわざとその場を外してしまう。

event_2_section_2_perf_3.additional_information: やがて2人のアルバニア貴族は、それぞれ相手に愛の告白をはじめる。まず妹のドベルラが誘惑に負けて、〈恋人を得たいまは死んでも悔いはない〉とグリエルモと二重唱しながら、手に手を取って退場する。いっぽうフィオルディリージは誘惑に負けかかるが、やっとのことで思いとどまる。しかし誘惑に負けかったことを後悔して、〈ああ、許して恋人よ〉とその気持を歌う。誘惑に失敗したフェルランドは、グリエルモから自分の恋人ドベルラが心変わりしたことを聞いて、信頼を裏切られたことを嘆き悲しむ。

event_2_section_2_perf_4.additional_information: 誘惑に負けたドベルラは、しきりに姉フィオルディリージに恋の楽しさを吹聴する。フィオルディリージは心を動かされながらも、戦地にいるグリエルモのことが気になってなかなかふんざりがつかない。ドベルラは何事も決心が大切だと〈恋は曲者〉と楽しそうに歌って部屋から出ていく。気持の追いつめられたフィオルディリージは、恋人を追って戦地に行こうとするが、そこにフェルランドがやってきて、以前より一層熱烈に恋の想いを打ち明けるので、すさがのフィオルディリージもついに気持が動いて、誘惑に負けてしまう。これをみたドン・アルフォンソは、わが計略成れりとばかり、すぐ結婚したほうがいいと入れ智恵する。そしてフィオルディリージとドベルラ姉妹は、以前の恋人を捨てて、新しい求婚者と結婚する決心をしてしまう。

event_2_section_2_perf_5.additional_information:
第二幕のフィナーレ、大詰めである。
式場の飾りつけがすむと、行進曲に合わせて2組の新郎新婦が登場する。すると公証人に変装したデスピーナが入って来て、結婚契約書を読みあげる。2組の新郎新婦は間違いのないことを確かめたうえで、それに署名する。ところがそのとき、勇ましい合唱が聞こえてくる。何事かと窓際に様子を見に行ったドン・アルフォンソは、一同に、フェルランドとグリエルモが帰ってきたことを知らせるので、2人のアルバニア貴族は急いで別室に逃れ去る。そしてすぐに軍服に着かえて、何喰わぬ顔で驚きあわてる姉妹の前にふたたび姿を現す。2人の士官は、さっさと署名したばかりの結婚契約書を手に入れ、これは一体何なのか、と大いに立腹した振りをする。気の毒なのは2人の姉妹で、彼女たちは〈こんなことなら一息に死んだほうがよい〉と嘆くと、2人の士官はアルバニア貴族に、デスピーナは医者に変装して出てくるので、やっと真相を知った姉妹は、取すかしさに耐えられない。しかし勝ち勝ったドン・アルフォンソが、女だって結局は生身の人間、女だけが悪いのではないと、巧妙なさばきで2組の恋人たちを元どおり円満に伸直りさせ、楽しいアンサンブルのうちに最後の幕が下りる。

event_11_section_1_perf_1.lyrics_transcript:
"O WHERE hae ye been, my long lost lover,
This seven lang years and mair?"
"O I'm come again to seek your love,
An' the vows that ye did swear."
"Now haud your tongue o' my love and vows,
For they can breed but strife;
Now haud your tongue o' my former vows,
For I am another man's wife."
"O fause are the vows o' womankind,
But fair is their fause bodie;
I wad never hae trodden on Irish ground,
Were it no for the love o' thee."
"Ye may leave your husband to himsel',
And your little son also,
And sail wi' me across the sea,
Sae fair the wind doth blow."
"See ye not seven pretty ships,
The eighth brought me to land,
With merchandise and mariners,
And music on every hand?"
"There's mantles warm to wrap my love,
O' the silk and soft velvet,
And rich attires to deck her head,
And costly shoon for her feet."
"O how do you like the ship?" he said,
"Or how do you like the sea?
And how do you like the bold mariners
That wait upon thee and me?"
"O weel I like the ship," she said,
"And weel I like the sea,
But where are a' your mariners?
I see nane but thee and me."
They hadna sailed a league, a league,
A league, but barely three,
When eerie grew the lift above,
And gurly grew the sea.
She hadna sailed a league, a league,
A league, but barely three,
When she espied the cloven hoof,
And wept right bitterlie.
"O what are yon, yon pleasant hills,
That the sun shines sweetly on?"
"O yon are the hills of heaven," he said
"Where you will never win."
"O whatna mountain is yon," she said,
"Sae dreary wi' frost and snow?"
"O yon is the mountain o' hell," he cried,
"Where you and I maun go."
The clouds grew black, and the wind grew loud,
And the levin filled her e'e;
And wesome wailed the snow-white sprites,
Out o'er the roaring sea.
He struck the mainmast wi' his hand,
The foremast wi' his knee;
He split the gallant ship in twain,
And sank her in the sea.

event_1_section_1_perf_4.additional_information:
(Faust, Part 2, Act 3.) (Composed specially for and dedicated to the Melbourne Liedertafel.) Life presented itself to the Greek mind as a series of manifestations of Power Omnipotent, irresistible, irrevocable, first in the order of forces, loom'd Fate, then the gods, the ancestral heroes, and the pre-eminent men of the times. Each State, surrounded by enemies, depended for its safety on the courage and power of its citizens, whom a reverse of war would convert into slaves with their wives and children. The actual experience of the Power and Tragedy of human existence, which to our modern comfortable plebian semi-vegetable life are almost unintelligible, lent an intensity to the moment which we can but faintly imagine. Power and its limitation were equally displayed in the sudden plunge from the height of prosperity to the depth of woe, and to find expression in the never equalled strength and restraint of Greek art, imparting a reverential solemnity even to its most joyous utterances. This is the key note of their art, energetic power, and fate:

Fate, whose horizons, narrowing from afar
Within their blind abysmal night immerse
Both gods and men, and all things else that be
In irremediable catastrophe.

In the following ode from Goethe's masterpiece, these qualities are passionately felt by one who was himself a Greek at heart though born in a barbarian age. The music is an endeavour to complete and enforce the poet's intention. The serenity, not untinged with a certain noble sadness, of the first stanza, is contrasted with those following, in which the power and majesty and terrible presence of the gods is imaged, to which succeeds the picture of limited fettered humanity.

event_1_section_1_perf_5.additional_information: In the Passacaglia we see, from a single idea by a development gradual, but resistless as fate, the growth of a huge superstructure almost overpowering in its nobility and grandeur, suggesting the unfolding of some mighty work of nature herself. When the watery ear-tickling organ music of the present age will have vanished into oblivion, such works as this will stand as the eternal monument to the imperishable glory of Bach.

event_1_section_1_perf_7.additional_information:
No. 1—Allegro molto. No. 2—Allegretto. In the wonderfully expressive and characteristic music of the Hungarians we find preserved the nobler and more significant phases of the Dance, before it had been corrupted by civilised larrkinism, and whilst it still remained among the people at large the one means through which their natural feelings and instincts found expression.

Not only at one time was the Dance a religious rite, but also it fulfilled the present office of the drama, and became an artistic representation of human passion and action. In the course of the various figures through which the dancers went, the joy and woe, love and hate, hope and despair, of mankind were represented. Youths would woo and maidens would play the coquette.

In Brahms' music we find not only those poetical moods which it once was the object of the dance to portray, but a delightful suggestion of the picturesque character of the people, and the free, wild naive aspect of Nature, which nowhere assumes a more beautiful or striking aspect than in the country of the Maygars.

event_1_section_1_perf_8.lyrics_transcript:
If a youth should meet a maiden,
    Need she run away with fright;
If his looks should win her favour,
    Sure the girl may use her sight.
Tho' she must, in maiden manner,
    Seem her glances to conceal;
Where's the harm, if she, unnoticed,
    Strive a sidelong look to steal.
Should perchance their eyes encounter,
    I no guilt therein can find;
Tho' her cheeks may blush a little,
    Yet it will not strike her blind.
Looking hither, looking thither,
    Looks are followed soon by sighs;
He sighs fairest, she smiles dearest,
    Soon a marriage we will see.
Come around me, dear companions,
    Would you like to see me bride?
Am I not a pretty maiden,
    And he is a smart young boy.

event_1_section_1_perf_9.lyrics_transcript:
A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
    Cries "Boatman, do not tarry!
And I'll give thee a silver pound
    To row us o'er the ferry."

"Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle
    This dark and stormy water?"
"Oh, I'm the chief of Ulvas' Isle,
    And this, Lord Ullin's daughter."

And fast before her father's men,
    Three days we've fled together,
And should he find us in the glen,
    My blood would stain the heather.

His horsemen hard behind us ride;
    Should they our steps discover,
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
    When they have slain her lover?

Out spake the hardy highland wight,
    "I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
    But for your winsome lady.

And by my word, the bonny bird
    In danger shall not tarry,
So though the waves are raging white,
    I'll row you o'er the ferry."

By this the storm grew loud apace,
    The water wraith was shrieking,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
    Grew dark as they were speaking.

But still as wilder blew the wind,
    And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
    Their tramping sounded nearer.

"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
    "Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
    But not an angry father."

The boat has left the stormy land,
    A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
    The tempest gather'd o'er her.

And still they rowed amidst the roar
    Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
    His wrath was changed to wailing.

For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
    He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
    And one was round her lover.

"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

'Twas vain: the loud waves lashed the shore,
    Return or aid preventing,
The waters wild went o'er his child,
    And he was left lamenting.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
The Chorus sing the praises of Colonos.

THOU comest here to the land, O friend,
Fam'd for fleet-footed steeds and blooming meadows;
Thou standest now in Colonos' grove,
Where the voices of nightingales
Resound, floating in dulcet strains
Thro' their temples of verdure;
Where the thick-woven ivy clings,
Spreading over the sacred aisles;
Where, in security, ripens the fruitful vine,
Unscath'd by beam or stormwind.
And here roameth the bounteous god
Gay and good Dionysos, ever greeted in lays,
Sung by the nymphs who rear'd him.

Fair and fragrant at dawn of day
See the beautiful heaven-bedewed Narcissus,
The flow'r that shone in the goddesses' crowns,
Worn by them in the days of old.
See the Crocus array'd in gold:
    Hear the slumberless waters,
While they glide in Cephisus' tide.
Still meandering day by day
Over the plains, bearing streams ever pure along,
    Enriching all the bowers
Embosomed in the favour'd land;
Ever loved by the tuneful choir of Muses,
    And Cythera, whose zone is golden.

Here, too, bloometh a tree
Crowned with a fruit not found in Asia;
Nor on Dorian plains doth it appear,
Gracing the island where the Pelops
Held sway; yet here it freely springeth;
    Rever'd by friends; and fear'd by foes,
    In native splendour it blossoms for Athens.
Behold ours is the rich oil-dropping olive!
    Aged and youthful, noble and peasant,
Never wantonly harm this holy tree.
    Guarded and cherished, it stands secure,
Ever heeded by Morian Jove.
    Lov'd and watch'd by Minerva,

Grateful, let me extol
Heaven's richest gifts designed to my country;
Presented by the Pow'r making our State
Fam'd for its wealth, honour, and glory:
    Our land and sea steeds, rein and rudder guided;
    O Chronos' son, by them we stand pre-eminent.
    Mighty god Poseidon,
Thou didst give us the rein form'd for the courser;
Guided thus, or curbed, he yields obedience.
Through the billows we dash, stemming the deep,
    Speeded along by the oar and helm,
    Bounding on with the dancing nymphs—
Nereus' hundred-footed daughters.

The Athenians are successful, and Thesens returns with Antigone and Ismene. Oedipus expresses his gratitude to the King, who announces the arrival of Polynices seeking an interview with his father. The chorus describes the sorrows of life, and the blessing of death when old age has come.

When the health and the strength are gone
He that still would be lingering here,
Borne down by a load of care,
Is, I consider, devoid of wisdom
Old age bringeth disease and pain,
Grief, anguish and regret remain.

For youth's bloom and its fleeting joys
Never, never return again.
Life's varied journeys lead to death;
Smooth or rugged, all its pathways,
Even its wishes, end in Hades.
Love hymeneal, revels, dances, strains of music
    Cease, when the Foe appeareth!

Better not to exist;
Or, if born, in early childhood to die,
And escape all the cares and pains.
They, living longest, endure the longest.
Youth and Folly and Sorrow roam
Hand in hand to their destined home:
For none liveth devoid of care;
None escapeth what all must bear.
Envy, Sedition, Murder, Strife,
Fear and Rage hover around us:
And, in conclusion, feeble, helpless,
Old and friendless, all these ills together meeting
    Crush their devoted victim.

On man, poor mourner, all these evils fall.
Fall as billows rushing beat the north strand,
Dashing onward, urged by the blast of winter.
Thus, then, storms of affliction, never-ending, assail us.
    Thus lowering sorrows around us gather;
    Whether from Helios' western bound,
        Or from his eastern gate,
        Or where his rays beam brightest,
        Or down from the home of Arcturus.

Theseus, followed by the citizens of Athens, again appears, and learning what Creon has done, sends for soldiers and renews his promises of protection to Oedipus, declaring that his daughters shall be restored to him, and that Creon shall not be allowed to bring such a disgrace upon Athens. The chorus describes the contest, and invokes the aid of the Gods in favour of Theseus and his followers.

    Ah, were I on yonder plain,
    Where now our undaunted sons
        Stand arm'd for the hostile fray;
    There, where the shrine of Phoebus gleams,
        And torches are burning;
    Where Mortals bow down to the awe-inspiring pair,
        Whose hallowed rites are mystic deeds,
        Wrought by Eumolpidan priests,
        And never breath'd to mortal ear.
    There, glowing with ardour,
        Panting to rush agains the foe,
        See, see all our legions,
    With Theseus they wave their swords, and cry.
        Rescue the sisters!

Or westward perchance they rush,
Where snow-cover'd mountains rise
O'er Gea's enamelled meads!
There dancing cars and prancing steeds
Will clash in the onset!
There on the foe soon will impending vengeance fall,
For Theseus leads our valiant bands:
See their arms and armour gleaming
Bright as the trappings that grace their steeds!
Now proudly exulting,
They, who honour the deeds of sage Minerva,
And Rhea's great son, earth encircling ocean's king,
Press to the battle!
Do they await, pursue or fight?
My heart thrills with hope
That they will soon rescue the captive maid,
Who hath endur'd, and still endures her kindred's woe.
This day, Jove will restore her.
Crown your deeds, heroes, with glory!
Like a dove high soaring,
Sped along by the storm-wind,
I, from the verge of a cloud,
Would look down on the contest,
And see my country's cause triumphant!
Dread Pow'r that fillest heaven's high throne,
O all-seeing Jove, defend our great ruler!
On him the victor's palm bestow!
With verdant laurels deck his brow!
We call on thee, Pallas Athena!
Mighty hunter, Phoebus, hear us!
And thy sister, fleet in chase, whose dart unerring
Pierceth the far-distant hart:
O come, defend our guardians!
We pray ye, aid our native heroes!

performance_5.additional_information: A. Borodin; The Melbourne Orchestral Society; Into the silence of the monotonous Steppes of Middle Asia come the first echoes of a peaceful Russian song. In the distance sound the trampling of horses and camels and the strange cries of the Orient. Under the protection of the Russian flag it moves safely on its weary journey through the immeasurable waste. It recedes further and further. The songs of Russia and the wild notes of the East merge into the solemn harmony of nature, slowly sinking into the echoes of the eternal Steppes.

performance_7.additional_information:
Max Bruch; Soprano Soloist: Miss Lilian Reid; Baritone Soloist: Mr. Horace Stevens; The Royal Victorian Liedertafel and Orchestra. The story of Frithjof the Bold and Ingeborg the Fair is told in "Frithjof's Saga," a poem in twenty-four cantos, by Esaias Tegner, published in 1820.

The hero, Frithjof, is son to Thorsten Vikingsson, who, though King Bele's best warrior and chosen friend, is of lowly origin. Frithjof the Strong and Bold dares to love Fair Ingeborg, daughter of his king and descendant of great Odin. Bele looks kindly on young Frithjof's love, but death takes from the youth at once a monarch and a friend. When Frithjof subsequently demands the hand of Ingeborg from Helge, son and successor of Bele, he is rejected with scorn. Later, old King Ring, a mighty monarch of the North, would make fair Ingeborg his queen, but Helge, influenced by soothsayers, sends a refusal, accompanied by a taunting message from brother Halfdan, to "Old Grey-beard." King Ring incensed, declares war against the brothers, and Ingeborg is sent for safety to the vale of Baldur, the god of innocence and virtue. While in the sacred grove, the maiden receives a visit from her lover, the joy of which is followed by the fear that she has angered the gods by keeping a love-tryst in that holy place. At a council of war assembled at Bele's cairn, Frithjof again demands from Helge the hand of Ingeborg, in return for which he offers his best aid in the impending battle. Helge again repels him, and forces him to make the fatal admission that he has visited Ingeborg in the sacred grove. He thereupon denounces him as a profaner of temples, and orders him to do penance for his sacrilege by sailing to the Orkneys to wring from fierce Earl Agantyr long-withheld tribute. Frithjof tries to persuade Ingeborg to fly with him, but in vain. Giving her his arm-ring, he departs, promising to return and make her his bride.

Borne through his perilous voyage by his charmed ship "Ellida," Frithjof returns at length to his native land to find his estates laid waste with fire and sword, and the fair Ingeborg given in marriage to victorious King Ring. He learns that at the marriage ceremony the cowardly Helge tore from his sister's arm her lover's ring, and hung it upon the arm of Baldur's image. Frithjof, furious, seeks out the King whilst he is in the act of offering sacrifice at Baldur's pyre. He flings Agantyr's tribute full in Helge's face, and, hastily snatching at the arm ring, he overturns the huge idol upon the sacred fire. The flames lap it about, and, leaping upward with angry roar, spread to the temple and the sacred grove, which are soon reduced to ashes.

Frithjof is now shunned by all as a perpetrator of sacrilege; he is banished from his country, and, sailing away in the "Ellida," he devotes himself to a life of wild adventure. The hero's troubled life is ultimately crowned with happiness. After many years he returns to his native land, and succeeds in gaining the goodwill of King Ring, who at his death bequeaths him his kingdom and his queen.

Bruch, Max, musical composer, born at Cologne 6th January, 1838, received his first musical instruction from his mother (nee Almenrider), who was a highly-esteemed teacher of music, and who often in her young days sang at the Rhenish musical festivals. At the age of eleven Bruch, then a pupil of Karl Breidenstein, attempted compositions on a large scale, and at the age of fourteen he had already brought out a Symphony at Cologne. From 1853 to 1857 he held the Mozart Scholarship at Cologne, and in that capacity he was a special pupil of Ferdinand Hiller in the theory of music and composition; and of Karl Reinecke (till 1854), and of Ferdinand Breunung in playing the piano. After a short stay in Leipzig, he resided from 1858 to 1861 as musical teacher at Cologne, and was very assiduous in composing. On the death of his father, in 1861 he set out on an extensive tour of study, which, after brief stays at Berlin, Leipzig, Vienna, Dresden, and Munich, ended at Mannheim, where his opera "Lorelei" (after the text written by Geibel for Mendelssohn) was produced in 1863. At Mannheim also, between 1862 and 1864, he wrote the chorus-works, "Frithjof," "Römischer Triumphgesang," "Gesang der heiligen drei Könige," and "Flucht der heiligen Familie." In 1864-65 he was again on his travels, visiting Hamburg, Hanover, Dresden, Breslau, Munich, Brussels, and Paris. Then he brought out his "Frithjof" with extraordinary success at Aix-la-Chapelle, Leipzig, and Vienna. From 1865 to 1867 he was musical director at Coblenz, and from 1867 to 1870 director of the court choir at Sonderhausen. At Coblenz he wrote, among other things, his well-known first concerto for the violin, and at Sonderhausen two symphonies and portions of a Mass. The opera "Hermione," which was produced in 1872 at Berlin, where Bruch resided from 1871 to 1873, had only a succès d'estime. The chorus "Odysseus" likewise belongs to the period of the composer's residence at Berlin. After he had been five years (1873-78) at Bonn, devoting his time exclusively to composing "Arminius," "The Song of the Bell," and his second concerto for the violin, and after he had paid two visits to England for the purpose of producing some of his works, he became in 1878, on the resignation of Hockhausen, Director of Stern's Singing Academy at Berlin; and in 1880 he was nominated to succeed Sir Julius Benedict as Director of the Philharmonic Society at Liverpool.
