performance_7.additional_information: FRITHJOF'S RETURN.

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
How bravely o'er the floods so bright,
Ellida flies to shore now in sight!
Although the king with demon spell
Invoked the horrid goblin brood,
And unloosed the wings of the tempest,
My Northland courage bore me
Through ardent strife
To glory's height;
From mighty Jarl the tribute I obtained!

I greet thee gladly, Baldur's grove,
Where oft by break of night
Hope filled my heart with sweet delight!
My Ingeborg, but where art thou now?
Beloved maiden, art thou true to me?
See I vie with the winds and their heavenly train.
Ellida, O hasten and fly o'er the main.

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
Oh, 'tis delight when the land afar appeareth,
And from the hearth of thy home beloved
The smoke curls upwards
And thou art near to childhood's scenes
For ever dear.

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
On the tomb of my father I planted the lime-tree,
Is the delicate stem still alive?
Give, earth, thy growth,
And thou, O heaven, send fostering dew.
Oh 'tis delight!

performance_11.additional_information: INGEBORG'S BRIDAL PROCESSION TO KING RING.

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
Sadly the Skald walks before the train.
Pale sits the bride on the coal black palfrey;
The angry Norna her arrow darteth.
She rules the mortals,
As their lot is cast.
From thunder-clouds ruin falls at last.

performance_14.lyrics_transcript:
My heart with sorrow overflowing,
Heeds not the flowers entwined with my ringlets;
Forever away from my home I go,
By my brother forced to wed his foe!
An endless woe in my bosom burneth,
But Bele's daughter pity spurneth!
Yet bear to Frithjof greetings from Ingeborg!
Great is my grief but I do not hate.
All-father judges
I bear my fate.

performance_16.lyrics_transcript:
Midnight sun on the mountain burns,
Red like blood appearing,
And through the strange mysterious light
Helge's train is nearing.
Lo, he comes, while the glare is spread,
Splendid crown adorns his head,
Helge, mighty monarch!

performance_17.lyrics_transcript:
Go to Hela's dark abode,
    Seek ye there the mighty rover;
Slain upon the horse he rode -
    Helge's life is over!

performance_19.lyrics_transcript:
Hush, wretched priests with gory knives,
    Moonlight's pallid princes!
Hush! or tremble for your lives,
    Long our blades have thirsted!
Where my father rests,
Where my childhood passed.
Nought save a ruin I found aghast!
And sold to the foe my beloved bride.
    The armlet, which to her I left,
Behold, now the God wears it proudly,
    And she is bereft!
Ah, Baldur! is this thy valiant deed?
By theft this armlet was given to thee!
Thou must, O Baldur, restore it to me!
How dar'st thou hold this ring in thy keeping,
Which once my Ingeborg blessed with weeping,
    No longer on thine arm it shall rest!
My hope, my joy, thou could'st destroy,
But, mind! not me shalt thou decoy!

performance_20.lyrics_transcript:
Woe! he tugs with all his might at the ring—O fright!
Ah! the God, now filled with wrath,
'Midst the flames is rushing,
And the consecrated hearth
    By his weight is crushing.
    Fane in flames!
    Pour water on!
The waves of the sea bring hither!
Lo! clouds of smoke are bursting forth,
Morning winds blow from the North!
How the flames are glaring!
What availleth human might!
Now from branch to branch they spring
Through the combat daring!
Blazing flames in the grove abound
Onward like rivers flowing
Sunlight smileth,
But fjord and sound
Blood-red with fire are glowing.
    Woe! Woe! Woe!

performance_21.lyrics_transcript: Mischief bringer! malediction on thy head! accurs'd!

performance_22.lyrics_transcript:
Mount, smoke, and upwards to heaven ascending,
    Valhalla enter, Valhalla enter.
Cry to the Gods, who o'er earth are bending.
And thou, O flame, the deed proclaim,
Fly, and proclaim to the Gods the accursed deed!

performance_25.lyrics_transcript:
Sun in the sky
Now mounteth high,
The winds are blowing
And gently flowing,
The waves advance
In joyful dance.

performance_26.lyrics_transcript:
Sadly Frithjof goes his way;
See, he weepeth, while morning gloweth!

performance_27.lyrics_transcript:
World's grandest region, thou mighty North,
From thy dominions I'm driven forth.
Within thy borders I lov'd to dwell!
Midsummer sun, fare thee well!
My love is foiled, my rooftree rent!
With honour soiled, in exile sent!
Cheerless is my soul within me,
Hopeless I must bear my lot.

Ye rugged mountains where heroes dwell,
And Thor commandeth clouds and winds;
Ye azure lakes that I love so well.
Ye woods and brakes, fare ye well!

performance_29.lyrics_transcript:
Storms wildly roar!
Billows break madly upon the shore.
Would 'neath the sod I were lying.
Winds o'er me sighing!
Sad and oppress,
Thee I did watch, flying sail in the west!
Onward with Frithjof thou glidest,
With him abidest.
Falcon, beloved! thee he left here;
Falcon, for his sake to me thou art dear.
Shake not thy pinions, stay near me,
O, why should'st thou fear me?

Here on his hand,
Worked on the canvas, thou proudly shall stand,
Silver thy pinions unfolden;
Thy claws shall be golden.
Thou darling bird!
Sit on my shoulder, and list to my word!
When I'm no more.
He will come hither, and his heart will be sore:
Greet from me. Frithjof,
Who loves me, and never forgets me.

performance_31.lyrics_transcript:
Now he crossed the floods of the salt desert waste,
Far off like a falcon he flew!
But for warriors on board, he wrote maxims and rules!
List to the laws of his crew!

performance_32.lyrics_transcript:
On this deck raise no tent,
And ashore do not sleep;
    Within houses the foe lurks for thee!
On thy shield sleep, Viking,
Thy sword in thy hand;
    Let the heavens thy canopy be.
Now hold high your lances—
    Your lances hold high—
Our banners unfold ye,
    The triumph is nigh.
To climes of the south we shall wander.
When hurricanes rage,
    Hoist the canvas on high!
Let them come as they may,
    He who flinches must die.
Rise, rise, unfold ye our banners!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Gurnemanz—
From bathing comes the king again,
    High stands the sun now:
So let me to the holy feast conduct thee,
    For, an thou'st pure:
The Grail will surely feed and refresh thee.

Parsifal—
What is the Grail?

Gurnem.—
I may not say;
But if to serve it thou art bidden,
Knowledge of it will not be hidden.
And lo! methinks I know thee now indeed,
No earthly road to it doth lead;
By no one can it be detected,
Who by itself is not elected.

Parsifal—
I scarcely move, yet swiftly seem to run.

Gurnem.—
My son, thou see'st,
Here space and time are one.
Now give good heed and let me see,
If thou'rt a fool and pure,
What wisdom thou can'st presently secure.

The Knights of the Grail—
The holy supper daily prepare we day by day,
As on that last time truly, the soul it still may stay.
Who lives to do good deeds,
This meal for ever feeds;
The cup his hand may lift,
And claim the purest gift.

Chorus—
As anguished and lowly,
His life stream's spilling for sinners
    He did offer.
For the saviour holy,
I now with heart free and willing my blood will proffer.
His body given our sins to shrive,
Through death becomes in us alive.
His love endures, the dove up-soars,
    The saviour's sacred token:
Take the wine red, for you it was shed,
    Let bread of life be broken!

Alti and Tenori—
Take my body and eat,
Take and drink my blood.
    Thus be our love remembered.

Soprani and Alti—
Take my body and eat,
Take and drink my blood,
    Do this and think of me.

Titurel—
Celestial rapture!
How light now the looks of the Lord!

Soprani and Alti—
Wine and Bread the Grail's Lord changed,
Which at that last meal was ranged,
    Through his pity's loving tide,
When he shed for you his gore,
    And his body crucified.
Blood and body which he offered,
Changed to food for you are proffered,
    By the Saviour ye revere,
In the wine which now ye pour,
    And the bread ye eat of here.

Tenori and Bussi—
Take of this bread, change it again,
    Your powers of body firing,
Living and dead, strive might and main,
    To work out the Lord's desiring.
Take of this wine, change it anew,
    To life's impetuous torrent,
Gladly combine, brothers so true,
    To fight as your duty shall warrant.

Chorus—
Blest in love and believing!
By pity lightened, the guileless fool,
    Blessed believing!
performance_1.additional_information: A Festival Drama By RICHARD WAGNER. WAGNER was sixty-five years old when he began the music of "Parsifal"—the poem of which he had published in 1877. This Festival Drama occupied him until April 1879, while the instrumentation was finished at Palermo, January 15th, 1882. "Parsifal" was first produced in July 1882. Wagner has certainly in "Parsifal" succeeded in giving the most exquisite expressions to the deepest religious feeling—for Parsifal is really an allegorical personification of Christ—and, if we consider religious feeling the most exalted of all emotions, we must agree that Wagner in "Parsifal" struck finer chords than in any other of his works. The "Forspiel" is based on three of the most deeply religious motives in the entire work. It opens with the Motive of the Sacrament. Through this motive we gain insight into the office of the Knights of the Grail, who from time to time strengthen themselves for their spiritual duties by partaking of the Communion, on which occasions the Grail itself is uncovered. The Second Motive is indicative of the Grail, and the trumpets announce the third—the Motive of Faith. The plot of "Parsifal" is briefly as follows:—Amfortas, as King of the Knights of the Holy Grail, who dwell in the castle of Montsalvat among the mountains of Gothic Spain, is enticed by Kundry, a lovely woman under the sway of Klingsor, an evil magician on the southern slope of the same mountains, supposed to be facing Arabian Spain, into Klingsor's magic garden. While in her arms Amfortas drops the holy spear, which is at once seized by Klingsor, who wounds the King therewith, and carries it off. Amfortas cannot recover from the wound until it has been touched by the spear, which can be wrested from Klingsor only by "the guileless fool," one who has been all his life ignorant of sin, who through deep sympathy with the anguish of Amfortas becomes conscious of the King's sin, and can resist temptation though it come to him ever so enticingly. Such an one is Parsifal. By resisting Kundry's charms he regains the spear, destroys Klingsor, and thus frees Kundry from his evil sway, heals the wound of Amfortas, and is proclaimed King of the Knighthood. The plot is allegorical. Parsifal is the personification of Christianity, and the triumph of Parsifal over Klingsor is the triumph of Christianity over Paganism. The performance this afternoon will—after the Vorspiel—begin at a point in Act I, where the Knights of the Grail are to celebrate the Love Feast or Communion that day. Gurnemanz—an old but vigorous knight—bids the youthful Parsifal accompany him to the castle. Then occurs a change of scene which, in itself is highly effective dramatically. Long sustained trombone notes softly swell; approaching peals of bells are heard. At last Gurnemanz and Parsifal arrive at a mighty hall, which looms itself overhead in a high vaulted dome, down from which alone the light streams in. The change of scene is ushered in by the solemn BELL MOTIVE, which is the basis of the powerful Orchestral Interlude accompanying the Panorama, and also of the scene in the hall of the Grail Castle. King Amfortas gives way to violent grief and the MOTIVE OF CONTRITION graphically portrays his spiritual suffering. The MOTIVE OF THE SACRAMENT (followed by the BELL MOTIVE and the sonorous and powerful GRAIL MOTIVE) is succeeded by the Knights intoning the chorus, "To the last love feast," while the Orchestra plays a solemn processional based on the Bell Motive. Amfortas is borne in preceded by pages who bear the covered Grail. A chorus based upon the Motive of Contrition and then the Motive of Faith floats down from the dome in ethereal beauty as it sung by angel voices. Tortured by contrition the King refuses Titurel's summons to uncover the Grail. Comforting voices chant the prophecy of Amfortas' redemption through the Guileless Fool. The Grail is uncovered and the voices chant the chorus, "Take of my body, take of my blood, to the Sacrament Motive. Amfortas is bowed in prayer. Through the dusk a ray of brilliant light darts upon the Grail; Amfortas raises the Grail and blesses the wine and bread, all kneeling, while voices in the dome chant a chorus based on the Sacrament Motive. When it has been repeated, one-half of the Knights intone a chant, the Bell Motive solemnly accompanying it in the Orchestra, the other half chorus repeats the chant, and then the entire chorus takes up the Grail Motive. To the Faith Motive the congregation prepares to go. Amfortas bows his head and touches his wound, his action being accompanied by the Motive of Contrition in union with the Bell Motive. Parsifal presses his hand to his heart. We again hear the Motive of the Prophecy. The Grail and Bell Motives lead once more to the Prophecy, and the Act closes amid the spiritual harmonies of the Prophecy of the Guileless Fool and of the Grail Motive. A. Vorspiel for Orchestra alone. B. Verwandlungs—Musik und Schluss-Scene des 1ten Aktes. First production in Australia of the latter. The Knightly Brotherhood of the Grail, &c.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
BUT who goes there apart? In the brake his pathway is lost,
Close behind clash the branches together, the grass rises again,
the desert engulphs him.
Who can comfort his anguish?
Who, if balsam be deathly,
If the hate of men from the fulness of love be drained?

He that was scorned turned to scorner, lonely now devours all he hath of worth in a barren self-seeking.
But if from Thy Psalter all-loving Father one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart!
Lift up his o'er-clouded eyes where are the fountains hard by the thirsty one in the desert.
But if from Thy Psalter, all-loving Father, one strain can but come to his hearing,
Oh! enlighten his heart, enlighten his heart.
performance_2.additional_information: (Fragment aus Goethe's Harzreise im Winter), FOR Contralto Solo, Chorus of Men's Voices and Orchestra. BY JOHANNES BRAHMS. Op. 53. LIEDERTAFEL AND ORCHESTRA. SOLOIST - Miss ADA CROSSLEY. The deep majestic expression which the greatest musical classic of our time has given to the Words of Gustle, establishes the work under notice as one of the highest manifestations of lofty subjectivity and profound contemplation that we worship in art. The Solo voice is responsible for the text throughout. The entry of Tenors and Basses—each in two parts—is made at the words, "But if thy Psalter."

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
AND it was Olav Trygvason,
    Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
    Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom their dark crest rearing,
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land.
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard upleaping.
Yonder snow covered peaks o'er cloud bands peeping.

And it was Olav Trygvason,
    Suddenly he seemed to sight,
Towering temples, domes and spires,
    Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vow'd the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring.
Swayed in the stormy wind, the forest strangely was murmuring
Sounds as of churchbells chiming.
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator.
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.
    On to God! On to God!

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Chorus—

To Palestine, the Holy Land,
Where the Redeemer's cross did stand,
Be thou our host's commander!
Come all by Christian zeal impelled
In holy war the sword to wield,
And be our faith's defender.
God wills it!

Ludwig—

Assembled are my faithful vassals,
At my command, ere my departure,
That they may swear to me allegiance
For comfort in the hour of parting.
The call divine, the holy cities
From pagan hordes idolatrous to ransom,
Upon my soul has ceaseless pressed:
And yet I am filled with sorrow,
To leave ye, ah, my loved ones, here alone.
Elizabeth!—Swear unto me
That you will guard her truly as your ruler,
And stand by her in weal and woe to serve her.

Chorus—

She is all goodness, she is all beauty,
We swear to her allegiance and duty;
We stand by thee in weal and woe to serve,
We stand by thee to serve thee faithfully.

Ludwig—

Farewell, my wife!

Elizabeth—

Oh tarry!
O shorten not the hour,
The last sweet hour of gladness,
The last we pass together.
My inmost spirit tells me
That I in grief and pain
In vain shall wait the moment
That brings thee back again.
Ah! must thou then forsake me!

Ludwig—

'Twas thou, my love, who gav'st me
Those higher aspirations
Toward which my heart is yearning—
The thirst for self-devotion.

Elizabeth—

With grief my spirit wrestles,
But in my inmost soul
One only thought is borne me,
That I shall ceaseless mourn thee—
This only do I know.
Around my pathway evil
Spreads forth its wings with might,
No star of hope beams comfort
To guide me through the night.
I tremble, awed and fearful,
I wrestle, lone and tearful,
And fall beneath this crushing blow,
Seized by despair and woe!

Ludwig—

Where is thy courage, O my love,
Thine ardour, all thy holy trust?

Elizabeth—

Ah, let me weep upon thy breast!
See where thy children pleading stand,
In loving silence they implore thee,
As though their sad fate they foresaw.

Chorus of Crusaders—
To Palestine, the Holy Land!
God wills it!

Ludwig—
Hear'st thou the warning call? Farewell!
Farewell, for I must part from thee.

Chorus—
To Palestine, the Holy Land,
Be thou our host's commander!

Ludwig—
Farewell, my children, fare ye well,
May God's peace ever with you dwell!

Elizabeth—
Thou goest? O God!

Ludwig—
In prayer remember me!
I must fulfil the mission I have chosen;
Farewell, my wife, farewell!

Elizabeth—
He goes!
Alas, he goes! I have forever lost him!

Chorus—
Come, all by Christian zeal impelled
In holy war the sword to wield,
    And be our faith's defender!
        God wills it!
To Palestine, the Holy Land,
Where the Redeemer's cross did stand,
Come, all by Christian zeal impelled
In holy war the sword to wield!
        God wills it!

section_1.additional_information: Cantata "Harald's Bridal Voyage" / Heinrich Hofmann / (WITH ORCHESTRAL ACCOMPANIMENT) / Solos by Mr. A. H. Gee and Mr. Henry Rofe / Liedertafel

performance_1.additional_information: Heinrich Hofmann. (WITH ORCHESTRAL ACCOMPANIMENT). Solos by Mr. A. H. Gee and Mr. Henry Rofe. Liedertafel.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Up, up, and away, every sail widely spanned,
The anchor set free, and the yards all bemanned.
Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

High swells his heart, and he longs for the bride,
Her all of his soul and his life doth confide,
Beauteous will adorn her with purple and gold,
With gems and pearls as his queen enfold.

An island hides her in ocean afar,
There brightly she shines as a radiant star,
The Maid of the Sea, demons guard day and night,
But our hero will win her all valiant in might.

Yohio, yohi! wind, bear us a tide,
Guard us and the hero when storm billows ride.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
An Old Sailor:

Depart, farewell! thou'lt see this port aye never,
    Your fatherland greets ye the last to-day,
Soon raging storm as foam the ship shall sever,
    Ye all shall be of fish and fowl the prey.

    Storm birds I see are flying,
    The wolf to forest hieing;
    Signs these that hell aye keepeth,
    When low the eagle sweepeth.

These signs full oft I read descrying,
    But younger folk their doubt will cast,
High rolls the tide, the winds are sighing,
    What is to be, must be, at last.

    Shout then and revel,
    Soon thy song shall die away,
    The raven croaks, deep caverns yawn,
    Thy fatherland greets ye the last to-day.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
Beauteous prize our zeal engageth,
    Be thou gracious, seaman's fate!
Lead us safe though tempest rageth,
    Back to native port elate.

Where we wander, where abiding
    In the hand of God we are,
On, great ship, the waves dividing,
    Aye before goes God's fair star.

So we're full of valour daring,
    Fear naught deep nor storm award,
Joy all earthly treasure sharing,
    For the Lord our house doth guard.

Harald's Song:

From the sea all darkly flowing,
    High the sun ascends and higher,
Fills the mead with radiance glowing,
    Wakes the Nereidian choir.
Love's bright star is beck'ning me,
    O! I'll follow, follow thee!

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.
I will listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

Swell, ye sails, and call, ye billows,
    Roar and blow, ye strong winds wild,
That I with my warriors daring,
    Soon may reach the darling child.

Where the cooling springs are plying,
    Lone she waketh, dream-bedight,
There I'll listen for her sighing
    Through the love-enraptured night.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
The God of Storms and the Demons of the South Sea:

Ye storms there on high,
    And fiends of the deep,
O tarry ye not,
    Where'er ye may sleep!

For battle prepared,
    Your God calleth ye,
Roll on as the thunder,
    And plough ye the sea.

O shiver the masts,
    Shake the bed of the sea,
Make known to them all
    Sons of hell ye be.

On the Ship:

Hark, storm-spirits dark are nighing,
    Threat'ning clouds all downward fly,
        For the storm spirit's nigh!
Reef the sails, the yards all lower,
    On the deck then every man.

Billow rises wild on billow,
    Piping raves the furious wind,
Is the anchor fast and steady?
    Still our hope to that we bind.

Woe! The mast broke, shrouds all shriven,
    Cleft the great ship's mighty bow,
Flash on flash red lightning driven
    Wraps in flame the anchor tow.

On and on the storm is waging,
    'Gainst the hellish rocks they dip.
See the furies, hear their raging,
    In the great deep sinks the ship.

The God of Storms:

To the deep she went down!
Come, O sun, here downward pour thee,
Ne'er that ship will sail before thee.

The Demons:

Victoria! That ship we sank for ever,
    Of shameless robbers quick revenge obtain
O'er us hath mortal had victory never,
    Ancient and mighty ocean race we reign.

Ill fares who seeks the prize 'tis ours to guard,
    And woe! shall sink in deepest wave.
Who his desire and hope our waves award,
    Earns for his daring bold an early grave.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
The Spirits of the Sea:

Slumber soft in deep sea lying,
    Lulled by billow-throng for aye.
Our ear heareth all your sighing,
    When ye plaint to plaint reply.

Calmly moon and stars are bending
    From high heaven unto the wave.
Far and wide night shadow blending,
    God doth guard your silent grave.

And the spirit choir are mourning
    With the nymphs thy fate's decree,
And the spirit choir are saying:
    Slumber soft in deepest sea!

performance_7.additional_information: Beethoven. Miss Florence Menk-Meyer.

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
The drowsy woods are wrapt in shadow;
    The dreamy clouds hang o'er the lake;
The quiet moon sleeps on the meadow;
    But love now watches for thy sake.

The ocean now in silence slumbers,
    Unheard the billows gently break,
And so to thee, in whispered numbers
    Comes love, who watches for thy sake.

Then rouse thee not, tho' love be singing,
    Or from thine eyes their slumbers shake,
If in thy soul the tones are ringing,
    Of love, who watches for thy sake.
performance_8.additional_information: (TENOR SOLO Mr. W. Clarence Fraser). Liedertafel.

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
2.—Easter Hymn

CHRIST is risen from the dead.
    Has broken the tomb,
    Gladly hail the token.
    Sin's fetters are broken,
Reversed is the doom,
Now the Master hath ascended,
    Rejoice for your bondage is o'er,
And the reign of sin is ended,
    Praise him for evermore!

    Alas! those He loved can but languish,
    Suffer mid pain and annoy.
    Master, we envy Thy joy,
Forget not the depth of our anguish.
    Hosanna!

4.—Chorus of Soldiers and Students

Soldiers.

Fortresses defended with strong ramparts high,
Fair maidens who daringly love's power defy,
Of conquest we're certain soon as we take the field,
We reck not of danger, to us they must yield.
At the sound of the trumpet we soldiers so
To revel or battle at once march away.

Students.

Jam nox stellata vel amina pandit,
Nunc bibendum et amandum est,
Vita brevis fugax que voluptas,
    Gaudeamus igitur.

Nobis sub ridente luna,
Per urbem quaerentes puellas eamus.
Ut cras fortunati Cæsares dicamus,
Veni, vidi, vici, gaudeamus igitur.

performance_12.lyrics_transcript:
Ah! must we part for ever?
One kiss before we sever.
Beside my bold commander
I far away must wander.
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!

I ne'er again may greet thee,
On sunny pathway meet thee;
The foe will stand before me,
And battle clouds roll o'er me.
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!

I long for thee when parted,
Weep thou for me true hearted!
When life's last pulses flutter,
My latest breath shall utter,
    Farewell, farewell, beloved maid!

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
Why should we sigh, and mirth decry,
And why from content seek banishment?
With care why alloy the cup of joy,
To vainly repent o'er days misspent?
No! cherish the hours, while youth is ours;
And give not to care life's better share;
    But the sage old device
    Let us prize,
That this world's both good and fair!
Though in lane and street,
Oftsoe'er you meet
    Gloomy faces, sorrow's traces,
Think that evermore.
When the clouds pass o'er,
Lips will smile that smil'd before, Once more!
Ever thus sweet Spring
Weaves his flow'ry ring,
    Gladness wooing, world renewing;
And like airy sprite,
Ceaseless day and night,
Joy doth weave a new delight, With micht.
    Her shapes are manifold
    Her voices all untold,
    She dwells in ev'ry place
    Where pure hearts may follow
        Her fairy trace.
She roams on sunlit hills,
Or lurks by babbling rills,
Or rocks on ocean's breast,
    Or sings where the woodlands
        In shadow rest.

But, oh! sweet is the image of joy,
    In human face that dwells,
When love new-born, of its pure ecstasy
    In humid glances tells.

O'er joy-illumined eye
Night spreads no starless sky;
And love-filled heart can hear
    The chime of earth's joy-bells
        Sound far and near.

O ye, that look through a darkening veil,
And ye, faint souls, that life's sorrows bewail,
Look up! and trust to Nature's decree:
    Where life is, love can be.

Come, haste your dull doleful creed to forsake,
To brighter faiths let your spirits awake,
Nor doubt that towards a heaven-lov'd end
    All joyful things will tend.

Then silence not the voice
That would in glee rejoice,
Nor dim in darksome night
Eyes made to bask in light;
Hush not the silv'ry note
That falls from Mirth's gay throat,
But when the maid thou hast,
    O hold her fast!

No wanton sprite is she,
That would avoided be,
But in each guileless breast
A gladly harbour'd guest;
Love that hath such bridesmaid,
By her more lovely's made—
Blest, where in cot or hall,
    Joy's footsteps fall.

And oft, when adrift in thought's rudderless boat,
    Calmly we float
    From life's noise remote,
Across the still waters her bright glances beam,
And bathe all in sunlight our dream.
Or when at Humanity's glorious shrine
    Men's hearts entwine
    In love half-divine,
'Tis joy that her glow to our pulses imparts,
And throbs in our grateful hearts.
    O rejoice! Heart and voice
    Raise to heav'n above, laud the Source of Love.
    He is good, great and wise;
    Wraft from earth to skies
    Hymns of gratitude!
Now to the gay dance's rhythmical sound
See the golden-haired hours circle round,
While our thoughts in harmonious rhyme
To their soul-stirring cadence keep time!
Stealing us far from the sorrows of life,
Shedding balm o'er its heart-paining strife,
Guiding gently to sweet spots of rest
For the heart that with gladness is blest!
    Joy and song
    Be our theme life-long,
    And in jocund strain
    Sound again the refrain!
    Sing and laugh, laugh and sing—
    Come what fate may bring!
    Let joy's paeans rise
    In glad songs to the skies!
        Then sing, yes sing, O sing!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
"O WHERE hae ye been, my long lost lover,
    This seven lang years and mair ?"
"O I'm come again to seek your love,
    An' the vows that ye did swear."
"Now haud your tongue o' my love and vows,
    For they can breed but strife;
Now haud your tongue o' my former vows,
    For I am anither man's wife."
"O fause are the vows o' womankind,
    But fair is their fause bodie;
I wad never hae trodden on Irish ground,
    Were it no for the love o' thee."
"Ye may leave your husband to himsel',
    And your little son also,
And sail wi' me across the sea,
    Sae fair the wind doth blow."
"See ye not seven pretty ships,
    The eighth brought me to land,
With merchandis
    And my..."
"O weel I like the ship," she said,
    "And weel I like the sea,
But where are a' your mariners?
    I see nane but thee and me."
They hadna sailed a league, a league,
    A league, but barely three,
When eerie grew the lift above,
    And gurly grew the sea.
She hadna sailed a league, a league,
    A league, but barely three,
When she espied the cloven hoof,
    And wept right bitterlie.
"O what are yon, yon pleasant hills,
    That the sun shines sweetly on?"
"O yon are the hills of heaven," he said
    "Where you will never win."
"O whatna mountain is yon," she said,
    "Sae dreary wi' frost and snow?"
"O yon is the mountain o' hell," he cried,
    "Where you and I maun go."
The clouds grew black, and the wind grew loud,
    And the levin filled her e'e;
And waesome wailed the snow-white sprites,
    Out o'er the roaring sea.
He struck the mainmast wi' his hand,
    The foremast wi' his knee;
He split the gallant ship in twain,
    And sank her in the sea.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land,
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard unleaping,
"Yonder snow-covered peaks o'er cloud-bands peeping."

And it was Olav Trygvason.
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring,
Swayed in the stormy wind the forest strangely was murmuring,
Sounds as of church bells chiming,
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.

"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator,"
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning.
God, to thee alone be glory
    On to God! On to God!

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
I KNOW not what it betokens
That I am so sad at heart,
A legend from bygone ages
Will not from my mind depart.
The air is cool and it darkens,
And calmly flows the Rhine,
The mountain's far summit sparkles
In gentle evening shine.
A lovely lady sitteth
Thereby, entrancing fair,
Her golden raiment glistens,
She combs her golden hair.
She combs it with comb all golden,
And sings a song the while,
That has a soul-betwitching
Resistless melody.
The boatman, as onward he fareth,
It seizeth with anguish dread,
He sees not the rocks fast shoaling,
He looks ever up overhead.
Meseems the wavelets swallow
At last both boatman and boat,
And this with her fatal singing
The Loreley has wrought.
performance_6.additional_information: Orchestrated by Professor Marshall-Hall. MISS MARGUERITE HENDERSON.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
Cries "Boatman, do not tarry!
And I'll give you a guinea and
To row
His horsemen hard behind us ride;
    Should they our steps discover,
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
    When they have slain her lover?
Out spake the hardy highland wight,
    "I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
    But for your winsome lady.
And by my word, the bonny bird
    In danger shall not tarry,
So though the waves are raging white,
    I'll row you o'er the ferry."
By this the storm grew loud apace,
    The water wraith was shrieking,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
    Grew dark as they were speaking.
But still as wilder blew the wind,
    And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
    Their tramping sounded nearer.
"Oh haste thee, haste!" the lady cries,
    "Though storms around us gather,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
    But not an angry father."
The boat has left the stormy land,
    A stormy sea before her,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
    The tempest gather'd o'er her.
And still they rowed amidst the roar
    Of waters fast prevailing:
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
    His wrath was changed to wailing.
For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
    He did his child discover:
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
    And one was round her lover.
"Come back, come back!" he cried in grief
    Across the stormy water,
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
    My daughter! oh, my daughter!"

performance_1.additional_information: THE ORCHESTRA. No sooner do the first few bars of this masterly comedy sound than stern Time seems to flag, falter, turn tail, and run back a few centuries, and, like the worthy golosh-clad councillor of Hans Andersen, we wake up to find ourselves a hundred or two years younger, sauntering through the queer old streets of Nürnberg, in the company of those famous master-singers of whose quaint customs we have so often read. We seem to see it all—the various guilds in procession with banners flying! the impetuous, passionate idealist Walther, head-over-ears in love with Master Goldsmith Pogner's daughter; tender little Eva, who shyly returns his passion; the frolicsome apprentices, mimicking the somewhat pompous airs of their masters; and, as, in a dream, scenes the most diverse succeed one another without incongruity conjured up by the spell of music.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
SUSANNA:—
At last the hour nears, when, O beloved! I shall possess thee entirely. Anxious doubts, begone! vanish for ever! disturb no more the joy of my heart! 'Ah! around me everything appears so gay: Hesperus looks down so smilingly, so smilingly upon my love! Come then, O my well-beloved! let the stillness of night watch over us. O finger no longer, beloved soul! thy friend waits for thee here, full of longing! The moon's silver torch not yet throws forth its light: stillness and peace reign in the fields. The murmur of the west-wind, and the gurgling brook attune every nerve to rapture; the flowers breathe o'er the glad meadows; all invites us to love, joy, and bliss. Come then, beloved! let me no longer await thee! Come that I may crown thy head with roses.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
1.
Ah! what can ail thee, wretched wight,
Alone and palely loitering?
The sedge is withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.

2.
Ah! what can ail thee, wretched wight,
So haggard and so woe-begone?
The squirrel's granary is full,
And the harvest's done.

3.
I see a lily on thy brow,
With anguish moist and fever dew;
And on thy cheek a fading rose
Fast withereth, too.

4.
I met a lady in the meads,
Full beautiful—a fairy's child:
Her hair was long, her foot was light,
And her eyes were wild.

5.
I set her on my pacing steed,
And nothing else saw all day long:
For sideways would she lean, and sing
A faery's song.

6.
I made a garland for her head,
And bracelets, too, and fragrant zone;
She looked at me as she did love,
And made sweet moan.

7.
She found me roots of relish sweet,
And honey wild, and mamma dew;
And sure in language strange she said,
I love thee true.

8.
She took me to her elfin grot,
And there she gazed and sighed deep,
And there I shut her wild, sad eyes—
So kissed to sleep.

9.
And there we slumbered on the moss,
And there I dreamed, ah, woe beside!
The latest dream I ever dreamed,
On the cold hillside.

10.
I saw pale kings, and princes, too,
Pale warriors—death-pale were they all—
Who cried—"La Belle Dame sans Merci
Hath thee in thrall."

11.
I saw their starv'd lips in the gloom
With horrid warning gaped wide,
And I awoke, and found me here,
On the cold hillside.

12.
And this is why I sojourn here
Alone and palely loitering,
Though the sedge is withered from the lake,
And no birds sing.

(Keats.)
performance_3.additional_information: MR. JAMES WADE. This wonderful poem represents in an ideal form the overpowering fascination which it is in the power of some women to exert over certain men—a fascination which makes or mars life. This the poets have pictured in "Antony and Cleopatra," "Launcelot and Guinevere," "Tristan and Isolde." The music is an attempt to realise the weird despair of the scene, and the strange irresistible magic of the love which usurps the man's whole being, with all its tender dreamy delight, of which the eighth stanza is the most marked instance, where the strange harmonic progressions seem to typify the "love-sleep" from which his life long he may never more awaken.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
AND it was Olav Trygvason,
A Sailing on the north sea wide,
Bearing the hope to found a kingdom,
Far on the other side.
Yonder the cliffs appearing,
Like a battlement loom, their dark crest rearing,
And it was Olav Trygvason,
Found he ne'er a spot to land,
E'en like the waves the royal desire,
Shattered upon the strand.
"See!" cried the bard unleaping,
"Yonder snow-covered peaks o'er cloud bands peeping."

And it was Olav Trygvason,
Suddenly he seemed to sight
Towering temples, domes and spires,
Glist'ning in virgin white.
Then vowed the king undaunted,
With his followers to tread that land enchanted,
Onward he went; the rushing streams
Heralded the coming spring;
Swayed in the stormy wind the forest strangely was murmuring,
Sounds as of church bells chiming,
And then spake the king,
Spake as tho' dreaming:
"Here the spot to found our kingdom!
Hell! these temple walls defy thee!
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory.
"Be my faith as yonder mountains,
Root as deeply, shine as purely;
And as these my faith strive upwards,
On to him, the All Creator,"
Olav's prayer be ours to utter,
As we near the throne of mercy.
Hearts are swelling, souls are yearning,
God, to thee alone be glory
    On to God! On to God!

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
Far in yon region of light, where pleasures fail not,
Wander the Spirits blest,
Breathed on by airs of glory, bright and divine,
Like a harp, when a master hand wakes it from silence;
Free from care, like a babe that is sleeping, are they in heaven that dwell:
Pure and lowly as half-open'd blossoms
In those fields of light they ever bloom;
And in bliss are their eyes still gazing on clearness calm and eternal.
But man may not linger, and nowhere finds he repose;
We stay not, but wander, we grief-laden mortals,
Blindly from one sad hour to another,
Like water from cliff unto cliff ever dropping
Blindly at last do we pass away.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
"Get thee up! there, thy offspring I do permit thee to behold, in darkness and in silence; then awhile thy blushes and my shame be hidden."

"No, not on him, on you fragile existence, be my blows directed elsewhere I'll find that which shall wipe out my dishonour, 'tis e'en thy life's blood. From thy base heart my dagger ere long shall bid it swiftly flow—vengeance sternly exacting for all my woe."

And would'st thou thus have sullied a soul so pure,
In whose chasteness my spirit delighted.
Thou betray me, in whose love I felt all secure?
Of my days thou hast poisoned the stream.
Treacherous heart! is it thus he's requitted who the first in thy friendship, yes the first in thy friendship did seem?
O the pangs of a joy aye departed, of caresses that made life a heaven! when Adelia, an angel pure hearted, in my arms grew resplendent with love!
All is over; and hate's bitter leaven my widow'd heart only can move:
Oh the pangs of joy departed; Hope can buoy me no more.

performance_8.additional_information: THE ORCHESTRA. He who can enter into the spirit of Shakespeare's "Midsummer Night's Dream," will need no other aid to throw himself into the mood in which this masterpiece is written. In delicacy of fancy it is unsurpassed, even by the great tragedian. The opening is delightful, where we hear the distant sound of Oberon's magic horn, and the following bars which so wonderfully depict the drowsy awakening of nature.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
"Perhaps I should have called this work 'Music for Japan from Australia', because I want the Australian Youth Orchestra to take to Japan music that says something of my own country. If the view of desert and sea, bush and city seems to be a personal one, it's because I want also to send music that says something about me. Some of the most memorable times of my life have been in Australia and Japan.

Written especially for the Australian Youth Orchestra, Music for Japan is quite adventurous in its sonorities and in the means required

to produce these. It might be called a 'sound piece', because, like my Sun Music series, it's made up of sound-impressions. Much as I enjoy writing melodies, in this work I've used no conventional melodic shapes, in order to get more fully an abstraction of my feelings.

Music for Japan is scored for a normal orchestra, with amplified percussion. Rather than provide a detailed programme note, I should like to say only that the work lasts for approximately twelve minutes; this may give the listener a sense of shape and flow within a certain period of time."

—Peter Sculthorpe.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Lars Porsena of Clusium
    By the Nine Gods he swore,
That the great house of Tarquin
    Should suffer wrong no more.
By the Nine Gods he swore it,
    And named a trysting day,
And bade his messengers ride forth,
East and west and south and north,
    To summon his array.

East and west and south and north
    The messengers ride fast,
And tower and town and cottage
    Have heard the trumpet's blast.
Shame on the false Etruscan
    Who lingers in his home,
When Porsena of Clusium
    Is on the march for Rome.

The horsemen and the footmen
    Are pouring in amain
From many a stately market-place;
    From many a fruitful plain
From many a lonely hamlet,
    Which, hid by beech and pine,
Like an eagle's nest, hangs on the crest
    Of purple Apennine.

There be thirty chosen prophets,
    The wisest of the land,
Who alway by Lars Porsena
    Both morn and evening stand:
Evening and morn the Thirty
    Have turned the verses o'er,
Traced from the right on linen white
    By mighty seers of yore.
And with one voice the Thirty
    Have their glad answer given:
"Go forth, go forth, Lars Porsena;
    Go forth, beloved of Heaven;
Go, and return in glory
    To Clusium's royal dome;
And hang round Nurscia's altars
    The golden shields of Rome."
And now hath every city
    Sent up her tale of men;
The foot are fourscore thousand,
    The horse are thousands ten:
Before the gates of Sutrium
    Is met the great array.
A proud man was Lars Porsena
    Upon the trysting day.

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
But by the yellow Tiber
    Was tumult and affright:
From all the spacious champaign
    To Rome men took their flight.
A mile around the city,
    The throng stopped up the ways;
A fearful sight it was to see
    Through two long nights and days.
For aged folks on crutches,
    And women great with child,
And mothers sobbing over babes
    That clung to them and smiled.
And sick men borne on litters
    High on the necks of slaves,
And troops of sun-burned husbandmen
    With reaping-hooks and staves,
And droves of mules and asses
    Laden with skins of wine,
And endless flocks of goats and sheep,
    And endless herds of kine,

And endless trains of waggons
    That creaked beneath the weight
Of corn-sacks and of household goods,
    Choked every roaring gate.

The Fathers of the City,
    They sat all night and day,
For every hour some horseman came
    With tidings of dismay.
Out spake the Consul roundly:
    "The bridge must straight go down;
For, since Janiculum is lost,
    Nought else can save the town."

Just then a scout came flying,
    All wild with haste and fear;
"To arms! to arms! Sir Consul:
    Lars Porsena is here."
On the low hills to westward
    The Consul fixed his eye,
And saw the swarthy storm of dust
    Rise fast along the sky.

And nearer fast and nearer
    Doth the red whirlwind come;
And louder still and still more loud,
From underneath that rolling cloud,
Is heard the trumpet's war-note proud,
    The trampling and the hum.
And plainly and more plainly
    Now through the gloom appears,
Far to left and far to right,
In broken gleams of dark-blue light,
The long array of helmets bright,
    The long array of spears.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
But the Consul's brow was sad,
    And the Consul's speech was low,
And darkly looked he at the wall,
    And darkly at the foe.
"Their van will be upon us
    Before the bridge goes down;
And if they once may win the bridge,
    What hope to save the town?"

Then out spake brave Horatius,
    The Captain of the Gate:
"To every man upon this earth
    Death cometh soon or late.

And how can man die better
Than facing fearful odds,
For the ashes of his fathers,
    And the temples of his gods,

"And for the tender mother
Who dandled him to rest,
And for the wife who nurses
    His baby at her breast,
And for the holy maidens
    Who feed the eternal flame,
To save them from false Sextus
    That wrought the deed of shame?

"Hew down the bridge, Sir Consul,
    With all the speed ye may;
I, with two more to help me,
    Will hold the foe in play.
In yon straight path a thousand
    May well be stopped by three.
Now who will stand on either hand,
    And keep the bridge with me?"

Then out spoke Spurius Lartius;
    A Ramnian proud was he:
"Lo, I will stand at thy right hand,
    And keep the bridge with thee."
And out spake strong Herminius;
    Of Titian blood was he:
"I will abide on thy left side
    And keep the bridge with thee."

"Horatius," quoth the Consul,
    "As thou sayest, so let it be,"
And straight against that great array
    Forth went the dauntless Three.
For Romans in Rome's quarrel
    Spared neither land nor gold,
Nor son nor wife, nor limb nor life,
    In the brave days of old.

performance_5.lyrics_transcript:
Meanwhile the Tuscan army,
    Right glorious to behold,
Came flashing back the noonday light,
    Rank behind rank like surges bright
Of a broad sea of gold.

Four hundred trumpets sounded
    A peal of warlike glee,
As that great host, with measured tread,
And spears advanced, and ensigns spread,
Rolled slowly towards the bridge's head,
    Where stood the dauntless Three.

And forth three chiefs came spurring
    Before that deep array;
To earth they sprang, their swords they drew,
And lifted high their shields, and flew
    To win the narrow way.

Stout Lartius hurled down Aunus
    Into the stream beneath:
Herminius struck at Seius,
    And clove him to the teeth:
At Picus brave Horatius
    Darted one fiery thrust;
And the proud Umbrian's gilded arms
    Clashed in the bloody dust.

Then Ocnus of Falerii
    Rushed on the Roman Three;
And Lausulus of Urgo
    The rover of the sea;
And Aruns of Volsinium,
    Who slew the great wild boar,
The great wild boar that had his den
Amidst the reeds of Cosa's fen,
And wasted fields, and slaughtered men,
    Along Albinia's shore.

Herminius smote down Aruns:
    Lartius laid Ocnus low:
Right to the heart of Lausulus
    Horatius sent a blow.
"Lie there," he cried, "fell pirate!
    No more, aghast and pale,
From Ostia's walls the crowd shall mark
The track of thy destroying bark,
    Thy thrice accursed sail."

But now no sound of laughter
    Was heard among the foes,
A wild and wrathful clamour
    From all the vanguard rose.
There lacked not men of prowess,
    Nor men of lordly race;
For all Etruria's noblest
    Were round the fatal place.

But all Etruria's noblest
    Felt their hearts sink to see
On the earth the bloody corpses,
    In the path the dauntless Three.

But meanwhile axe and lever
    Have manfully been plied;
And now the bridge hangs tottering
    Above the boiling tide.
"Come back, come back, Horatius!"
    Loud cried the Fathers all.
"Back, Lartius! back, Herminius!
    Back, ere the ruin fall!"

Back darted Spurius Lartius;
    Herminius darted back:
And, as they passed, beneath their feet
    They felt the timbers crack.
But when they turned their faces,
    And on the farther shore
Saw brave Horatius stand alone,
    They would have crossed once more.

But with a crash like thunder
Fell every loosened beam,
And, like a dam, the mighty wreck
    Lay right athwart the stream.
And a long shout of triumph
    Rose from the walls of Rome,
As to the highest turret-tops
    Was splashed the yellow foam.
Alone stood brave Horatius,
    But constant still in mind;
Thrice thirty thousand foes before,
    And the broad flood behind.

"Down with him!" cried false Sextus
    With a smile on his pale face.
"Now yield thee," cried Lars Porsena,
    "Now yield thee to our grace."

Round turned he, as not deigning
    Those craven ranks to see;
Nought spake he to Lars Porsena,
    To Sextus nought spake he;
But he saw on Palatinus
    The white porch of his home;
And he spake to the noble river
    That rolls by the towers of Rome.

"Oh, Tiber! Father Tiber!
    To whom the Romans pray,
    A Roman's life, a Roman's arms,
        Take thou in charge this day!"
So he spake, and speaking sheathed
    The good sword by his side,
And with his harness on his back,
    Plunged headlong in the tide.

No sound of joy or sorrow
    Was heard from either bank;
But friends and foes in dumb surprise,
With parted lips and straining eyes,
    Stood gazing where he sank:
And when above the surges
    They saw his crest appear,
All Rome sent forth a rapturous cry,
And even the ranks of Tuscany
    Could scarce forbear to cheer.

But fiercely ran the current,
    Swollen high by months of rain:
And fast his blood was flowing;
    And he was sore in pain,
And heavy with his armour,
    And spent with changing blows:
And oft they thought him sinking,
    But still again he rose.

Never, I ween, did swimmer,
    In such an evil case,
Struggle through such a raging flood
    Safe to the landing-place.
    But his limbs were borne up bravely
By the brave heart within,
    And our good father Tiber
Bore bravely up his chin.

And now he feels the bottom;
    Now on dry earth he stands;
Now round him throng the Fathers
    To press his gory hands;
And now, with shouts and clapping,
    And noise of weeping loud,
He enters through the River-Gate,
    Borne by the joyous crowd.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
They gave him of the corn-land,
    That was of public right,
As much as two strong oxen
    Could plough from morn till night;

performance_3.lyrics_transcript:
I hear thee speak of the Better Land,
Thou call'st its children a happy band;
Mother, where is that radiant shore?
Shall we not seek it and weep no more?
Is it where the flow'r of the orange blows,
And the fireflies dance thro' the myrtle boughs?
    Not there, not there, my child

Is it far away in some region old,
Where the rivers wander o'er sands of gold,
Where the burning rays of the ruby shine
And the diamond lights up the secret mine,
And the pearl gleams forth from the coral strand?
Is it there, sweet mother, that better land?
    Not there, not there, my child.

Eye hath not seen it, my gentle boy;
Ear hath not heard its sweet songs of joy;
Dreams cannot picture a world so fair;
Sorrow and death may not enter there;
Time doth not breath on its fadeless bloom;
Far beyond the clouds, beyond the tomb,
    It is there, my child, it is there.

performance_6.lyrics_transcript:
Mine host, fill up!
What joy to drink of rosy wine!
    Fill the glass; drink it up!
Fill the goblet to the brim.
    Drink it off! Drink it off!
By the clink of glass,
By song and glee,
    Toujours fidèle.

When I kiss the foaming goblet,
    Dearest love, I think of thee.
When the landlord seeks his reckoning,
    Then I drink; love, to thee.
Mine host, this goblet fill with wine!
[SPOKEN—One! two! three!]    Hurrah!

Sweetheart, dearest sweetheart,
    Dearest love, I think of thee;
Dearest love, I daily pledge thee
    In the cup filled to thee.
Drink it up! My glass is gone!
    Mine host, fill up!

What joy to drink of rosy wine!
Boys, take another glass of wine,
That drives all sorrow from the heart of man.
Now drain the goblet! Quick the goblet drain!
[SPOKEN—One! two! three!]    Hurrah!

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
HALLO! Hallo!
Now hunters come away, for early breaks the day;
With rifles prov'd and tried we range the mountain side;
Keep distance every man, each nook and covert scan,
From by the forest end to where the two ways blend.

Yoho, yoho, yoho!  There something crouches low;
What eyes can shine like that?  It is a mountain cat.
'Tis only so I fear: It is a crouching deer;
Surround it every way, before it steals away.

See now he springs and flies, and for the forest tries,
But there the hunters stand, with steady eye and hand.
And crack it goes, yoho!  the ball has laid him low;
A noble beast is he, and killed most manfully.

Here from the waterfall we send a hunter's call,
To glad the list'ning ear of wives and sweethearts dear,
So gently timid they, that if we shoot they say—
"Ah me! there's someone hurt to day."

O sweethearts in the vale, you from afar we hail,
With joyful notes that tell that all with us is well,
Yet here awhile we roam; and with the evening come
To seek our dear and quiet home.

Tra la, la la, la la! then here's hurrah, hurrah!
For such a bonny land, for vales and mountains grand.
And here's hurrah, hurrah! for wives and maidens true.
Sweethearts, we shout for you, hurrah!

An eye that never fails, a heart that never quails,
A cheek aglow with health, is more than idle wealth.
Hallo! hallo! hallo! a-hunting we will go:
By topmost crag and peak our timid prey we seek.
Hallo! hallo! hallo! a-hunting we will go:
Full quickly flies the day; Hallo, hallo, away!

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Leaping in silvery, swirling cascades;
Pour the libation in fizzing champagne,
Gushing in tremulous, prancing, proud courses.
Flowing in boiling and high foaming ardours,
Like to the olden-time streamlets and sources
Deeply in Ida's dun thickets concealed.

Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam;
Seething they climb from their specular home.
Mould there thy pearl drops from silvery foam.
There are the sharp infundibular goblets,
Sparkling and glistening like bubbling fountains,
Pour'd from the mouth of the broken sealed magnum
Deeply in Ida's dun thickets concealed.

Swaying and thinking in aureate room,
Clink now the glasses with resonant swing;
Rolling and swaying like zephyrs in spring-time.
Dance frolicsome genii of champagne:
Backward and forward enlacing departing,
Glistening, vanishing, lost in the crystal vase;
Brief as the day of youth's gay effervescence.

performance_4.lyrics_transcript:
If thou art sleeping maiden,
Awake, awake and open thy door,
'Tis the break of day and we must away
O'er meadow and mount and moor.
Wait not to find the silken feet,
But come with thy silken feet,
We shall have to pass through the dewy grass
And the waters wide and fleet.

performance_7.lyrics_transcript:
The Nation's glory into your hands is now given.
    Oh, guard it well.
To sink with you, or with you rise to heaven.
    The magic spell of heart and song
    Links all the worlds that roll along,
So may they ever blended be in richest harmony.
Her voice is like the dreadful thunder,
    Terrible in its might and anger;
It rises on victorious planks, and vengeance
    takes on foes and minions—
    Strikes terror to the tyrant's heart.
If truth to exile e'er be driven;
Then to her aid the Muse arisen
Shall find revenge in lofty music's song.
    Oh, freedom's soul of arise!
Lift up your head to beauty's throne,
And as with her you mount the skies,
All lesser crowns disown.
The thousand various ways unending
Of rich humanity explore,
Till from the summit's height extending,
Behold the vast eternal shore.

performance_9.lyrics_transcript:
THE drooping flowers their buds are closing.
The silver stars keep watch above!
The world in tranquil sleep reposing
My wakeful bosom yields to love.
While here in hopeless grief I languish,
Could I behold thy vision bright,
Then would I fondly breathe my anguish,
Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.

Tho' all unmoved by love's appealing,
No kindling passion lights thy brow?
No voice of love thy heart revealing,
Still, still, the silver stars above.
Bend softly down, ye golden tresses,
Beam kindly once, bright orbs of light;
List, lady, list to love's distresses—
Thou art my dream thro' stilly night.
performance_9.additional_information: Gail Hofmann. Performed by THE LIEDERTAFEL.

performance_10.additional_information: Popper; Cossmann. HERR LOUIS HATTENBACH.

performance_11.lyrics_transcript:
THRO' forest deep at dead of night,
The mail is slowly borne;
While sleep the weary travellers,
The post-boy winds his horn.

The forest-ranger's dwelling
Within the wood is seen,
The horn a tale is telling—
What can its echoes mean?

Its tunes so soft and sweetly flow,
The mails, in passing by,
Pause at the open window,
And mingling with them fly.

Where sleeps the forest maiden,
While beams the moon above;
With love her dreams are laden—
With melody and love.
performance_11.additional_information: (Cornet Solo—Mr. ARTHUR HAIGH). Schafer. Performed by THE LIEDERTAFEL.

performance_13.lyrics_transcript:
On land we find but scanty honour,
A vagrant folk without a home;
Exiles to-day on shore we wonder,
To-morrow monarchs of the foam!
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

When o'er the deep our sails are flying,
All things must bow to our control;
On every hand a tax we levy
And ocean's pride must pay us toll.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Our coats are good broad-cloth from England,
And heavy silk from Genoa;
Our scores we reckon with the grapnel,
And we receipt them with "Hurrah!"
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!

On land we find but scanty honour,
A vagrant folk without a home;
Exiles to-day on shore we wonder,
To-morrow monarchs of the foam!
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

When o'er the deep our sails are flying,
All things must bow to our control;

And ocean's pride must pay us toll.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Our coats are good broad-cloth from England,
And heavy silk from Genoa;
Our scores we reckon with the grapnel,
And we receipt them with "Hurrah!"
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Here's glorious beer! That comes from Hamburg!
Or is your taste for Spanish wine?
All climes are pledged to feed and clothe us,
All fill the cup when we would dine.
    Clink again!
    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

Gay go the hours with wine and singing,
A merry life beyond compare!
And when at last our skulls lay bleaching,
Why there's an end to further care.

    Glasses drain!
    Drink amain!

=== Page 2 ===
博物館の歩み

武蔵野音楽大学楽器博物館は、当大学図書館の付属施設として、昭和42年10月に開設された。

昭和28年福井直弘学長は、学生たちの研究資料とするために、ドイツから一個のヴィオラ・ダモーレを持ち帰った。それが当博物館の第一号の資料となった。これに端を発して徐々に資料としての楽器が集められ、昭和35年には楽器陳列室が設けられた。

昭和41年、来学された伊丹市の邦楽器研究家故水野佐平氏は、邦楽器関係の資料の欠如を指摘されると共に、同氏の貴重な邦楽器コレクション寄贈の申し出をされ、これが契機となって陳列室は博物館として発足することになった。

所蔵品は、邦楽器、外国楽器、楽器付属品、音楽に関係した装置・器具類の4つの部分に大別でき、邦楽器部門には数々の逸品が、外国楽器部門にはヨーロッパの多くの名器の他アジア、アフリカなど世界の民族楽器が、楽器付属品部門にはヴァイオリンやチェロの名弓210本以上のコレクションが、そして装置器具類にはエジソンの蝋管器を含む蓄音機の歴史的蒐集がそれぞれ含まれており、その総数は2,000点に及びとんとしている。

event-7_10.event_name: SCENES FROM THE SONG OF HIAWATHA
event-7_10.additional_information:
Page references in this chunk: === Page 31 ===, === Page 33 ===, === Page 35 ===.
In performance a few words have been altered to bring the narrative into the present tense. The story of this Opera forms a part of Longfellow's "Song of Hiawatha." It is divided into three Acts: "Hiawatha's Wedding Feast," "The Death of Minnehaha," and "Hiawatha's Departure."
To understand the story it is necessary to know that it had been revealed to the Indian tribes by Gitche Manitou, the Great Spirit and Creator of all living things, that he would send to them from the land where there is no sin and no darkness, and where all is bathed in the glory of light and love, a great prophet who would teach them to adore the beauty of peace and who, after suffering with them the sorrows and privations of mankind, would lead them into the golden dawn of a new world.
In the fulness of time, Hiawatha was born, and became a great prophet, teacher and statesman. Under his influence five adjacent tribes buried the hatchet and welded themselves together as a powerful confederation which became allied to the British settlers and fought beside them against the Hurons and their allies, the French. Thus, Hiawatha played a considerable part in the history of the formation of the British Empire, in that he assisted to a great extent in the acquisition of Canada.

event-7-section-1.additional_information:
Hiawatha was a man as other men, and wooed and won sweet Laughing Water, Minnehaha from the land of the Dacotahs. The Opera opens with the festivities at their marriage, and gay are the guests as they offer their presents and receive the generous hospitality of their host. Quip and jest pass round, and Chibibabos, the singer of sweet songs, sounds the keynote of passionate love in the ears of his entranced listeners. Dance follows song, Pau-Puk-Keewis leaps and twines with the grace of a barbaric savage. The Medicine Man brews a Peyote plant potion, of which the guests partake, and through its magic visualize a dream ballet of childhood days. Then follows a thrilling totem dance, in which all the tribe take part, and give vent to their feeling in the hiss of the serpent, the bark of the fox, the shriek of the eagle or the bellow of the buffalo, according to the nature of their totem.
The Marriage Feast is over. Happy and joyous, the guests depart to their wigwams, and alone in the moonlight are Hiawatha and Minnehaha.

event-7-section-1-performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
You shall hear how Pau-Puk-Keewis,
How the handsome Yenadizze,
Danced at Hiawatha's wedding;
How the gentle Chibibabos,
He the sweetest of musicians,
Sang his songs of love and longing,
How Iago, the great boaster,
He the marvellous storyteller,
Told his tales of strange adventure,
That the feast might be more joyous,
That the time might pass more gaily
And the guests be more contented.
Sumptuous was the feast Nokomis
Made at Hiawatha's wedding.
All the bowls were made of bass-wood
White and polished very smoothly,
All the spoons of horn of bison,
Black and polished very smoothly.

She had sent through all the village
Messengers with wands of willow,
As a sign of invitation,
As a token of the feasting;
And the wedding-guests assembled,
Clad in all their richest raiment,
Robes of fur and belts of wampum,
Splendid with their paint and plumage,
Beautiful with beads and tassels.
First they ate the sturgeon, Nahma,
And the pike, the Maskenoza,
Caught and cooked by old Nokomis,
Then on pemmican they feasted,
Pemmican and buffalo marrow,
Haunch of deer and hump of bison,
Yellow cakes of the Mondamin,
And the wild rice of the river.
But the gracious Hiawatha,

And the lovely Laughing Water,
And the careful old Nokomis,
Tasted not the food before them,
Only waited on the others,
Only served their guests in silence.
    And when all the guests had finished,
Old Nokomis, brisk and busy,
From an ample pouch of otter,
Filled the red stone pipes for smoking
With tobacco from the South-land,
Mixed with bark of the red willow,
And with herbs and leaves of fragrance.
    Then she said, "O Pau-Puk-Keewis,
Dance for us your merry dances,
Dance the Beggar's Dance to please us,
That the feast may be more joyous,
That the time may pass more gaily,
And our guests be more contented!"
    Then the handsome Pau-Puk-Keewis,
He the idle Yenadizze,
He the merry mischief-maker,
Whom the people called the Storm-Fool,
Rose among the guests assembled.
    Skilled was he in sports and pastimes,
In the merry dance of snow-shoes,
In the play of quoits and ball-play;
Skilled was he in games of hazard,
In all games of skill and hazard,
Pugasaing, the Bowl and Counters,
Koomtassoo, the Game of Plum-stones.
    Though the warriors called him Faint-Heart
Called him coward, Shaugodaya,
Idler, gambler, Yenadizze,
Little heeded he their jesting,
Little cared he for their insults,
For the women and the maidens
Loved the handsome Pau-Puk-Keewis.
    He was dressed in shirt of doe-skin,
White and soft, and fringed with ermine,
All inwrought with beads of wampum;
He was dressed in deer-skin leggings,
Fringed with hedgehog quills and ermine,
And in moccasins of buck-skin
Thick with quills and beads embroidered.
On his head were plumes of swan's down,
On his heels were tails of foxes,
In one hand a fan of feathers,
And a pipe was in the other.
    Barred with streaks of red and yellow,
Streaks of blue and bright vermilion,
Shone the face of Pau-Puk-Keewis,
From his forehead fell his tresses,
Smooth and parted like a woman's,
Shining bright with oil, and plaited,
Hung with braids of scented grasses,
As among the guests assembled,
To the sound of flutes and singing,
To the sounds of drums and voices,
Rose the handsome Pau-Puk-Keewis,
And began his mystic dances.
    First he danced a solemn measure,
Very slow in step and gesture,
In and out among the pine trees,
Through the shadows and the sunshine,
Treading softly like a panther,
Then more swiftly and still swifter,
Whirling, spinning round in circles,
Leaping o'er the guests assembled,
Eddying round and round the wigwam,
Till the leaves went whirling with him,
Till the dust and wind together
Swept in eddies round about him.

Of the Lake, the Big-Sea-Water,
On he sped with frenzied gestures,
Stamped upon the sand, and tossed it
Wildly in the air around him;
Till the wind became a whirlwind,
Till the sand was blown and sifted
Like great snowdrifts o'er the landscape,
Heaping all the shores with Sand Dunes,
Sand Hills of the Nagow Wudjoo!

Danced his Beggar's Dance to please them,

There among the guests assembled,
Sat and fanned himself serenely
With his fan of turkey-feathers.
    Then they said to Chibiabos,
To the friend of Hiawatha,
To the sweetest of all singers,
To the best of all musicians,

Songs of love and songs of longing,
That the feast may be more joyous,
That the time may pass more gaily,
And our guests be more contented!"
    And the gentle Chibiabos
Sang in accents sweet and tender,
Sang in tones of deep emotion,
Songs of love and songs of longing,
Looking still at Hiawatha,
Looking at fair Laughing Water,
Sang he softly, sang in this wise:

"Onaway! Awake, beloved!
Thou the wild-flower of the forest!
Thou the wild-bird of the prairies!
Thou with eyes so soft and fawn-like!
"If thou only lookest at me,
I am happy, I am happy,
As the lilies of the prairie,
When they feel the dew upon them!
"Sweet thy breath is as the fragrance
Of the wild-flowers in the morning,
As their fragrance is at evening,

"Does not all the blood within me

Onaway! awake, beloved!"

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Summer is over, and Winter grips valley and mountain in its icy clutch. Fever and Famine stalked abroad. Clinging to each other for warmth, the stricken Indians cower and shiver beneath their blankets. And what of the lovely Minnehaha—"Minnehaha, Laughing Water, Loveliest of Dacotah women"? In the absence of Hiawatha—who has gone to seek vainly for food for his people, succour for his bride—she is sick unto death, and dread phantoms bend over her couch. Finally, with a wild cry of "Hiawatha! Hiawatha!" she dies in delirium. "Far away amid the forest, miles away among the mountains" the wanderer hears that cry. Homeward hurries Hiawatha. Passionately, despairingly, he flings himself beside the dead body of his beloved, and the old nurse Nokomis sobs out her anguish. The sorrowing Indians moan and wail forth their sorrow, and over the mountains falls the snow.

There is a pause to show the passage of seven days, and then the body of Minnehaha is borne away in stately procession, clothed in her richest garments, wrapped in her robes of ermine, ready for her journey to the Islands of the Blessed.

performance-2.lyrics_transcript:
O the long and dreary Winter!
O the cold and cruel Winter!
Ever thicker, thicker, thicker.
Froze the ice on lake and river,
Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
Fell the snow o'er all the landscape,
Fell the covering snow, and drifted
Through the forest, round the village.
Hardly from his buried wigwam
Could the hunter force a passage;
With his mittens and his snow-shoes
Vainly walked he through the forest,
Sought for bird or beast and found none,
Saw no track of deer or rabbit,
In the snow beheld no footprints,
In the ghastly, gleaming forest
Fell, and could not rise from weakness,
Perished there from cold and hunger.
O the famine and the fever!
O the wasting of the famine!
O the blasting of the fever!
O the wailing of the children!
O the anguish of the women!
All the earth was sick and famished,
Hungry was the air around them,
Hungry was the sky above them,
And the hungry stars in heaven
Like the eyes of wolves glared at them!

Into Hiawatha's wigwam
Came two silent guests and gloomy,
Waited not to be invited,
Did not parley at the doorway,
Sat there without word of welcome
In the seat of Laughing Water;
Looked with haggard eyes and hollow
At the face of Laughing Water.
And the foremost said, "Behold me!
I am Famine, Buckadawin!"
And the other said, "Behold me!
I am Fever, Akhosewin!"
And the lovely Minnehaha
Shuddered as they looked upon her,
Shuddered at the words they uttered,
Lay down on her bed in silence,
Hid her face, but made no answer;
Lay there trembling, freezing, burning
At the looks they cast upon her,
At the fearful words they uttered.
Forth into the empty forest
Rushed the maddened Hiawatha;
In his heart was deadly sorrow,
In his face a stony firmness;
On his brow the sweat of anguish
Started, but it froze, and fell not.
Wrapped in furs, and armed for hunting,
With his mighty bow of ash-tree,
With his quiver full of arrows,
With his mittens, Minjekahwun,
Into the vast and vacant forest
On his snow-shoes strode he forward.

"Gitche Manitou, the Mighty!"
Cried he with his face uplifted
In that bitter hour of anguish,
"Give your children food, O father!
Give us food, or we must perish!
Give me food for Minnehaha,
For my dying Minnehaha!"

Through the far-resounding forest,
Through the forest vast and vacant,
Rang the cry of desolation,
But there came no other answer
Than the echo of his crying,
Than the echo of the woodlands
"Minnehaha! Minnehaha!"
All day long roved Hiawatha
In than melancholy forest,
Through the shadow of whose thickets,
In the pleasant days of Summer,
Of that ne'er-forgotten Summer,
He had brought his young wife homeward,
From the land of the Dacotahs;
When the birds sang in the thickets,
And the streamlets laughed and glistened,
And the air was full of fragrance,

And the lovely Laughing Water
Said, with voice that did not tremble,
"I will follow you, my husband!"
In the wigwam with Nokomis,
With those gloomy guests that watched her,
With the Famine and the Fever,
She was lying, the Beloved,
She the dying Minnehaha.
"Hark!" she said, "I hear a rushing,
Hear a roaring and a rushing,
Hear the Falls of Minnehaha
Calling to me from a distance!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the night-wind in the pine trees!"
"Look!" she said, "I see my father
Standing lonely at his doorway,
Beckoning to me from his wigwam,
In the land of the Dakotahs!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the smoke that waves and beckons!"
"Ah!" she said, "the eyes of Pauguk
Glare upon me in the darkness;
I can feel his icy fingers
Clasping mine amid the darkness!
Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

And the desolate Hiawatha,
Far away amid the forest,
Miles away among the mountains,
Heard that sudden cry of anguish,
Heard the voice of Minnehaha
Calling to him in the darkness,
"Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"
Over snow-fields waste and pathless
Under snow-encumbered branches.
Homeward hurried Hiawatha,
Empty-handed, heavy-hearted,
Heard Nokomis, moaning wailing,
"Wahonomin! Wahonomin!
Would that I had perished for you,
Would that I were dead as you are!
Wahonomin! Wahonomin!"
And he rushed into the wigwam
Saw the old Nokomis slowly
Rocking to and fro and moaning,
Saw his lovely Minnehaha
Lying dead and cold before him
And his bursting heart within him
Uttered such a cry of anguish,
That the forest moaned and shuddered,
That the very stars in heaven
Shook and trembled with his anguish.

Then he sat down, still and speechless,
On the bed of Minnehaha,
At the feet of Laughing Water,
At those willing feet, that never
More would lightly run to meet him,
Never more would lightly follow.
With both hands his face he covered,
Seven long days and nights he sat there,
As if in a swoon he sat there,
Speechless, motionless, unconscious
Of the daylight or the darkness.

Then they buried Minnehaha:
In the snow a grave they made her,
In the forest deep and darksome,
Underneath the moaning hemlocks;
Clothed her in her richest garments,
Wrapped her in her robes of ermine,
Covered her with snow, like ermine;
Thus they buried Minnehaha.

And at night a fire was lighted,
On her grave four times was kindled,
For her soul upon its journey
To the Islands of the Blessed.
From his doorway Hiawatha
Saw it burning in the forest,
Lighting up the gloomy hemlocks;
From his sleepless bed uprising,
From the bed of Minnehaha,
Stood and watched it at the doorway,
That it might not be extinguished,
Might not leave her in the darkness.
"Farewell!" said he, "Minnehaha
Farewell, O my Laughing Water!
All my heart is buried with you,
All my thoughts go onward with you!
Come not back again to labour,
Come not back again to suffer,
Where the Famine and the Fever
Wear the heart and waste the body.
Soon my task will be completed,
Soon your footsteps I shall follow
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah!
To the land of the Hereafter!"

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Nature is eternally young. The Third Act opens with a Ballet of Spring, symbolizing life bursting forth throughout a rejuvenated world. Then Iago, the boaster, tells of how he had seen 100 warriors coming over a great water—"bitter so that none could drink it"—in a "great canoe with pinions." He is mocked at by the Indians. "Kaw?" they say, "what lies you tell us!" But Hiawatha declares that Iago speaks truth. The strangers are the coming White Race—traders, settlers and missionaries—bringing to the depths of the virgin forest civilization and the Faith and Hope of Christianity.

And presently this prophecy is fulfilled. The Black-Robe Chief, with the cross upon his bosom, accompanied by his guides and companions, lands on the sandy margin of the lake—bearing a message of Peace and Goodwill on earth.

Hiawatha's mission is at an end. Bidding his people cultivate friendship and unity, he steps into his magic canoe, and as it floats down the stream, the whole tribe raise their arms and their voices in final farewell. As their voices sound and swell and triumph, the vast crowd, the camp, valleys, trees and distant mountain peaks are mantled in solemn light, and in a blaze of sound and colour, Hiawatha westward passes away into the golden sunset. So ends the "Song of Hiawatha."
