"I beheld, too, in that vision
All the secrets of the future,
Of the distant days that shall be.
I beheld the westward marches
Of the unknown, crowded nations.
All the land was full of people,
Restless, struggling, toiling, striving,
Speaking many tongues, yet feeling
But one heart-beat in their bosoms.
In the woodlands rang their axes,
Smoked their towns in all the valleys,
Over all the lakes and rivers
Rushed their great canoes of thunder.

"Then a darker, drearier vision
Passed before me, vague and cloud-like,
I beheld our nations scattered,
All forgetful of my counsels,
Weakened, warring with each other;
Saw the remnants of our people
Sweeping westward, wild and woeful,
Like the cloud-rack of a tempest,
Like the withered leaves of Autumn!"

By the shore of Gitche Gumee,
By the shining Big-Sea-Water,
At the doorway of his wigwam,
In the pleasant Summer morning
Hiawatha stood and waited.

All the air was full of freshness,
All the earth was bright and joyous,
And before him through the sunshine,
Westward toward the neighbouring forest
Passed in golden swarms the Ahmo,
Passed the bees, the honey-makers,
Burning, singing in the sunshine.

Bright above him shone the heavens,
Level spread the lake before him;
From its bosom leaped the sturgeon,
Sparkling, flashing in the sunshine,
On its margin the great forest
Stood reflected in the water,
Every tree-top had its shadow,
Motionless, beneath the water.

From the brow of Hiawatha
Gone was every trace of sorrow,
As a fog from off the water,
As the mist from off the meadow,
With a smile of joy and triumph,
With a look of exultation,
As of one who in a vision
Sees what is to be, but is not,
Stood and waited Hiawatha.

Towards the sun his hands were lifted,* Both the palms spread out against it,
And between the parted fingers
Fell the sunshine on his features,
Flecked with light his naked shoulders,
As it falls and flecks an oak-tree
Through the rifted leaves and branches.
O'er the water floating, flying,
Something in the hazy distance,
Something in the mists of morning,
Loomed and lifted from the water,
Now seemed floating, now seemed flying,
Coming nearer, nearer, nearer.

Was it Shingebis, the diver?
Was it the pelican, the Shada?
Or the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah?
Or the white goose, Waw-be-wawa,
With the water dripping, flashing
From its glossy neck and feathers?

It was neither goose nor diver,
Neither pelican nor heron,
O'er the water floating, flying,
Through the shining mist of morning,
But a birch canoe with paddles,
Rising, sinking on the water,
Dripping, flashing in the sunshine.
And within it came a people
From the distant land of Wabun,
From the farthest realms of morning
Came the Black-Robe chief, the Prophet,
He the Priest of Prayer, the Pale-face,
With his guides and his companions.
And the noble Hiawatha,
With his hands aloft extended,
Held aloft in sign of welcome,
Waited, full of exultation,
Till the birch canoe with paddles
Grated on the shining pebbles,
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
With the cross upon his bosom,
Landed on the sandy margin.

Then the joyous Hiawatha
Cried aloud, and spake in this wise:
"Beautiful is the sun, O strangers,
When you come so far to see us!
All our town in peace awaits you,
All our doors stand open for you:
You shall enter all our wigwams,
For the heart's right hand we give you.
"Never bloomed the earth so gaily,
Never shone the sun so brightly,
As to-day they shine and blossom,
When you come so far to see us!
Never was our lake so tranquil,
Nor so free from rocks and sand-bars;
For your birch canoe in passing
Has removed both rock and sand-bar!
"Never before had our tobacco
Such a sweet and pleasant flavour,
Never the broad leaves of our corn-fields
Were so beautiful to look on,
As they seem to us this morning,
When you come so far to see us!"

And the Black-Robe chief made answer,
Stammered in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar:
"Peace be with you, Hiawatha,
Peace be with you and your people,
Peace of prayer, and peace of pardon,
Peace of Christ, and joy of Mary!"

Then the generous Hiawatha
Led the strangers to his wigwam,
Seated them on skins of bison,
Seated them on skins of ermine,
And the careful old Nokomis
Brought them food in bowls of basswood,
Water brought in birchen dippers,
And the calumet, the peace-pipe,
Filled and lighted for their smoking.
All the old men of the village,
All the warriors of the nation,
All the Jossakeeds, the prophets,
The magicians, the Wabenos,
And the medicine-men, the Medas,
Came to bid the strangers welcome;
"It is well," they said, "O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"
In a circle round the doorway,
With their pipes they sat in silence,
Waiting to behold the strangers,
Waiting to receive their message;
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
From the wigwam came to greet them.
Stammering in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar;
"It is well," they said, "O brother,
That you come so far to see us."

Then the Black-Robe chief, the prophet,
Told his message to the people,
Told the purport of his mission.
Told them of the Virgin Mary,
And her blessed Son, the Saviour:
How in distant lands and ages
He had lived on earth as we do;
How he fasted, prayed, and laboured;
How the Jews, the tribe accursed,
Mocked him, scourged him, crucified him;
How he rose from where they laid him,
Walked again with his disciples,
And ascended into heaven.

And the Chiefs made answer, saying:
"We have listened to your message,
We have heard your words of wisdom.
We will think on what you tell us.
It is well for us, O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

Then they rose up and departed
Each one homeward to his wigwam,
To the young men and the women
Told the story of the strangers
Whom the Master of Life had sent them
From the shining land of Wabun.

Heavy with the heat and silence
Grew the afternoon of summer;
With a drowsy sound the forest
Whispered round the sultry wigwam,
With a sound of sleep the water
Rippled on the beach below it;
From the cornfields shrill and ceaseless
Sang the grasshopper, Pah-puk-keena;
And the guests of Hiawatha,
Weary with the heat of Summer,
Slumbered in the sultry wigwam,
Slowly o'er the simmering landscape
Fell the evening's dusk and coolness.
And the long and level sunbeams
Shot their spears into the forest,
Breaking through its shields of shadow,
Rushed into each secret ambush,
Searched each thicket, dingle, hollow;
Still the guests of Hiawatha
Slumbered in the silent wigwam.

From his place rose Hiawatha,
Bade farewell to old Nokomis,
Spake in whispers, spake in this wise,
Did not wake the guests that slumbered:

"I am going, O Nokomis,
On a long and distant journey,
To the Portals of the Sunset,
To the regions of the home-wind.
But these guests I leave behind me,
In your watch and ward I leave them;
See that never harm comes near them,
See that never fear molests them,
Never danger nor suspicion,
Never want of food or shelter,
In the lodge of Hiawatha!"

Musashino High School
武蔵野高等学校
●弦楽合奏 String ensemble
event_2_80.additional_information: Page 32. Expository and promotional text about 武蔵野高等学校 and its educational environment, including Japanese and English paragraphs. Text includes: 本学園では青少年の高潔な人格、円満な情操、健全な心身をはぐくむ教育環境として、45万㎡の美しい自然を誇る入間校地に理想的な教育施設の整備を進めてきたが、昭和48年に武蔵野高等学校音楽科を開設した。 この高等学校においても教育方針として、音楽芸術の研鑽とともに人間形成を掲げ、これを実現する手段として専門教科と一般教科との均衡、授業と教室内外の生活指導の一体化に重点を置いているが、本校が原則として全寮制を採用しているのもこの趣旨からである。 本校は大学との関連における一貫教育ならびに適切な早期教育の重要性を認識し、優れた専任教諭と武蔵野音楽大学からの指導陣を擁し、生徒の指導に万全を期している。 卒業生の大部分は武蔵野音楽大学への進学を希望するが、このうち学業、人物が特に優れたものには、同大学音楽学部(第一部)に推薦入学の特典が与えられる。 English text also present beginning 'In order to provide an environment suitable for fostering well-rounded character development of young people...'

Descriptive text: 幼児教育の重要性と地域社会への貢献を考え、本学園では次頁の４幼稚園を設置している。いずれも学校教育法に基づいて、４才児、５才児の２年保育を行う。幼児期が基本的人格の形成に極めて重要、かつ音楽教育においても非常に大切な時期であることを認識し、幼児にふさわしい教育環境を整備して、人間形成の基礎を築くことを目指している。この目的を達成するために学園と４幼稚園が協力、連繋して、幼稚園教育要領をもとに健康、社会、自然、言語、音楽リズム、絵画制作の６領域から適質、適量の教育内容を選択し、カリキュラムを編成している。加えて音楽の基礎指導にカール・オルフのメソッドを、さらにヴァイオリンその他の楽器を採用して、大きな教育成果を挙げている。 English description also present. Captions: ・保育風景 A kindergarten class; • 屋外保育 Outside the kindergarten; • 運動会 Athletic activities; • バス送迎 Boarding the school bus; • 遠足 A school excursion.

event_4_45.additional_information: Page 40. Descriptive text: 音楽教育においてとくに大切な幼少年期を正しく導き、その天分を豊かに伸ばす目的をもって本学園内に設置されている。指導者は外人教授を含め80名。本学園の充実した施設を活用し、個人レッスンのほかソルフェージュ、合唱、合奏などのクラス授業を全生徒に課し、技巧偏重を避けるとともに、音楽に対する歓びと広い視野を養い、また各生徒の適性に応じたきめこまかな指導を行なっている。授業は週2回。 English description also present.

event_5_33.additional_information: Pages 41-43. Student Life heading includes 演奏会／特別講座・特別演奏会. Main heading on page 42: Student Concerts / 演奏会. Introductory text: 武蔵野音楽大学では、学生諸君が豊かな経験をとおして技術と創造性を練習し、同時にその実績を広く学外に紹介するために次のような演奏会を企画開催している。 English parallel description on page 43 begins: The following concerts are regularly scheduled at Musashino Academia:.

section_2.additional_information: 前期（7月）と後期（12月）の年2回、定期的に開催される演奏会。7月は教職員と管・弦・打楽器専攻から選抜された学生で編成されるオーケストラによる演奏会で、古典から現代にいたる管弦楽曲や協奏曲がプログラムにとりあげられる。協奏曲の独奏者は全学から公募し、オーディションによって選出された学生が起用される。12月にはこのオーケストラに声楽学生を主体とした混声合唱団が協演し、古今のレクイエム、パッション、オラトリオあるいはミサ曲などを上演するのが恒例である。毎年全国各地または昭和52年度には西独に演奏旅行を行ない（別掲）大成功を収めている。 English parallel title: Orchestra Concert/Choir Recital.

section_3.additional_information: 本大学では過去においてたびたびオペラを上演し好評を博してきたが、昭和48年度から新しい構想のもとに正規のカリキュラムに組込まれたオペラコースを発足させ、多くの外国人教授の協力、指導も得て、平素の歌唱、基礎演技の勉学をとおし、音楽大学におけるオペラ研究のあり方、上演の意義を追求している。従来毎年発表を行っているが、昭和53年度にはモーツァルト“コシ・ファン・トゥッテ”を上演した。 English parallel title: Opera Performance.

performance_1.performance_name: モーツァルト“コシ・ファン・トゥッテ”
performance_1.additional_information: 昭和53年度にはモーツァルト“コシ・ファン・トゥッテ”を上演した。

section_4.section_name: ●管楽合奏団（ウィンドアンサンブル）演奏会
section_4.additional_information: 管楽器専攻学生によるウィンドアンサンブルは、古典から現代に至るオリジナル曲を中心に毎週練習に励んでおり、学内外で数多くの演奏の実績を誇っている。毎年全国各地に演奏旅行を行っているが、昭和53年は東北地方での演奏が行なわれる。 English parallel title: Wind Ensemble Recitals.

section_5.section_name: ●室内合奏団、室内合唱団、室内楽、ソロコンサート
section_5.additional_information: それぞれ選抜された大学院生、学生が多くの指導者の指導を得て意欲的なプログラムと取組み、学内外で演奏会を開き好評を得ている。 English parallel title: Chamber Ensembles, Chamber Choral Recitals, Chamber Music, Solo Concerts.

section_6.additional_information: 教職員、学生の研究発表、外来演奏家による演奏、あるいは邦楽鑑賞会など、学生に音楽全般にわたる広い知識と経験を与えるために、江古田校舎では水曜および土曜日にベートーヴェンホール、モーツァルトホールで、また入間校舎では木曜日に、カリキュラムの一環として企画開催される演奏会。 English parallel title: Wednesday, Thursday and Saturday Concerts.

event_6_28.event_name: ●海外演奏旅行● Overseas Performing Tour
event_6_28.event_venue: ベートーヴェンホール
event_6_28.presenter_sponsor: ボン市およびドイツ音楽協議会
event_6_28.additional_information: Pages 44-45. 昭和52年9月8日から約1ヶ月間、西独ボン市およびドイツ音楽協議会の主催になる、ベートーヴェン没後150年祭の公式行事に参加するとともに、同国13都市で演奏を行なった武蔵野音楽大学管弦楽団は、訪問地先々で大成功を収めた。 大統領府におけるシェール大統領への感激の対面、ベートーヴェンホールでの熱演、日・独・英の若人達の共演による「第9シンフォニー」、各都市における心温まる歓迎レセプション、民宿先でのドイツ人家族との交歓、史跡や音楽関係施設の見学など、この旅行が教育上または文化交流と国際親善に果した役割は大きい。 English parallel text present. Captions: ・本学演奏会 / ボン・ベートーヴェンホールにて / Concert at Beethoven Hall, Bonn; ・シェール西ドイツ大統領と… West German President Scheel greets the Academia's musicians; ・民宿先での練習 Rehearsal at the chateau; ・シュヴェッパー城にて Schloss Schwebber (Chateau Schwebber); ・本学オーケストラの成功を報道する西ドイツ各紙 German newspapers praised the Musashino concerts; ・各地演奏会プログラム、ポスター Concert programs and posters.

event_2_82.additional_information: Page 1 title: 亞洲青年音樂營（香港）一九七九 / Asian Youth Music Camp 1979 Hong Kong. Page 2 contents include: Introduction; Message from the Acting Governor Sir Jack Cater K.B.E., J.P.; Message from the Secretary for Home Affairs Mr F.K. Li C.M.G., J.P.; The Music Administrator's Office; Urban Council; Repertorie; Message from the Asian Composers' League; Programme Notes; Personalities; Camp Diary; Participants; Staff; Acknowledgement. Chinese contents also listed. Page 3 describes the camp history and purpose. The Inaugural Asian Youth Music Camp was held at Mount Makiling of the Philippines from 1st to 15th of May, 1977. The 2nd Asian Youth Music Camp was held in Singapore in December 1978. The 1979 Asian Youth Music Camp will be held at the Wu Kwai Sha Youth Village, Hong Kong, from 1st to 15th December. Over a hundred participants from Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Macau and Australia will come and join the best young players from Hong Kong. At the Camp the 1979 Asian Youth Orchestra will be formed and the Orchestra will give four public concerts for Hong Kong audience. The camp will also encourage ethnic music on ethnic instruments; in Hong Kong, the term "ethnic" refers to Chinese music and traditional Chinese instruments. The Singapore Youth Chinese Orchestra will join the Hong Kong Youth Chinese Orchestra and eighteen other Hong Kong Chinese orchestras, choirs and dance groups in the rehearsal and performance of Chinese instrumental music, songs and dances. Chinese text on page 3 gives parallel information and says 本届亚洲青年音乐营由香港主办，于本年十二月一日至十五日在中华基督教青年会乌溪沙青年新村举行. Page 4 contains a welcome message signed ( Jack Cater ) Acting Governor. Page 5 contains MESSAGE 獻辭 FROM THE SECRETARY FOR HOME AFFAIRS, signed (F.K. Li), dated 26th November 1979; Chinese date 一九七九年十一月廿六日. Pages 6-9 provide descriptive institutional information about The Music Administrator's Office and The Urban Council: Cultural Programmes and Facilities, including statistics, ensembles, exchange programmes, festivals, venues, and cultural facilities.

event_10_15.additional_information:
=== Page 12 ===
"Great music harmonizes with the Universe"—this is a common belief of Chinese philosophers. Music is the best communication medium among the races.

During the coming two weeks, all the young musicians from the Austral-Asian region will work and study together; this will not only improve the musicianship of each participant but also help to develop mutual understanding and friendship. With the development of this type of activities, we can foresee a brightful future in the music world of Austral-Asia.

During the music camp, various compositions from all over the world will be performed. In particular, some of the best compositions by Asian composers will also be played. On this point, the Asian Youth Music Camp is sharing the same goal with the Asian Composers' League, and this is something we are pleased and proud of.

Therefore, on behalf of the Asian Composers' League, I wish to send the best wishes and most sincere congratulations to all the participants and organisers of the 1979 Asian Youth Music Camp.

English text includes: "1972 — Teeside Music Festival (won the 2nd prize in Folk Music Group). 1973 — Goodwill tour and performances to West Malaysia which was a great success. 1974 — Participation in the Llangollen International Eisteddfod in Wales, UK (The Ensemble won 2nd place in the Folk Group Section). — Performance in London for the students of Singapore and Malaysia. 1975 — Goodwill tour and performances in the Philippines to foster greater understanding between the ASEAN countries. 1976 — Invitation to perform in Muar, Kuala Lumpur and Penang. A musical workshop was organized on the request of the Chinese orchestra enthusiasts in West Malaysia, to share with our Malaysian neighbours our instrumental expertise. 1977 — Invitation by the Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall to conduct a week-long workshop on Chinese Instrumental Music in Kuala Lumpur. The workshop was a great success and it concluded with the combined 100 strong orchestra performing in an evening of instrumental music." Also: "The Singapore Youth Chinese Orchestra has been actively engaged in promoting Chinese music since its inception in 1970. With the great interest created in schools for Chinese instrumental music, the orchestra has plans to go to schools to give concerts and to conduct workshops for school Chinese orchestra members." Chinese text repeats similar information. Cross-instrument notes preserved in source include "(Di Zi)", "(Yang Qin)", "(BAN HU)" and in Chinese "（兼笛子）", "（兼揚琴）", "（兼板胡）". credits.composer: Liu Tian-hua, Lau Tak-hoi, Wong Yin-chiu, Wong Shue-chiu, Jian Guang-yi, Wang Zhi-wei, Tong Leung-tak, Tung Tak-leong

event_3_67.additional_information: Pages 24-26 vicinity. Introductory note: "The music items rehearsed and performed by the Singapore Youth Chinese Orchestra and the combined Chinese orchestras, dance troupes and chorus from Hong Kong fall into three main categories: classical pieces for solo and ensemble playing, compositions for the Chinese orchestra and music rewritten or re-arranged for accompanying folk dances. The following notes briefly describe selected items in each of the three categories." Chinese pages continue with parallel notes and additional item descriptions.

section_1.additional_information: Includes English and Chinese notes, some with lyrics or descriptive text.

performance_1.additional_information: "Legend has it that the piece was composed during or before the Song Dynasty (960 – 1280 A.D.). It is one of the best loved compositions for the qin, an ancient instrument. The music is composed in such a way to form the effect of a dialogue between a fisherman and a woodcutter. There are imitations of the sounds of rowing and wood-cutting and the listener could almost visualise the leisurely life of the fisherman and the woodcutter." Chinese note: "此曲的作者不考。明代「藏春塢琴譜」在此曲解題中引及「紫霞洞考」，倘宋代的「紫霞洞琴譜」實有此曲，則其年代可提前到宋或以前。現存琴譜載有此曲的，最早是明代「杏莊太音續譜」（1560），明清琴譜轉載的極多，為流行最廣的琴曲之一。 此曲前段用悠悠自得的樂句重複或移位再現，形成問答對話的效果。另有些琴聲船和砍木的音調，造成了對漁樵生活的聯想。明揚論「太古遺音」說：『按斯曲，想亦隱君子所作也。因見青山綠水，萬古常新，其間識山水之趣者，惟漁與樵。…………是以金蘭同契，拉伴清談，數治亂，論興亡，千載得失，盡付於漁樵談笑之中矣。』這段話頗足以解釋此曲的含意。

performance_2.additional_information: "one of the eight most famous tunes of southern China. A composition of the Qing Dynasty (1644 – 1911 A.D.), the crisp and rhythmic melody describes the joyful celebration of a good harvest in a picturesque village setting."

performance_3.performance_name: Tai Hua Qiao (The Bride in the Wedding Sedan Chair)
performance_3.additional_information: "it was customary in the past in many rural areas of Chona for villagers to carry a bride on a sedan chair from one village to another on her wedding day. This piece of joyful folk music, re-arranged now for solo on the suo-na (a double reed ethnic wind instrument) could well have been played by the small instrumental ensemble which would accompany the bride on her ride to her new home;" Chinese note for "抬花橋": "這是首民間吹鼓曲。描寫過去鄉村村民在喜慶佳日，奏樂抬轎迎新娘的那種熱鬧場面。"

performance_4.additional_information: "composer Liu Tian-hua (1895 – 1932 A.D.) is one of the most famous Chinese composers. His er-hu (a two-string bowed instrument) compositions are standard studies for virtually every er-hu soloist. Liang Xiao was composed on 22nd January, 1928. The music is of typical southern Chinese flavour. It paints a peaceful picture of a Chinese family happily celebrating New Year's Eve and joyfully awaiting the arrival of the Lunar New Year;" Chinese note for "良宵": "作曲者劉天華先生為中國著名中樂大師，生於一八九五年二月四日，卒於一九三二年六月一日。作品計有十首二胡獨奏曲，三首琵琶獨奏曲及一首合奏曲等。其二胡曲更為每個二胡演奏家之必修課，其中以「良宵」、「光明行」、「空山鳥語」最為著名。『良宵』作於一九二八年一月廿二日，又名『除夜小唱』。樂曲具有江南風味，描寫在除夕之夜，人們合家聚一堂，守歲過年之情景。"

performance_5.performance_name: Mei Li Di Xi-Shuang-Ban-Na (The Beautiful Xi-Shuang-Ban-Na)
performance_5.additional_information: "Xi-Shuang-Ban-Na is the name of a district in the Yun-nan Province. Based on a folk melody, the music describes the life of the hard-working peasants living in the area." Chinese note: "雲南民歌，由湯良德改編為樂隊合奏曲。樂曲描繪，雲南美麗的西雙版納（地方名）世世代代居住着傣族人民，他們能歌善舞，勤勞勇敢，如詩似畫的美景，給傣族人們帶來無限的歡樂。"

performance_6.performance_name: Cao Yuan Xiao Zi Mei (Sisters of the Pasture)
performance_6.additional_information: "a 1974 composition by Lau Tak-hoi and Wong Yin-chiu, originally for performance by a symphony orchestra. The music describes the life of the nomadic shepherd who live on the pasture of Mongolia." Chinese note for "草原小妹妹": "這首樂曲由劉德海，吳祖強，王燕樵初作於一九七四年，樂曲描繪了內蒙草原上有一對英雄小姊妹，在一次牧羊時，突然遇到暴風雪，通過她們英雄頑強，不屈不撓的鬥爭，終於戰勝了風雪，保護了羊群。"

performance_7.performance_name: Gang Shui Ben Liu (The Rolling Steel Mill)
performance_7.additional_information: "a 1977 composition, the Chinese orchestra is used to portray the bustling life in a modern steel mill and the perseverance and dedication of those who work in it."

performance_8.additional_information: "these two compositions were written in June 1979 by Tong Leung-tak in commemoration of the holding of the Asian Youth Music Camp in Hong Kong. In the music, Tong describes two familiar scenes in Hong Kong — one on a soccer field with two teams of youngsters playing in a feverish game". Chinese note for "小波迷": "一九七九年六月湯良德先生特意為亞洲青年音樂營演出而作此曲。樂曲以詼諧的兒歌來表現一群天真活潑的少年，在課餘時間裏，展開了一場你爭我奪的足球比賽。運動給少年帶來歡樂，促進他們的健康成長，鍛鍊堅強意志。"

performance_9.performance_name: Yu Jia Gu Niang (The Young Lady from the Fishing Village)
performance_9.additional_information: "these two compositions were written in June 1979 by Tong Leung-tak in commemoration of the holding of the Asian Youth Music Camp in Hong Kong. In the music, Tong describes ... the other in one of the many fishing villages around the territory." Chinese note for "漁家姑娘": "樂曲描寫居住在香港的漁家姑娘，她們勤勞勇敢，從小隨着父母，迎烈日，踏風浪，生活在海洋上。樂曲以三段體組成（1）姑娘織網（2）出海捕魚（3）滿載而歸。"

performance_10.performance_name: You Tian Di Zao Chen (The Oil Field in the Morning)
performance_10.additional_information: "composer Wong Shue-chiu wrote this piece of music in 1968 and used the Chinese orchestra to tell the story of one day's event at an oil field — sunrise, followed by a song of the workers; then the exhilaration when oil is struck at the field and finally, a chorus sung by those who had a job well done." Chinese note: "這是一首四段體的樂曲。 第一段引子奏出油田早晨太陽初升，鳥鳴花香的景色，接著奏出優美如歌的慢板，使人聯想到大自然的美麗。 第二段為快板，樂曲模仿鑽機聲響徹四方，奏出工人們愉快的勞動心情。 第三段表現更為熱烈，是歡慶油田順利建成的熱鬧場面。 結尾以一個壯麗的進行曲式結束，表現出工程之宏偉及對油田的歌頌。 作者王樹銘，寫於一九六八 年左右。"

performance_11.performance_type: transcription or variation based on folk tune
performance_11.based_on_tune: a folk song in her praise
performance_11.additional_information: "A-La-Mu-Han is the name of a beautiful young lady who lived in the Xin Jiang Province — a folk song in her praise;" Chinese note: "這是一首新疆民歌，由謝功成編曲，描繪一個美麗勤勞的姑娘叫『阿拉木汗』。"

performance_12.performance_type: transcription or variation based on folk tune
performance_12.lyrics_transcript: 「一年四季百花開，百花開放人人愛，人人愛來人人戴，姑娘呀小伙子戴起來」
performance_12.based_on_tune: a folk tune from the An Hui Province
performance_12.additional_information: Chinese note: "安徽民歌，用了鄉土的風味，歡快的旋律，唱出一年四季人們所最愛戴的花朵。真如歌詞中所說的…"

performance_13.performance_type: transcription or variation based on folk tune
performance_13.performance_name: Bu-Gu-Niao Jiao Chi Liao (The Cuckoo is late this Spring)
performance_13.based_on_tune: a folk song of the Shan Bei Province
performance_13.additional_information: "where the farmers were earnestly awaiting the first call of the cuckoo, the arrival of Spring;" Chinese note: "陝北民歌描寫農家春耕時節，等待布谷鳥在枝頭上迎春歌的情景。"

performance_14.performance_type: transcription or variation based on folk tune
performance_14.performance_name: Wu-Su-Lei Xiang Dong Liu (The Wu-Su-Lei River flows eastwards)
performance_14.lyrics_transcript: 「莊稼綠油油，遍山種花集，魚兒滿江游，歌聲傳山坡」
performance_14.based_on_tune: a folk song of the He-Zhe tribe
performance_14.additional_information: "who depend on the Wu-Su-Lei River for their livelihood." Chinese note for "烏蘇里向東流": "赫哲族人們生活愉快…"

performance_15.performance_name: Mu Min Xin Ge (Song of the Herdsman)
performance_15.based_on_tune: the melody is based on a folk tune from Mongolia
performance_15.additional_information: "composed in 1973 by Jian Guang-yi and Wang Zhi-wei for solo on the di-zi (the Chinese bamboo flute), the melody is based on a folk tune from Mongolia. The Mongolians are herdsman and the music describes the peaceful and joyful Mongolians travelling with their herd in the wide pastures of Mongolia." Chinese note: "『牧民新歌』作於一九七三年，作曲者簡易勇、王志偉兩位本身也是笛子演奏家。樂曲採用了蒙古族的音調編寫而成。歌曲用曲笛來演奏，曲笛音色優美柔和。樂曲描繪年青一代的內蒙牧民，在藍色遼闊的天空下，無邊無際的草原上盡情高歌的場面。"

performance_16.additional_information: "a classical duet of a brother and sister who were performing frontier duties in bright moonlight;" Chinese note: "這是首古典雙人舞，舞蹈表現了一對兄妹，爲了保衛邊疆，在一個月光瑩瑩的夜晚，手執利劍，一邊巡邏，一邊練武的情景。舞蹈由陳華，林阿梅合編，樂曲由符任之先生編配。"

performance_17.performance_name: Da Yan Nan Fei (South Fly the Snow Geese)
performance_17.lyrics_transcript: 「深秋季節裏，大雁南去，在途中遇到了暴風雪。一對小雁受傷失落，它們掙扎飛翔，終於在大雁的護衛下，回到了隊伍，繼續南飛」
performance_17.additional_information: English note: "an episode during the flight of a flock of snow geese towards the south, in search of warmer weather. The flock was blown off course in a snow storm and two young ones lost touch with the main team. The whole flock turned back to search for the lost ones and, as all good stories would end, the young ones were found and they flew on in search of peace and warmth." Chinese note: "一九七九年邢浪平先生用這故事編成舞蹈表現蒙族人民，不畏艱難，勇敢堅強的性格。"

performance_18.based_on_tune: the dance is based on two extracts from the Butterfly Lovers Violin Concerto
performance_18.additional_information: English note: "the dance is based on two extracts from the Butterfly Lovers Violin Concerto which was written in 1958-9 by two young composers attached to the Shanghai Conservatory. The concerto might best be described as a programme-concerto in Chinese idiom, its narrative taken from a classic Chinese Opera story..." Chinese note: "舞蹈採用了小提琴協奏曲『梁祝片斷』（樓台會）及『化蝶』的音樂編成。故事發生在明末，一對同窗友好，叫梁山伯和祝英台。他們互相敬慕，願做終生伴侶，可是封建的祝員外以父母之命媒妁之言，強行把自己的女兒祝英台許配給有財有勢的馬文才。樓台會相見後，使梁山伯知情憂鬱而死，當祝英台聞訊後悲切斷腸，終於在祝英台出嫁路過梁山伯的墓前撞墓而死。"

performance_19.lyrics_transcript:
Ah! Sing Gloria!
Cheerfully we sing!
We are Asian young musicians.
United as one, cheerfully we sing,
To our friendship,
To our progress,
To advancement.
Through our fellowship we are united.
Joyfully we sing!
performance_19.additional_information: "And finally, to commemorate the occasion of the 3rd Asian Youth Music Camp, 3 officers of the Music Administrator's Office wrote a song as a dedication to the Asian Youth Music Camp movement, with accompaniment by a Chinese orchestra. The music is written by Tung Tak-leong, with the lyrics by Tong Leung-tak and Lui Ki-ling."

performance_20.lyrics_transcript:
「鑼鼓震天響，鞭炮沖雲霄
調龍舞獅迎新春，風調雨順年年好」
performance_20.additional_information: 「本曲作於一九七七年春節，樂曲描寫了在中國的傳統節日裏，人們歡度新春的那種熱烈場面。」

performance_21.lyrics_transcript:
「巍巍寶塔山，高高入雲天
潺潺延河水，源遠幾千載」
performance_21.based_on_tune: 根據一首陝北歌曲改編而成
performance_21.additional_information: 「一九七五年劉明沅先生根據一首陝北歌曲改編而成，樂曲描繪了古都延安的壯麗景色，人們過着和平幸福的生活。」

performance_22.lyrics_transcript: 「梭羅河水源流長，世世代代熱愛它，河水流不盡，贊歌唱不完」。

performance_23.based_on_tune: 歌曲「滿江紅」是以岳飛的詞譜成一首中國古曲
performance_23.additional_information: 「中國南宋名將岳飛是一位傑出的民族英雄。歌曲『滿江紅』是以岳飛的詞譜成一首中國古曲。歌曲表達了英雄『盡忠報國』的偉大胸懷和『還我河山』的必勝信心。」

performance_24.based_on_tune: 曾試配以唐代詩人李白的同名詩
performance_24.additional_information: 「此曲始見於王賓魯先生『梅庵琴譜』（一九三一年），為梅庵古琴派之名曲。中國民族音樂理論家楊隆勳先生，曾試配以唐代詩人李白的同名詩，以表現古代征人遠戍邊疆的不滿情緒。」

performance_25.lyrics_transcript:
「馬兒啊，你慢些走，慢些走！我要把這迷人的景色看個夠。肥沃的土地好像浸透了油，良田萬畝好像用黃金鋪就。青山滴翠美如畫，人在畫中鬧豐收…………。」
林蔭小道多清幽，姑娘樓前在刺繡。
路旁的小溪撥動了琴弦，好像為姑娘的歌聲伴奏，晚風揚起了溫柔的翅膀，永遠隨着我的馬兒走。家鄉啊，我愛你多彩的風姿，我想看個夠，總也看不夠。
performance_25.additional_information: 「這是一首家鄉的贊歌，抒情、優美、親切、熱情，是一幅美麗的圖畫：」

performance_26.additional_information: 「新疆有位美麗的姑娘叫阿依莎。她美麗勤勞。她的歌聲比百靈鳥都好聽。她歌唱能把千年荒山變綠洲，唱歌能使麥穗金黃棉桃大。」

performance_27.based_on_tune: 樂曲以河南音樂作基調
performance_27.additional_information: 「描寫了河南人民為了改變窮山溝為米糧川的那種艱苦奮鬥的精神。」

performance_28.based_on_tune: 舞蹈是根據一九七五年王國潼，李秀琪所創作的一首二胡齊奏曲所編成
performance_28.additional_information: 「在那遼闊無際，綠草茵茵，如詩似畫的大草原上，蒙族牧民揚鞭躍馬，奔馳在千里草原上。」

performance_29.based_on_tune: 這首樂曲是歌劇音樂改編

performance_30.lyrics_transcript:

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
O'ER verdant meadows to the mountain height,
    In rays of morning do thou rise, O song,
And greet the sea and land, the day so bright,
    Rise to empyreal spheres where angels throng.

The solemn Sabbath bells intone the lay,
    That sweetly with the sylvan choir doth chime;
The brook doth gush, and thund'ring far away
    Roll hoary, crumbling rocks, e'en old as time.

Sublime, divine the pow'r of melodies
    That wakes the heart to worthiness and grace.
Sound forth o'er earth, ye wondrous harmonies,
    Resound in song throughout all time and space.

    Rejoice, O human-kind!
The pow'r of tone o'er life doth shed
    A happy ray of light.
Like sunshine spreading forth from zone to zone,
    So song shall quicken, waking pure delight.

Sovereign Lord, to Thee we bow.

Grand as organ nobly pealing,
    Let this vow to Heaven ascend;
Heart and voice the power revealing,
    Verse and harmony to blend.
Native country, native tongue,
Bind our hearts in union strong.

Word and weapon nobly plighted,
    To defend thee and to save;
We, thy children, stand united,
    Glorious shall thy banner wave.
Life we pledge at thy command,
O, thou dearest Fatherland.

Honour to the man who foldeth
    Truth and beauty to his breast;
But on him who sacred holdeth
    Woman's love let blessing rest.
Curse the dastard who doth prove
Traitor to a woman's love.

In full chorus now uniting,
    Pledged to love, be all agreed;
Friendship's sacred name now plighting,
    True to be in word and deed;
Swear by love to faithful stand;
Honour God and Fatherland.

performance_8.lyrics_transcript:
STREAM and mill, your murmurs cease,
Sounds, to silence all decline;
Now, ye woodbirds, rest in peace,
Or in this my burthen join,
She is mine, she is mine; she has said she is mine.

Lovely springtime, thee I welcome merrily,
All thy flowrets blooming smile so cheerily,
Now no more, with care o'ergrown,
Feels my beating heart alone.
She is mine, yes, the miller's daughter now is mine.
performance_8.additional_information: Liedertafel

performance_10.lyrics_transcript:
O Sons of Art, man's dignity to you is given:
    Preserve it man!
It falls with you, with you ascends to heaven!
The hallowed themes of Magian dreams,
Founded in Wisdom's vast creation,
Gliding like rivers find their ocean,
    That great harmonious plan.

Eternal truth, tho' oft rejected,
Exists not ever unprotected;
She finds a refuge with the tuneful throng.
She there appears in all her glory,
Mighty when veil'd in mystic story;
She wakes the lay of lofty voices,
And over all her foes rejoices,
Her vengeance flashing, peals in song.

To your free mother homage render,
Boldly to gain her height aspire;
Enthron'd she dwells in radiant splendour
No other crown than hers desire.
While you her thousand paths are tracing
Press onward, keeping Truth in sight;
Come altogether, stand embracing
Before the Throne where paths unite!
performance_10.additional_information: Liedertafel

performance_11.additional_information: (With Cello Obbligato by Herr Theo. Liebe). Signor Buzzi

performance_12.lyrics_transcript:
Pull away, boys, steer for the cove,
Yonder lie dreaming the hearts that we love.
Let us now banish all trouble and sorrow,
We shall have cause to be joyful to-morrow.
Glittering moonbeams bespangle the deep,
O'er the wide ocean the winds are asleep.

Storms are o'er, and land is in sight,
Calmly we glide thro' the waters to-night.
Many a heart will to-morrow be leaping,
Which in the bosom is quietly sleeping.
Rowing and singing we draw near the shore,
Where there are joys for us seamen in store.

performance_13.additional_information: Miss Juliet Flegeltaub

performance_14.lyrics_transcript:
Great Caesar, with our dying breath,
    Thus we hail thee!
The body thou canst doom to death,
But the soul shall hold fast her faith.
O Caesar, with our dying breath,
    Thus we hail thee!
Great lord of life and death!

    See, the town keeps holiday to-day,
The circus in festive array!
Now raise a merry shout to the gods,
With cymbals clashing, and trumpets blowing.
Before them the stern lictors' rods
See the consuls in crimson glowing.
See the pale Vestals' white robes flowing,
All attend till great Caesar nods.

    And we, all amid the dread arena,
Naked, defenceless, in God our sole reliance,
We hear with calm defiance
The roaring lion and hyena,
Soon to be our living tomb.

    Heard ye that ringing cheer?
They open now the cage,
And the tiger and panther in their rage,
They come madly bounding along.
Brethren, be strong!
Lift up your heart in prayer and song.

    God of the martyr and the slave,
O Christ, who hast triumphed over death!
Come, oh come, thy suff'ring saints to save.
Now they draw their parting breath!

    'Tis the hour of joyful compensation,
Hark! it greets us from eternity.
Now comes the long-looked-for salvation,
Now dawns the day of liberty.

And when the life-blood is pouring,
And day is dark'ning into night,
O living God, to Thee our souls are soaring,
And death is the dawning of endless light.

performance_16.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Dioscuri! shining twin stars,
    Ye who light us o'er the ocean;
Mighty helpers, guide us safely,
    Still the waves to gentle motion.

Tho' with firm hearts, fear unknowing,
    Undismayed with storms contending,
We would see your mild rays beaming,
    Hope and courage to us lending.

This strong oar that bears us onward,
    O'er the waves your rule obeying,
At your shrine we then will offer,
    At your altar homage paying.

Again fill your glasses with bright sparkling wine,
Once more will I pledge ye, dear comrades of mine!
Farewell, hoary mountains and dear native home,
Farewell! to a far distant land I must roam.

The bright sun above us at rest does not stand,
His course he fulfils over ocean and land;
The billows disperse and recede from the shore,
The storm rushes onward its fury to pour.

With swift-speeding pinion the bird flies away,
Still singing and soaring it pours out its lay.
Thus youth's glowing visions will urge to the race,
Thus earth wanders on thro' regions of space.

The birds of his own land the wanderer greet,
Its flowr's meet his eye with their odour so sweet;
They bring to his heart thoughts of home and of love,
The meadow beneath and the blue sky above.

He dreams that once more he his fatherland sees,
And sweet scents of home life come borne on the breeze;
Thus love e'er will follow the lov'd one afar,
And shine through the distance his one guiding star.

event_1_120.event_name: SCENES FROM THE SONG OF HIAWATHA

credits.composer: S. COLERIDGE-TAYLOR

event_1_120.additional_information: Visible source pages include Page 24, 25, 27, 31, 33. Cast/credit list appears fragmentary and may continue from earlier or later pages. Program note states: "In performance a few words have been altered to bring the narrative into the present tense." The story note reads: "The story of this Opera forms a part of Longfellow's "Song of Hiawatha." It is divided into three Acts—"Hiawatha's Wedding Feast," "The Death of Minnehaha," and "Hiawatha's Departure.""

section_1.additional_information:
Program note/summary preceding and within this section: "Hiawatha was a man as other men, and wooed and won sweet Laughing Water, Minnehaha from the land of the Dacotahs. The Opera opens with the festivities at their marriage, and gay are the guests as they offer their presents and receive the generous hospitality of their host. Quip and jest pass round. Pau-Puk-Keewis leaps and twines in dance with the grace of a barbaric savage. The Medicine Man brews a Peyote plant potion, of which the guests partake, and through its magic visualise an ancient myth of a Young Chief who relinquishes his earthly body to seek his beloved in the Land of the Hereafter. He finds her, and soul meets soul in the Happy Hunting Grounds. Supreme happiness is his till he is reminded by Gitche Manitou, the Mighty, that he is mortal, and must return to fulfil his destiny on Earth. The return of the Young Chief to his people is celebrated by a thrilling totem dance, in which all the tribe takes part, and give vent to their feeling in the hiss of the serpent, the bark of the fox, the shriek of the eagle or the bellow of the buffalo, according to the nature of their totem. Song follows dance, and Chibabos, the singer of sweet songs, sounds the keynote of passionate love in the ears of his entranced listeners.

The Marriage Feast is over. Happy and joyous, the guests, led by Iagoo, the marvellous storyteller, depart to their wigwams, and alone in the moonlight are Hiawatha and Minnehaha.

performance_1.lyrics_transcript:
You shall hear how Pau-Puk-Keewis,
How the handsome Yenadizze,
Danced at Hiawatha's wedding;
How the gentle Chibabos,
He the sweetest of musicians,
Sang his songs of love and longing,
How Iagoo, the great boaster,
He the marvellous storyteller,
Told his tales of strange adventure,
That the feast might be more joyous,
That the time might pass more gaily
And the guests be more contented.
Sumptuous was the feast Nokomis
Made at Hiawatha's wedding.
All the bowls were made of bass-wood
White and polished very smoothly,
All the spoons of horn of bison,
Black and polished very smoothly.

She had sent through all the village
Messengers with wands of willow,
As a sign of invitation,
As a token of the feasting;
And the wedding-guests assembled,
Clad in all their richest raiment,
Robes of fur and belts of wampum,
Splendid with their paint and plumage,
Beautiful with beads and tassels.
First they ate the sturgeon, Nahma,
And the pike, the Maskenoza,
Caught and cooked by old Nokomis,
Then on pemican they feasted,
Pemican and buffalo marrow,
Haunch of deer and hump of bison,
Yellow cakes of the Mondamin,
And the wild rice of the river.
But the gracious Hiawatha,

And the lovely Laughing Water,
And the careful old Nokomis,
Tasted not the food before them,
Only waited on the others,
Only served their guests in silence.

And when all the guests had finished,
Old Nokomis, brisk and busy,
From an ample pouch of otter,
Filled the red stone pipes for smoking
With tobacco from the South-land,
Mixed with bark of the red willow,
And with herbs and leaves of fragrance.

Then she said, "O Pau-Puk-Keewis,
Dance for us your merry dances,
Dance the Beggar's Dance to please us,
That the feast may be more joyous,
That the time may pass more gaily,
And our guests be more contented!"

Then the handsome Pau-Puk-Keewis,
He the idle Yenadizze,
He the merry mischief-maker,
Whom the people called the Storm-Fool,
Rose among the guests assembled.

Skilled was he in sports and pastimes,
In the merry dance of snow-shoes,
In the play of quoits and ball-play;
Skilled was he in games of hazard,
In all games of skill and hazard,
Pugasaing, the Bowl and Counters,
Koomtassoo, the Game of Plum-stones.

Though the warriors called him Faint-Heart
Called him coward, Shaugodaya,
Idler, gambler, Yenadizze,
Little heeded he their jesting,
Little cared he for their insults,
For the women and the maidens
Loved the handsome Pau-Puk-Keewis.

He was dressed in shirt of doe-skin,
White and soft, and fringed with ermine,
All inwrought with beads of wampum;

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
And, returning, sat down laughing
There among the guests assembled,
Sat and fanned himself serenely
With his fan of turkey-feathers.

Then they said to Chibiabos,
To the friend of Hiawatha,
To the sweetest of all singers,
To the best of all musicians,
"Sing to us, O Chibiabos!
Songs of love and songs of longing,
That the feast may be more joyous,
That the time may pass more gaily,
And our guests be more contented!"

And the gentle Chibiabos
Sang in accents sweet and tender,
Sang in tones of deep emotion,
Songs of love and songs of longing,
Looking still at Hiawatha,
Looking at fair Laughing Water,
Sang he softly, sang in this wise:

"Onaway! Awake, beloved!
Thou the wild-flower of the forest!
Thou the wild-bird of the prairie!
Thou with eyes so soft and fawn-like!

"If thou only lookest at me,
I am happy, I am happy,
As the lilies of the prairie,
When they feel the dew upon them!

"Sweet thy breath is as the fragrance
Of the wild-flowers in the morning,
As their fragrance is at evening,
In the Moon when leaves are falling.

"Does not all the blood within me
Leap to meet thee, leap to meet thee,
As the springs to meet the sunshine,
In the Moon when nights are brightest?

"Onaway! my heart sings to thee,
Sings with joy when thou art near me,

As the sighing, singing branches
In the pleasant Moon of Strawberries!
"When thou art not pleased, beloved,
Then my heart is sad and darkened,
As the shining river darkens
When the clouds drop shadows on it!
"When thou smil'st, my beloved,
Then my troubled heart is brightened,
As in sunshine gleam the ripples
That the cold wind makes in rivers.
"Smiles the earth, and smile the waters,
Smile the cloudless skies above us,
But I lose the way of smiling
When thou art no longer near me!
"I myself, myself! behold me!
Blood of my beating heart, behold me!
O awake, awake, beloved!
Onaway! awake, beloved!"

Thus the gentle Chibiabos
Sang his song of love and longing;
And Iagoo, the great boaster,
He the marvellous storyteller,
He the friend of old Nokomis,
Jealous of the sweet musician,
Jealous of the applause they gave him,
Saw in all the eyes around him,
Saw in all their looks and gestures,
That the wedding-guests assembled
Longed to hear his pleasant stories,
His immeasurable falsehoods.
Very boastful was Iagoo:
Never heard he an adventure
But himself had made a greater;
Never any deed of daring
But himself had done a bolder;
Never any marvellous story
But himself could tell a stranger
Would you listen to his boasting,
Would you only give him credence,
No one ever shot an arrow
Half so far and high as he had;
Ever caught so many fishes,
Ever killed so many reindeer,
Ever trapped so many beaver!

None could run so fast as he could,
None could dive so deep as he could.
None could swim so far as he could;
None had made so many journeys,
None had seen so many wonders,
As this wonderful Iagoo,
As this marvellous storyteller!
Thus his name became a by-word
And a jest among the people!
And whene'er a boastful hunter
Praised his own address too highly,
Or a warrior, home returning,
Talked too much of his achievements,
All his hearers cried, "Iagoo!
Here's Iagoo come among us!"
He it was who carved the cradle
Of the little Hiawatha,
Carved its framework out of linden,
Bound it strong with reindeer's sinews;
He it was who taught him later
How to make his bows and arrows,
How to make the bows of ash-tree,
And the arrows of the oak-tree.
So among the guests assembled
At my Hiawatha's wedding
Sat Iagoo, old and ugly,
Sat the marvellous storyteller.
And they said, "O good Iagoo,
Tell us now a tale of wonder,
Tell us of some strange adventure,
That the feast may be more joyous,
That the time may pass more gaily,
And our guests be more contented!"
And Iagoo answered straightway,
"You shall hear a tale of wonder,
You shall hear of strange adventures."
So he told the strange adventures
Of Osco, the Magician,
From the Evening Star descended.

Such was Hiawatha's Wedding,
Thus the wedding-banquet ended,
And the wedding-guests departed,
Leaving Hiawatha happy
With the night and Minnehaha.

performance-1.lyrics_transcript:
Summer is over, and Winter grips valley and mountain in its icy clutch. Fever and Famine stalk abroad. Clinging to each other for warmth, the stricken Indians cower and shiver beneath their blankets. And what of the lovely Minnehaha—"Minnehaha, Laughing Water, Loveliest of Dacotah women"? In the absence of Hiawatha—who has gone to seek vainly for food for his people, succour for his bride—she is sick unto death, and dread phantoms bend over her couch. Finally, with a wild cry "Hiawatha! Hiawatha!" she dies in delirium.

Far away amid the forest, miles away among the mountains" the wanderer hears that cry. Homeward hurries Hiawatha. Passionately, despairingly, he flings himself beside the dead body of his beloved, and the old nurse Nokomis sobs out her anguish. The sorrowing Indians moan and wail forth their sorrow, and over the mountains falls the snow.

There is a pause to show the passage of seven days, and then the body of Minnehaha is borne away in stately procession, clothed in her richest garments, wrapped in her robes of ermine, ready for her journey to the Islands of the Blessed.

O the long and dreary Winter!
O the cold and cruel Winter!
Ever thicker, thicker, thicker,
Froze the ice on lake and river,
Ever deeper, deeper, deeper,
Fell the snow o'er all the landscape,
Fell the covering snow, and drifted
Through the forest, round the village.
Hardly from his buried wigwam
Could the hunter force a passage;
With his mittens and his snow-shoes
Vainly walked he through the forest,
Sought for bird or beast and found none,
Saw no track of deer or rabbit,
In the snow beheld no footprints,
In the ghastly, gleaming forest
Fell, and could not rise from weakness,
Perished there from cold and hunger.
O the famine and the fever!
O the wasting of the famine!
O the blasting of the fever!
O the wailing of the children!
O the anguish of the women!
All the earth was sick and famished,
Hungry was the air around them,
Hungry was the sky above them,
And the hungry stars in heaven
Like the eyes of wolves glared at them!

Into Hiawatha's wigwam
Came two silent guests and gloomy,
Waited not to be invited,
Did not parley at the doorway,
Sat there without word of welcome
In the seat of Laughing Water;
Looked with haggard eyes and hollow
At the face of Laughing Water.
And the foremost said, "Behold me!
I am Famine, Buckadawin!"
And the other said, "Behold me!
I am Fever, Ahkosewin!"
And the lovely Minnehaha
Shuddered as they looked upon her,

Shuddered at the words they uttered,
Lay down on her bed in silence,
Hid her face, but made no answer;
Lay there trembling, freezing, burning
At the looks they cast upon her,
At the fearful words they uttered.
Forth into the empty forest
Rushed the maddened Hiawatha;
In his heart was deadly sorrow,
In his face a stony firmness;
On his brow the sweat of anguish
Started, but it froze, and fell not.
Wrapped in furs, and armed for hunting,
With his mighty bow of ash-tree,
With his quiver full of arrows,
With his mittens, Minjekahwun,
Into the vast and vacant forest
On his snow-shoes strode he forward.

"Gitche Manito, the Mighty!"
Cried he with his face uplifted
In that bitter hour of anguish,
"Give your children food, O father!
Give us food, or we must perish!
Give me food for Minnehaha,
For my dying Minnehaha!"

Through the far-resounding forest,
Through the forest vast and vacant,
Rang that cry of desolation,
But there came no other answer
Than the echo of his crying,
Than the echo of the woodlands,
"Minnehaha! Minnehaha!"
All day long roved Hiawatha
In that melancholy forest,
Through the shadow of whose thickets,
In the pleasant days of Summer,
Of that ne'er-forgotten Summer,
He had brought his young wife homeward,
From the land of the Dacotahs;
When the birds sang in the thickets,
And the streamlets laughed and glistened,
And the air was full of fragrance,

And the lovely Laughing Water
Said, with voice that did not tremble,
"I will follow you, my husband!"
In the wigwam with Nokomis,
With those gloomy guests that watched her,
With the Famine and the Fever,
She was lying, the Beloved,
She the dying Minnehaha.
"Hark!" she said, "I hear a rushing,
Hear a roaring and a rushing,
Hear the Falls of Minnehaha
Calling to me from a distance!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the night-wind in the pine-trees!"
"Look!" she said, "I see my father
Standing lonely at his doorway,
Beckoning to me from his wigwam,
In the land of the Dacotahs!"
"No, my child!" said old Nokomis,
"'Tis the smoke that waves and beckons!"
"Ah!" she said, "the eyes of Pauguk
Glare upon me in the darkness;
I can feel his icy fingers
Clasping mine amid the darkness!
Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

And the desolate Hiawatha,
Far away amid the forest,
Miles away among the mountains,
Heard that sudden cry of anguish,
Heard the voice of Minnehaha
Calling to him in the darkness,
"Hiawatha! Hiawatha!"

Over snow-fields waste and pathless
Under snow-encumbered branches.
Homeward hurried Hiawatha,
Empty-handed, heavy-hearted,
Heard Nokomis moaning, wailing,
"Wahonomin! Wahonomin!
Would that I had perished for you,
Would that I were dead as you are!
Wahonomin! Wahonomin!"
And he rushed into the wigwam,
Saw the old Nokomis slowly
Rocking to and fro and moaning,
Saw his lovely Minnehaha
Lying dead and cold before him;
And his bursting heart within him
Uttered such a cry of anguish,
That the forest moaned and shuddered,
That the very stars in heaven
Shook and trembled with his anguish.

Then he sat down, still and speechless,
On the bed of Minnehaha,
At the feet of Laughing Water,
At those willing feet, that never
More would lightly run to meet him,
Never more would lightly follow.
With both hands his face he covered,
Seven long days and nights he sat there,
As if in a swoon he sat there,
Speechless, motionless, unconscious
Of the daylight or the darkness.

Then they buried Minnehaha:
In the snow a grave they made her,
In the forest deep and darksome,
Underneath the moaning hemlocks;
Clothed her in her richest garments,
Wrapped her in her robes of ermine,
Covered her with snow, like ermine;
Thus they buried Minnehaha.
And at night a fire was lighted,
On her grave four times was kindled,
For her soul upon its journey
To the Islands of the Blessed.
From his doorway Hiawatha
Saw it burning in the forest,
Lighting up the gloomy hemlocks;
From his sleepless bed uprising,
From the bed of Minnehaha,
Stood and watched it at the doorway,
That it might not be extinguished,
Might not leave her in the darkness.
"Farewell!" said he, "Minnehaha
Farewell, O my Laughing Water!
All my heart is buried with you,
All my thoughts go onward with you!
Come not back again to labour,
Come not back again to suffer,
Where the Famine and the Fever
Wear the heart and waste the body.
Soon my task will be completed,
Soon your footsteps I shall follow
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah!
To the land of the Hereafter!"

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
Nature is eternally young. The Third Act opens with a Ballet of Spring, symbolising life bursting forth throughout a rejuvenated world. Then Iago, the boaster, tells of how he had seen 100 warriors coming over a great water—"bitter so that none could drink it"—in a "great canoe with pinions." He is mocked at by the Indians. "Kaw," they say, "what lies you tell us!" But Hiawatha declares that Iago speaks truth. The strangers are the coming White Race—traders, settlers and missionaries—bringing to the depths of the virgin forest civilisation and the Faith and Hope of Christianity.

And presently this prophecy is fulfilled. The Blackrobe Chief, with the cross upon his bosom, accompanied by his guides and companions, lands on the sandy margin of the lake—bearing a message of Peace and Goodwill on earth.

Hiawatha's mission is at an end. Bidding his people cultivate friendship and unity, he steps into his magic canoe, and as it floats down the stream, the whole tribe raise their arms and their voices in final farewell. As their voices sound and swell and triumph, the vast crowd, the camp, valleys, trees and distant mountain peaks are mantled in solemn light, and in a blaze of sound and colour, Hiawatha westward passes away into the golden sunset. So ends the "Song of Hiawatha."

Spring had come with all its splendour
All its birds and all its blossoms,
All its flowers and leaves and grasses,
Sailing on the wind to northward,
Flying in great flocks, like arrows,
Like huge arrows shot through heaven,
Passed the swan, the Mahnabhezee,
Speaking almost as a man speaks;
And in long lines waving, bending
Like a bowstring snapped asunder,
The white goose, the Waw-be-wawa;
And in pairs, or singly flying,
Mahng the loon, with clangorous pinions,
The blue heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
And the grouse, the Mushkodasa.
In the thickets and the meadows
Piped the blue-bird, the Owaisa;
On the summit of the lodges
Sang the robin, the Opechee;
And the sorrowing Hiawatha,
Speechless in his infinite sorrow,
Heard their voices calling to him,
Went forth from his gloomy doorway,
Stood and gazed into the heaven,
Gazed upon the earth and waters.

From his wanderings far to eastward,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun,
Homeward now returned Iago,
The great traveller, the great boaster,
Full of new and strange adventures,
Marvels many and many wonders.
And the people of the village
Listened to him as he told them
Of his marvellous adventures,
Laughing answered him in this wise:
"Ugh! it is indeed Iago:
No one else beholds such wonders!"

He had seen, he said, a water
Bigger than the Big-Sea-Water,
Broader than the Gitche Gumee,
Bitter so that none could drink it!
At each other looked the warriors,
Looked the women at each other,
Smiled, and said, "It cannot be so!
Kaw!" they said, "it cannot be so!"

O'er it, said he, o'er this water
A canoe with wings came flying,
Bigger than a grove of pine-trees,
Taller than the tallest tree-tops!
And the old men and the women
Looked and tittered at each other.
"Kaw!" they said, "we don't believe it!"

From its mouth, he said, to greet him,
Came Waywassimo, the lightning,
Came the thunder, Annemeekie!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed aloud at poor Iago;
"Kaw!" said they, "what tales you tell us!"

In the great canoe with pinions
Came, he said, a hundred warriors;
Painted white were all their faces,
And with hair their chins were covered!
And the warriors and the women
Laughed and shouted in derision,
Like the ravens on the tree-tops,
Like the crows upon the hemlocks.
"Kaw!" they said, "what lies you tell us!
Do not think that we believe them!"

Only Hiawatha laughed not,
But he gravely spake and answered
To their jeering and their jesting:

"True is all Iagoo tells us;
I have seen it in a vision,
Seen the great canoe with pinions,
Seen the people with white faces,
Seen the coming of this bearded
People of the wooden vessel,
From the regions of the morning,
From the shining land of Wabun.

"Gitche Manito, the Mighty,
The Great Spirit, the Creator,
Sends them hither on his errand,
Sends them to us with his message.
Wheresoe'er they move, before them
Swarms the stinging fly, the Ahmo,
Swarms the bee, the honey-maker;
Wheresoe'er they tread, beneath them
Springs a flower unknown among us,
Springs the White-man's Foot in blossom.

"Let us welcome, then, the strangers,
Hail them as our friends and brothers,
And the heart's right hand of friendship
Give them when they come to see us.
Gitche Manito, the Mighty,
Said this to me in my vision.

"I beheld, too, in that vision
All the secrets of the future,
Of the distant days that shall be.
I beheld the westward marches
Of the unknown, crowded nations.
All the land was full of people,
Restless, struggling, toiling, striving,
Speaking many tongues, yet feeling
But one heart-beat in their bosoms.
In the woodlands rang their axes,
Smoked their towns in all the valleys,
Over all the lakes and rivers
Rushed their great canoes of thunder.

"Then a darker, drearier vision
Passed before me, vague and cloud-like,
I beheld our nations scattered,
All forgetful of my counsels,
Weakened, warring with each other;
Saw the remnants of our people
Sweeping westward, wild and woeful,
Like the cloud-rack of a tempest,
Like the withered leaves of Autumn!"

By the shore of Gitche Gumee,
By the shining Big-Sea-Water,
At the doorway of his wigwam,
In the pleasant Summer morning
Hiawatha stood and waited.

All the air was full of freshness,
All the earth was bright and joyous,
And before him through the sunshine,
Westward toward the neighbouring forest
Passed in golden swarms the Ahmo,
Passed the bees, the honey-makers,
Burning, singing in the sunshine.

Bright above him shone the heavens,
Level spread the lake before him;
From its bosom leaped the sturgeon,
Sparkling, flashing in the sunshine,
On its margin the great forest
Stood reflected in the water,
Every tree-top had its shadow,
Motionless, beneath the water.

From the brow of Hiawatha
Gone was every trace of sorrow,
As a fog from off the water,
As the mist from off the meadow,
With a smile of joy and triumph,
With a look of exultation,
As of one who in a vision
Sees what is to be, but is not,
Stood and waited Hiawatha.

Towards the sun his hands were lifted,* Both the palms spread out against it,
And between the parted fingers
Fell the sunshine on his features,
Flecked with light his naked shoulders,
As it falls and flecks an oak-tree
Through the rifted leaves and branches.
O'er the water floating, flying,
Something in the hazy distance,
Something in the mists of morning,
Loomed and lifted from the water,
Now seemed floating, now seemed flying,
Coming nearer, nearer, nearer.

Was it Shingebis, the diver?
Was it the pelican, the Shada?
Or the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah?
Or the white goose, Waw-be-wawa,
With the water dripping, flashing
From its glossy neck and feathers?

It was neither goose nor diver,
Neither pelican nor heron,
O'er the water floating, flying,
Through the shining mist of morning,
But a birch canoe with paddles,
Rising, sinking on the water,
Dripping, flashing in the sunshine.
And within it came a people
From the distant land of Wabun,
From the farthest realms of morning
Came the Black-Robe chief, the Prophet,
He the Priest of Prayer, the Pale-face,
With his guides and his companions.
And the noble Hiawatha,
With his hands aloft extended,
Held aloft in sign of welcome,
Waited, full of exultation,
Till the birch canoe with paddles
Grated on the shining pebbles,
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
With the cross upon his bosom,
Landed on the sandy margin.

* In this manner, and with such salutations, was Father Marquette received by the Illinois. See his Voyages et Découvertes, Section V.

Then the joyous Hiawatha
Cried aloud, and spake in this wise:
"Beautiful is the sun, O strangers,
When you come so far to see us!
All our town in peace awaits you,
All our doors stand open for you:
You shall enter all our wigwams,
For the heart's right hand we give you.
"Never bloomed the earth so gaily,
Never shone the sun so brightly,
As to-day they shine and blossom,
When you come so far to see us!
Never was our lake so tranquil,
Nor so free from rocks and sand-bars;
For your birch canoe in passing
Has removed both rock and sand-bar!
"Never before had our tobacco
Such a sweet and pleasant flavour,
Never the broad leaves of our corn-fields
Were so beautiful to look on,
As they seem to us this morning,
When you come so far to see us!"

And the Black-Robe chief made answer,
Stammered in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar:
"Peace be with you, Hiawatha,
Peace be with you and your people,
Peace of prayer, and peace of pardon,
Peace of Christ, and joy of Mary!"

Then the generous Hiawatha
Led the strangers to his wigwam,
Seated them on skins of bison,
Seated them on skins of ermine,
And the careful old Nokomis
Brought them food in bowls of basswood,
Water brought in birchen dippers,
And the calumet, the peace-pipe,
Filled and lighted for their smoking.
All the old men of the village,
All the warriors of the nation,
All the Jossakeeds, the prophets,
The magicians, the Wabenos,
And the medicine-men, the Medas,
Came to bid the strangers welcome;
"It is well," they said, "O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

In a circle round the doorway,
With their pipes they sat in silence,
Waiting to behold the strangers,
Waiting to receive their message;
Till the Black-Robe chief, the Pale-face,
From the wigwam came to greet them.
Stammering in his speech a little,
Speaking words yet unfamiliar;
"It is well," they said, "O brother,
That you come so far to see us."

Then the Black-Robe chief, the prophet,
Told his message to the people,
Told the purport of his mission.
Told them of the Virgin Mary,
And her blessed Son, the Saviour:
How in distant lands and ages
He had lived on earth as we do;
How he fasted, prayed, and laboured;
How the Jews, the tribe accursed,
Mocked him, scourged him, crucified him;
How he rose from where they laid him,
Walked again with his disciples,
And ascended into heaven.

And the Chiefs made answer, saying:
"We have listened to your message,
We have heard your words of wisdom.
We will think on what you tell us.
It is well for us, O brothers,
That you come so far to see us!"

Then they rose up and departed
Each one homeward to his wigwam,
To the young men and the women
Told the story of the strangers
Whom the Master of Life had sent them
From the shining land of Wabun.

Heavy with the heat and silence
Grew the afternoon of summer;
With a drowsy sound the forest
Whispered round the sultry wigwam,
With a sound of sleep the water
Rippled on the beach below it;
From the cornfields shrill and ceaseless
Sang the grasshopper, Pah-puk-keena;
And the guests of Hiawatha,
Weary with the heat of Summer,
Slumbered in the sultry wigwam,
Slowly o'er the simmering landscape
Fell the evening's dusk and coolness.
And the long and level sunbeams
Shot their spears into the forest,
Breaking through its shields of shadow,
Rushed into each secret ambush,
Searched each thicket, dingle, hollow;
Still the guests of Hiawatha
Slumbered in the silent wigwam.

From his place rose Hiawatha,
Bade farewell to old Nokomis,
Spake in whispers, spake in this wise,
Did not wake the guests that slumbered:

"I am going, O Nokomis,
On a long and distant journey,
To the Portals of the Sunset,
To the regions of the home-wind.
But these guests I leave behind me,
In your watch and ward I leave them;
See that never harm comes near them,
See that never fear molests them,
Never danger nor suspicion,
Never want of food or shelter,
In the lodge of Hiawatha!"

Forth into the village went he,
Bade farewell to all the warriors,
Bade farewell to all the young men,
Spake persuading, spake in this wise:

"I am going, O my people,
On a long and distant journey:
Many moons and many winters
Will have come, and will have vanished,
Ere I come again to see you.
But my guests I leave behind me;
Listen to their words of wisdom,
Listen to the truth they tell you,
For the Master of Life has sent them
From the land of light and morning!"

On the shore stood Hiawatha.
Turned and waved his hand at parting;
On the clear and luminous water,
Launched his birch canoe for sailing,
From the pebbles of the margin
Shoved it forth into the water;
Whispered to it, "Westward! westward!"
And with speed it darted forward.
And the evening sun descending
Set the clouds on fire with redness,
Burned the broad sky, like a prairie,
Left upon the level water
One long track and trail of splendour,
Down whose stream, as down a river,
Westward, westward Hiawatha
Sailed into the fiery sunset,
Sailed into the purple vapours,
Sailed into the dusk of evening.
And the people from the margin
Watched him floating, rising, sinking,
Till the birch canoe seemed lifted
High into that sea of splendour,
Till it sank into the vapours
Like the new moon, slowly, slowly
Sinking in the purple distance.

And they said, "Farewell for ever!"
Said, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the forests, dark and lonely,
Moved through all their depths of darkness,
Sighed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the waves upon the margin
Rising, rippling on the pebbles,
Sobbed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"
And the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
From her haunts among the fenlands,
Screamed, "Farewell, O Hiawatha!"

Thus departed Hiawatha,
Hiawatha the Beloved,
In the glory of the sunset,
In the purple mists of evening,
To the regions of the home-wind,
Of the Northwest wind, Keewaydin,
To the Islands of the Blessed,
To the kingdom of Ponemah,
To the land of the Hereafter!

event-1_38.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for Andrew Imbrie and the work DREAM SEQUENCE. Korean and English text. DREAM SEQUENCE was commissioned by Mr. Frank Taplin and was completed on June 17, 1986. Includes movement descriptions: first movement, second movement, last movement. Page number visible: === Page 34 ===.

event-1-section-1.additional_information: Completed on June 17, 1986.

event-1-section-1-perf-1.additional_information: The first movement opens rather feverishly with a long phrase characterized by dynamic surges, unstable texture, and a quick dissolution. This is followed by a halting viola melody, supported intermittently by a low, fitful accompaniment. The development of this idea is interrupted, but at the same time answered, by the flute, soon joined by oboe and clarinet; whereupon all instruments participate in a more sustained drive toward the goal of the first section. This consists of an insistent disjunct passage for the piano in its and subsequent collapse. The middle part of the movement strongly contrasts with all this: it is ushered in by muted strings, and characterized by a reflective English horn melody. Eventually the piano joins the strings and the bass clarinet recalls the English horn melody. Following this, elements derived from the first section reappear in new guises and positions. At the same time these disparate elements are more tightly woven together by means of an overarching melodic line. The climax of this line coincides with the return of the high disjunct music (previously for piano), now played by the piccolo. A coda brings the movement to a close.

event-1-section-1-perf-2.additional_information: The second movement is really a scherzo, but this description ought to be qualified in the following way. A traditional scherzo moves in fast triple time, and the listener is consistently aware of its dance-like quality. In this movement the quick triple meter is always present, but although sometimes in the foreground it is merely latent, owing to the tendency of the music to broaden into a kind of evanescent lyricism, or else to redivide the measure into fours or fives, etc., rather than into threes. The scherzo quality therefore derives as much from shifts of metrical focus as from an evocation of the dance. The "persona" behind the scherzo adopts changing disguises.

event-1-section-1-perf-3.additional_information: The last movement is an adagio, begun and ended by a long oboe melody.

event-2-section-1.section_name: TWO MOVEMENTS FOR STRING QUARTET AND PIANO
event-2-section-1.additional_information: Originally commissioned in 1957 by the Berkshire Music Center (Tanglewood) where it was awarded the Wechslar Prize given to outstanding alumni.

event-2-section-1-perf-1.additional_information: The first movement is a kind of "permuted passacaglia" where, instead of returning to the beginning of the recurring theme, each variation begins one measure further on; first with the second measure, then the third, and so on. When the end of the theme is reached, the process is reversed until the music works itself back to the opening solo theme which this time is heard as a canon in the string quartet while the piano "heralds" the theme of the second movement.

event-2-section-1-perf-2.additional_information: The second movement is a highly developed sonata-form type of piece which, in a climactic moment towards the end, recalls the pitch pattern of the first movement's theme. The entire piece is based on a twelve-note row which is the same backwards as it is forwards, although, of course, at a different transposition.

event-4-section-1.section_name: THREE SONGS FOR VIOLIN AND PIANO
event-4-section-1.additional_information: In my childhood, it was a great pleasure for me to read tragic fiction. My heart was always absorbed in these books and quite often I could not help but explore my emotional response. I was especially impressed by reading the tragedies of Nietzsche, Goethe and Boris Pasternak. Three Songs for Violin and Piano represent my emotional reaction to these works. My feeling is that tragedy is the one and eternal condition for us, so it exists equally in our heart, beyond the ages and the world.

credits.composer: David Ocker

event-5_18.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for David Ocker and PRIDE AND FOOLISHNESS. Presented as Five often un-asked questions about Pride and Foolishness. Page number visible: === Page 37 === and === Page 38 ===.

event-5-section-1.additional_information: Q: Why did you call your piece Pride and Foolishness? A: I named it after the two most important qualities a composer can have while writing music. if you don't try to make the work as well-crafted as your previous musical experience will allow, you can't feel pride in it. If you don't take chances and thus risk appearing foolish, you and your music won't grow and change. Q: Why did you write Pride and Foolishness? A: I don't Know. It won't have much effect in the GNP, nor will it solve the problems of homelessness, illiteracy or television. I guess it kept me off the streets. Q: Are there formal musical structures in Pride and Foolishness which you have developed in previous pieces? A: Yes. Q: What could someone listen for during a performance of Pride and Foolishness? A: There's a melody which is supposed to be quite prominent, and two supporting lines: continuous running notes which move from instrument to instrument, and a punctuating octave figure. These three elements change their overall relationships about half way through the piece. There are also gradual modulations and tempo changes.

credits.composer: Steven Stucky

event-6_17.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for Steven Stucky and Son et lumiere ("Sound and Light,"). Korean and English text. Son et lumiere, commissioned by the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra, was composed between June and December 1988 in Ithaca (N.Y.), in Los Angeles, and at the artists’ colony Yaddo, in Saratoga Springs (N.Y.). David Zinman conducted the first performance in Baltimore on 18 May 1989. Page numbers visible: === Page 39 ===.

event-6-section-1.additional_information: ("Sound and Light," a kind of show staged for tourists at historic sites or famous buildings) is an orchestral entertainment whose subject is the play of colors, bright surfaces, and shimmery textures. Throughout its brief nine-minute span, the piece is built almost exclusively of short, busy ostinato figures. Surprisingly, the musical materials seemed determined to shape themselves into an approximation of nineteenth-century sonata form. In the coda a second surprise: As if another, different music has been lurking all the while behind the shiny surface, the strings now unexpectedly split off from the rest of the orchestra to assert a new, more passionate, more “serious” voice, transcending the external show of sound and light.

credits.composer: William Kraft

event-7_15.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for William Kraft and INTERPLAY. Interplay was commissioned by the Los Angeles Philharmonic for the occasion of the 80th birthday of Dorothy Chandler, and received its premiere on November 1, 1984, in the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion with Simon Rattle conducting. Page number visible: === Page 40 ===.

event-7-section-1.additional_information: The title tells much about the piece: there are three ideas which form the basis for the ensuing interplay, or variations. The three ideas are presented in an introductory section. The first idea is stated by way of a cello cadenza, second by flutes, and then, later, strings. While the second idea is still being played, the third enters. It consists simply of four parallel thirds played by an ensemble of three percussionists on vibraphone, orchestra bells and crotales. Ideas one and two are never again stated completely, but rather, they are fragmented, and it is the elements resulting from that fragmentation which are exploited and varied. The interplay consists not only of the interaction of the elements themselves, but also in the way they are thrown about the orchestra.

event-8-section-1.section_name: CONCERTINO FOR TAEGUM AND STRING ENSEMBLE
event-8-section-1.additional_information: This music, consisting of a single movement, has a simple tone structure and a mood of Oriental atmosphere. The tones are applied vertically and linearly with contrasting dynamics, spacing, tone color, density and so on. This piece pursues the possibilities of expressing beauty in an Oriental idiom combining one of the famous Korean traditional woodwind instruments, the Taegum, and Western string instruments.

event-9_10.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for Donald Erb and PRISMATIC VARIATIONS. PRISMATIC VARIATIONS was completed on August 18, 1983. It was written on commission of Leonard Slatkin, Music Director of the St. Louis Symphony, who with his orchestra gave the first performance of the work on January 28, 1984. Page number visible: === Page 42 ===.

event-9-section-1.additional_information: Mr. Erb writes: "Composers are often surprised by the qualities their music presents to the public, but this work will, I think, have a couple of qualities that will be exemplified by the title I have chosen. One thing I have tried to achieve in this piece is to fill the hall with bright, transparent sound. This is accomplished by the orchestra, but it is also enhanced by participants in the audience who are called upon to play, separately or in combination, such instruments as harmonicas, soda bottles and telephone bells. The other quality that this piece should have has to do with the fact that much of the music is repeated during the course of the work, but is, altered by being radically reorchestrated for each successive appearance. In other words, some of the variations are simply changes in orchestration and not changes in the shape of the theme—or that of the preceeding variation. This gives the work a quality similar in some ways to a rondo as much as to a theme and variations." The score calls for two flutes and piccolo, two oboes and English horn, two clarinets and bass clarinet, two bassoons and contrabassoon, four horns, three trumpets, three trombones, tuba, timpani, a large percussion ensemble, three harmonicas, slide whistle, piano, electric piano, electric organ, harp, strings and approximately eighty young people in the audience playing harmonicas, soda bottles, stemmed glasses and telephone bells.

credits.composer: Karel Husa

event-10_10.additional_information: Program note and biographical material for Karel Husa and MUSIC FOR PRAGUE 1986. The work was commissioned by the Ithaca Band and composed during the summer and fall of 1968 for the capital city of Czechoslovakia. The work was first performed in its orchestral version on January 31, 1970, with the composer conducting the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra. The premiere of the original version for concert band took Place in Washington, D. C. on January 31, 1989, with Dr. Kenneth Snapp conducting the Ithaca College Concert Band in concert for the Music Educator's National Conference. Page numbers visible: === Page 43 === and === Page 44 ===.

event-10-section-1.additional_information: Three main ideas bind the composition together. The first and most important is an old Hussite war song from the 15th century, "Ye Warriors of God and His Law", a symbol of resistance and hope for hundreds of years, whenever fate lay heavy on the Czech nation. The second idea is the sound of bells throughout. The last idea is a motive of three chords first appearing very softly under the piccolo solo at the beginning of the piece. Different techniques of composing as well as orchestration have been used in Music for Prague 1968 and some new sounds explored, such as the percussion section in the Interlude, and at the ending of the work. Much symbolism also appears: in addition to the distress calls in the first movement (Fanfares), the unbroken hope of the Hussite song, sound of bells, or the tragedy (Aria), there is also the bird call at the beginning (piccolo solo), symbol of the liberty which the City of Prague has seen only for moments during its thousand years of existence.

event-10-section-1-perf-1.based_on_tune: Ye Warriors of God and His Law
event-10-section-1-perf-1.additional_information: The beginning of this religious song is announced very softly in the first movement by the timpani and concludes in a strong unison (Chorale).

event-10-section-1-perf-2.additional_information: Later it reappears at extremely strong dynamic levels, for example, in the middle of the Aria.

event-10-section-1-perf-3.additional_information: Some new sounds explored, such as the percussion section in the Interlude.

event-17-section-1.additional_information: The Association of Korean Symphonies was founded on September 15, 1945, and the Korean Symphony Orchestra (KSO) was born. In October of 1945, the KSO gave its first concert under the baton of Maestro Chung-Shik Kye at the Sudo Theatre in Seoul. The Seoul Symphony Orchestra (SSO) was established in January, 1948. The inaugural concert in November, 1950, of the Navy Symphony and Chorus was held at Shi-Gong Hall. On August 14th of 1957, the Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra (SPO), with its 82 members under the baton of Maestro Kim, was officially founded. In March of 1965, the orchestra made a successful concert tour of Japan. In May 1977, the orchestra went on a successful Asian tour. In November 1982, the orchestra toured the Western United States. In May of 1986, the SPO embarked on another American tour.

performance_2.lyrics_transcript:
(a) Hier soll ich dich denn sehen,
    Konstanze! dich mein Glück!
    Lass Himmel es geschehen,
    Gib mir die Ruh zurück,

    Ich duldet der Leiden,
    O Liebe, allzuviel!
    Schenk' mir dafür nun Freuden,
    Und bringe mich ans Ziel.

    Here as I now to meet thee
    My Constance, thou, my joy!
    Heaven grant me soon to greet thee
    In peace without alloy.

    Too long I've pined in sadness,
    My darling, far from thee!
    'Twill fill my heart with gladness
    Thy face once more to see.

    Klopf't mein liebevolles Herz!
    Und des Wiedersehens Zähre

section-1.additional_information: Program note text: "Claude Achille Debussy was born at St. Germain, August 12, 1862; died at Paris, March 26, 1918." "Iberia", composed in 1909, received its first performance at the Concerts Colonne, at Paris, February 20, 1910, with Gabriel Pierné as conductor. In those days the Debussy idiom was not readily acceptable to all of the concert-goers, even of Paris, and the public reception of this performance of "Iberia" brought forth both applause and shrill whistles. Debussy calls for a slightly enlarged orchestra in the score of "Iberia" especially in the percussion group where tambourine, castanets, xylophone, celesta, cymbals, and bells are used with definite color values.

performance-4.lyrics_transcript:
"See, friend, how others get on well.
Knock, knock, knock."
Others without trouble have riches, youth and renown;
Their merry songs are heard and wine makes them sport.
For long their noisy feasting's heard; but suddenly the guests grow pale and silent.
With hand trembling with rage, fate knocks at their window:
"Knock, knock, knock;
A new friend has come to see you; make place for him.
Knock, knock, knock,"
But there is happiness on earth, once full of expectation.
With youthful joy upon his face, a lucky fellow came to a tryst.
Still he's alone. All is silent. Sunset expires behind the grove,
And the nightingale falls silent, his heart beats and knocks:
"Knock, knock, knock."
Dear friend, are you coming to our rendezvous?"
Knock, knock, knock.
But there she comes, and in a moment love, disquiet, expectation, bliss—
All combine for them in one wild kiss.
Dumb night looks down on them, all heaven's alight with fires.
And someone quietly behind the bushes with tiresome iteration hammers:
"Knock, knock, knock, an old friend has come to see you; enough of bliss.
Knock, knock, knock."
